meta.scope: Global. Eurasia in depth; Europe, the Americas, Africa, and the Middle East as a first expansion
method: Defense spending figures are SIPRI's 2025 data (released in April 2026); nuclear warhead counts are estimates from the SIPRI Yearbook 2026.
Active-duty troop numbers come mainly from the 2025 edition of the IISS Military Balance, with figures for some countries drawn from the 2024–2026 editions.
GDP and growth projections come from the IMF World Economic Outlook: the October 2026 edition for the 50 main countries and the April 2026 edition for the rest.
The globe's military-power colors show SIPRI's 2025 military expenditure on a logarithmic scale.
Forecast probabilities are judgment estimates; outcomes are reported once their resolution dates pass.
uncertain: Because the full text of the IISS Military Balance 2026 could not be obtained, active-duty troop numbers are the IISS figures cited in Wikipedia's compiled tables (mainly the 2025 edition, with some from the 2024 and 2026 editions).
IMF figures were taken from the IMF DataMapper API (for the 50 main countries, retrieved on October 27, 2026, from the October edition).

RUS.leader: President Vladimir Putin (Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin)
RUS.situation: In the fifth year of its war in Ukraine, Russia is pressing a war of attrition aimed at seizing what remains of Donetsk under Ukrainian control. Moscow has engaged with mediation by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner without yielding on its core territorial demands, and in September's Duma election United Russia won its largest-ever share of seats, a display of the Kremlin's grip at home.

mil.note: Military spending at 7.5 percent of GDP (SIPRI estimate), the highest since the end of the Cold War; world's largest nuclear warhead stockpile

pol.stability: Tightened wartime controls keep the regime stable, but economic fatigue is building
pol.next_election: Presidential election, March 2030

econ.note: A low-growth war economy, with the policy rate at 14 percent and inflation forecast at 6–7 percent; under Western sanctions, high oil prices (Brent above $100) prop up the budget

recent.text: The Defense Ministry claimed the capture of Kostiantynivka in Donetsk region; Ukraine denied it, and fighting continued inside the city
United Russia won about 58 percent of the vote in the Duma election, taking 349 of 450 seats, its largest-ever haul
After meeting U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow, Putin ordered a 72-hour halt to strikes on Kyiv starting September 5; Ukraine reciprocated by refraining from attacks on Moscow
The central bank held its policy rate at 14 percent and forecast 2026 inflation of 6–7 percent
The Kremlin rejected a proposal for a limited energy ceasefire; around the same time, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace

President Zelensky said Washington had proposed preparing and hosting a trilateral technical-level meeting of Ukraine, Russia and the United States in the United Arab Emirates, but no date has been set; the Kremlin reiterated that it is not seeking a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to rearm.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russian forces had advanced west of Kostiantynivka but had made almost no net gains across the front since March, and that Putin appears to be shifting emphasis from ground offensives to a long-range strike campaign for the winter of 2026–27.

watch: Whether the proposed U.S.-Russia-Ukraine technical talks in the UAE actually resume
The pace of offensives toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk after Kostiantynivka
Signs of escalation, such as airspace violations along NATO's eastern frontier (Poland and the Baltic states)

gs.core: Great-power status and regime survival. To secure both, Moscow demands a privileged sphere of influence over the former Soviet space.
goals: Ukrainian neutrality and legal recognition of the occupied territories (including all of the Donbas)
A permanent halt to NATO's eastward expansion
Non-Western economic networks that bypass sanctions (China, India, the global South)
give: Adjustments to parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson fronts
Ukrainian membership in the EU, so long as it does not amount to a military alliance
Technical agreements such as prisoner exchanges and Black Sea navigation
Some of its support for North Korea and Iran
never: Ukrainian membership in NATO
Returning Crimea and the Donbas
Outside measures that deny the regime's legitimacy
gs.summary: Moscow calculates that a war of attrition favors it, and it wants not a ceasefire but a final settlement that locks in its territorial gains in law, so that no future Western government can reverse them. It is buying time while Washington's attention is drawn to the Middle East, and although its dependence on China has deepened, it has widened an alternative network of partners through its ties with North Korea and Iran.
gs.contra: The war economy props up short-term growth (1.1 percent in 2026), but the cumulative losses in manpower, technology and public finances are heavy. Lopsided dependence on China runs head-on into the goal of great-power status.

hist.meaning: A plains country without natural barriers, Russia has long bought security with space, that is, with buffer zones.

episodes.t: Napoleon and Hitler both marched on Moscow across the western plains
The Crimean War: Russia lost to Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire in a fight over its outlet from the Black Sea
Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War led to the 1905 revolution
The tsarist empire collapsed under the attrition of World War I
The Soviet Union dissolved after the drain of the Afghan war and economic stagnation

hist.learned: That losing the buffer on the western plains invites invasion. Ukraine and Belarus are the core of that buffer.
hist.read: Russia has rarely yielded to outside pressure alone. Decisive change has come when it lost a war or was worn down by a long one and then crumbled from within (1905, 1917, 1991).

drivers.why: Plains without barriers are the root of Russia's fixation on buffer zones, and regime survival determines whether the war goes on. Memories of invasion deepen this geographic insecurity.

signals.t: Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said North Korean denuclearization is a "closed issue."
Signed a mutual defense treaty with North Korea.
Vetoed the renewal of the UN Security Council's panel of experts monitoring sanctions on North Korea.

Russia sent North Korean troops into the Kursk fighting in 2024–2025, and Ukraine's military intelligence agency said in August 2026 that a new contingent of 8,500 North Korean troops would not fight inside Ukraine but would reinforce Russia's rear. In return, Moscow gives Pyongyang technology and money.
Suspected of providing technical help for North Korea's nuclear-powered submarine.

intent.read: Moscow has effectively accepted North Korea's nuclear arsenal and keeps Pyongyang close through the mutual defense treaty, its Security Council veto, and military-technical assistance. With the war continuing since the 32-hour ceasefire collapsed in April, this policy of embracing North Korea will not change for as long as the fighting goes on.

watch.t: A Russia-Ukraine ceasefire and the return of North Korean troops
Russian technology revealed by the launch of North Korea's nuclear-powered submarine
Signals of economic cooperation with South Korea after the war

uncertain: Active-duty troop numbers are IISS Military Balance figures cited in Wikipedia's "List of countries by number of military and paramilitary personnel," and may mix the 2024–2026 editions across countries (e.g., Russia 1.264 million, Ukraine 677,000). They need to be checked against the original Military Balance 2026.
Sources differ on the dates of Russia's Duma election (September 18–20 or 20–22), so it is listed as September 2026. United Russia's roughly 58 percent and 349 seats follow The Moscow Times.

The exact share of territory occupied on Ukraine's eastern front (percentage of Donetsk region) could not be confirmed. Kostiantynivka has been reported as contested since Russia's claim of capture in July.
The size of the North Korean contingent deployed to Russia rests on Ukrainian claims (about 8,500 additional troops; estimates of 30,000 to 50,000) and has not been independently verified.
It could not be confirmed whether Russia has formally accepted the U.S.-proposed trilateral technical-level meeting in the UAE, or when it would take place.

UKR.leader: President Volodymyr Zelensky (Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, appointed July 16, 2026)
UKR.situation: Ukraine is fighting a defensive war in eastern Donetsk while using drones and missiles to strike Russia's rear, including Novorossiysk, and its shadow fleet. Talks stalled as Washington's attention shifted to the Iran war; a September visit by U.S. envoys has put a resumption of trilateral talks back on the table. A major cabinet reshuffle in July reset Kyiv's wartime economic and diplomatic course.

mil.note: Military spending equals 40 percent of GDP, the heaviest burden in the world; partners provided $52.2 billion in state budget support in 2025 (SIPRI counts military aid as spending by the donor countries)

pol.stability: Elections are suspended under martial law and cabinet reshuffles are frequent, but the wartime state continues to function

econ.note: Dependent on Western financial support; energy and steel facilities come under repeated air attack

recent.text: The Verkhovna Rada accepted Prime Minister Yuliia Svyrydenko's resignation (Zelensky announced the reshuffle on July 12) and appointed Serhii Koretskyi prime minister on July 16

President Zelensky said Ukraine struck the port of Novorossiysk, a Black Sea Fleet base, with drones, Neptune missiles and uncrewed surface vessels (Russian authorities did not disclose military damage)
The EU approved €7.5 billion in military aid, and Ukraine's largest steel plant halted operations after repeated strikes
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv to discuss ways to get through the winter, but no breakthrough emerged

A large-scale Russian drone attack that began on the night of September 24 (295 drones nationwide overnight alone) killed at least seven people in Kyiv; the same day, Russia and Ukraine confirmed plans to resume trilateral talks hosted by the UAE

Zelensky said the United States had proposed preparing and hosting a technical-level trilateral meeting of Ukraine, Russia and the United States in the United Arab Emirates, though no date has been set; the Kremlin reiterated that it is not seeking a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to rearm.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a U.S. think tank, assessed that Russian forces had advanced west of Kostiantynivka but had made almost no net gains along the front as a whole since March, and that Putin appears to be shifting emphasis from ground offensives to a long-range strike campaign for the winter of 2026–27.

South Korea's presidential office called Zelensky's disclosure at the UN General Assembly on September 24 that two North Korean prisoners of war had been transferred to South Korea a breach of a confidential agreement, and demanded an explanation and an apology from Ukraine; on September 28 it expressed "strong regret" over Ukraine's denial that any such agreement existed.

watch: Winter strikes on energy infrastructure and whether the power grid holds
Washington's negotiating priorities (competing with the Iran war) and pressure to compromise on territory
The staying power of EU financial and military support

gs.core: Survival and sovereignty as an independent state.
goals: Binding security guarantees that deter another invasion
Integration with the West (EU membership first)
Funding for postwar reconstruction
give: Accepting the reality of de facto Russian control of occupied territory (not legal recognition)
The timing of NATO membership
Some limits on the size of its armed forces
never: Legal cession of occupied territory
A security arrangement in which Russia holds a veto
Demilitarization
gs.summary: Ukraine has shifted its priority from recovering territory to national survival and preventing another invasion. Its current course is to raise the cost of the war by hitting Russia's rear—oil refineries, the Black Sea Fleet and the shadow fleet—while moving in step with Europe to reject unfavorable terms in U.S.-led negotiations.
gs.contra: Manpower shortages and uncertain U.S. support. It is unclear whether holding out strengthens or weakens Ukraine's bargaining position.

hist.meaning: As its name suggests, a borderland. It was the Russian Empire's breadbasket and outlet to the Black Sea, and it is the passage between Europe and Russia.

episodes.t: The Pereiaslav Agreement, which placed the Cossack state under Moscow's protection
A bid for independence that failed when outside support was cut off
The Great Famine (Holodomor)
Independence with the dissolution of the Soviet Union
The Budapest Memorandum. Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in return for security assurances, which Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 rendered void

hist.learned: That security assurances on paper, without the force to back them, are meaningless (the Budapest Memorandum). Ukraine therefore cannot lay down its arms without binding guarantees.
hist.read: Ukraine has won independence only when its powerful neighbor was weakened (1918, 1991). As in 1918–21, independence can collapse if outside support is cut off.

drivers.why: Geography—living next to Russia—has set Ukraine's fate, and the memory of the Budapest Memorandum sets the lines it cannot concede.

uncertain: Active-duty troop numbers are IISS Military Balance figures cited in Wikipedia's "List of countries by number of military and paramilitary personnel," and may mix the 2024–2026 editions across countries (e.g., Russia 1.264 million, Ukraine 677,000). They need to be checked against the original Military Balance 2026.
The exact share of eastern Ukraine under occupation (percentage of Donetsk Oblast) could not be confirmed. Kostiantynivka has been reported as contested since Russia claimed its capture in July.
The size of the North Korean force deployed to Russia rests on Ukrainian claims (about 8,500 additional troops; estimates of 30,000 to 50,000) and has not been independently verified.
Moldova and Transnistria were left out because, following the joint Ukrainian-Moldovan blockade in January 2026, no new signs of abrupt change had been confirmed as of September.

BLR.situation: Belarus is deepening military and judicial integration with Russia under their Union State while running a transactional diplomacy that trades the release of political prisoners for U.S. sanctions relief. Washington has lifted some sanctions, including those on the potash producer and state banks, but human rights groups still count political prisoners in the 900s.

mil.note: Has no nuclear weapons of its own but serves as Russia's forward base, with announced deployments of Russian tactical nuclear weapons and the Oreshnik missile

pol.stability: Lukashenko's one-man rule is firmly entrenched and depends on Russian patronage
pol.next_election: Presidential election, 2030

econ.note: Heavily dependent on Russian markets and subsidies; the lifting of U.S. sanctions on potash has provided some breathing room

recent.text: Signed a memorandum with Russia on "harmonizing" their judicial systems
Met U.S. special envoy John Coale and called for lifting the remaining sanctions and unfreezing assets
Lukashenko pardoned 15 people, but their names were not released

watch: Whether the U.S.-Belarus trade of sanctions relief for prisoner releases expands
Deployments of Russian troops and tactical nuclear weapons, and tensions on the Polish and Lithuanian borders

gs.core: The survival of the Lukashenko regime.
goals: Keeping Russia's economic and security shield
Limited deals with the West to win sanctions relief
give: Releasing political prisoners
Small-scale cooperation with the West
never: Leaving the Union State with Russia
Opening up in ways that could lead to regime change
gs.summary: Minsk entrusts its security to Russia while pursuing transactional diplomacy, using political prisoners as bargaining chips to extract U.S. sanctions relief. Its reliance on Russia leaves it little autonomy, but it exploits that narrow space to the fullest.
gs.contra: The deeper its integration with Russia, the fewer cards it has to play with the West.

hist.meaning: The corridor between Moscow and Warsaw. The invasion route to Moscow by way of Smolensk ran across this land.

episodes.t: The route of Napoleon's and Germany's advances on Moscow
Operation Bagration: Germany's Army Group Center collapsed here
After protests over the disputed presidential election, dependence on Russia deepened decisively

hist.learned: That the Lukashenko regime cannot survive without Russian patronage (2020).
hist.read: Belarus's direction is tied to Russia's strength. If Russia weakens, that direction could change.

drivers.why: The survival of the Lukashenko regime explains nearly every choice it makes.

KAZ.leader: President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev (Vice President Yerlan Karin, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov)
KAZ.situation: A March referendum adopted a new constitution that reorganized the structure of power, creating a unicameral Kurultai and the post of vice president. Kazakhstan maintains multivector diplomacy between Russia and China while expanding cooperation with South Korea, the United States and others.

mil.note: A CSTO member, but its military is limited in size

pol.regime: Authoritarian presidential system (under the new constitution)
pol.stability: With the constitutional overhaul and the parliamentary election completed without incident, Tokayev's rule is secure
pol.next_election: Presidential election in 2029 (single seven-year term)

econ.note: An oil and uranium exporter that benefits from high oil prices, but the 12.5 percent U.S. tariff is a burden

recent.text: The referendum on the new constitution passed with about 90 percent support, and the constitution took effect on July 1
The United States imposed a 12.5 percent tariff, citing allegations of forced labor
The ruling party won about 71 percent of the vote in the first election to the unicameral Kurultai
The Kurultai approved Yerlan Karin's appointment as vice president and kept Bektenov on as prime minister
Tokayev attended the first Korea–Central Asia Summit in Seoul

watch: How the new vice presidency shapes the succession
Keeping open both the CPC oil export route through Russia and the trans-Caspian Middle Corridor

gs.core: Protecting its sovereignty and territory between Russia and China.
goals: Multivector diplomacy that leaves it subordinate to no single power
Raising its economic value through resources and the trans-Caspian corridor
Stability under the new constitutional order
give: Remaining in Russian-led bodies (the CSTO and the EAEU)
Attracting Chinese investment
never: Outside interference in the ethnic-Russian regions of the north
Open support for Russia's war in Ukraine
gs.summary: Kazakhstan's strategy is multivector diplomacy: staying close to both Russia and China while belonging to neither. Its defense lies in widening its options through broader cooperation with South Korea, the United States, the EU and Turkey.
gs.contra: A Russian victory in Ukraine could increase pressure over the ethnic-Russian regions in the north.

hist.meaning: A crossroads of the steppe, where the Russian Empire's southward expansion met China's westward reach.

episodes.t: Absorbed into the Russian Empire in stages
Lost a large share of its population to forced collectivization
The Semipalatinsk nuclear test site
Handed over all the nuclear weapons the Soviet Union had left behind
Called in Russian-led CSTO troops during the January unrest

hist.learned: That between two great powers, multivector diplomacy is the formula for survival.
hist.read: Calling in Russian-led CSTO troops during the January 2022 unrest cuts both ways: the support saved the regime, but it could become a channel of dependence on Russia.

drivers.why: Its landlocked position between two great powers compels multivector diplomacy.

uncertain: The ruling party's name in Kazakhstan's August 23 Kurultai election (Ädilet, 71.17 percent) rests on a single source, Wikipedia, so the main text refers to it only as the ruling party.

TUR.situation: Turkey is expanding its regional influence, hosting the NATO summit in Ankara in July and casting itself as a mediator in both the Iran war and the Ukraine war. It acts as patron of Syria's new government and has signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, forming a new security axis; at home, legislation to dissolve the PKK is moving forward alongside a crackdown on the opposition.

mil.note: The second-largest armed forces in NATO; a special defense-industry fund accounts for 22 percent of military spending

pol.stability: Erdogan's grip is firm, but the detention of Ekrem Imamoglu, among other moves, has deepened conflict with the opposition
pol.next_election: Presidential and parliamentary elections in 2028 (an early election is possible)

econ.note: High inflation persists, and as an energy importer Turkey is vulnerable to high oil prices

recent.text: Turkey hosted the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7–8
The ruling alliance submitted a bill on strengthening national solidarity and social cohesion that sets out a framework for PKK disarmament; it cleared the justice committee on the 8th
Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
Tensions with Israel have grown, with Israeli hard-liners labeling a Turkey-Syria axis a greater threat than Iran

watch: The fall plenary vote on the bill setting out the PKK disarmament framework, and verification of disarmament
Possible clashes with Israel over spheres of influence in Syria
Management of the Black Sea and the Turkish Straits, and its role as mediator between Russia and Ukraine

gs.core: Standing as an independent regional power that belongs fully to neither the Eastern nor the Western camp.
goals: Influence in Syria, the Caucasus and the Black Sea
A self-reliant defense industry and arms exports
Bargaining leverage from the mediator's seat in the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars
give: Case-by-case cooperation within NATO
Parts of its economic relationship with Russia
Its mediating stance in individual disputes
never: Autonomy or statehood for Kurdish armed groups
Control of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles (the Montreux regime)
gs.summary: A NATO member that does business with Russia, Turkey has formed a new security axis through a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Its strategy is to take the mediator's seat in every war to increase its leverage.
gs.contra: A strategy of dealing with everyone risks winning no one's trust at the decisive moment. Economic instability at home eats into its capacity abroad.

hist.meaning: The Straits and Anatolia: gatekeeper of the Black Sea and crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and the Caucasus.

episodes.t: The Crimean War: the Ottomans drew in Britain and France to halt Russia's southward push
Gallipoli: repelled the Allied landings aimed at the Straits
Nearly partitioned under the Treaty of Sèvres, it reversed the outcome with the Treaty of Lausanne
Secured control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention
Joined NATO after Stalin's demands on the Straits

hist.learned: That in the face of Russia's southward push it can draw in the West to restore the balance—but the West, too, once tried to carve it up (Sèvres). So it trusts no one completely.
hist.read: Turkey has used control of the Straits as leverage to extract concessions from both Russia and the West. Its current mediator strategy continues a pattern of behavior centuries old.

drivers.why: The geography of the Straits and Anatolia has produced the same balancing act for centuries.

IRN.leader: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei (succeeded March 2026); President Masoud Pezeshkian
IRN.situation: Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded his father, Ali Khamenei, who was killed in U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, and Iran has now been at war with the United States and Israel for seven months. After a June ceasefire memorandum collapsed in July, Tehran has used its control of the Strait of Hormuz as leverage under a U.S. naval blockade. On September 25 it offered a road map to reopen the strait within seven days, which Trump rejected.

mil.note: The IAEA has been unable since June 2025 to verify the whereabouts of about 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent

pol.regime: Theocratic republic (rule of the supreme leader)
pol.stability: The leadership succession went through, but economic collapse and a split between hard-liners and pragmatists leave the system unstable
pol.next_election: Presidential election, 2028

econ.note: With the U.S. naval blockade, oil sanctions and the halt in trade with the UAE, Iran is expected to suffer the worst economic contraction in the region

recent.text: Signed a 14-point ceasefire memorandum with the United States and entered a 60-day negotiating period
As attacks on merchant ships continued, Trump declared the ceasefire over, struck 90 targets inside Iran and reimposed the naval blockade in mid-July
Citing missile attacks, the UAE suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran indefinitely
Authorities arrested 30 protest organizers, while officials in the Pezeshkian government floated a halt to enrichment as a way to avert airstrikes
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a seven-day road map conditioned on the release of frozen assets and the lifting of the blockade (for Trump's rejection, see the September 26 entry)

Trump rejected Iran's road map to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days in exchange for the release of $12 billion in frozen assets, the lifting of oil sanctions, an end to the naval blockade and a cessation of hostilities, including in Lebanon; The Wall Street Journal reported that he is considering resuming bombing after the November midterm elections.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed to have seized a U.S. unmanned underwater vehicle (a REMUS 600) in the Strait of Hormuz and to have targeted 19 ships it called violators over two days; Washington disputed the claim that advanced equipment had been seized (the figure of 122 merchant ships turned back comes from a U.S. Central Command announcement on September 25).

The U.S. Treasury pressed a campaign to isolate Iran with some 50 countries; in response, the UAE grounded all Iranian airlines and cut off transactions with Bank Melli, and Turkey and Oman barred Mahan Air.

Araghchi said Iran was awaiting a formal U.S. reply through mediators, but by Iran's account no further talks are scheduled, and some members of parliament have renewed calls to consider withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

watch: Whether large-scale U.S. airstrikes resume around the November midterm elections
Shipping volumes through Hormuz, and mines and attacks on merchant vessels
The power struggle between IRGC hard-liners and pragmatists under Mojtaba

gs.core: Survival of the Islamic Republic.
goals: Ending the war without the regime collapsing
Lifting the blockade and sanctions and recovering frozen assets
Preserving nuclear latency (enrichment capability)
give: Caps on enrichment levels, or a temporary halt to enrichment
Reopening Hormuz to shipping
Reining in the Houthis and other proxies
never: Permanently renouncing the right to enrich
Terms that would lead to regime change
Dismantling its missile force
gs.summary: Though losing militarily, Iran holds Hormuz, the chokepoint of the world's energy supply, as a bargaining chip. It is enduring the blockade and the bombing and playing for time, waiting for rising oil prices and the November midterms to unsettle U.S. domestic politics first.
gs.contra: Closing the strait gives Tehran leverage, but it also deepens economic collapse (a 2026 growth forecast of −6.1 percent) and discontent at home.

hist.meaning: A plateau fortress guarded by mountains and an ancient civilization, Iran commands Hormuz from the northern shore of the Persian Gulf.

episodes.t: Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence
Britain and the Soviet Union jointly occupied the country
A coup backed by the United States and Britain toppled the Mosaddegh government
The Islamic Revolution
After eight years of war with Iraq, Khomeini accepted a ceasefire, likening the decision to drinking poison

hist.learned: That foreign powers manipulate Iran's internal affairs (1907, 1953). The memory of international silence during Iraq's chemical attacks bred a fixation on an independent deterrent.
hist.read: When the regime's survival was at stake, Iran accepted even a humiliating ceasefire (1988). At the same time, it is a country that has endured for millennia without losing much territory. Endurance is part of its culture.

drivers.why: The survival of the Islamic Republic explains its nuclear, Hormuz and proxy policies alike. Memories of foreign intervention justify them.

signals.t: Put forward a seven-day road map for a ceasefire and the reopening of the strait.
Holds de facto control of Hormuz through attacks on merchant ships and mines.
About 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent remain outside IAEA verification.

intent.read: Tehran is using its grip on the strait as leverage while offering to reopen it. Its stated readiness to bargain for the regime's survival matches what it is actually doing.

watch.t: The whereabouts of the enriched uranium

uncertain: Sources differ on where the June 17 U.S.-Iran ceasefire memorandum was signed (an Islamabad memorandum, Switzerland, Versailles), so only the date is given.

The intensity of fighting in the Iran war in August and September (an Iranian attack on U.S. forces in Jordan in late August, IRGC claims of attacks on U.S. warships in early September, etc.) has been confirmed only at the headline level.

The June 17 memorandum effectively collapsed after Trump said on July 8 that it was over, and formally lapsed when its deadline expired on August 17. As of late September the state of ceasefire talks is unclear (there are reports of a meeting between Trump and an Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly).

Sources disagree on the state of the ceasefire in the Iran war. A June France24 headline described the ceasefire as taking hold, but Al Jazeera reported in August that there was no comprehensive ceasefire. As of August, the British- and French-led Hormuz escort mission had not yet launched.

ISR.leader: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (President Isaac Herzog)
ISR.situation: Israel is fighting on multiple fronts: waging the war on Iran alongside the United States, occupying a buffer zone in southern Lebanon south of the Litani River and continuing airstrikes in Syria. In Gaza, the Board of Peace announced a deal in late July for Hamas's phased disarmament, but implementation is uncertain. The Knesset has dissolved, and a general election is set for October 27.

mil.note: Military spending at 7.8 percent of GDP; an undeclared nuclear power (SIPRI estimates 90 warheads)

pol.stability: The wartime coalition has broken up and the country is in campaign mode, with Likud contending against Yashar, Gadi Eisenkot's new party
pol.next_election: Knesset election, October 27, 2026

econ.note: The multifront war weighs heavily on public finances and reserve mobilization, but the technology export base remains solid

recent.text: The Knesset dissolved, locking in an October 27 election
The Trump-led Board of Peace announced an agreement on Hamas's phased disarmament and a phased Israeli withdrawal, but Israel has not formally accepted it
Israel struck Abu al-Duhur air base in Syria's Idlib province, and on the 24th held de-escalation talks with Syria under U.S. mediation
Israel continues to occupy about 55 villages in southern Lebanon as a "security zone," with sporadic clashes with Hezbollah

Netanyahu reportedly made an unannounced visit to Abu Dhabi to meet the UAE president, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for annexing the part of Lebanon south of the Litani River and most of Gaza.
Israel's election remains set for October 27, and opposition leaders announced that they would cooperate after the vote to form a government of recovery.

watch: The October 27 election result and Netanyahu's political future
Renewed strikes on Iran if U.S.–Iran talks collapse
Implementation of the Gaza disarmament deal and deployment of an international stabilization force

gs.core: The physical security of the state: ensuring that no hostile force acquires the ability to threaten its existence.
goals: Permanent elimination of Iran's nuclear capability
Disarmament of Hezbollah and Hamas
Normalization of relations with Saudi Arabia
give: How Gaza is governed (international administration, for example)
The timing of withdrawal from parts of the occupied territories
Tactical concessions in coordination with Washington
never: A nuclear-armed Iran
Handing control of its security to outsiders
The rebuilding of armed groups near its borders
gs.summary: Israel has extended its preemptive principle—eliminate threats before they grow—to Iranian soil. It maintains buffer zones in southern Lebanon and southern Syria and sustains several fronts at once. The October 27 election is the variable that will decide whether this strategy endures.
gs.contra: Its military edge is large, but a prolonged multifront war is piling up costs in manpower, the economy and international opinion.

hist.meaning: A narrow strip of land without strategic depth, which gave rise to its doctrine of preemptive strikes and short, decisive wars.

episodes.t: The Six-Day War: a preemptive strike greatly expanded its territory
The Yom Kippur War: caught by surprise after an intelligence failure
Bombed Iraq's Osirak reactor (the Begin Doctrine)
The invasion of Lebanon, in whose aftermath Hezbollah was born
Bombed Syria's nuclear reactor

hist.learned: That an enemy's capability must be destroyed before it is complete (the Begin Doctrine); today's attacks on Iran extend that principle. The trauma of the 1973 surprise attack was repeated in Hamas's surprise attack of October 7, 2023.
hist.read: Military victory has often failed to produce a political settlement. The 1982 invasion of Lebanon created a stronger enemy, Hezbollah.

drivers.why: The memories of the Holocaust and the 1973 surprise attack established the principle of "never again," and geography without strategic depth compels preemption. It is a rare case in which memory drives strategy.

uncertain: That some heads of state—among them Israeli President Herzog, Georgian President Kavelashvili and the leaders of the UAE and Tajikistan—remained in office in September 2026 is based on the absence of reports of any change, not on articles directly confirming it.

SAU.leader: King Salman bin Abdulaziz (Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman)
SAU.situation: Since the opening days of the Iran war, Saudi Arabia has come under Iranian missile and drone attacks that damaged facilities including the Ras Tanura refinery, and since July, Houthi offensives and drone attacks from Iraq have piled on. Even the East-West Pipeline, the alternative export route around the Hormuz closure, was halted by an attack on September 11 and restarted at a low level on the 22nd, leaving export capacity severely constrained. Riyadh has moved to diversify its security by signing a joint defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan.

mil.note: The largest defense spender in the Middle East; the defense pact with Pakistan has prompted discussion of a nuclear umbrella

pol.stability: MBS-centered rule is firm, but war damage and Houthi offensives have sharply increased the security burden

econ.note: Oil prices are high, with Brent above $100, but the closure of Hormuz and the shutdown of the East-West Pipeline have cut export volumes

recent.text: Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan
A Houthi attack on Aramco facilities wounded 73 people
Saudi Arabia halted the East-West Pipeline (Abqaiq-Yanbu) after a drone attack launched from Iraq's Maysan province
A Houthi drone was intercepted south of Mecca, and King Salman condemned the attack as a disgraceful crime
The East-West Pipeline resumed operations at a low level through bypass lines, and crude loadings at the port of Yanbu restarted. Full restoration is likely to take six to eight weeks.

Houthi offensives along Yemen's Red Sea coast and the intensity of the Saudi response
Whether civil nuclear cooperation with the United States is tied to normalization with Israel

gs.core: Stability of the monarchy and the economic transformation of Vision 2030.
goals: Secure oil export routes (bypassing Hormuz)
U.S. security guarantees and civil nuclear cooperation
Checking Iran's regional hegemony
give: OPEC+ production adjustments
The terms of normalization with Israel (the question of a Palestinian state)
The level of its relations with China
never: The legitimacy of the monarchy
The security of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina
A nuclear-armed Iran
gs.summary: When the Iran war brought direct attacks on its oil infrastructure, Saudi Arabia acted on the conclusion that the United States alone was not enough. Its joint defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and NATO member Turkey is a sign of that.
gs.contra: Economic transformation requires peace and foreign investment, but the security environment is moving in the opposite direction.

hist.meaning: A land of oil and holy places: the center of world energy and the wellspring of Islamic legitimacy.

episodes.t: The meeting between Roosevelt and Ibn Saud began a relationship that traded oil for security
The oil embargo showed that oil could be a weapon
The seizure of the Grand Mosque in Mecca and the Iranian revolution happened in the same year
The Gulf War: Riyadh called in U.S. forces to stop Iraq
The Abqaiq oil facilities were attacked, but the United States made no military response

hist.learned: That Abqaiq in 2019 confirmed the limits of U.S. guarantees. The current diversification of security (the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement) is the product of that lesson.
hist.read: When threats grew, Saudi Arabia drew in the United States (1990); when Washington hesitated, it spread its risk by seeking other security partners (after 2019).

drivers.why: Regime stability and economic transformation set the goals, and the geography of oil and holy places supplies both the means and the vulnerabilities.

Played in the FIFA World Cup finals for the first time

CHN.leader: Xi Jinping (general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, president and chairman of the Central Military Commission); Premier Li Qiang
CHN.situation: Since the October 2025 truce in Busan, Washington and Beijing have kept up summit diplomacy—Trump's visit to China in May, Xi's visit to the United States on September 23–25—and built a framework of "strategic stability"; the tariff truce has been extended by two months, to January 2027. Beijing has pocketed diplomatic gains, including a U.S. statement that it does not support Taiwan independence, while keeping up pressure on Japan for an 11th month since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's remarks on Taiwan: a ban on dual-use exports, curbs on seafood and restrictions on tourism. At home, the purge of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli has shrunk the Central Military Commission to the point of near dissolution, and growth slowed to 4.3 percent in the second quarter.

mil.note: By SIPRI's count, defense spending has risen for 31 consecutive years (up 7.4 percent), and China's nuclear arsenal is growing faster than any other in the world. The sweeping purge of the military leadership continues to leave gaps in the chain of command.

pol.regime: Communist Party one-party rule (Xi in his third term)
pol.stability: Xi's grip on power is secure, but the serial purges of the top brass are read as a sign of internal instability.
pol.next_election: 21st Party Congress, second half of 2027

econ.note: Growth slowed to 4.3 percent in the second quarter, against a 2026 target of 4.5–5.0 percent; weak consumption and the property slump persist.

recent.text: On May 13–15, President Trump made a state visit to China, where the two sides agreed on the purchase of 200 Boeing airliners and on allowing exports of Nvidia's H200 chips, and defined their relationship as one of "constructive strategic stability."
On June 8–9, Xi made his first state visit to Pyongyang in seven years; the two sides agreed to deepen China–North Korea "strategic cooperation."

Zhang Youxia, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, and Liu Zhenli, chief of the Joint Staff Department, were formally removed from the state Central Military Commission (and expelled from the Party on September 21), leaving only two of the commission's seven members.
Xi attended the SCO summit in Bishkek, then stressed de-dollarization and AI cooperation at the BRICS summit in India on September 12–13.

Xi wrapped up his first state visit to the White House in 11 years. The two sides extended the tariff truce by two months (to January 2027) and set up a new U.S.–China dialogue channel on AI, but concrete results were thin.

David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said Trump had asked Xi at the Washington summit whether China would be interested in buying American weapons, and that no date has yet been set for approving a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan that has been on hold since the May summit in Beijing.

watch: Whether a grand bargain is struck before the tariff truce expires in January 2027, and whether chip export controls are eased
How the purge of the military leadership affects readiness for Taiwan operations and appointments at the 2027 Party Congress
Whether economic retaliation against Japan (rare earths, seafood) continues or is lifted

gs.core: The perpetuation of Communist Party rule, and the "great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation"—matching or surpassing the United States—by the middle of the century.
goals: Unification with Taiwan (creating the conditions comes before any deadline)
Technological self-reliance in chips and AI (the core of the 15th Five-Year Plan)
Completing the capability to deny U.S. forces access inside the first island chain
Loosening the U.S. alliance network
give: Part of the trade imbalance (purchase commitments)
The pace and intensity of export controls on rare earths and other goods
The level of support for North Korea and Russia
Temporary stabilization of individual territorial disputes, such as the border with India
never: Taiwan independence, or a formal foreign military commitment to defend Taiwan
The Party's political monopoly, and Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong
Formally abandoning its South China Sea claims
gs.summary: China's strategy is to avoid a head-on clash with the United States while making time work in its favor. Summit diplomacy that stages "strategic stability" slows tariff and technology pressure, and Beijing uses the breathing room to push technological self-reliance and military modernization. With its neighbors, it calibrates economic retaliation (Japan) and gray-zone pressure (Taiwan, the Philippines) without crossing the threshold of all-out war.
gs.contra: Slowing growth (4.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026) and a shrinking population weaken the premise that time is on China's side. The serial purges of the top brass tighten control but leave questions about operational readiness.

hist.meaning: A great power facing both continent and sea. For 2,000 years the threat came from the northern steppe; since the 19th century it has come from the sea.

episodes.t: The Opium War, which opened the so-called century of humiliation
Defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War forced China to cede Taiwan to Japan
Entry into the Korean War, to keep the peninsula, a buffer zone, from falling to a hostile power
After border clashes with the Soviet Union, Beijing aligned with the United States to counter Moscow
The Taiwan Strait missile crisis. After backing down in the face of two U.S. aircraft carriers, China set out to build naval power

hist.learned: That the weak get carved up. Beijing therefore treats concessions on sovereignty and territory as a question of regime legitimacy, and it intervenes when a buffer zone is about to fall to a hostile power (1950).
hist.read: China backed down when it lacked the capability and came back once it had built it; the retreat of 1996 produced today's anti-access forces. China was weakest when it was divided at home (the late Qing, the Cultural Revolution). Internal stability is the precondition for action abroad.

drivers.why: The Party's survival is the overriding goal, and the narrative of the century of humiliation underpins its legitimacy. Growing national power has steadily widened its range of action.

signals.t: China's foreign ministry did not confirm the White House announcement of a shared goal of denuclearization, speaking only of continuity and consistency.
At the White House summit, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence.
When Xi visited Pyongyang, Kim Jong Un pledged to make China-North Korea friendship "the most important top-priority strategic work"; denuclearization went unmentioned.
China-North Korea trade rose 25 percent, returning to pre-pandemic levels.
Expelled Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli from the Party and the military, concentrating military decision-making further in Xi's hands.
Staged large-scale blockade-style exercises around Taiwan (Justice Mission-2025).
Its arms control white paper, China's Arms Control, Disarmament, and Nonproliferation in the New Era, dropped any reference to denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula.
It joined Russia in vetoing a Security Council resolution that would have imposed additional sanctions over North Korea's ICBM tests.
It abstained in the vote to extend the panel of experts that monitors sanctions on North Korea.
Taiwan's defense ministry said 10 of the 27 rockets fired in the Justice Mission-2025 exercises landed inside Taiwan's contiguous zone (24 nautical miles).
Imposed export controls on dual-use items and rare earths bound for Japan in retaliation for remarks about Taiwan.
Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's visit to China, pressed Seoul to state its position on Taiwan clearly.
Sanctions on five U.S. subsidiaries of Hanwha Ocean (suspended November 10, 2025)
Implementation of the October 9, 2025, rare-earth export control announcement suspended until November 10, 2026
Customs told to block H200 imports; companies urged to hold off on purchases
Ban on exports of dual-use items to Japan
China-South Korea supply-chain hotline reactivated; cooperation to keep South Korean chip plants running smoothly

intent.read: On the Korean Peninsula, Beijing has dropped denuclearization even from its rhetoric while embracing North Korea in practice. It talks of peaceful reunification, yet it has made pressure around Taiwan routine and has retaliated economically against a neighbor, Japan, over the Taiwan question. No country shows a wider gap between words and deeds.

watch.t: Monthly China-North Korea trade data (China's General Administration of Customs) — forecast that China-North Korea trade holds steady in 2027 (f23)
Whether Kim Jong Un visits China
Military personnel changes ahead of the Party Congress
