thinkers.name: Mao Zedong
thinkers.role: Leader of the Chinese Communist Party and founding leader of the People's Republic of China
thinkers.works: "On Protracted War" (1938), "On Policy" (1940), interview with Anna Louise Strong (the "paper tiger" remark, 1946), conversation with Kenneth Kaunda (the Three Worlds theory, 1974)
thinkers.bio: Mao Zedong was born on December 26, 1893, in Shaoshan, Hunan Province, and died on September 9, 1976. From 1913 to June 1918 he studied at a normal school in Hunan under the ethics teacher Yang Changji, and in April 1918 he founded the New People's Study Society with fellow students. From October 1918 he worked as an assistant to Li Dazhao, head of the Peking University library, and in July 1919 he published "The Great Union of the Popular Masses" in the Xiang River Review, arguing that the people had to unite against the alliance of the powerful, the aristocracy, and the capitalists. He attended the founding congress of the Chinese Communist Party in July 1921. At the Zunyi Conference in January 1935, during the Long March, he took the lead in military command, and in March 1943 he became chairman of the Politburo and thus the party's top leader. From the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 until his death, he led the country.
thinkers.claim: In his lectures "On Protracted War," delivered in Yan'an in May and June 1938, he rejected both the theory that China would be subjugated and the theory that it would win quickly. Japan was strong but a small country, short of land, resources, population, and troops, and would grow increasingly isolated internationally; China was weak but a large country whose international support would grow. The war therefore had to be long, passing through three stages: the enemy's offensive and China's defense, stalemate, and China's counteroffensive. In the meantime, since the temporary and partial loss of territory was the price of holding and recovering all of it permanently, China had to avoid decisive battles and wear the enemy down through mobile and guerrilla warfare. The other pillar was the united front. "On Policy" (1940) extended to foreign affairs the principle of exploiting contradictions to win over the many, oppose the few, and crush enemies one by one, calling for Japan's allies, Germany and Italy, to be treated differently from Britain and the United States, which opposed Japan.
thinkers.develop: In an interview with Anna Louise Strong on August 6, 1946, he said of the atomic bomb and the U.S.-backed Chiang Kai-shek that all reactionaries were paper tigers, and described an immense zone lying between the United States and the Soviet Union, an idea that later became the starting point of his intermediate-zone theory. In December 1958 he summarized the point: because the enemy is both a paper tiger and a real tiger, it should be despised strategically and taken seriously tactically. After the armed clash with the Soviet Union on Zhenbao Island in March 1969, he made the Soviet Union the principal enemy and met Nixon on February 21, 1972. On February 22, 1974, he set out the Three Worlds theory to Zambian President Kenneth Kaunda: the United States and the Soviet Union formed the First World; Japan, Europe, and Canada the Second; and Asia except Japan, together with Africa and Latin America, the Third.
thinkers.critique: First, "On Protracted War" held that the final counteroffensive would rely mainly on China's own strength, supplemented by international support and changes inside Japan; in practice the weights were reversed. Japan's surrender was decided by the U.S. war in the Pacific, the atomic bombings of August 1945, and the Soviet entry into the war, and Rana Mitter (Forgotten Ally) concludes that it was mainly Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist army that tied down large Japanese forces in China. Second, the paper-tiger argument has been criticized for treating the risk of nuclear war lightly. In Moscow on November 18, 1957, he said that a nuclear war might kill a third, or perhaps as much as half, of the world's 2.7 billion people, but that the other half would remain; and China, which had called the atomic bomb a paper tiger, acquired nuclear weapons with its first test on October 16, 1964. Third, his military and diplomatic judgment did not carry over to governing at home. The Chinese Communist Party's own historical resolution of June 27, 1981, concluded that the Cultural Revolution had brought the most severe setback and the heaviest losses since the founding of the People's Republic, and that Mao bore the chief responsibility. The same resolution, however, held that his achievements were primary and his mistakes secondary.
thinkers.now: The Russia-Ukraine war has become a war of attrition in which each side waits for the other to tire first, and the chance that a full ceasefire takes effect by the end of the year is put at 10 percent. Mao's protracted war, however, was a strategy in which the weak but large side buys time to reverse the balance of strength, a different configuration from a war of attrition in which both sides simply hold out. In the Taiwan Strait, Beijing's dual strategy (avoiding the use of force until Taiwan's presidential election in January 2028 while extracting concessions from Washington on joint-statement language and arms sales and leaning on Taiwan's opposition to influence the vote) resembles the logic of protracted war and the united front: avoid a decisive battle and make time an ally. In semiconductors, its approach of courting South Korea as a whole while singling out particular companies for pressure has the same structure as the principle of winning over the many and crushing the few one by one.
thinkers.record: His forecast to Edgar Snow on July 16, 1936, that Japan would not stop at China but would push on to the Philippines, Vietnam, the Malay Peninsula, and beyond came true with Japan's move into southern Indochina in 1941 and the outbreak of the Pacific War that December. In line with his 1938 forecast that China could not win quickly but would not be subjugated, the war dragged on for seven more years and ended with Japan's surrender in August 1945. His judgment in August 1946 that the U.S.-backed Nationalists were a paper tiger was borne out by victory in the civil war in 1949, and his decision in 1969 to make the Soviet Union the principal enemy led to U.S.-China rapprochement in February 1972. By contrast, after he set the goal in November 1957 of catching up with or surpassing Britain in 15 years, the Great Leap Forward he launched in 1958 ended in a famine in which, depending on the researcher, an estimated 15 million to 55 million people starved to death.

props.t: A side that is weak but large in territory and population can reverse the balance of strength against a strong but small opponent by avoiding decisive battle and prolonging the war.
One should exploit contradictions within the opposing camp to win over the many, oppose the few, and defeat enemies one by one.
A strong enemy should be despised strategically but taken seriously tactically.

quote.ko: "Will China be subjugated? Answer: No, it will not be subjugated; final victory will be China's. Can China win quickly? Answer: No, it cannot win quickly; the War of Resistance Against Japan is a protracted war."

thinkers.name: John Rawls
thinkers.works: A Theory of Justice (1971; revised edition 1999), Political Liberalism (1993), "Fifty Years after Hiroshima" (1995), The Law of Peoples (1999)
thinkers.bio: Rawls was born in Baltimore in 1921 and died in Lexington, Massachusetts, in 2002. He graduated from Princeton in 1943, enlisted that year, and fought as an infantryman in New Guinea and the Philippines; after Japan's surrender he served with the occupation forces and saw Hiroshima in the aftermath of the atomic bombing. Fifty years later, in "Fifty Years after Hiroshima" (1995), he confronted the bombing directly, though the essay makes no mention of his own service. He received his doctorate from Princeton in 1950 and, after Cornell and MIT, taught at Harvard from 1962 to 1991.
thinkers.claim: A Theory of Justice sought the principles people would agree to behind a "veil of ignorance," not knowing their own circumstances, talents, or values. The first principle is equal basic liberties for all; the second permits social and economic inequalities only under fair equality of opportunity and only when they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle). The Law of Peoples took peoples, not individuals, as its unit, and recognized as members of international society "decent" peoples that, though not liberal, do not commit aggression and respect basic human rights. "Outlaw states" that commit aggression and disregard human rights are not members. Toward "burdened societies," which lack the institutions and resources to order themselves, he set a duty of assistance that lasts until they can do so on their own, but he rejected extending the difference principle across borders. Clisa Geopolitics always identifies those who stand to lose most in its "What it means for people" section but, unlike Rawls, does not use this as the criterion for ranking.
thinkers.develop: In Political Liberalism (1993) he turned to "overlapping consensus," in which citizens of differing religions and philosophies endorse the same political conception of justice for their own reasons, and to "public reason"; his essay "The Law of Peoples," published the same year, grew into the 1999 book. In "Fifty Years after Hiroshima" (1995) he argued that leaders, soldiers, and civilians must be distinguished in war, and that, unlike Britain early in the war, when it stood alone against Germany, the United States fighting Japan never faced the "supreme emergency" that could justify bombing cities; he called the firebombing of Japanese cities and the atomic bombing of Hiroshima "very great wrongs." President Truman, who made no attempt at negotiation, failed as a statesman, he concluded.
thinkers.critique: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Robert Nozick argued that the difference principle can be sustained only by constant interference in free transactions. On justice beyond borders, well before The Law of Peoples, Charles Beitz (1979), citing interdependence among states, and Thomas Pogge (1989), arguing that nationality is as much a matter of chance as race or class, contended that the veil of ignorance should extend across borders. Kok-Chor Tan (1998) found the case for tolerating nonliberal "decent" societies weak, and Allen Buchanan (2000) criticized The Law of Peoples as a set of rules for a Westphalian world that no longer exists. In his 1979 lecture "Equality of What?" Amartya Sen observed that a disabled person can do less with the same income and proposed looking at "basic capabilities" rather than goods; this is the origin of the capability concept Clisa Geopolitics uses. In The Idea of Justice (2009) he proposed comparing the options actually available rather than first sketching perfect justice, as ideal theory does.
thinkers.now: Taking individual lives as the yardstick, Clisa Geopolitics has put the return of prisoners of war and of children forcibly deported to Russia first on the agenda for ceasefire talks in the Russia-Ukraine war, and in the Russia-NATO standoff has placed the protection of civilians and safeguards against accidental clashes ahead of the Polish government's priorities. This runs close to the principle of "Fifty Years after Hiroshima" that civilians, who bear no responsibility for a war, must be distinguished from leaders and soldiers. Rawls's duty of assistance is also cited in the site's philosophy questions, but on October 9 Kim Yo Jong rejected the plan of South Korea's Ministry of Unification to provide medical equipment. Clisa Geopolitics leaves open how to distinguish a regime from its people in a system like North Korea's, where regime and state are effectively one, and this is precisely where The Law of Peoples, which takes peoples as its unit, has drawn criticism.
thinkers.record: Where he was borne out: the demand of A Theory of Justice (1971) to look first to the least advantaged became the starting point for half a century of debate over distributive and international justice. In experiments reported in 1987 by Norman Frohlich, Joe Oppenheimer, and Cheryl Eavey, groups placed in conditions modeled on the veil of ignorance were able to reach agreement, as Rawls's account predicts. Where he missed: the groups in the same experiments chose not the difference principle but a principle of maximizing average income subject to a guaranteed minimum. Buchanan pointed out that, contrary to the premise of The Law of Peoples, cross-border economic structures had already become a subject of justice. And its diagnosis, which locates the causes of poverty mainly in a society's own political culture, remains in dispute between Pogge, who stresses the responsibility of international institutions, and Joshua Cohen (2011), who stresses political culture and geography.

props.t: Social and economic inequalities are permissible only when they are to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.

Peoples that do not commit aggression and that respect basic human rights are members of international society even if they are not liberal, and the duty to assist burdened societies lasts until those societies can order themselves.
In war, leaders and soldiers must be distinguished from civilians, and civilians must not be attacked directly except in a "supreme emergency."

Each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override. ... It does not allow that the sacrifices imposed on a few are outweighed by the larger sum of advantages enjoyed by many."

thinkers.name: Henry Kissinger
thinkers.role: U.S. national security adviser and secretary of state
thinkers.works: A World Restored (1957), Diplomacy (1994), On China (2011), World Order (2014)
thinkers.bio: Kissinger was born on May 27, 1923, into a Jewish family in Fürth, Germany, and in August 1938 fled Nazi persecution with his family to the United States. Of that experience he said, in an interview published in The New York Times Magazine in November 1971, "That part of my childhood is not a key to anything." Drafted into the U.S. Army in 1943, he did intelligence work in Europe. He graduated summa cum laude from Harvard in 1950, and his 1954 doctoral dissertation on the diplomacy of Castlereagh and Metternich was published in 1957 as A World Restored. As national security adviser from January 1969 to November 1975 and secretary of state from September 1973 to January 1977, he directed U.S. Cold War diplomacy, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize for the 1973 Vietnam peace agreement. He died on November 29, 2023, at the age of 100.
thinkers.claim: A stable international order, he held, requires two things together. One is a balance of power in which no state can easily subjugate another; the other is legitimacy. Legitimacy here means not justice but a minimal agreement among the major powers on the shape of a workable order and on the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy. His conclusion was that once a great power rejects this agreement and seeks to overturn the order itself, balance alone cannot preserve the peace. In practice, through his secret trip to China in July 1971 and President Nixon's visit in February 1972, he built a configuration in which the United States had closer relations with both the Soviet Union and China than the two had with each other, so that the two Communist giants checked each other.
thinkers.develop: A World Restored analyzed the Vienna settlement after the Napoleonic Wars and established his framework of balance combined with legitimacy, and Nuclear Weapons and Foreign Policy (1957) argued that instead of a strategy of massive retaliation that threatened all-out nuclear war, the United States should prepare for limited war, including the use of tactical nuclear weapons. In Diplomacy (1994) he wrote that American foreign policy, which since Wilson had leaned on the ideal of collective security, had to be joined to a calculation of national interest. On China (2011) proposed a "Pacific Community" in which the United States and China would build order together without excluding each other. In World Order (2014) he argued that in a world where civilizations hold different conceptions of legitimacy, regional orders should be built first and then linked into a Westphalian system for the 21st century.
thinkers.critique: In The Trial of Henry Kissinger (2001), Christopher Hitchens accused him of responsibility for war crimes, citing the bombing of Cambodia, the coup in Chile, and East Timor, among other cases. In The Blood Telegram (2013), Gary Bass documented how, as the Pakistani army carried out mass killings in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) in 1971, President Nixon and Kissinger ignored cables from the U.S. consulate in Dhaka warning of genocide in order to protect the Yahya Khan regime, their secret channel to China. On the theoretical side, Angelo Codevilla argued in a 2016 Hoover Institution essay that Kissinger's 1957 theory of limited nuclear war assumed that both the United States and the Soviet Union wanted restraint, and so missed the possibility that the adversary might understand war in an entirely different way.
thinkers.now: The triangle he designed now stands on its head: China and Russia are closer to each other than either is to the United States. With President Trump's visit to China in May 2026 and President Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September, the U.S.-China tariff truce has been extended to January 10, 2027, and the leaders' staging of coexistence resembles, on the surface, his proposal for a Pacific Community. By his own standard, however, the element of legitimacy, an agreement on permissible aims and methods, is missing. Semiconductor export controls were left off the agenda, and Washington has floated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip while imposing Section 301 tariffs on its allies as well. In Ukraine, no compromise that would reach what he called "balanced dissatisfaction" is yet in sight. Russia makes the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from all of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire and rejects any stationing of Western troops at all.
thinkers.record: In an op-ed on March 5, 2014, he argued that Ukraine should be not an outpost of either East or West against the other but a bridge between them, and advised it not to join NATO but to adopt a posture comparable to Finland's. His warning that a contest between blocs over Ukraine was dangerous came true with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The prescription of neutrality, however, was not adopted, and he himself abandoned it after the invasion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos on May 23, 2022, he proposed a ceasefire along the prewar line, drawing protests from Ukraine, and in an essay in The Spectator that December he wrote that a peace process should link Ukraine to NATO. On January 17, 2023, he said that a neutral Ukraine no longer made sense and accepted NATO membership as an appropriate outcome. The détente of the 1970s rested on the premise that the Soviet Union would endure for a long time. At a 2007 State Department conference he recalled that Nixon and he had expected the satellite regimes of Eastern Europe to collapse, though not so quickly, and that neither Nixon nor he, nor the Soviet experts they consulted, had ever spoken of the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself.

props.t: Unless the major powers agree on the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy, a balance of power alone does not stabilize international order.
The United States is better off maintaining closer relations with China and with Russia than those two countries have with each other.

The success of a settlement should be judged not by the complete satisfaction of any one side but by "balanced dissatisfaction," in which all parties are equally dissatisfied and still accept the outcome.

quote.ko: "The test is not absolute satisfaction but balanced dissatisfaction."
quote.orig: The test is not absolute satisfaction but balanced dissatisfaction.

thinkers.name: Lee Kuan Yew
thinkers.works: From Third World to First (memoir, 2000); Lee Kuan Yew: The Grand Master's Insights on China, the United States, and the World (interviews, edited by Graham Allison, Robert D. Blackwill, and Ali Wyne, 2013; Korean edition 2015)
thinkers.bio: Lee was born in Singapore on September 16, 1923, and died on March 23, 2015. In February 1942, while he was a student at Raffles College, Japan occupied Singapore and his studies were cut short. In his 1998 memoir, The Singapore Story, he wrote that the three and a half years of Japanese occupation taught him more than any university, and that he had seen how Japanese bayonets and terror could change not only people's behavior but even their loyalties. In 1946 he went to Britain, studied at the London School of Economics, and then read law at Fitzwilliam, Cambridge, graduating with first-class honors in 1949. He co-founded the People's Action Party in 1954, served as prime minister from 1959 to 1990, and then remained in the cabinet as senior minister and later minister mentor until May 2011.
thinkers.claim: His argument proceeds in two steps. First, China wants to be accepted as China, not as an "honorary member" of a Western order, and as a country with an ancient civilization and an enormous population it cannot help aiming to become the strongest power in Asia and, eventually, in the world. At the same time, he judged that China would not become a Western-style liberal democracy. Second, because Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and ASEAN combined cannot balance China, the United States must remain the regional balancer if the smaller countries are to have room to maneuver. He said that competition between the United States and China is inevitable but conflict is not, and warned that if the United States wants to influence Asia's strategic direction, it cannot keep going back and forth.
thinkers.develop: In the early 1960s he saw Singapore's way forward in merger with Malaysia; in 12 radio talks in September and October 1961 he made the case for it, and the merger was achieved in 1963. When Singapore was expelled from Malaysia in 1965, he revealed his anguish at an August 9 press conference, saying he had believed in merger all his life, and thereafter concentrated on the survival strategy of an independent city-state. In the 1990s he advanced "Asian values," the view that East Asia's growth rested on a culture that puts the community ahead of the individual (in a 1994 Foreign Affairs interview). In a speech on November 20, 2000, he stressed the United States' role as balancer, and in a speech in Washington on October 27, 2009, he set out both principles for managing U.S.-China competition and the case for a continued U.S. presence in the region.
thinkers.critique: The rebuttal best known to Korean readers is Kim Dae-jung's. After Lee's interview appeared in the March/April 1994 issue of Foreign Affairs, Kim, who would later become South Korea's president, answered with "Is Culture Destiny?" in the November/December issue of the same year. Asia, he argued, has its own roots of democracy, such as Mencius's doctrine that a ruler who loses the mandate of heaven may be overthrown and the Donghak teaching that every person is heaven, and what blocks democratization is not culture but authoritarian rulers. In a lecture on May 25, 1997, the economist Amartya Sen pointed out that the so-called Lee thesis, that authoritarianism is better for growth, rests on selected cases, and that systematic studies do not confirm a conflict between democratic rights and economic performance. Critics have also consistently argued that Singapore's achievements were bought at the cost of restrictions on individual freedom.
thinkers.now: ASEAN countries are hedging, expanding economic and diplomatic cooperation with China without cutting off security cooperation with the United States, so as to avoid lining up behind either side. By his reasoning, such hedging depends on the United States remaining the regional balancer. In 2026, however, Washington extended its tariff truce with China through summit diplomacy while floating arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, and imposed Section 301 tariffs on its allies as well. This can be read as a sign of the vacillating United States he warned against. The sharp drop in traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war has also raised the strategic weight of the Strait of Malacca, raising the stakes of the choices facing Southeast Asian countries.
thinkers.record: Start with the judgments that held up. In the 2013 interview collection he said that China would not become a liberal democracy and that if it did, it would collapse; the first part has proved right, as the Communist Party's one-party rule continues to this day. He also said China would not submit its South China Sea territorial disputes to international adjudication, and when the arbitral tribunal in The Hague constituted under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled in the Philippines' favor on July 12, 2016, China rejected the award as "null and void." Some judgments missed. The merger with Malaysia that he had urged in his 1961 radio talks as Singapore's way forward, achieved in 1963, ended just two years later with Singapore's expulsion in August 1965, and the independent Singapore whose survival many doubted at the time went on to prosper. In a 2005 interview with Germany's Der Spiegel he correctly diagnosed that North Korea's leadership had staked its survival on nuclear weapons, but his forecast that the regime would eventually collapse from within has not come true more than 20 years later. In a May 2012 interview with Germany's Die Zeit he said the European Union had expanded too quickly and would probably fail, yet the EU has not broken apart, having survived even Britain's 2016 decision to leave.

Small Asian countries have room to maneuver between the great powers only if the United States remains the regional balancer.
Competition between the United States and China is inevitable, but conflict is not.

thinkers.name: Samuel Huntington
thinkers.works: The Soldier and the State (1957), Political Order in Changing Societies (1968), "The Clash of Civilizations?" (1993), The Clash of Civilizations (1996)
thinkers.bio: Born in New York City in 1927, he died on December 24, 2008, on Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts. He graduated from Yale in 1946, earned a master's degree from the University of Chicago in 1948, and received his doctorate from Harvard in 1951. At Harvard he held the Albert J. Weatherhead III University Professorship and directed the Center for International Affairs (now the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs). In 1977–78 he served as coordinator of security planning on the National Security Council in the Carter administration. He was president of the American Political Science Association in 1986–87 and a co-founder of the quarterly Foreign Policy.
thinkers.claim: In an essay in the Summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs, Huntington argued that the fundamental source of conflict after the Cold War would be culture rather than ideology or economics. States would remain the principal actors, but the principal conflicts would occur between nations and groups belonging to different civilizations. A civilization, in his account, is the broadest level of cultural identity, defined by history, language, tradition, and above all religion. He named the Western, Confucian, Japanese, Islamic, Hindu, Slavic-Orthodox, and Latin American civilizations and, with a qualification, an African one. His reasons included that civilizational differences form over long periods and change slowly; that growing interaction makes people more aware of those differences; that religion fills the gap left when modernization unsettles older identities; and that the West's position at the peak of its power drives non-Western societies back to their own roots. He did not deny conflict within civilizations, but he held that conflicts between them are more frequent, longer lasting, and more violent, and the most likely to escalate into global war.
thinkers.develop: The Soldier and the State (1957) contrasted liberal American society with the "conservative realist" ethic of the professional officer and argued for "objective civilian control": professionalizing the military and keeping it out of politics. Political Order in Changing Societies (1968) argued that disorder and violence follow when institutions cannot keep pace with the rate at which modernization brings new groups into politics, and that the most important difference among countries is not their form of government but their degree of government. The Third Wave (1991) analyzed the global wave of democratization that began in Portugal in 1974. The doubt he had voiced in 1968, that economic development does not automatically bring stability or Western-style institutions, was recast in cultural terms in the 1993 essay, in the 1996 book The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order, and in an article from the same year, "The West: Unique, Not Universal."
thinkers.critique: In "The Clash of Ignorance," published in The Nation on October 22, 2001, Edward Said argued that Huntington personified vast entities such as "the West" and "Islam" as if they were single individuals and treated civilizations as closed units, erasing the debates within each civilization and centuries of exchange among them. Fouad Ajami countered in 1993 that "civilizations do not control states, states control civilizations." In a 2000 article in the Journal of Peace Research, Bruce Russett, John Oneal, and Michaelene Cox analyzed militarized interstate disputes from 1950 to 1992 and reported that pairs of states divided by civilizational lines were not more likely to become embroiled in conflict. Huntington responded that because the data came mostly from the Cold War, the findings could neither confirm nor refute his hypothesis about the post–Cold War era.
thinkers.now: As of 2026, the Russia-Ukraine war has ground on as a war of attrition into its fifth year, a war between two countries that belong to the same Slavic-Orthodox civilization. The Mecca joint defense pact concluded by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan in August 2026 fits his "kin-country syndrome," in which countries of the same civilization close ranks, yet Pakistan is also fighting the Taliban regime in Afghanistan, a fellow member of the Islamic world. The 2024 treaty between North Korea and Russia is, in his classification, anti-Western cooperation linking the Confucian and Orthodox civilizations, a cross-civilizational alignment like the "Confucian-Islamic connection" he described in 1993. The relationship between North Korea and China, restored in June, amounts to solidarity within a single Confucian civilization.
thinkers.record: Some of his judgments have held up. His 1993 diagnosis that culture and religion would become the main axes of conflict once ideological rivalry ended fits a trend of great powers invoking civilization as justification, as Russia did in March 2023 when its foreign policy concept defined the country as a "state-civilization" and the center of the "Russian world." Ajami, who had criticized him in 1993, wrote in 2008 that Huntington's argument now seemed more persuasive than his own critique. Among his misses, he wrote in 1993 that violence between Ukraine and Russia was unlikely because both are Slavic and Orthodox peoples, yet the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the full-scale invasion of February 2022 followed. The 2014 uprising by armed separatists in the east partly overlapped with the split between a Catholic-leaning west and an Orthodox east that he had judged in 1996 to be more likely than war, but what Russia chose in 2022 was an all-out interstate war. As for the hypothesis that civilizational conflicts grow more frequent and more intense, Jonathan Fox analyzed data on domestic conflicts from 1945 to 2001 and reported in 2005 that conflicts between civilizations were consistently fewer than other conflicts and did not become relatively more intense after 1990.

props.t: After the Cold War, the principal conflicts occur between nations and groups belonging to different civilizations, and these conflicts are more frequent, longer lasting, and more violent than conflicts within a civilization.
A nation or group drawn into conflict with an adversary from another civilization seeks support from countries of its own civilization, and those countries tend to take its side.
Disorder and violence arise when institutions cannot keep pace with the rate at which modernization brings new groups into politics.

quote.ko: "It is my hypothesis that the fundamental source of conflict in this new world will not be primarily ideological or primarily economic. The great divisions among humankind and the dominating source of conflict will be cultural. ... The clash of civilizations will dominate global politics. The fault lines between civilizations will be the battle lines of the future."

thinkers.name: Zbigniew Brzezinski
thinkers.works: The Grand Failure (1989), The Grand Chessboard (1997), Strategic Vision (2012)
thinkers.bio: Born in Warsaw on March 28, 1928, he died on May 26, 2017. At McGill University in Canada he earned a bachelor's degree in 1949 and, in 1950, a master's degree with a thesis on the nationalities within the Soviet Union; his 1953 Harvard dissertation was published in 1956 as The Permanent Purge. After studying the communist world at Harvard and Columbia, he served as President Jimmy Carter's national security adviser from 1977 to 1981. His tenure saw the establishment of diplomatic relations between the United States and China on January 1, 1979, and the Camp David Accords, as well as the Iran hostage crisis and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
thinkers.claim: The Grand Chessboard (1997) treated Eurasia as the central arena of global power and defined the task of the United States after the Cold War as preventing the emergence of any dominant power or coalition that could push it out of the continent. Brzezinski called countries that shape the fate of great powers by virtue of their location rather than their strength "geopolitical pivots," and he named Ukraine as the leading example. Without Ukraine, he argued, Russia cannot become a Eurasian empire; if it subordinates Ukraine again, it automatically becomes one. The most dangerous scenario, in his view, was an "antihegemonic" coalition of China, Russia, and Iran, bound not by ideology but by complementary grievances, and he expected that this time China would lead and Russia would follow. But he described it as a contingency to be averted, however remote it might be.
thinkers.develop: In The Grand Failure (1989), Brzezinski concluded that reform of the communist system was blocked by a barrier that would be hard to overcome: Leninist dogma. As early as 1994, in "The Premature Partnership" in Foreign Affairs, he identified Ukraine as the key to any revival of a Russian empire, and in The Grand Chessboard (1997) he offered the eastward enlargement of NATO and the EU as the response. In Strategic Vision (2012) he acknowledged the relative decline of the United States and proposed a "larger West" that would take in Turkey and even a reformed Russia. In a Financial Times article on February 24, 2014, he proposed a Finland model under which Ukraine would not join any military alliance directed against Russia.
thinkers.critique: In the September/October 2014 issue of Foreign Affairs, John Mearsheimer argued that the eastward expansion of NATO and the EU and Western support for democratization in Ukraine had provoked Russia and lay at the root of the problem, and that the West bore most of the responsibility for the crisis. Brzezinski's Afghanistan policy is also disputed. In a January 1998 interview with the French weekly Le Nouvel Observateur, he was reported as saying that Carter first authorized covert aid to the rebels on July 3, 1979, before the Soviet invasion, and that the administration had thereby knowingly increased the likelihood of Soviet intervention. The historian Conor Tobin, by contrast, argued in a 2020 article in Diplomatic History that the story of Brzezinski deliberately luring the Soviet Union into a trap is a "myth."
thinkers.now: Russia signed comprehensive strategic partnership treaties with North Korea in 2024 and with Iran in January 2025, and North Korea restored its relationship with China as well when Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang in June 2026. The result resembles the coalition Brzezinski warned about. Because it is bound by grievances rather than ideology, however, the limits of its cohesion show up in a crisis. With the Iran war now in its seventh month, the test is what China and Russia do for an Iran under a U.S. naval blockade. His proposition that Russia becomes an empire if it subordinates Ukraine again is also being tested. Russia is demanding the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from all of Donetsk Oblast as a precondition for a ceasefire.
thinkers.record: In The Grand Failure (1989), Brzezinski judged that the Soviet Union was more likely to head toward one of four outcomes than to succeed at pluralization: prolonged crisis, Brezhnev-style stagnation, a coup by the military and the KGB, or fragmentation along ethnic lines. With the attempted coup of August 1991 and the dissolution of the Soviet Union that December, two of them came to pass. His 1997 warning about an antihegemonic coalition also pointed in the right direction and took partial shape in the Russia-Iran treaty of January 2025. That treaty, however, contains no mutual defense clause, and China has signed no new alliance treaty with either country, so the China-led grand coalition he anticipated has not yet materialized. One judgment proved only half right: in The Grand Chessboard (1997) he expected Ukraine to be ready for serious negotiations with the EU and NATO sometime between 2005 and 2010. Negotiations with the EU on an association agreement began in March 2007, bearing out that forecast, but the NATO summit in Bucharest on April 3, 2008, stated only the principle of future membership and deferred a Membership Action Plan (MAP) to a later stage. Another missed the mark: events ran directly counter to his 2012 vision of bringing a reformed Russia into a "larger West," with the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Whether the NATO and EU enlargement he supported intensified Russia's backlash remains in dispute.

props.t: Russia becomes a Eurasian empire if it subordinates Ukraine again, and it cannot become one without Ukraine.
If China, Russia, and Iran form an antihegemonic coalition, China will lead and Russia will follow.
The central task of U.S. foreign strategy should be to prevent the emergence of any dominant power or coalition that could push the United States out of Eurasia.

quote.ko: "Potentially, the most dangerous scenario would be a grand coalition of China, Russia, and perhaps Iran, an 'antihegemonic' coalition united not by ideology but by complementary grievances."
quote.orig: Potentially, the most dangerous scenario would be a grand coalition of China, Russia, and perhaps Iran, an "antihegemonic" coalition united not by ideology but by complementary grievances.
quote.src: The Grand Chessboard, 1997 (verified against the passage as reproduced in a May 2021 Brookings Institution paper by Cheng Li)

thinkers.idea: The Grand Chessboard (1997) treated Eurasia as the central arena of global power and defined the task of the United States after the Cold War as preventing the emergence of any dominant power or coalition that could push it out of the continent. Brzezinski called countries that shape the fate of great powers by virtue of their location rather than their strength "geopolitical pivots," and he named Ukraine as the leading example. Without Ukraine, he argued, Russia cannot become a Eurasian empire; if it subordinates Ukraine again, it automatically becomes one. The most dangerous scenario, in his view, was an "antihegemonic" coalition of China, Russia, and Iran, bound not by ideology but by complementary grievances, and he expected that this time China would lead and Russia would follow. But he described it as a contingency to be averted, however remote it might be.

thinkers.name: Graham Allison
thinkers.role: Harvard political scientist; former U.S. assistant secretary of defense
thinkers.works: Essence of Decision (1971), "The Thucydides Trap" (The Atlantic, 2015), Destined for War (2017)
thinkers.bio: Born in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1940, he earned a bachelor's degree in history from Harvard in 1962 and a degree in philosophy, politics, and economics from Oxford in 1964. His Harvard dissertation, which explained the 1962 Cuban missile crisis through three models, was accepted in January 1968 and led to a 1969 article in the American Political Science Review and to Essence of Decision in 1971. He was dean of Harvard's Kennedy School from 1977 to 1989, and from August 1993 to March 1994 he served in the Clinton administration as assistant secretary of defense for policy and plans, handling the reduction of nuclear weapons in the former Soviet republics. He directed the Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs from 1995 to 2017 and is now the Douglas Dillon Professor at the Kennedy School.
thinkers.claim: The Thucydides Trap is the hypothesis that when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling power, the structural stress created by the shift in power between them makes ordinary crises prone to escalate into war, even if neither side wants one. The name comes from Book 1, Chapter 23, Section 6 of the History of the Peloponnesian War, where Thucydides wrote that, contrary to the publicly stated grounds, the truest cause was that the growth of Athenian power instilled fear in Sparta and drove it to war. Allison's research team selected 16 cases over 500 years, from Portugal and Spain around the time of the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas to Britain and France versus Germany from the 1990s on, and counted 12 that ended in war (1,000 or more battle deaths per year). The team sought to collect every qualifying case rather than a sample, followed standard histories in its judgments, and relied on The New Cambridge Modern History where accounts differed. In the four cases that avoided war, Allison argues, both the challenger and the ruling power made major adjustments in their attitudes and actions.
thinkers.develop: In Essence of Decision, Allison added two explanations, organizational process and bureaucratic politics, to the view of the state as a single rational actor. In 2004 he wrote Nuclear Terrorism. He first applied the phrase "Thucydides Trap" to U.S.-China relations in a Financial Times article in August 2012, made the 16 cases public in an article in The Atlantic in September 2015, and consolidated the argument in Destined for War in 2017. He did not claim that war is inevitable, and he presented the case list not as a finished product but as work to be revised in response to criticism and additions.
thinkers.critique: The most frequently cited weakness is case selection. In January 2017, Joseph Nye argued that it is unclear what counts as a single case, asking whether the 1914 war between Britain and Germany should be counted as one case or two, and, citing Donald Kagan's work, pointed out that Athenian power was not growing on the eve of the war. Arthur Waldron countered that in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 and the Pacific War of 1941, it was the rising power, Japan, not the established power, that attacked first. In 2021, Richard Hanania argued that the war rate was bound to be high because only rivals that threatened each other had been selected; adding the 14 cases the team had said it was considering, he calculated that 19 of 30 ended in war, and that only one of seven did after 1950. A limitation was evident from the start: only two cases postdate the advent of nuclear weapons, the United States versus the Soviet Union and reunified Germany, and both ended without war.
thinkers.now: After President Donald Trump's visit to China in May 2026 and Chinese leader Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September, the U.S.-China tariff truce was extended to January 10, 2027. This amounts to managing the relationship a few months at a time rather than the major adjustment in attitudes and actions that Allison describes; semiconductor export controls were left off the agenda, and the Chinese chipmaker CXMT's share of the DRAM market rose from 4 percent to 10 percent in a year. In the Taiwan Strait, no crisis has escalated into war since 1954, but the level of pressure has risen with each one: the effective erasure of the median line in 2022, regular Chinese coast guard patrols around Kinmen from 2024, and the announcement by China's Maritime Safety Administration of navigation controls in August 2026. What Allison warned against is a chain reaction in which such ordinary crises spread along alliance lines.
thinkers.record: In 2004, Allison wrote that on the current path, a nuclear terrorist attack on the United States within the next decade was more likely than not, but no such attack had occurred by 2014. His warning in August 2012 that structural tension between the United States and China would grow fits the course that ran from the trade war that began in 2018 to the U.S. semiconductor export controls on China in October 2022. His core claim of September 2015, however, that in light of the historical record a U.S.-China war in the coming decades is more likely than not, cannot yet be judged right or wrong because its time frame has not run out. There has been no war between the United States and China through 2026, but a lengthening period of managing tensions without war, by itself, neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis.

props.t: When a rising power threatens to displace a ruling power, ordinary crises are prone to escalate into war even if neither side wants it.
On the current trajectory, a U.S.-China war in the coming decades is much more likely than currently recognized, and judging by the historical record, more likely than not.
A state's foreign policy decisions result not only from a single rational calculation but also from the standard procedures of organizations and from bureaucratic politics.

thinkers.name: John Mearsheimer
thinkers.works: "Back to the Future" (1990), "The Case for a Ukrainian Nuclear Deterrent" (1993), The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001; updated edition 2014), "Why the Ukraine Crisis Is the West's Fault" (2014)
thinkers.bio: Born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1947, he served as an enlisted soldier in the Army in 1965–66, graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1970, and served as an Air Force officer until 1975, earning a master's degree in international relations from the University of Southern California in 1974. In a 2019 interview, he said that his time in uniform coincided with the Vietnam War, and that the lesson he drew from it, that great powers should avoid invading and occupying developing countries, profoundly shaped his scholarly outlook. He received his doctorate from Cornell in 1981, began teaching at the University of Chicago in 1982, and became the R. Wendell Harrison Distinguished Service Professor in 1996.
thinkers.claim: Offensive realism starts from five assumptions: an anarchic system with no authority above states, the offensive capabilities of great powers, uncertainty about others' intentions, survival as the overriding goal, and states as rational actors. Because a state cannot know when another state might become an enemy, the surest guarantee of security is to be more powerful than its competitors, and great powers therefore seek to maximize their power. Global hegemony, however, is impossible because of the "stopping power of water": oceans impede the projection of military force. The realistic goal is therefore hegemony in one's own region. Mearsheimer holds that the United States, as a regional hegemon, should act as an offshore balancer, relying first on the states of other regions to keep a peer competitor from emerging there and keeping direct intervention as a last resort. By this logic, he predicted that a powerful China would seek to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, that the United States would try to stop it, and that neighbors such as India, Japan, South Korea, and Vietnam would side with the United States.
thinkers.develop: In "Back to the Future," published in International Security in the summer of 1990, Mearsheimer argued that once the Cold War ended and U.S. and Soviet forces withdrew from Central Europe, the likelihood of crises and war would rise sharply in a multipolar Europe, and he proposed carefully managed proliferation that would allow only Germany to acquire nuclear weapons. In the summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs, he applied the same logic to argue that Ukraine's nuclear weapons were the only reliable deterrent against Russian aggression. The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001) set this out as a general theory, and the 2014 updated edition added a new final chapter on whether China can rise peacefully. In the September/October issue of Foreign Affairs that same year, he argued that NATO enlargement was the root cause of the crisis and proposed making Ukraine a neutral buffer, like Austria during the Cold War.
thinkers.critique: In the same summer 1993 issue of Foreign Affairs, Steven Miller countered that Russia effectively held operational control of the nuclear weapons on Ukrainian territory, so an attempt to seize them could invite Russian military intervention, and he cited the costs of possessing nuclear weapons, Western sanctions and isolation, and the collapse of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty. Responding to the 2014 article in the November/December issue that year, Michael McFaul argued that Russia had not sent troops into Ukraine for more than a decade after NATO enlargement and that Russia's hard line grew out of domestic politics following the antigovernment protests of 2011–12, while Stephen Sestanovich pointed out that Viktor Yanukovych's removal was not a coup but a unanimous vote of parliament in which even members of the ruling party took part. Mearsheimer replied that the vote did not meet the requirements for impeachment under Ukraine's constitution. In 2012, Jonathan Kirshner criticized the prescription of slowing China's rise as not only wrong but dangerous.
thinkers.now: As of October 2026, the Russia-Ukraine war continues into its fifth year. Russia makes the withdrawal of Ukrainian forces from the remaining parts of Donetsk Oblast a precondition for a ceasefire and rejects any stationing of Western troops. Its demands extend beyond neutrality to territory, a cap on the size of Ukraine's armed forces, and legal recognition of the annexed lands, which sits uneasily with his 2014 prescription that a neutral buffer would suffice. The United States has asserted its dominance of the Western Hemisphere through the capture of President Nicolás Maduro in January, an energy blockade of Cuba, and a Greenland security agreement with Denmark in September, consistent with his theory that a regional hegemon first secures its primacy in its own region. By contrast, Washington's floating of arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, its tariffs on allies, and its unilateral scaling back of combined U.S.-South Korean exercises diverge from his picture of the United States concentrating its strength on containing China, with China's neighbors lining up behind Washington.
thinkers.record: His prediction in the Chicago Tribune on January 15, 1991, that U.S. combat deaths in the Gulf War would be fewer than 1,000 proved correct. His 1993 warning that a Ukraine without nuclear weapons would be vulnerable to Russia gained weight when Ukraine, having handed its last nuclear warheads to Russia in June 1996, was invaded in 2014 and 2022. Whether nuclear weapons would have prevented the invasions, however, cannot be tested, and his 1993 expectation that Ukraine would not give up its nuclear weapons was proved wrong within three years. In 1990 he warned of instability in Europe on the premise that U.S. and Soviet forces would leave Central Europe and NATO would effectively cease to function, yet NATO grew to 32 members with Sweden's accession in March 2024. In 2014 he wrote that Putin's response was defensive rather than offensive and that Russia lacked the capability to conquer even eastern Ukraine easily; the full-scale invasion of February 2022 ran counter to the first judgment, while Russia's failure to take Kyiv that March bore out the second.

props.t: Great powers are always sensitive to threats arising near them and do not tolerate a rival great power bringing military forces into a neighboring country.
A powerful China will seek to dominate Asia as the United States dominates the Western Hemisphere, and the United States and China's neighbors will join together to stop it.
The United States should act as an offshore balancer, relying first on the states of other regions to keep a peer competitor from emerging there and keeping direct intervention as a last resort.

quote.ko: "This is Geopolitics 101: great powers are always sensitive to potential threats near their home territory. After all, the United States does not tolerate distant great powers deploying military forces anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, much less on its borders."

digest.t: North Korea says it will restart loudspeakers as Seoul again proposes military talks
digest.d: In an October 21 statement, Kim Yo Jong, head of the Workers' Party's General Affairs Department, said North Korea would switch on its psychological-warfare loudspeakers aimed at South Korea along the entire border before the end of the month. In a statement the next day, she claimed the loudspeakers would go on standby within days and that new means of response were on mission standby. On October 23, South Korea's Ministry of National Defense formally proposed military talks with the North to confirm the location of the Military Demarcation Line, restore military communication lines, and prevent accidental clashes, and said three-way talks including the United Nations Command were also possible. The offer repeats one made in November 2025, and no official reply from the North has been confirmed. Reuters reported that South Korean and U.S. officials see little chance of a Trump-Kim summit this year and that Washington has received no answer from Pyongyang.

digest.t: Resumed Hormuz blockade passes 100 days as Brent tops $116
digest.d: U.S. Central Command said on October 22 that 100 days had passed since it resumed its naval blockade of Iran, that no seaborne trade other than humanitarian goods was moving in or out, and that it had blocked more than $25 billion in Iranian oil exports. The same day, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed that four tankers transferring cargo in the northern Persian Gulf had been hit and three damaged by mines; President Trump and Central Command denied the claim, and there has been no independent confirmation. Brent crude settled at $116.72 a barrel on October 23, its highest close since April 29. U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz said the Navy could keep up the blockade for the time being, and on October 25 Trump said he was deciding between a deal with Iran and military action.

digest.t: Houthi strikes spread to airports and oil fields as U.S. orders staff out of Saudi Arabia
digest.d: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have spread to airports and oil fields. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was attacked on the night of October 21, killing two people and wounding eight, and debris from a drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field killed two people the same day. The State Department ordered nonemergency staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia on October 21, and on October 23 it also cut staff at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted Houthi missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu on October 24, and the Houthis claimed on October 25 that they had again struck Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which had resumed flights.

digest.t: U.S.-China summitry projects calm, but allies pay the price
digest.d: With Trump's visit to China in May and Xi Jinping's visit to the United States in September, the U.S.-China tariff truce was extended to January 2027. Over the same period, Washington floated arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip, unilaterally scaled back joint South Korea-U.S. exercises, and slapped Section 301 tariffs on allies as well.

digest.t: U.S.-China AI chip race rolls on despite the truce
digest.d: The U.S.-China summit in September extended the tariff truce to January 10, 2027, but kept chip export controls off the agenda. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are running their plants in China on one-year U.S. licenses that expire at the end of the year, and China has put in place a legal basis for sanctioning companies that comply with U.S. controls. Meanwhile, China's CXMT has lifted its share of the DRAM market from 4 percent to 10 percent in a single year.

digest.t: Three-way talks slip to November in Abu Dhabi as Russian strikes go on
digest.d: U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met President Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo on October 20 and President Putin in St. Petersburg on October 21. Afterward, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia was in principle ready to resume three-way talks around November 10, and Zelensky said on October 23 that the negotiating teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November. In the meantime, Russia struck 12 regions with 21 ballistic missiles from the evening of October 21 into the early hours of October 22, an attack Zelensky denounced as a show of force right after the talks. The two sides exchanged 270 prisoners each on October 23, and the White House announced the same day that they had agreed to a local ceasefire in occupied Oleshky. Three-way technical talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine, which Washington had proposed holding by the end of October, now look less likely to take place in October.

digest.t: Cargo ship sinks just outside Romanian waters as Russia-NATO tension spreads to the Black Sea
digest.d: The Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv sank on October 23 after a drone attack about 13 nautical miles off Constanța, just outside Romania's territorial waters; one Ukrainian crew member was killed and three are missing. Romanian President Nicușor Dan called the attack part of Russia's escalation of its war in Ukraine, and Russia made no public response. The same day, a Russian Geran drone entered Moldovan airspace and fell near homes in a village, and Moldova declared a Russian embassy staff member persona non grata.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, and on October 5 the three countries invoked "collective deterrence measures" against Houthi attacks and decided to deploy forces rapidly to Saudi Arabia. North Korea, already bound to Russia by the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty it signed in 2024, has also restored relations with China following Xi Jinping's visit to Pyongyang in June.

digest.t: Pakistan faces two fronts, east and west, and an emergency in its northwest
digest.d: Pakistan has been fighting the Taliban government in Afghanistan since February, and after strikes on Kandahar in late September it bombed Kunar and Helmand provinces on the night of September 30. The U.N. Assistance Mission in Afghanistan said the strikes killed at least 10 civilians, most of them children. On the Indian front, Pakistani and Indian warships collided in the Arabian Sea on September 15. A court of arbitration has ruled on the Indus Waters Treaty, but India does not recognize the court's jurisdiction. President Zardari declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11, citing a surge in militant activity in the northwest. On October 17, Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban clashed at several points along the border around Kurram.

digest.t: Washington puts the Monroe Doctrine into practice
digest.d: In January the U.S. military captured President Maduro, and the United States then signed an oil agreement with Venezuela's transitional government. Washington has imposed an energy blockade on Cuba since January and is waging tariff wars with Canada and Brazil. In September it signed a security agreement on Greenland with Denmark. On October 14, a report said a U.S. Army battalion had begun deploying to Panama for counter-cartel training; Southern Command did not comment on the deployment. On October 21, the U.S. Embassy in Canada alleged that Canadian politicians were trying to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections.

digest.t: Wars flare at once across the Horn of Africa and the Sahel
digest.d: The Tigray war resumed on September 22, and on October 6 and 7 a string of witness accounts said Eritrean troops had crossed the border and entered towns in northern Tigray. In a letter dated October 8, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos called this a "full-scale invasion" and cited the right of self-defense; the Eritrean government denied it and countered that Ethiopia has designs on the port of Assab. Sudan's civil war and the offensives of jihadist insurgents in the Sahel continue. On October 19, a drone attack on a market and a fuel depot in Abyei, an area contested by Sudan and South Sudan, killed at least 153 people. In September, Yemen's Houthi rebels seized the port of Mocha and Perim Island, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea.
