Whether the United States resumes large-scale airstrikes is likely to determine the timing of the next round of fighting.

trends.t: U.S. offshore balancing and allied self-reliance
trends.d: As the United States hands primary responsibility for defense to its allies, self-strengthening is under way on several fronts at once: Japan's normalization of its defense posture, Europe's rearmament, and the Mecca pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. A by-product is mounting pressure toward nuclear proliferation. Conditions are forming for debates over independent nuclear capabilities to grow in South Korea, Japan, and Saudi Arabia.

Cooperation among Russia, North Korea, and Iran has tied Ukraine, the Middle East, and the Korean Peninsula together. How the war on one front ends changes each country's calculations on the others. Once the Russia-Ukraine war ends, North Korea will be of less use to Russia, and Pyongyang will have more incentive to turn toward the United States and China.

India, Turkey, Indonesia, Vietnam, and Saudi Arabia join neither camp, lining up issue by issue. Small arrangements such as the Mecca pact, the Quad, and AUKUS, rather than grand alliances, are moving the board.

The Hormuz blockade is forcing Asian importers to diversify their crude oil supply routes. The Strait of Malacca gains weight, India's and China's dependence on Russian oil deepens, and Saudi Arabia's bypass pipelines become both strategic assets and targets.

Technological self-reliance and military modernization put time on China's side, but slowing growth, a shrinking population, and military purges work in the opposite direction. The most dangerous moment will come when China concludes that the time working in its favor is running out.

trends.t: AI concentrates value in a few hubs and turns those hubs into targets
trends.d: AI cannot escape geography. Leading-edge chipmaking is concentrated in Taiwan and helium production in the United States and Qatar, and as the 2026 attacks on data centers in the Gulf and in Kyiv showed, such hubs become targets. The more these choke points are threatened, the faster rerouting and dispersal proceed, with the exception of irreplaceable choke points such as Hormuz.

scenarios.name: Managed competition
scenarios.d: The U.S.-China tariff truce is extended, the Russia-Ukraine war freezes without a legal end, and an interim compromise with Iran trades nuclear limits for lifting the blockade. Tensions run high, but war is kept under control.
signals: Tariff truce extended before January 2027
U.S.-Russia-Ukraine trilateral talks become regular
Announcement that Hormuz is reopening
scenarios.korea: Economically the most favorable scenario for South Korea, but direct U.S.-North Korea dealings could push Seoul to the sidelines of talks on the Korean Peninsula.

scenarios.name: Armed multipolarity
scenarios.d: The U.S. retreat accelerates and allies arm themselves. A revision of Japan's three non-nuclear principles, South Korea's debate over nuclear-powered submarines and nuclear armament, and Saudi demands for enrichment become open items on the agenda. Minilateral security pacts multiply.
signals: Announcement of cuts to U.S. Forces Korea
Formal revision of Japan's three non-nuclear principles
Saudi demand for uranium enrichment
scenarios.korea: For South Korea, this is both an opportunity to widen its security autonomy and a cost. Soaring defense spending and the nuclear debate move to the center of domestic politics.

scenarios.name: Protracted linked wars
scenarios.d: U.S. airstrikes on Iran resume after November and spread across the Gulf. The Russia-Ukraine war also continues, and the oil shock drags on. Cooperation among Russia, North Korea, and Iran grows tighter.
signals: Large-scale airstrikes resume after the midterm elections
Renewed attacks on Saudi pipelines
Confirmation of Russian arms supplies to Iran
scenarios.korea: In this scenario the Strait of Hormuz, through which 70 percent of South Korea's crude oil imports pass, stays closed. Energy prices and the trade balance take a direct hit.

scenarios.name: Taiwan Strait crisis
scenarios.d: The crisis arrives not as a full-scale invasion but as Chinese coast guard inspections and quarantine or a partial blockade. How Washington responds will decide the credibility of the entire alliance system.
signals: Resumption of named, large-scale encirclement exercises
Coast guard inspections of Taiwan-bound ships
A U.S. freeze on arms sales to Taiwan
scenarios.korea: The strategic flexibility of U.S. Forces Korea, semiconductor supply chains, and tensions in the Yellow Sea all come into play at once.

scenarios.name: Internal fracture in one pole
scenarios.d: Russia's war economy collapses, the Iranian regime falls, or China suffers a financial crisis. As one pole of the board crumbles from within, the others compete to fill the vacuum.
signals: A plunging ruble and expanded conscription
Mass protests and military defections in Iran
Cascading defaults on Chinese local government debt
scenarios.korea: If Russia or Iran collapses, North Korea loses a patron. If China is shaken, the South Korean economy will be the first to feel it.

grand.drivers_note: The weights of the four factors (geography, power, regime, and memory) are analytical judgment estimates, and together they add up to 100.

tensions.memory: Memories of colonial rule and wartime forced labor.
tensions.structure: North Korea's nuclear weapons and missiles, China's rise, and U.S. burden-shifting all call for security cooperation between South Korea and Japan.
tensions.note: Memory does not disappear; it goes dormant. When domestic politics shift, it comes back to the fore.

tensions.memory: Memories of the vast territory ceded to Russia under the 19th-century treaties of Aigun and Peking, and of the 1969 border clashes.
tensions.structure: Confrontation with the West calls for anti-Western coordination.
tensions.note: If Western pressure eases, memory will regain its weight. This is a latent path to a Sino-Russian rift.

tensions.structure: Balancing China has drawn the two countries into a comprehensive strategic partnership.
tensions.note: Even so, Vietnam offers neither an alliance nor bases. Memory persists in the form the relationship takes.

tensions.memory: The memory of 1971, when the United States sided with Pakistan in the Bangladesh war and sent a carrier task force into the Bay of Bengal.
tensions.structure: Balancing China drives the Quad and defense cooperation.
tensions.note: India cooperates but refuses an alliance. Memory survives in the form of nonalignment.

tensions.memory: Roughly a dozen Russo-Ottoman wars between the 16th century and 1918.
tensions.structure: Energy trade and a shared distance from the West call for cooperation, but interests collide in the Black Sea, Syria, and the Caucasus.
tensions.note: Structure and memory point in different directions depending on the issue, which makes the relationship transactional and unstable.

laws.d: The Korean Peninsula (1953–), Kashmir (1949–), Cyprus (1974–). Armistice lines that harden without a legal end to the war last for decades.

laws.t: Alliances are tested when commitments blur
laws.d: The Korean War, five months after Dean Acheson's 1950 defense-perimeter speech; the fall of Saigon in 1975, two years after the 1973 Paris accords; the fall of Singapore in 1942. Deterrence broke down over signals of resolve before it broke down over capability.
The Russian Empire (1917), the Soviet Union (1991), and the Qing dynasty (1911) fell to prolonged attrition and internal fracture rather than to a blow from outside.

laws.t: Ideological solidarity breaks on borders and asymmetry
laws.d: The Sino-Soviet alliance of 1950 split within a decade, and in 1969 the two sides exchanged fire on their border. Kissinger drove a wedge into that crack.

laws.t: Energy shocks leave permanent policy shifts
laws.d: After the 1973 oil embargo, Japan and South Korea diversified their crude oil suppliers and built stockpiling systems, and the West founded the International Energy Agency. The shock ended; the policies remained.

laws.t: Those left out pay for great-power deals
laws.d: The Korean Empire under the 1905 Taft-Katsura agreement, South Vietnam under the 1973 Paris accords, and South Korea, which shouldered the costs of the 1994 Agreed Framework.

laws.t: Outmatched challengers back down, build up, and return
laws.d: China, which backed down in the Taiwan Strait in 1996, had built anti-access forces two decades later to keep the U.S. military at bay. India, defeated by China in their 1962 border war, modernized its military and acquired nuclear weapons.

laws.t: The fate of states that gave up the bomb hardens others' resolve to possess it
laws.d: Ukraine, which handed over its nuclear weapons (1994), was invaded; Libya's Muammar Gaddafi, who abandoned his nuclear program (2003), was overthrown. North Korea and Iran have drawn lessons from both cases.

analogies.now: The Russia-Ukraine war of attrition and ceasefire talks
cases: Finland's Winter War and the Moscow Peace Treaty (1940)
analogies.then: After the front lines stalled, the Korean War went on for two more years of fighting and negotiating, and it ended in an armistice without a peace treaty that remains in place today. In 1940 Finland preserved its independence by ceding about a tenth of its territory, but in 1941 it was drawn into war again.
analogies.implies: The most common outcome history points to is a Korean-style armistice: front lines harden without legal recognition, and an armed buffer zone remains. A ceasefire comes when Russia and Ukraine both conclude that further fighting will gain them nothing. That moment has not arrived while one side still believes it is advancing.
analogies.breaks: After 1953 South Korea had an enforceable guarantee in the form of U.S. troops stationed on its soil. Ukraine has no such guarantee. Even if an armistice comes, it is therefore likely to be one that, like Finland's, leaves the risk of a renewed invasion.

analogies.now: The Iran war and the Hormuz blockade
cases: The Tanker War within the Iran-Iraq War (1984–88)
analogies.then: In the 1980s Iran attacked tankers in the Gulf, and the U.S. Navy countered with escort operations and retaliatory strikes (Operation Praying Mantis in 1988). In 1988 Khomeini finally accepted a ceasefire, likening the decision to drinking poison. The 1973 embargo permanently changed importing countries' energy policies.
analogies.implies: The Iranian regime has a precedent of accepting a humiliating ceasefire when it judged its survival to be at stake. The question is when that threshold will be reached. Even after the blockade ends, Asian importers' diversification of supply routes will not be reversed.
analogies.breaks: In 1988 the United States was not the main belligerent, and the supreme leader was firmly in place. Today the United States is fighting directly, and the supreme leader has changed. It is unclear whether the new leadership has the political room to accept a humiliation.

analogies.now: Managed competition between the United States and China
analogies.then: Détente staged stability through arms control and grain deals, but competition in the Third World continued, and it collapsed with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979. Before 1914 Britain and Germany were among each other's most important trading partners, and Norman Angell's argument that war profits not even the victor (The Great Illusion, 1910) had spread as a belief that interdependence prevents war.
analogies.implies: The tariff truce is détente-style stability: it does not halt competition but puts rules around it. Stability of this kind was broken by events on the periphery, not at the center. Today the candidates for such peripheral flashpoints are the Taiwan Strait, the South China Sea, and the Korean Peninsula.
analogies.breaks: Nuclear deterrence and the depth of supply chain interdependence put today in a different league from 1914. The threshold for all-out war is high, but by the same token gray-zone attrition may drag on longer.

analogies.then: The 1958 shelling of Kinmen eventually settled into a ritual of shelling on odd-numbered days; the crisis was calibrated through political signaling. In 1996 China backed down in the face of U.S. aircraft carriers, and that humiliation became the starting point for its buildup of naval and missile forces.
analogies.implies: When China lacked capability, it backed down, but it always came back with greater capability. Now that its capabilities have grown, it has less need to back down as it did in 1996. Weakening signals of U.S. commitment are therefore far more dangerous than they were in 1996.
analogies.breaks: In the 1950s and the 1990s the U.S. commitment was clear. Today the United States floats arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip. The variable that stopped China in past crises is wavering.

analogies.now: Direct U.S.-North Korea dealings and South Korea
analogies.then: In 1905 the United States and Japan acknowledged each other's hold on the Philippines and Korea in what amounted to a swap. In 1973 the United States reached a deal directly with North Vietnam, and South Vietnam, left out, fell two years later. In the 1994 Agreed Framework, South Korea was outside the negotiating room yet bore most of the cost of the light-water reactors.
analogies.implies: Parties left out of great-power deals ended up bearing the costs or losing control of their fate. If a Trump-Kim Jong Un summit takes place, this is the pattern South Korea must guard against first.
analogies.breaks: Unlike in 1905 or 1973, South Korea today ranks among the world's top 10 economic and military powers. It has the capacity to reject a deal or to set conditions for bearing its costs. The question is whether it has the will and the preparation to use that capacity.

cases: The Nixon Doctrine (1969) and the withdrawal of the U.S. 7th Infantry Division from South Korea (1971)
Britain's withdrawal from east of Suez (1968–71)
analogies.then: After the Nixon Doctrine, Park Chung-hee's government proclaimed a policy of self-reliant defense and secretly attempted to develop nuclear weapons, stopping only under strong U.S. pressure. Jimmy Carter's 1977 plan to withdraw U.S. troops was eventually abandoned. When Britain pulled out of the Gulf, the United States filled the vacuum by setting up Iran and Saudi Arabia as its "twin pillars."
analogies.implies: Signs of U.S. retreat prompted allies to pursue nuclear weapons, and to stop them the United States ended up reaffirming its commitments. Today's nuclear debates in South Korea, Japan, and Saudi Arabia could be a replay of the 1970s.
analogies.breaks: In the 1970s the United States put nonproliferation first. Whether today's United States would block allies' nuclear capabilities in the same way or tolerate them as part of burden sharing is an open question.

analogies.now: The links among Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran
analogies.then: The 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance, and Mutual Assistance marked the high point of anti-Western solidarity. Yet within a decade the Soviet advisers had been withdrawn, and in 1969 the two sides clashed on the Ussuri River border. Kissinger exploited the rift to bring about the U.S.-China rapprochement of 1972.
analogies.implies: Even solidarity bound by ideology and anti-Western sentiment broke apart over asymmetry and borders. Today the point at which a Sino-Russian rift could open is the moment Russia feels its subordination to China. That is also the source of Washington's incentive to attempt a "reverse Kissinger," that is, to pry Russia away from China.
analogies.breaks: In the 1950s China was the weaker party; now Russia is. As the weaker party, Russia has less room to break with China. Even if a split comes, it is likely to come more slowly than it did in 1960.

analogies.now: The Russia-NATO standoff on the eastern flank
analogies.then: In Berlin, a Western garrison too small to defend the city, together with the airlift, left the Soviet Union with the burden of using force first, and deterrence held. In 1961, though, the garrison protected West Berlin but could not stop East Germany from building a wall on its own side. Britain's 1939 guarantee was a promise with no troops on the ground, and it covered only a German attack, so it did not apply to the Soviet invasion on September 17. Germany and the Soviet Union partitioned Poland between them.
analogies.implies: The precedents indicate that allied troops on the ground matter more than promises. Allied forces in place deter an open ground attack, but they cannot stop sub-threshold attacks such as sabotage, drones or damage to undersea infrastructure, so Russia's costs have to be raised through resilience and retaliation.
analogies.breaks: During the Berlin crises the United States had both nuclear superiority and a firm commitment to Europe. Today Washington is cutting troops in Germany while sending more to Poland alone, on the strength of the relationship between President Trump and President Nawrocki, so how long U.S. troops will stay in Poland is less settled than it was in Berlin. Kaliningrad, moreover, is like West Berlin in 1948: an isolated enclave that can be supplied only across the other side's territory. If land transit is cut, the burden of using force first shifts to whoever blocks supply by sea and air. That is why Russia leads with the word 'blockade.'

questions: How does the other side read this side's actions?
What does the other side fear most?
What would the other side need to be able to tell its domestic audience in order to back down?
Are the other side's aims limited or unlimited?

cases.name: The Russia-Ukraine War

parties.reads: Moscow sees Ukraine's integration into the West as NATO advancing to Russia's borders, and Western ceasefire proposals as a way of buying time to rearm Ukraine. As evidence, it cites former Chancellor Angela Merkel's remark in a December 2022 interview that the Minsk agreements of 2014–2015 had bought Ukraine time.
parties.fear: That the occupied territories never gain legal recognition, so that the question reopens every time a Western government changes hands; and that the question of what the war was fought for spreads within the system.
parties.say: We liberated the Donbas and stopped NATO.
parties.aim_note: Russia's current demands stop at neutrality and territory, but its advance on Kyiv in early 2022 aimed at regime change. It has a record of widening its aims when its capabilities allow.

parties.reads: Kyiv sees every Russian ceasefire proposal as preparation for the next invasion, because the Minsk agreements that followed the 2014 annexation of Crimea ended in the full-scale invasion of 2022.
parties.fear: Giving up territory and still not gaining security — a repeat of 1994, when Ukraine surrendered its nuclear weapons under the Budapest Memorandum, only to be invaded later.
parties.say: We saved the country and secured guarantees that we will not be invaded again.
parties.aim_note: The aim is national survival and sovereignty. Ukraine has no designs on Russian territory proper.

parties.reads: Washington sees the war as a cost that drains resources it needs for China and the Western Hemisphere, and tends to treat Russia's demands as a deal to be bargained over.
parties.say: We ended the war and saved American money.
parties.aim_note: The aim is an early end to the war.

cases.misread: The most dangerous misreading would be for Washington to become convinced that Russia's aims are limited ones that a territorial deal would satisfy. If that conviction is wrong, it would repeat Chamberlain's misjudgment at Munich in 1938, when he believed Hitler's demands were limited. Conversely, Moscow may overinterpret American impatience as fatigue across the entire West, when Europe is preparing to hold out even if the United States pulls back.

exits.title: A Korean-style armistice that leaves legal status unresolved

claims.UKR: We did not give up our territory in law

exits.precedent: The 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement has held for more than 70 years while leaving the territorial question unresolved. Through its Ostpolitik in 1970, West Germany accepted its borders in practice while preserving its legal right to seek unification.
exits.obstacle: Russia wants not just de facto control of the occupied territories but legal recognition, because it fears that de facto control alone could let a future Western government reverse the outcome.

exits.title: Armed neutrality and bilateral guarantees instead of NATO

claims.USA: We ended it without sending U.S. troops

exits.precedent: In 1955, Austria pledged permanent neutrality and signed the State Treaty, securing the withdrawal of Soviet troops.
exits.obstacle: Russia demands limits on the size of Ukraine's military; Ukraine demands that the guarantees be enforceable. The two demands collide head-on.

exits.title: Phased lifting of sanctions, with frozen assets redirected to reconstruction
exits.precedent: The phased sanctions relief built into the Iran nuclear deal (2015).
exits.obstacle: Europe holds many of the keys to the sanctions, and deciding what to do with the frozen assets requires agreement within Europe.

signals: Whether three-way U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks actually take place
Whether Russia softens the language of its territorial demands from legal recognition to de facto control
Whether Europe agrees to provide troops for security guarantees

cases.name: The Iran war and Hormuz

parties.reads: Tehran sees American offers to negotiate as a prelude to regime change. Its evidence is memory: the 1953 coup in which the United States had a hand, the U.S. withdrawal from the nuclear deal in 2018, and airstrikes launched while negotiations were under way.
parties.fear: Giving up its nuclear potential and then collapsing, as Libya did.
parties.say: We did not surrender, we broke the blockade, and we defended our right to enrich.
parties.aim_note: The aim is regime survival, though Iran pursues greater regional influence even in peacetime.

parties.reads: Washington sees the closing of the strait as holding the world economy hostage, and Iran's ceasefire proposals as a way of buying time.
parties.fear: A nuclear-armed Iran, and higher oil prices upsetting the November midterm elections.
parties.say: We opened the strait and stopped Iran's bomb.
parties.aim_note: The stated aims are eliminating Iran's nuclear capability and reopening the strait. Washington has not made regime change an official aim.

parties.reads: Israel sees any agreement as giving Iran time to rebuild its nuclear and missile capabilities.
parties.fear: A U.S. deal with Iran that leaves Israel out.
parties.aim_note: The aim is eliminating Iran's nuclear and missile capabilities. But Israel sets a high bar for what counts as elimination, which makes it prone to clash with any agreement between the United States and Iran.

cases.misread: The most dangerous misreading would be for Washington to see Iran as it was in 1988, near the end of the Iran-Iraq War: a regime that will give in once it is hurt enough. For Mojtaba Khamenei, who inherited power after losing his father, capitulation could turn into a crisis of legitimacy. He has less room to back down than Khomeini had in 1988.

exits.title: A 1988-style ceasefire: yielding to the international community rather than to the United States

claims.IRN: We did not give in to the United States; we accepted the demands of the international community
claims.ISR: Nuclear limits were written into the terms for ending the war

exits.precedent: In 1988, Iran ended its eight-year war with Iraq by accepting UN Security Council Resolution 598. This time, Pakistan, Qatar, and Oman are mentioned as possible mediators.
exits.obstacle: Washington does not favor going through the United Nations, and Israel opposes any ceasefire with weak nuclear limits.

exits.title: Separating the right to enrich from the act of enriching

claims.IRN: We defended our right to enrich
claims.ISR: Iran's capabilities were frozen for years

exits.precedent: The right stays on paper, while actual enrichment is suspended for years and handed to an international consortium. As in the 1962 Cuban missile crisis, when Washington privately promised to withdraw its missiles from Turkey, the deal could also be split between a public agreement and private assurances.
exits.obstacle: Israel opposes putting the right in writing at all. And a private assurance becomes a political liability for both sides the moment it leaks.

exits.title: Releasing frozen assets into humanitarian accounts

claims.USA: The money goes only to food and medicine, not weapons

exits.precedent: In the 2023 prisoner exchange, $6 billion in Iranian funds frozen in South Korea was transferred to humanitarian accounts in Qatar.
exits.obstacle: The money was frozen again after Hamas's attack on October 7 of that year. Iran remembers the episode as proof that American promises can be withdrawn at any time.

signals: Whether the names of mediating countries and a venue are made public
Whether Iran uses language that distinguishes the right to enrich from the act of enriching
Washington's first move after the November midterm elections

cases.name: The Taiwan Strait

parties.reads: Beijing sees U.S. arms sales and high-level exchanges as salami-slice support for independence, and the Lai Ching-te government as a pro-independence force.
parties.fear: That Taiwan's legal independence becomes a fait accompli and time is no longer on China's side; and that a failed use of force shakes the Party's legitimacy.
parties.say: The great trend toward national reunification cannot be stopped. We need only show progress, with no deadline.
parties.aim: Uncompromising on the goal, flexible on timing
parties.aim_note: China will not compromise on the goal of unification, but it is flexible about timing and methods. That sets it apart from the unlimited expansionism of Nazi Germany in 1938.

parties.reads: Taipei sees China's offers of exchanges as a prelude to absorption. Its evidence is Hong Kong, whose autonomy collapsed after the National Security Law took effect in 2020.
parties.fear: That Washington uses Taiwan as a bargaining chip with China.
parties.aim_note: The aims are preserving the status quo and ensuring the survival of its democracy.

parties.reads: Washington sees Chinese pressure as part of a strategy for regional hegemony. At the same time, the Trump administration shows signs of treating Taiwan as a bargaining chip with China.
parties.fear: Being dragged into a war, and losing access to semiconductors.
parties.say: We avoided war and protected our chip supply.
parties.aim_note: The aims are preserving the status quo and avoiding war.

cases.misread: The most dangerous misreading would be for China to take Washington's talk of using arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip and overinterpret it as a sign that the United States will abandon Taiwan. In 1950, Kim Il Sung and Stalin read the Acheson speech as America abandoning the Korean Peninsula, and that misreading led to war. When war actually came, the United States fought.

exits.title: Restoring strategic ambiguity

claims.CHN: We confirmed that the United States does not support Taiwanese independence
claims.TWN: The U.S. defense commitment was preserved

exits.precedent: In the 1972 Shanghai Communiqué, a single sentence — "The United States acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China" — accommodated different readings and has held for more than 50 years.
exits.obstacle: Once Washington starts using strategic ambiguity as a bargaining chip, the ambiguity itself loses credibility.

exits.title: Institutionalizing the status quo with no deadline

claims.TWN: The threshold for using force has been raised

exits.precedent: The 1972 U.S.-Soviet Incidents at Sea Agreement created rules to prevent collisions at sea even between adversaries. A U.S.-China military hotline and rules of conduct for coast guards could be its modern counterpart.
exits.obstacle: China is reluctant because it believes rules of conduct would treat the waters around Taiwan as if they were international waters.

exits.title: Resuming economic exchanges

claims.CHN: We demonstrated the great trend toward unification

exits.precedent: Cross-strait tensions were at their lowest around the time the two sides signed the Economic Cooperation Framework Agreement (ECFA) in 2010.
exits.obstacle: Taiwanese public opinion is wary of economic dependence as a channel for absorption, and Beijing refuses to deal with the DPP government.

signals: Whether the Taiwan language in U.S.-China joint documents changes
The tone of Lai Ching-te's October 10 speech and China's response
Whether U.S. arms sales to Taiwan are actually put on hold

cases.name: The Korean Peninsula

parties.reads: Pyongyang sees joint U.S.-South Korean exercises as rehearsals for invasion, and demands for denuclearization as demands to dismantle the regime.
parties.fear: The path of Libya, which collapsed after giving up its nuclear program; and a decline in Russian patronage once the Russia-Ukraine war ends.
parties.say: We have been recognized as a nuclear power and stand as an equal of the United States.
parties.aim_note: The aim is regime survival. The "two states" doctrine is a threat, but it can also be read as formally setting aside the offensive goal of unification by force.

parties.reads: Seoul sees North Korea's "two states" doctrine as a declaration of hostility. But another reading is possible: a North Korea that has given up the goal of unification could become a partner in coexistence.
parties.fear: Being cut out of a direct U.S.-North Korean deal, and facing North Korea's nuclear weapons with weakened U.S. deterrence.
parties.say: The Korean Peninsula question is ours to settle. We kept the peace.
parties.aim_note: The aims are preventing war and peaceful coexistence.

parties.reads: Washington sees North Korea as a problem of managing ICBMs aimed at the U.S. homeland. It has handed conventional deterrence to South Korea.
parties.fear: ICBMs that can reach the U.S. homeland.
parties.aim_note: The aim is removing the threat to the homeland.

cases.misread: The most dangerous misreading could occur within the alliance. If Washington strikes a homeland-first deal that settles for an ICBM freeze, Seoul could take it as an official endorsement of North Korea's nuclear status, and public support for South Korea's own nuclear weapons could explode. At the same time, Pyongyang may overinterpret the Trump administration's scaling back of joint U.S.-South Korean exercises as a sign that the alliance is loosening. That is the lesson of the 1950 misjudgment that read the Acheson speech as America abandoning the Korean Peninsula.

exits.title: A phased freeze: a Geneva deal with South Korea at the table

claims.PRK: We negotiated as a nuclear power
claims.USA: We reduced the threat to the homeland
claims.KOR: We lowered tensions and took part in the negotiations

exits.precedent: The 1994 Agreed Framework traded a freeze of North Korea's nuclear activities for compensation, including light-water reactors. South Korea, though left outside the negotiating room, ended up bearing most of the cost of the reactors. This time, South Korea must sit at the table as a party to avoid the same mistake.
exits.obstacle: North Korea wants to talk only to the United States, shutting South Korea out.

exits.title: Four-party talks to turn the armistice into a peace regime

claims.KOR: We led the creation of a peace regime as a party to it
claims.USA: We can use the role of U.S. forces in Korea as a bargaining chip

exits.precedent: South Korea did not sign the 1953 Armistice Agreement. Four-party talks among the two Koreas, the United States, and China provide a framework that fills the gap left by South Korea not being a signatory.
exits.obstacle: Because the status of USFK and the United Nations Command is at stake, differences within the alliance run deep.

exits.title: Normalizing relations by turning "two states" to advantage

claims.PRK: We were recognized as two states

exits.precedent: Under the 1972 Basic Treaty, East and West Germany coexisted by treating each other as states, while West Germany kept the goal of unification in its constitution. Unification, 18 years later, came within that framework.
exits.obstacle: This approach conflicts with Article 3 of South Korea's Constitution (the territorial clause). But in 1973 West Germany's Federal Constitutional Court upheld the Basic Treaty, treating East Germany as a state under international law but not as a foreign country in relation to West Germany, and South Korea has the framework of the special relationship defined in the 1991 Inter-Korean Basic Agreement. The domestic political backlash would still be strong.

signals: Whether South Korea takes part in preparations for a Trump-Kim Jong Un meeting
Whether North Korea makes recognition of two states a condition for talks
How public support in South Korea for its own nuclear weapons shifts

cases.name: The Russia-NATO standoff (Baltic Sea, Kaliningrad, Suwałki Gap)

parties.reads: Russia sees NATO's forward deployment on the eastern flank, exercises around Kaliningrad and Western seizures and inspections of tankers as an encirclement aimed at isolating Kaliningrad. In a diplomatic note to NATO members on September 30, 2026, it claimed NATO was preparing an air and sea blockade of Kaliningrad and said it would respond by all available means, including nuclear weapons.
parties.fear: Kaliningrad being cut off, and NATO's forward deployment becoming permanent even after the war in Ukraine ends.
parties.say: We defended Kaliningrad and stopped NATO at our border.
parties.aim_note: Russia avoids open, full-scale war while stepping up sub-threshold attacks, and seeks limits on NATO's eastern posture through a deal with the United States. Yet its December 2021 draft treaty, which demanded that NATO station no forces in countries that joined after 1997, suggests its aims may not be limited.

parties.reads: Poland sees Russian sabotage and airspace violations as rehearsals for a larger attack. It fears that direct U.S.-Russian talks could repeat the pattern of 1939's secret Nazi-Soviet protocol or 1945's Yalta, when great powers decided Poland's fate without it.
parties.fear: The United States and Russia trading a ceasefire in Ukraine for limits on the eastern flank, and the alliance's promises remaining on paper without troops on the ground, as in 1939.
parties.say: Allied troops are now permanently stationed on our soil, and we did not face Russia's provocations alone.
parties.aim_note: Poland's aims are territorial integrity and an alliance commitment that works. It does not seek Russian territory. Because the president and the government clash over security policy, any face-saving line has to be one both can use.

parties.reads: The United States sees Europe's defense as primarily Europe's responsibility and strategic stability with Russia as a condition for concentrating on the homeland, the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific (December 2025 National Security Strategy). The January 2026 National Defense Strategy called Russia a 'persistent but manageable threat' to NATO's eastern members.
parties.fear: Being dragged into a direct clash with Russia by events in Europe, and having forces it needs for the Indo-Pacific tied down there.
parties.say: We lowered tensions without a war and made Europe bear more of the cost.
parties.aim_note: The aim is to reduce U.S. forces in Europe overall while sending more troops to countries whose leaders are on good terms with the president and that spend heavily on defense. The cut in U.S. forces in Germany, the halt to a long-range fires deployment there and the announcement of 5,000 troops for Poland all came in May 2026.

parties.reads: Germany sees Russia's hybrid attacks as a threat that has become routine, yet it tries to hold the line Chancellor Merz drew: 'We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace.'
parties.fear: German territory being attacked directly as a rear base for supporting Ukraine, and being left with the burden of defending the eastern flank if the United States pulls out.
parties.say: We stood by the alliance without being drawn into war.
parties.aim_note: Germany aims to keep up support for Ukraine and deterrence without seeking to destabilize the Russian regime. Its permanent forward-deployed brigade is in Lithuania. Any face-saving line has to take account of supporters of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has gained ground in state elections in the east.

parties.reads: Lithuania sees transit to Kaliningrad as a channel through its territory for Russian military movements and sanctions evasion, and holds that it has the right to stop it if necessary (foreign minister, October 2025).
parties.fear: The Suwałki Gap being cut so that NATO reinforcements cannot get through, and facing Russian retaliation alone over the transit issue.
parties.say: We kept our sanctions and our right to halt transit, and the EU decided together with us.
parties.aim_note: Lithuania aims to preserve its territory and its control over its borders.

cases.misread: The most dangerous misreading could come from two directions. First, Russia could overinterpret the U.S. troop cut in Germany as a weakening of NATO's commitment to the eastern flank and escalate sub-threshold attacks to the point of causing deaths. An often-cited precedent is the argument that the 1949 withdrawal of U.S. troops from Korea and Secretary of State Dean Acheson's January 1950 defense-perimeter speech signaled to the attackers that the United States would not intervene. Second, Russia could mistake Polish and Baltic action against the shadow fleet and their infrastructure protection measures for preparations to blockade Kaliningrad and respond with naval escorts or shows of force. The September 30 diplomatic note shows that this misperception has already begun.

exits.title: Risk-reduction arrangements decoupled from forward deployment

claims.RUS: NATO put Russia's security concerns on the negotiating agenda
claims.POL: Not a single forward-deployed unit was cut
claims.DEU: We stabilized the eastern flank without war

exits.precedent: The 1972 U.S.-Soviet Incidents at Sea Agreement reduced dangerous approaches by ships and aircraft without touching military posture. Advance notification and observation of large exercises began with the 1975 Helsinki Final Act and the 1986 Stockholm Document and were broadened by the 1990 Vienna Document.
exits.obstacle: Russia demands cuts to forward deployment in return for risk-reduction arrangements, and a United States that puts strategic stability with Russia first may be open to that deal (A6b). Russia has resisted modernizing the Vienna Document, and accepting risk reduction alone would amount to accepting NATO's forward deployment, so it has little incentive to accept.

exits.title: Reaffirming the rules for transit to Kaliningrad (at EU level)

claims.RUS: We secured guaranteed land access to Kaliningrad
claims.LTU: We kept our right to halt transit and our sanctions
claims.DEU: We settled it within EU rules

exits.precedent: Under a 2002 EU-Russia agreement, travel by Kaliningrad residents was guaranteed through a simplified transit document even after Lithuania joined the EU. When Lithuania blocked rail transit of sanctioned goods in June 2022, the European Commission's interpretive guidance of July 13 allowed rail freight to pass (within the average volume of the previous three years, excluding military and dual-use goods) while keeping the ban on road transport, defusing the crisis.
exits.obstacle: Russia may demand not only land transit but an end to the air and sea 'blockade' and limits on NATO exercises around Kaliningrad, which Lithuania and Poland would see as one-sided concessions.

exits.title: Codifying the rules for maritime inspections in the Baltic

claims.RUS: We protected the sea route to Kaliningrad
claims.POL: We kept up action against the shadow fleet
claims.USA: A clash at sea was avoided

exits.precedent: In the 1962 Cuban missile crisis the United States called its measure a 'quarantine' rather than a blockade and let ships not carrying offensive weapons pass.
exits.obstacle: Russia seeks to protect even reflagged or uninsured tankers as its own ships, while the West sees any narrowing of inspections as a retreat on sanctions.

signals: Whether limits on troops and exercises on NATO's eastern flank appear on the U.S.-Russia negotiating agenda
Whether Russia follows up its claim of a Kaliningrad 'blockade' with official documents or military action such as naval escorts
Whether tanker inspections and seizures in the Baltic, and Russian naval escorts, increase
Whether Lithuania restricts or halts transit to Kaliningrad
Whether the 5,000 U.S. troops President Trump announced are actually stationed on a permanent basis
The opening and closing of the Belarusian border and the course of U.S.-Belarus talks
Whether military hotlines or incident-prevention talks between NATO and Russia resume

items.t: The ultimate purpose of every strategy is the happiness of individual human beings. Happiness is understood as capability: the conditions under which each person can pursue the life he or she considers good.

The happiness of individual human beings is this site's mission. It is not entered into the calculation of any particular strategy, nor used as a filter on options; instead, every assessment carries a separate section, What it means for people (Ⅲ).

Analysis has four parts: Situation assessment (Ⅰ), Strategy evaluation (Ⅱ), What it means for people (Ⅲ), and Verification (Ⅳ). Situation assessment (Ⅰ) forecasts what will happen without bringing values to bear. Strategy evaluation (Ⅱ) judges options against the strategic actor's own goals. What it means for people (Ⅲ) shows how the results bear on individual lives. Under Verification (Ⅳ), every assessment comes with a forecast that states its resolution date, and forecasts that miss are kept on the record rather than deleted.

Acts that international humanitarian law clearly prohibits — deliberately targeting civilians, using starvation as a method of warfare, taking hostages, and the like — are not recommended. Analysis of such options, however, is kept in full in Situation assessment (Ⅰ). Basis: Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Articles 51 and 54; Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, Article 8.

questions.title: Whose happiness?
questions.scene: Sanctions on North Korea put pressure on the regime, but they hurt ordinary North Koreans first. If a strategy that makes South Korea more secure leaves North Koreans less happy, is it a good strategy?

positions.view: Distance and nationality do not change moral weight. The suffering of someone far away counts as much as the suffering of someone nearby ("Famine, Affluence, and Morality," 1972).
People live within communities, and members of the same community owe one another special obligations.
Justice is first a matter within a single society, but the duty to assist burdened societies extends across borders (The Law of Peoples, 1999).

questions.objection: Treat every human being identically, and no strategy for South Korea can be formulated. Consider only South Koreans, and the phrase "individual human beings" rings hollow.
questions.answer: The What it means for people section (Ⅲ) treats all human beings equally. Strategy evaluation (Ⅱ), by contrast, takes the strategic actor's goals as its standard. When South Korea is the strategic actor, that goal is the one named in the preamble to its constitution: "security, liberty and happiness for ourselves and our posterity." When the two standards collide, neither is used to override the other; the gap between them is made explicit.
questions.remains: Making the gap explicit does not by itself settle the question. What to recommend when the two standards collide is decided issue by issue.

rule.text: Every strategic analysis names everyone affected: the strategic actor's citizens, the people of the opposing country, third countries, and future generations.

questions.title: What is happiness?
questions.scene: Some countries have high per capita income but no freedom of speech. People in a country at war want safety above all. Can the circumstances of people in the two countries be measured against a single yardstick of happiness?

positions.view: Happiness is the presence of pleasure and the absence of pain. The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right and wrong.
Happiness (eudaimonia) is not a feeling but a life lived by exercising one's distinctively human capacities well.
Do not try to measure happiness directly. Look instead at capabilities: people's real ability to live lives they have reason to value.
Asked whether they would enter a machine that supplied every experience they wanted, most people refuse. Pleasure is not the whole of happiness (the experience machine, 1974).

questions.objection: Happiness is subjective. The moment it is defined from the outside, the result is paternalism: the presumption to know what someone else's happiness is.
questions.answer: Happiness itself is left undefined. The aim instead is the conditions that allow each person to pursue the life he or she considers good—that is, capabilities. The capabilities that geopolitical strategy affects are defined by the seven categories of human security set out by the UN: personal safety, community, political, economic, food, health, and environment. They are measured through proxy indicators such as violent deaths, forced displacement, state violence, and income, while food, health, and environment are shown as alerts when a threshold is crossed. Surveys of subjective happiness serve as a supplement.
questions.remains: When the categories collide—when freedom of movement is curtailed for the sake of safety, for example—which should take precedence is taken up again in Q6 (When freedom and happiness collide).

rule.text: The effects of a strategy are stated separately for each of the seven categories of human security (personal safety, community, political, and economic, plus alerts for food, health, and environment) and are never combined into a single number.

questions.title: The problem of aggregation: may the few be sacrificed for the many?
questions.scene: Shows of force for deterrence, sanctions, and war always buy the security of the many with someone's sacrifice. That is why the 1945 atomic bombings are still debated today.

positions.view: The right choice is the one that maximizes total happiness.
Utilitarianism does not take seriously the distinction between persons. The position of the least advantaged must be considered first (A Theory of Justice, 1971).
Never treat a person merely as a means, but always at the same time as an end.

Even war is bound by principles: proportionality (what is gained must outweigh what is lost) and distinction (civilians are not to be targeted). Unintended collateral harm differs from intended harm (the doctrine of double effect).

questions.objection: Every strategy harms someone, so refusing to aggregate makes any action impossible. Yet doing nothing is also a choice, and someone pays for it too.
questions.answer: Aggregation itself is not rejected, and no option is excluded from analysis on moral grounds. Every option is judged by its consequences in Situation assessment and Strategy evaluation. Those who stand to lose the most are always identified in the What it means for people section, but their losses are not used to rank the options. The only things not recommended are acts that international humanitarian law clearly prohibits, and that line is an editorial principle, not part of the analytical method.
questions.remains: Measures such as sanctions, whose toll on ordinary people is foreseeable, do not fall under the editorial principle. That toll is spelled out concretely in the What it means for people section. Whether spelling it out is enough can be judged only after more issues have been analyzed.

rule.text: Every option is included in the analysis. A do-nothing option (A0) is always included, and no option is dropped on moral grounds. Those who stand to lose the most are identified in the What it means for people section, but their losses are not used to rank the options.

questions.title: The state and the individual: does the survival of the state come before individual happiness?
questions.scene: Ukraine is trying to lower its conscription age, and Israel keeps reservists at the front for months at a time. Can a state demand that individuals give their lives for its survival?

positions.view: Without a common power, the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short (Leviathan, 1651). The state comes first.
The power of government is entrusted to it by the people to protect their lives, liberty, and property; a government that abandons that purpose loses its legitimacy.
民爲貴 社稷次之 君爲輕. The people matter most, the state comes next, and the ruler counts for least.
The international system has no authority above states, so the survival of the state is the precondition for everything else.

questions.objection: The state is a precondition for individual happiness. As Syria and Sudan show, when the state collapses, individual happiness collapses with it.
questions.answer: The state is a means, not an end — but an irreplaceable one. Its survival and security are therefore given heavy weight as conditions for individual happiness. A distinction is drawn, however, between the survival of a regime and the lives of its people. A strategy that sacrifices people's lives to preserve a regime cannot be justified in the name of national survival.
questions.remains: How should this distinction apply to a system in which regime and state are effectively one, such as North Korea?

rule.text: Whenever the word "state" is used, the text specifies whether it refers to the regime, the institutions of the state, or the people.

questions.title: This generation and the next
questions.scene: Nuclear armament makes the current generation safer but passes the risks of accidents and proliferation on to the next. War debt, climate, and demographics follow the same pattern.

positions.view: Society is a partnership between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are yet to be born (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790).

Economics discounts the value of the future. The Stern Review (2006), by contrast, held that people cannot be valued less merely because they are born at a different time, and set the pure rate of time preference close to zero (0.1 percent a year).
Because present choices change who will be born at all, what it means to harm future people has to be reconsidered from the ground up (the non-identity problem, 1984).

questions.objection: The distant future is too uncertain to calculate. And the urgent suffering at hand comes first.
questions.answer: Future generations are not discounted merely because of when they are born. Uncertainty, however, is expressed as probability. And irreversible outcomes — nuclear proliferation, territorial annexation, the dispersal of peoples, ecological collapse — are given greater weight.
questions.remains: How much extra weight irreversibility should carry has not yet been fixed in numbers. That has to be settled as cases accumulate.

rule.text: Every strategy states the reversibility of its outcomes (reversible, difficult to reverse, irreversible), and irreversible outcomes are given greater weight.

questions.title: When freedom and happiness collide
questions.scene: China holds up stability and prosperity as the basis of its system's legitimacy. In 1994, Lee Kuan Yew invoked "Asian values," arguing that Western-style democracy does not suit Asia; that same year, Kim Dae-jung rebutted him in "Is Culture Destiny?"

positions.view: Negative liberty, the freedom from interference, differs from positive liberty, the freedom to govern one's own life. Oppression is easily justified in the name of positive liberty ("Two Concepts of Liberty," 1958).
So long as it harms no one else, individual liberty should not be restricted (On Liberty, 1859).
Huxley depicted a society in which everyone is content but no one is free (Brave New World, 1932).
No major famine has ever occurred in a functioning democracy. Freedom is also a means of survival.

questions.objection: In poor societies, bread comes before freedom. Putting freedom first is a luxury of the well fed.
questions.answer: Freedom is the condition that lets people decide for themselves what their happiness is, so it is set out separately and not merged with the other dimensions. It is not, however, treated as always taking precedence over them. Doing so would build into the method a ranking of values fixed by a particular ideology. Treating freedom as an absolute standard would also rule out policies that actually expanded freedom, such as Freikauf, under which West Germany paid to secure the release of political prisoners held by East Germany.
questions.remains: The freedom scores currently rest on the ratings of a single organization, Freedom House. Other measures, such as V-Dem, have yet to be brought in.

rule.text: Changes in freedom are set out separately and not merged with the other dimensions, but freedom is not treated as always taking precedence over them. The text also notes that the freedom scores come from a single organization, Freedom House.

questions.title: How can anyone know whether a strategy advanced happiness?
questions.scene: Did the 1994 Agreed Framework prevent a war, or merely slow North Korea's nuclear program? The consequences of the road not taken cannot be observed.

positions.view: Causation is estimated by comparison with cases in which a different choice was made under similar conditions.
Anyone can explain events after the fact. The only evidence of good judgment is whether forecasts made in advance came true.
The observation that happiness does not rise in step with income (1974) counsels caution in measuring happiness through proxies such as income.

questions.objection: Controlled experiments are impossible in geopolitics. Judging a strategy's contribution amounts to nothing more than telling a plausible story.
questions.answer: Causation cannot be proven. What can be checked is whether forecasts stated in advance came true. Every strategy is therefore presented together with a forecast of the form "if this strategy is adopted, X will be observed by date Y," and whether that forecast came true is checked on the Forecasts and Track Record tab.
questions.remains: A correct forecast does not mean the strategy was right; it may simply have been luck. Only as cases accumulate can luck be told apart from skill.

rule.text: No strategy is presented without a forecast. Each forecast is posted to the Forecasts and Track Record tab with a resolution date and the conditions under which it counts as fulfilled.

questions.title: The realist objection: international politics is a realm of survival
questions.scene: Well-intentioned interventions have often ended in disaster — Iraq in 2003 and Libya in 2011 among them. In the Melian Dialogue recounted by Thucydides, the Athenians declare that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

positions.view: Prudence — weighing the consequences of alternative courses of action — is the supreme virtue in politics (Politics Among Nations, 1948).
Individuals can be moral, but groups are selfish (Moral Man and Immoral Society, 1932).

An ethic of conviction, which puts purity of intention first, is not enough for a politician; it must be joined by an ethic of responsibility, which answers for foreseeable consequences ("Politics as a Vocation," 1919).

questions.objection: A strategy that proclaims happiness as its goal is either naive or, worse, hypocritical.
questions.answer: The realist diagnosis is accepted as it stands in Situation assessment and Strategy evaluation. Situations are judged by power and interest; strategies, by the strategic actor's interests and their foreseeable consequences. Happiness is the site's mission and is treated separately, in the What it means for people section (Ⅲ). Following Weber's ethic of responsibility, judgments rest on consequences rather than intentions, and prudence is the core principle of the method.
questions.remains: Prudence can breed a bias toward the status quo. How to deal fairly with strategies that would change an unjust status quo remains an unsolved problem.

rule.text: Strategies are evaluated by their foreseeable consequences. An option that carries a high risk of escalation or of irreversible outcomes is marked down one notch, even if its expected payoff is large.

tree.root: Purpose · The happiness of individual human beings (capability) · This site's mission

layers.name: Situation assessment
layers.d: The analysis excludes value judgments. Every option open to every actor is examined as the actors themselves weigh it.

layers.name: Strategy evaluation
layers.q: What should the strategic actor do?
layers.d: The strategic actor is named first, and options are evaluated against goals drawn from the actor's own documents.

layers.name: What it means for people
layers.q: How do the outcomes change people's lives?
layers.d: Options are not excluded on this basis; this assessment is presented separately from the strategy evaluation. Where Clisa's ranking by this standard differs from the strategic actor's, the gap is made explicit.

layers.name: Verification
layers.d: Forecasts are issued with stated resolution dates, and once a resolution date passes, accuracy is scored with the Brier score.

tree.editorial: Acts that international humanitarian law clearly prohibits — deliberately targeting civilians, using starvation as a method of warfare, taking hostages, and the like — are not recommended. Analysis of such options, however, is kept in full in Situation assessment (Ⅰ). Basis: Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Articles 51 and 54; Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, Article 8.
tree.quality: No assessment is issued without a forecast that carries a resolution date. Judgment estimates are given with ranges.

philosophy.note: The provisional answer to each question will be revised as new objections and cases emerge.

strategies.title: The Korean Peninsula: What should South Korea do about North Korea?
strategies.recipient: The government and people of the Republic of Korea
facts: At its Ninth Party Congress in February 2026, North Korea's ruling party formally enshrined both the country's status as a nuclear weapons state and a "two-state" doctrine that defines the Republic of Korea as a "hostile state." Between January and September 2026, Pyongyang conducted at least nine ballistic missile launches involving more than 15 missiles; it tested a new hypersonic missile on September 20 and fired a hypersonic intermediate-range missile on October 3, which flew more than 700 kilometers, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff. Its arsenal is estimated at about 60 nuclear warheads.
North Korea signed a mutual defense treaty with Russia in 2024 and has since supplied it with troops and weapons; Xi Jinping's visit to Pyongyang in June 2026 also restored its ties with China.

The 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy shifted primary responsibility for conventional deterrence of North Korea to South Korea. In August, President Donald Trump unilaterally scaled back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, and he is pursuing a meeting with Kim Jong Un before the end of the year.

At the UN General Assembly in September, the Lee Jae-myung government set out three principles of "peaceful coexistence" and urged Washington to pursue a trade of sanctions relief for a nuclear freeze. It turned down a U.S. request to send forces to the Strait of Hormuz.

About 33,000 members of separated families are still alive, two-thirds of them aged 80 or older. Family reunions and confirmations of whether relatives are alive have been suspended since 2018, now for eight years.

Multilateral talks have never required the two Koreas to recognize each other as states. They took part as separate delegations in the Four-Party Talks in Geneva (South Korea, North Korea, the United States, and China) from December 1997 to August 1999 and in the Six-Party Talks from 2003 to 2008. The two Koreas joined the United Nations simultaneously in 1991, and the Basic Agreement signed the same year describes their relations as "not being a relationship between states" but "a special interim relationship."

Seoul has already formally proposed a four-party framework. At the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on June 4, 2026, Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed beginning with four-way talks among the two Koreas, the United States, and China and then widening them to include Mongolia, Japan, and Russia; the government envisions a sequence in which U.S.-North Korean talks open the door to four-party peace negotiations. North Korea has demanded recognition as a nuclear weapons state and the lifting of sanctions while ruling denuclearization off the agenda, and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, while referring to a "constructive role" for Beijing, made it conditional on Washington abandoning its hostile policy.

At the Ninth Party Congress in February 2026, North Korea declared that it had no business dealing with the South and demanded that the United States respect its nuclear status and withdraw its hostile policy. On September 24, 2026, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui declared that the country's nuclear status is irreversible and that sanctions and military pressure are incompatible with dialogue.

After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed at the UN General Assembly on September 24 that two captured North Korean soldiers had been transferred to South Korea, the South Korean presidential office called the disclosure a breach of a confidential arrangement and demanded an apology from Kyiv (September 27–28), and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned Ukraine's chargé d'affaires in Seoul on September 28 to protest. No official North Korean reaction has yet been confirmed.

On September 21, a land mine exploded south of the Military Demarcation Line inside the Demilitarized Zone, wounding South Korean soldiers. On September 29, the defense minister said it was certainly a North Korean mine and that North Korean troops appeared to have crossed the line to plant it. In a statement by Kim Yo Jong, North Korea denied responsibility and called the incident "the farce of their own making," and on October 2 it said it would allow no room for any entanglement with South Korea.
On September 29, the Cabinet approved a special bill on the acquisition, operation, and safety management of nuclear-powered submarines, which the government aims to enact before the end of the year.

actors.t: The regime's goal is its own perpetuation, and nuclear weapons are its insurance policy. It fears Libya's fate and worries that Russian patronage will fade once the Russia-Ukraine war ends. When this analysis speaks of "North Korea," it distinguishes the regime from the people: the regime's interests and the lives of 26 million North Koreans are not the same.

Washington's attention centers on ICBMs that can reach the U.S. homeland. It has handed conventional deterrence to South Korea. That gives it a strong incentive to accept a deal that limits only the threat to the homeland.
Beijing wants North Korea stable as a buffer and most dislikes any scenario that brings U.S. forces up to the Yalu River. A nuclear North Korea is uncomfortable for China; a collapsed one is worse.

Russia has been North Korea's ally under a mutual defense treaty since 2024. It pays in technology and money for North Korean troops and artillery shells. Its posture after the Russia-Ukraine war ends is the biggest variable.

Tokyo has a stake in both the missile threat and the abduction issue. If Washington and Pyongyang agree to limit only ICBMs, Japan will feel left alone to bear the threat from medium- and short-range missiles.

law.title: Article 3 of the Constitution and the two-state doctrine
points: Article 3 of the Constitution of the Republic of Korea states, "The territory of the Republic of Korea shall consist of the Korean peninsula and its adjacent islands." Article 4 commits the country to peaceful unification. Recognizing North Korea as a fully foreign country would collide head-on with Article 3.

The tension is not new. When the two Koreas joined the United Nations together in 1991, Article 3 stayed as it was. The Basic Agreement signed that year described inter-Korean relations as "not being a relationship between states" but "a special interim relationship stemming from the process towards reunification," and the Development of Inter-Korean Relations Act of 2005 wrote that formula into law. The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court treat North Korea as having a dual status: an anti-state organization and a partner in dialogue and cooperation.

West Germany faced the same problem. In 1973, its Federal Constitutional Court upheld the Basic Treaty between East and West Germany, holding that East Germany was a state under international law but not a foreign country to West Germany, and that Germany as a whole continued to exist. The two states exchanged permanent missions instead of embassies. The arrangement institutionalized coexistence while preserving the legal basis for unification.

The territorial clause also matters decisively for North Korean defectors. The Supreme Court has consistently held that North Koreans are nationals of the Republic of Korea, which is why defectors hold citizenship the moment they arrive. Amending Article 3 to make North Korea a foreign country would undermine that protection.
law.result: Coexistence within the special-relationship framework (A2) should therefore not be a "recognition of two states" that requires amending the Constitution, but "coexistence within the special-relationship framework" that leaves the Constitution intact. The remaining obstacle lies on the North Korean side. Since 2024, Pyongyang has been erasing references to unification and demanding recognition as two fully separate states, so it is likely to reject the special-relationship framework itself.

Livelihoods, freedom, family

people.who: About 33,000 surviving members of separated families
people.how: Two in three are 80 or older. Time lost cannot be recovered
Families left in the North, their status in South Korea
