Nuclear proliferation in Northeast Asia, a hardened division

alts.name: Staying the course (doing nothing new)
alts.desc: Seoul proposes dialogue but, if North Korea does not respond, simply maintains deterrence. Negotiations with North Korea are left to Washington.

eff.safety: The near-term risk of war is low. But risk accumulates as North Korea's nuclear program advances and U.S. deterrence weakens.
eff.living: North Koreans' poverty continues under sanctions.
eff.freedom: No change in North Koreans' freedom.
eff.bond: The inter-Korean rupture and the suspension of family reunions continue. Every year, thousands of separated-family members die without seeing their relatives again.

alts.loser: Elderly members of separated families; North Koreans
alts.rev: Reversible, though the losses to separated families are not

G1.t: Risk accumulates (North Korea's nuclear advances, gaps in deterrence)

G2.t: Leaving negotiations with North Korea to Washington risks South Korea's exclusion

ev.esc2: Low in the short term, cumulative in the long term

alts.name: A phased freeze with South Korea at the table
alts.desc: North Korea freezes nuclear tests, ICBM tests, and the production of fissile material and accepts verification in exchange for phased sanctions relief. South Korea takes part as a party at the negotiating table and as a contributor to the costs.

eff.safety: The pace of the nuclear buildup slows and the risk of accidental clashes falls. But because it effectively accepts North Korea's nuclear status, it could strengthen public support for nuclear armament in South Korea and Japan.
eff.living: Sanctions relief could improve North Koreans' livelihoods, though the regime may capture the resources first. South Korea bears part of the cost of implementing the agreement.
eff.freedom: No direct effect. Greater exchanges would let a little more outside information into North Korea.
eff.bond: Humanitarian exchanges and family reunions can be written into the terms of the agreement.

alts.loser: Future generations, who bear the proliferation risk; Japan, which remains exposed to medium- and short-range missiles
alts.prob: Low to medium. North Korea seeks to exclude South Korea, and Washington leans toward a deal limiting only the ICBMs that can reach the U.S. homeland

G1.t: A ceiling on nuclear and missile buildup

G2.t: Secures a seat at the table

ev.cost: Medium (some sanctions relief, adjustment of joint exercises)

alts.name: Institutionalized coexistence within a special relationship (German Basic Treaty model)
alts.desc: Seoul treats North Korea as an entity under international law while keeping the two Koreas in a "special relationship" in which neither is a foreign country to the other, and it institutionalizes permanent missions (rather than embassies), trade, and humanitarian exchanges. The territorial clause in Article 3 of the Constitution and the goal of unification remain unchanged.

eff.safety: Institutionalized liaison channels reduce accidental clashes. North Korea's nuclear weapons remain.
eff.living: Resumed trade would benefit both Koreas, though it could also enlarge the North Korean regime's resources.
eff.freedom: North Korean human rights could be pushed aside in the course of normalization. On the other hand, West Germany, while dealing with East Germany, paid to secure the release of about 33,000 East German political prisoners between 1963 and 1989. Normalization can also become a channel for expanding freedom.
eff.bond: Family reunions and exchanges can be institutionalized. Of the four dimensions — life and safety, livelihood, freedom, and relationships and community — this is the one that improves the most.

alts.loser: North Korean political prisoners and defectors, if human rights are pushed aside
alts.prob: Low. North Korea demands full recognition as a separate state, not a "special relationship," and domestic opposition is strong

G1.t: Small direct effect

G4.t: Coexistence that preserves the legal basis for unification

alts.name: An independent nuclear arsenal
alts.desc: South Korea withdraws from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and develops and deploys its own nuclear weapons.

eff.safety: Deterrence against North Korea grows stronger. But it brings a vulnerable window during development, cascading nuclear armament in Japan and Taiwan, a backlash from China, and the risk of accidents.
eff.living: International sanctions and disruptions to nuclear fuel supplies would deal a heavy blow to the export economy. The United States also has a law, the Glenn Amendment, that mandates sanctions on countries that conduct nuclear tests.
eff.bond: The U.S.-South Korean alliance is shaken and inter-Korean hostility hardens.

alts.loser: Future generations, who inherit a proliferated Northeast Asia; workers in export industries
alts.prob: Feasible but extremely costly. South Korea currently has no capacity to produce fissile material, so it would take years even after a decision

G1.t: Short-term deterrence grows, but proliferation cascades

G2.t: Rift in the alliance, nonproliferation sanctions

G3.t: Controls on nuclear fuel and exports, and sanctions

alts.name: Latent nuclear capability (conditional, transparent)
alts.desc: South Korea acquires enrichment and reprocessing capabilities and nuclear-powered submarines within the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. It does so not unilaterally or in haste but conditionally, announcing in advance that it will move to the next stage if North Korea does not agree to a freeze (on the model of NATO's 1979 Double-Track Decision), within a joint U.S.-South Korean framework, and while actually expanding inspections.

eff.safety: It yields no usable weapon now. Its value lies in the signal it sends North Korea and in insurance for the future. The time between a decision to build nuclear weapons and their completion (breakout time) would shrink from several years to several months over the five to 10 years it takes to build enrichment and reprocessing facilities.
eff.living: Because Washington supports this path, the risk of sanctions is small. The facilities require investment.
eff.bond: It invites suspicion from China and North Korea. Prior coordination with Japan is needed to keep it from turning into a competition.

alts.loser: Northeast Asia as a whole, if a race in latent capabilities takes hold, and companies exporting to China, which bear the costs of Chinese suspicion
alts.prob: Under way: U.S. support in November 2025 and a master plan for nuclear-powered submarines in May 2026. A conditional design tied to whether North Korea freezes its program does not yet exist
alts.rev: Largely reversible, though the facilities remain
alts.esc: Medium; high the moment South Korea moves to actually build nuclear weapons (breakout)

G1.t: Insurance

ev.esc2: Low to medium (chain reaction in Japan)

alts.name: U.S. nuclear sharing or redeployment of tactical nuclear weapons
alts.desc: Seoul asks for NATO-style nuclear sharing or the redeployment of the U.S. tactical nuclear weapons withdrawn in 1991.

eff.safety: The credibility of deterrence rises. But the host bases become targets for a preemptive strike.
eff.living: Chinese economic retaliation could exceed what followed the THAAD deployment.
eff.bond: The U.S.-South Korean alliance deepens, but relations with China deteriorate sharply and inter-Korean hostility hardens.

alts.loser: Residents near the deployment sites; companies exporting to China
alts.prob: Low. It runs against the burden-shifting thrust of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy
alts.rev: Reversible; the 1991 U.S. withdrawal of tactical nuclear weapons is the precedent

G1.t: Reinforces deterrence

G2.t: Alliance cohesion, though Washington may refuse

alts.name: Maximum pressure and engineered collapse
alts.desc: Seoul tightens comprehensive sanctions and increases the flow of information into North Korea to hasten the regime's collapse.

eff.safety: The risk of a desperate "gamble" by a North Korea convinced that its system cannot survive rises sharply.
eff.living: North Koreans' livelihoods deteriorate badly; North Korea's great famine of the 1990s is the precedent.
eff.freedom: If collapse succeeds, freedom could grow in the long run, but the outcome is highly uncertain.
eff.bond: Hostility hardens.

alts.loser: North Koreans
alts.prob: The probability of collapse is low, and the risk of provoking a gamble is high

G1.t: China and Russia plug the gaps in sanctions, so the deterrent effect is small while the incentive for provocation grows

G2.t: It runs against the Trump administration's negotiating current, and South Korea gets bypassed

ev.feas: Low (Security Council resolutions are blocked and China and Russia do not cooperate)

alts.name: Stronger conventional deterrence
alts.desc: South Korea builds up its own strike capabilities, missile defenses, and surveillance assets to actually take on primary responsibility for conventional deterrence of North Korea. This is the direction the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy demands.

eff.safety: South Korea's greater deterrent capability reduces the risk of war but sets off an arms race.
eff.living: Higher defense spending strains public finances. The North Korean regime channels even more resources to the military.
eff.bond: Little change.

alts.loser: South Korean taxpayers, who bear the fiscal burden; North Koreans caught in the arms race

G1.t: Directly strengthens deterrence

alts.name: Using information tools aimed at North Korea
alts.desc: Seoul uses the switching on and off of loudspeakers, radio and TV broadcasts, and private leaflet launches as leverage in itself. These have in fact served as bargaining chips several times: in the August 2015 agreement, the 2018 Panmunjom Declaration, and the 2025 halt of loudspeaker broadcasts.

eff.safety: Switching the tools on raises tensions in border areas (North Korean countermeasures such as trash balloons).
eff.living: Little change.
eff.freedom: Switching them on increases North Koreans' access to information; switching them off reduces it.
eff.bond: Little change.

alts.loser: North Koreans (access to information) when a deal to switch them off is struck; border-area residents (tension) when they are switched on

G1.t: Border tensions

G2.t: Switching on and off is itself a card

G4.t: Long-term change in North Korean society

alts.name: Humanitarian exchange with something given in return
alts.desc: Like West Germany's Freikauf, in which Bonn bought the release of East German political prisoners with money and goods, Seoul offers goods or other compensation in return for family reunions, confirmations of whether relatives are alive, and the repatriation of detainees and abductees. It is designed as in-kind payment within the humanitarian exemption procedures of UN sanctions.

eff.safety: Little change.
eff.living: The goods sent in return reach the regime first.
eff.freedom: If detainees and abductees are released, their freedom is restored.
eff.bond: Family reunions and confirmations of whether relatives are alive become possible.

alts.loser: Criticism that the payments help the regime; the credibility of the sanctions regime

G1.t: Neutral

ev.cost: Goods given in return, sanctions-exemption procedures, domestic criticism

excluded: Maximum pressure and engineered collapse (A4) is not put forward as an option because it crosses the first line: never deliberately using innocent people as a means to an end. Targeted sanctions against materials used directly in nuclear and missile programs can, however, be maintained under staying the course (A0) or a phased freeze (A1).

ranked.t: Pursue two tracks together: a phased freeze in which South Korea sits at the table as a party, and institutionalized coexistence within a special relationship that keeps the constitutional framework intact. Normalization should come with the condition that it is not bought with silence on human rights or the repatriation of defectors, and family reunions should be the first item of any agreement. Add a conditional, transparent latent nuclear capability (A3b) as both negotiating leverage and insurance. A latent capability pursued unilaterally and in haste does not make the top rank.
Staying the course (A0) is the baseline for comparison. It is not a neutral choice: it means accepting, year after year, irreversible losses for separated families.
Nuclear sharing or the redeployment of tactical nuclear weapons is reversible, but Washington is unlikely to accept it, and it would provoke the strongest backlash from China and North Korea.

An independent nuclear arsenal does not cross the first line (never deliberately using innocent people as a means to an end), but it is irreversible and carries a high risk of cascading proliferation and escalation, so it ranks last. It should be reconsidered if U.S. extended deterrence actually collapses.

verdict.undecided: On the sequence of a phased freeze (A1) and special-relationship coexistence (A2), a second review from the standpoint of the deciding powers tilted toward putting A1 first, because what North Korea rejects is not a freeze but contact with the South. This procedure still does not settle which should weigh more when South Korea's security and North Koreans' livelihoods conflict. The question left open under Q1 ("Whose well-being?") on the Methodology tab remains open.

responses.note: The assumption is not that adversaries will protest loudly, but that they will respond in the most capable way: neutralizing the signals the South Korean government sends and leaving South Korea with nothing but costs.

rows.CHN: Beijing would welcome it as serving China's interest in stability on the peninsula, but it would want it handled within a four-party framework of the United States, China, and the two Koreas, or within a U.S.-China deal, rather than in a framework with South Korea seated as a party.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would refuse to let South Korea sit as a party and insist on a direct deal with Washington. It would signal to the United States that leaving South Korea out makes for a faster deal.
rows.JPN: Tokyo would support it if medium- and short-range missiles are included in what is frozen.
rows.RUS: Moscow would be indifferent, or at least would not obstruct it.
rows.USA: Washington would welcome it publicly but prepare negotiations through the U.S.-North Korean channel and simply inform Seoul of the results.

rows.CHN: Rather than retaliating loudly, Beijing would concentrate on driving a wedge between Washington and Seoul. It would invoke international nonproliferation norms to push the U.S. Congress toward sanctioning South Korea, and use South Korean nuclear weapons to justify its own nuclear buildup.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would exploit South Korea's development period as an opportunity for provocation or, more cleverly, propose "mutual recognition of nuclear status and arms control talks between the two Koreas" to win formal acceptance of its own nuclear weapons.
rows.JPN: Tokyo would cite South Korean nuclear weapons to abandon the Three Non-Nuclear Principles and pursue its own arsenal. With more than 40 tons of plutonium, Japan would reach nuclear armament before South Korea.
rows.RUS: Moscow would increase transfers of submarine and missile technology to North Korea and portray South Korean nuclear weapons as proof that the nonproliferation regime has collapsed.
rows.USA: Within the United States, pressure for sanctions under nonproliferation laws (such as the Glenn Amendment) and calls to review the alliance would arise at the same time.

rows.CHN: Beijing would not react strongly. It would watch quietly and apply economic pressure at the moment South Korea takes a step toward nuclear weapons. Meanwhile it would encourage a chain reaction in Japan to split Seoul and Tokyo, and link South Korea's latent capability to the Taiwan question in bargaining with Washington. The move is to erase South Korea's signals by ignoring them and leave South Korea with only the costs.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would use South Korea's latent capability to justify developing its own nuclear weapons and nuclear-powered submarines (unveiled in December 2025, with suspected Russian technology transfers) and close the denuclearization agenda for good.
rows.JPN: Tokyo would use South Korea's latent capability as a pretext to "normalize" its own (reprocessing facilities and plutonium). South Korea opens the door, and Japan walks through first.
rows.RUS: Moscow would openly expand technical support for North Korea's nuclear-powered submarine on the grounds that "South Korea is doing it too."
rows.USA: Washington would seek to use South Korea's latent capability as leverage in containing China, and could also use it as a bargaining chip with China if needed.

rows.CHN: Beijing would retaliate more strongly than it did over THAAD and use the deployment of tactical nuclear weapons to justify a missile buildup in Northeast Asia and its refusal of arms control.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would declare the host bases targets for preemptive strikes and entrench a doctrine that lowers the threshold for nuclear use.
rows.JPN: Tokyo would broadly welcome it, but a debate over deployment in Japan would follow.
rows.RUS: Moscow would use it as a pretext for deploying its own intermediate-range missiles in Northeast Asia.
rows.USA: Washington would likely refuse, since it runs against the 2026 National Defense Strategy's thrust of shifting burdens to allies.

rows.CHN: Beijing would quietly fill the gaps in sanctions with trade and crude oil supplies. China-North Korea trade rose 25 percent in 2025.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would step up provocations and deepen its reliance on Russia. It would block the influx of information with controls that extend to executions.
rows.RUS: Moscow would block additional sanctions at the Security Council (it vetoed the extension of the panel of experts on North Korea sanctions in 2024) and pay for the troops and artillery shells North Korea has sent.
rows.USA: Because it would run against the administration's negotiating current, Washington would have a stronger incentive to bypass South Korea and deal with North Korea directly.

rows.CHN: Beijing would view it warily as part of U.S.-Japan-South Korea solidarity but would stop short of retaliation on the scale of the THAAD episode.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would use it as a pretext for an arms race and ask Russia for more technology. It would also cite it as a reason to refuse negotiations.
rows.RUS: Moscow would use it as a pretext for technology transfers to North Korea.
rows.USA: Washington would welcome it as consistent with the demands of the National Defense Strategy, and could also use it to justify reducing U.S. Forces Korea.

rows.CHN: Beijing would be indifferent.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would retaliate with trash balloons and loudspeakers of its own, and try to minimize what it gives up in return for South Korea switching off its information tools.
rows.RUS: Moscow would be indifferent.
rows.USA: Washington might see it as an obstacle to U.S.-North Korean dialogue.

rows.CHN: Beijing would be indifferent.
rows.PRK: Pyongyang would refuse publicly but might accept if the payment were large and the deal quiet. Family reunions in the 2000s, too, took place amid payments.
rows.JPN: Tokyo would demand that the abduction issue be raised as well.
rows.RUS: Moscow would be indifferent.
rows.USA: Washington would insist on sanctions-exemption procedures and oppose payment in cash.

responses.lesson: Assuming that adversaries respond in the most capable way changed the character of latent nuclear capability. Its value lies in the signal it sends. But a capable adversary erases that signal by ignoring it, leaving only the costs of suspicion and chain reactions. And it times its counterattack for the moment South Korea moves to actually build nuclear weapons (breakout), when South Korea is most vulnerable. Latent capability is therefore weak on its own and has value only when designed so that adversaries cannot ignore it. The design has three elements: a conditional announcement that ties each stage to North Korea's behavior (NATO's 1979 Double-Track Decision announced in advance that it would deploy missiles unless the Soviet Union negotiated the withdrawal of its intermediate-range missiles, and it led to the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty); a joint U.S.-South Korean framework (which keeps China from driving a wedge between Washington and Seoul); and prior coordination with Japan together with expanded inspections (which turns a competitive chain reaction into a shared norm). Maximum pressure (A4) is the option whose effect shrinks the most when China and Russia respond capably by quietly plugging the gaps in sanctions.

predictions.q: If a U.S.-North Korean summit takes place without South Korea formally taking part in the preparatory negotiations, the resulting agreement will contain no provisions on inter-Korean relations or on medium- and short-range missiles
predictions.note: Tests whether a U.S.-North Korean agreement becomes a deal covering only the threat to the U.S. homeland (ICBMs)

predictions.q: If the current trend (A0) continues, inter-Korean military communication lines will not be restored
If the current trend (A0) continues, family reunions and confirmations of whether relatives are alive will not resume
China will not retaliate with open, large-scale economic measures, as it did over THAAD, against South Korea's pursuit of enrichment, reprocessing, and nuclear-powered submarines
predictions.note: Tests the assumption that the adversary responds in the most capable way

falsify: If North Korea formally declares that it will not accept South Korea as a negotiating partner and its missile launches become more frequent, the premise of a phased freeze combined with special-relationship coexistence (A1+A2) — that South Korea can sit at the table as a party — will have collapsed, and the sequence will be reconsidered.

If Washington concludes an agreement that limits only ICBMs without South Korean participation, the analysis will check whether the credibility of extended deterrence has actually collapsed and reconsider the ranking of an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) and of nuclear sharing or tactical nuclear redeployment (A3c).

If Japan formally moves to expand reprocessing or enrichment, or to revise its Three Non-Nuclear Principles, before South Korea does, the prior coordination with Japan on which latent nuclear capability (A3b) depends will have broken down, and its ranking will be reconsidered.

If China answers South Korea's pursuit of enrichment and reprocessing with open, large-scale economic retaliation, the assumption that "China waits quietly instead of retaliating loudly" will have proved wrong.

If a reduction of U.S. Forces Korea is actually carried out, the credibility of extended deterrence will be reassessed and the ranking of an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) and of nuclear sharing or tactical nuclear redeployment (A3c) reconsidered. This signal is the same as external variable X1 (a substantive U.S. retreat).
If North Korea-China trade falls sharply and Beijing tightens sanctions enforcement, the effect of maximum pressure (A4) will be recalculated.

If the final National Defense Authorization Act includes a provision that makes completion of the OPCON transfer wait for the secretary of defense's certification (Section 1235 of the Senate Armed Services Committee's bill), the forecast that the transfer will be completed by 2030 and the timeline assumed for stronger conventional deterrence (A5) will be revisited.

conclusions.t: Through 2030, the most likely future is "armed stalemate" (37%, range 27–47%), followed by "a U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea" (22%, range 14–30%).
conclusions.why: Armed stalemate is the only future that none of the five deciding powers (the United States, China, North Korea, Russia, and Japan) rejects. A U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea is a future that the Trump administration and North Korea prefer and that China can accept, and it is also the best move North Korea can choose on its own.
conclusions.flip: If military communication lines are restored and family reunions take place by the end of 2028, the probability of managed coexistence will be raised.

conclusions.t: For South Korea, a risk as real as war is being shut out of agreements on North Korea. Exclusion here is less about having a seat at the negotiating table than about whether South Korea's interests are reflected at the moment decisions are made.
conclusions.why: The 1994 Agreed Framework was concluded in bilateral U.S.-North Korean talks, yet South Korea paid 70 percent ($3.2 billion) of the cost of building the light-water reactors. Right after the 2018 Singapore summit, President Trump announced a halt to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises without consulting Seoul in advance — and this happened at a time when South Korea was mediating between Washington and Pyongyang. The risk of war is low in peacetime but rises sharply right after negotiations break down; the U.S. consideration of bombing the Yongbyon nuclear facilities during the first North Korean nuclear crisis in June 1994 is an example.
conclusions.flip: If a U.S.-North Korean agreement concluded without South Korea nonetheless includes provisions on inter-Korean relations and limits on the medium- and short-range missiles aimed at South Korea (f14 resolves no), this judgment that exclusion means loss will have proved wrong.

conclusions.t: Judged by the South Korean government's goals, the top choice is a package of three: build up conventional deterrence (A5), secure a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as insurance, and, in freeze negotiations (A1), secure a seat at the table for the implementation and peace-regime stages that follow a U.S.-North Korean agreement rather than at the opening stage. The cards to play early are not sanctions relief but tension-reducing steps such as adjusting joint U.S.-South Korean exercises or restoring inter-Korean liaison channels, and information tools aimed at the North (A6), such as loudspeakers and broadcasts, serve as bargaining chips.
conclusions.why: Since Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020, North Korea has put "withdrawal of hostile policy," including a halt to joint exercises and to deployments of U.S. strategic assets, ahead of sanctions relief. Adjusting joint exercises is an area in which South Korea has a say, but as the announcement of a halt to joint exercises without consulting Seoul right after the 2018 Singapore summit showed, what South Korea holds is not a veto but limited influence. In the inter-Korean high-level agreement that followed the August 2015 wooden-box mine provocation, South Korea traded a halt to loudspeaker broadcasts for an expression of regret from North Korea — a case in which information tools served as an actual bargaining chip.
conclusions.flip: If North Korea ultimately refuses to negotiate, citing South Korea's stronger deterrence, and Washington reaches an agreement with North Korea without South Korea (f21 resolves yes), the place of freeze negotiations (A1) in the top-ranked package will be reconsidered.

conclusions.t: Maximum pressure (A4) ranks low even when judged by the South Korean government's own goals.
conclusions.why: Its effect is small because China and Russia are plugging the holes in sanctions (China-North Korea trade rose 25 percent in 2025, and Russia pays for North Korean troops and weapons). It also runs against the Trump administration's push to negotiate with North Korea, leaving South Korea alone on the sidelines, and it closes the door to freeze negotiations.
conclusions.flip: If China tightens sanctions enforcement and China-North Korea trade falls sharply (f23 resolves no), the effect of maximum pressure will be recalculated.

conclusions.t: An independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) ranks last.
conclusions.why: It would inflict irreversible losses on the U.S.-South Korean alliance (G2) and the economy (G3), and it could set off a proliferation cascade in which Japan, with its more advanced technological base, arms first.
conclusions.flip: If Washington concludes an agreement limiting only ICBMs without South Korean participation and actually scales back its extended deterrence commitment, the ranking of an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) and of U.S. nuclear sharing or tactical nuclear redeployment (A3c) will be reconsidered.

conclusions.t: Judged by individual lives rather than by the government, the ranking changes in two places. Anything received in return for switching off the information tools aimed at the North should take only forms that benefit people directly, such as family reunions, and a humanitarian exchange that offers something in return for family reunions and the repatriation of detainees (A7) should be raised into the top-ranked package.
conclusions.why: When elderly members of separated families die, that loss is irreversible, and switching off the information tools narrows North Koreans' access to news from outside. The costs of a humanitarian exchange are the domestic political burden of giving North Korea something in return and the hassle of going through the humanitarian exemption procedures of UN sanctions. On September 29, 2026, the National Assembly's National Defense Committee failed to adopt a resolution condemning the North Korean land-mine incident because the parties could not agree on wording calling for a review of planned aid to the North — an instance of that domestic political burden surfacing in the legislature.
conclusions.flip: If the number of surviving separated-family members falls so far that there is no one left to exchange for (about 20,000 are expected by 2030), the ranking of a humanitarian exchange (A7) will change.

conclusions.t: Even by North Korea's own goals, its best move is a direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out. But what North Korea seeks is not sanctions relief but de facto acceptance of its nuclear status and a scaling back of joint U.S.-South Korean exercises and deployments of U.S. strategic assets; what it offers in return is a moratorium on nuclear and ICBM tests.
conclusions.why: At the 2019 Hanoi summit, North Korea offered to dismantle its Yongbyon nuclear facilities — a bigger concession than a freeze — and still failed to win sanctions relief, and Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020 recast the formula of exchange as "withdrawal of hostility versus resumption of DPRK-U.S. negotiations." The Four-Party and Six-Party Talks, in which North Korea sat down with South Korea, were respectively a format co-proposed by Washington and Seoul and one hosted by Beijing, and since February 2026 North Korea has said it will not deal with the South, whatever the agenda.
conclusions.flip: This judgment will be revised if North Korea again makes sanctions relief the center of the exchange or voluntarily joins consultations in which South Korea takes part.

conclusions.t: South Korea and China share an interest in preventing Washington and Pyongyang from bypassing them to strike a deal. But China is not a guarantor that will bring North Korea to the table, and the real value of a four-party framework of the two Koreas, the United States, and China lies in guaranteeing South Korea a place in peace-regime negotiations after a U.S.-North Korean agreement.
conclusions.why: In the 1997–1999 Four-Party Talks, China was merely one of the rotating chairs, and in 2008, as the Six-Party Talks were collapsing, it sided with North Korea by continuing to supply heavy fuel oil. China's 2017 "dual suspension" proposal (a simultaneous halt to North Korean nuclear and missile tests and to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises) was rejected by North Korea, only to be carried out the following year bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang, without China. The price China will demand (South Korean restraint on Taiwan and THAAD) should not be paid up front but doled out stage by stage.
conclusions.flip: This judgment will be reconsidered if Washington and Pyongyang sign an agreement that excludes South Korea from the implementation and peace-regime stages as well (f22 resolves yes).

why.risk: South Korea is in a state of armistice with a nuclear-armed hostile state, and the Seoul metropolitan area lies within range of long-range artillery. Domestic state violence is low. Hence "medium" (50).
On top of the same exposure to war, state violence such as political prison camps, public executions, and collective punishment of relatives hangs over daily life. Hence "high" (75).
Because most live in South Korea, the same exposure value as for South Koreans (50) is used.
why.contact: Reunions, confirmations of whether relatives are alive, and letters have all been suspended since 2018. Hence 0.

facts.PRK: 74 years (healthy life expectancy 64.7 years; South Korea 72.5)
facts.src: Statistics Korea · UN World Population Prospects

facts.PRK: 1.87 million won (3.6% of South Korea's) · 3.5% growth in 2025

facts.ROK: About 32,948 survivors, two-thirds aged 80 or older · about 3,000 die each year
facts.src: Ministry of Unification, Integrated Information Center for Separated Families

wellbeing.status: Baseline values are calculated from measured data; only exposure to risk is a judgment estimate by the analyst

items.name: Armed stalemate
items.story: A hostile two-state relationship hardens. North Korea expands its nuclear weapons and missiles and builds nuclear-powered submarines with Russian help. Washington wants dialogue, but North Korea refuses on the grounds that denuclearization is on the agenda, or the two sides meet without reaching agreement. There is no major clash, but there are no communication lines and no reunions either. The number of surviving separated-family members falls to about 20,000 by 2030.
items.test: If none of the conditions for managed coexistence (F2), nuclear dominoes (F3), sudden upheaval (F4), or a deal without South Korea (F5) is met, the outcome is armed stalemate (F1). If several conditions are met at once, the first in the order F4, F3, F2, F5 applies.
signs: A U.S.-North Korean summit falls through, or takes place without producing an agreement
North Korea repeats language formally rejecting dialogue with South Korea
Military communication lines stay cut into another year
North Korea resumes ICBM flight tests
items.why: South Korea's exposure to risk is set at 55 to reflect North Korea's nuclear buildup. Incomes are assumed to grow 1.8 percent a year in South Korea and 2 percent a year in North Korea (on trade with Russia).

items.name: A deal without South Korea
items.story: Washington and Pyongyang strike a deal that leaves South Korea out. North Korea halts ICBM and nuclear tests, and the United States lifts some sanctions and scales back joint exercises. Denuclearization is pushed off as a distant goal, and North Korea's nuclear weapons are accepted in practice. Inter-Korean relations remain blocked, and medium- and short-range missiles are left out of the agreement.
items.test: If Washington and Pyongyang agree on a nuclear and missile freeze or sanctions relief but fewer than two of the three conditions for managed coexistence (F2) are met, the outcome is a deal without South Korea (F5).
signs: The schedule of a Trump-Kim meeting is announced without prior consultation with South Korea
North Korea repeatedly signals that it will deal only with the United States (statements by Kim Yo Jong that do not target Washington directly)
Washington begins deferring denuclearization as a "long-term goal" and talking about a freeze and arms control
North Korea publicly ties an ICBM test moratorium to talks with Washington
items.why: Because North Korea's nuclear weapons remain and are accepted, South Korea's exposure to risk (50) does not fall. North Korea's exposure is set at 70 because the risk of conflict with the United States declines, and partial sanctions relief is assumed to raise its incomes 4 percent a year and bring undernourishment down to 40 percent. There are no exchanges for separated families.

items.name: Managed coexistence
items.story: A phased freeze with South Korea at the table begins, and a liaison office, trade, and humanitarian exchanges are institutionalized within a special-relationship framework. Because North Korea's system stays the same, freedom barely expands, but hunger and the risk of war decline and separated families meet again.
items.test: If at least two of the following occur — restoration of military communication lines, resumption of family reunions or confirmations of whether relatives are alive, and agreement on a nuclear and missile freeze — the outcome is F2.
signs: Military communication lines are restored
A U.S.-North Korean agreement includes provisions on inter-Korean relations or on medium- and short-range missiles
Food and health aid to North Korea resumes through UN channels
items.why: Exposure to risk is set at 40 for South Korea and 65 for North Korea (the risk of war falls, but state violence remains). North Korean incomes are assumed to grow 5 percent a year and undernourishment to fall to 35 percent with the help of aid, and separated families are assumed to reach the level at which confirmations of whether relatives are alive and letters are possible (50).

items.name: Nuclear dominoes
items.story: Doubts about U.S. extended deterrence grow, and Japan and South Korea move beyond latent capability toward developing nuclear weapons. China quietly drives wedges between Washington and Seoul and between Seoul and Tokyo, and Russia gives North Korea more technology. The number of nuclear powers in Northeast Asia grows.
items.test: If, by the end of 2030, South Korea or Japan formalizes any of the following — a decision to develop nuclear weapons, withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, or abandonment of its non-nuclear principles — the outcome is F3.
signs: Japan formally debates revising its Three Non-Nuclear Principles
With public support for an independent nuclear arsenal above 70 percent, the South Korean government says it is considering the option
Washington concludes an agreement limiting only ICBMs without South Korean participation
items.why: Exposure to risk is set at 65 for South Korea and 80 for North Korea. South Korean incomes are assumed to grow only 1.2 percent a year because of sanctions pressure and security costs, and its freedom score is assumed to slip slightly (83→81) as security-driven controls tighten.

items.name: Sudden upheaval
items.story: North Korea's supreme leader is replaced, internal turmoil breaks out, or a large-scale armed clash occurs. The range of outcomes is the widest of all: at the bad end, war and mass casualties; at the good end, regime transition and opening. It is therefore presented as a range rather than a single point.
items.test: If, by the end of 2030, North Korea's supreme leader changes or an armed clash on the Korean Peninsula kills 100 or more people, the outcome is F4.
signs: Rumors about Kim Jong Un's health coincide with a formal designation of a successor
Russian support drops sharply and food prices soar
Military clashes recur in the Yellow Sea or elsewhere
items.why: The bad case is one in which war lowers life expectancy to 82 in South Korea and to 66 in North Korea. The good case assumes a freedom score of 35 for North Koreans after regime transition (the low end of Eastern Europe's transition period in the early 2000s) and free movement between the Koreas.

expect.note: Expected values are the probability-weighted sums of each future's 2030 values (for F4, the midpoint between the bad and good cases). They are calculated separately for each dimension — life and safety, livelihood, freedom, and relationships and community — and the dimensions are not combined. Because expected values alone hide risks that are unlikely but highly damaging, the values for the worst future are shown alongside.
expect.read: If the recommendation is followed, expected values rise slightly for all three groups, but only by small margins. The biggest movement is in the relationships dimension for separated families (0 in 2026, 11.0 under the current trend, 18.5 if the recommendation is followed). South Koreans' life and safety, at 73.2 even if the recommendation is followed, stays below the 2026 level of 74.0. This means that, with North Korea's nuclear buildup already under way, no choice can fully preserve the current level. North Koreans' freedom remains in single digits in every future (except the good case of sudden upheaval). What strategy can change is the probability of futures, not the futures themselves, and the margin South Korea can change on its own is not large.

futures.note: The probabilities and the inputs for each future are judgment estimates by the analyst. Figures in parentheses are ranges. "If the recommendation is followed" assumes that South Korea begins the top-ranked package (stronger conventional deterrence A5, a phased freeze A1, and a conditional latent nuclear capability A3b, plus information tools aimed at the North A6 as bargaining chips) by the end of 2027.

items.means: The alliance and the nuclear umbrella, U.S. Forces Korea, the design of the sanctions regime, U.S.-North Korean summits
items.frame: The North Korea problem is a problem of ICBMs that can reach the U.S. homeland. The Korean Peninsula is both a forward base for containing China and a cost to be cut.
goals: Limit the ICBM threat to the homeland
Cut alliance costs and hand conventional deterrence to South Korea
Use South Korea in the competition with China (shipbuilding, semiconductors, the strategic flexibility of U.S. Forces Korea)
items.strategy: Washington is downgrading the North Korea problem from something to "solve" to something to "manage" and shifting resources toward China. But there are two strands within the United States: the administration wants results from a leader-level deal with North Korea, while Congress and the national security bureaucracy want to preserve the alliance framework.
tactics: The 2026 National Defense Strategy shifted primary responsibility for conventional deterrence of North Korea to South Korea
It unilaterally scaled back the August joint exercise and is pursuing a meeting with Kim Jong Un before year's end
After the May summit in Beijing, it announced that the two sides had affirmed denuclearization as a shared goal, keeping denuclearization alive in name
It supports South Korean enrichment and nuclear-powered submarines, as the price of enlisting South Korea in containing China
Congress is using the defense authorization bill to block reductions in U.S. Forces Korea, and the White House opposes that provision
red: Completion of a nuclear strike capability that can reach the homeland, or its transfer to a third country
South Korea acquiring its own nuclear weapons (the collapse of the nonproliferation regime)
Being dragged into a war it does not want
items.ext: Taiwan comes first; the Korean Peninsula is a variable attached to it. Washington believes it must be able to draw on U.S. Forces Korea in a Taiwan crisis. It sees an end to the Russia-Ukraine war as an opportunity for negotiations, since it would reduce North Korea's dependence on Russia.
items.want: That Seoul take on more of conventional deterrence and defense spending, not oppose the containment of China, and not slow down a U.S.-North Korean deal
items.onrec: Washington would publicly welcome a freeze with South Korea at the table (A1) but regard it as a demand that would slow the deal. The most capable U.S. response would be to prepare negotiations solely through the U.S.-North Korean channel and simply inform Seoul of the results. It would welcome a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as leverage against China while keeping any decision to move to actual weaponization subject to U.S. consent.
items.lever: Things that cannot be implemented without South Korea: the practical work and funding of sanctions relief, shipbuilding and defense-industrial cooperation, South Korea's share of conventional deterrence, and its ties to a Congress intent on preserving the U.S.-South Korean alliance.

F5: A win for the administration; Congress and the bureaucracy are uneasy
F2: Stable, but slower if South Korea leads
F3: Divided between those who welcome shifting burdens to allies and those who want to uphold nonproliferation

intent.read: In words, Washington upholds denuclearization and the alliance; the movement of money and troops points toward cutting costs on the Korean Peninsula and opening a deal with North Korea. The split between the administration and Congress is itself a signal. This is the basis for the judgment that the Trump administration prefers "a deal without South Korea" (F5).

watch.t: USFK provisions in the final NDAA
Scale of the spring 2027 joint exercises
Whether a Trump-Kim meeting takes place (f22)

items.means: Most of North Korea's trade, a veto on the UN Security Council, the 1961 Sino-North Korean Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, the border
items.frame: The Korean Peninsula is a buffer that keeps China from directly facing U.S. forces. North Korea's nuclear weapons are uncomfortable, but better than collapse.
goals: Stability of the North Korean regime and preservation of the buffer
Prevent the U.S.-South Korean alliance from turning into an anti-China alliance (deployment of U.S. Forces Korea to a Taiwan contingency, U.S.-Japan-South Korea solidarity)
Use the Korean question as a card in U.S.-China bargaining
items.strategy: Beijing began dropping "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" from its official statements in 2024 and, in its November 2025 arms control white paper, left it out of a policy document for the first time. It now speaks only of a "political settlement," effectively tolerating North Korea's nuclear weapons while regaining the influence over Pyongyang that it lost to Russia during the war in Ukraine. It uses economic ties to keep Seoul from leaning too far toward Washington.
tactics: In June, Xi Jinping visited Pyongyang, where Kim Jong Un pledged to make China-North Korea friendship its "most important top-priority strategic work"; denuclearization went unmentioned
China's Foreign Ministry did not confirm the shared denuclearization goal announced by the White House
China-North Korea trade rose 25 percent in 2025, returning to pre-pandemic levels
In September, Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were expelled from the Party and the military, tightening Xi's grip on the armed forces. Decisions are concentrating even further in Xi alone
red: Collapse of the North Korean regime and U.S. forces approaching the Yalu River
Absorption of the North under South Korean leadership
Nuclear armament by South Korea or Japan
Use of U.S. Forces Korea in Taiwan operations
items.ext: Taiwan is everything; the Korean Peninsula is an appendage to the Taiwan negotiations. Beijing sees U.S. retreat as an opportunity and the close North Korea-Russia relationship as something to guard against.
items.want: That Seoul make no further THAAD-style deployments, slow the pace of U.S.-Japan-South Korea military cooperation, and stay neutral on Taiwan
items.onrec: Beijing would welcome a freeze (A1) as consistent with stability on the peninsula, but it would prefer to handle it within a U.S.-China deal or a four-party framework of the United States, China, and the two Koreas rather than in a framework with South Korea seated as a party. On latent nuclear capability (A3b), it would ignore Seoul's signals and wait, then apply economic pressure the moment South Korea takes a step toward nuclear weapons.
items.lever: The pace of U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation, the choice not to deploy additional THAAD batteries, and how fast and how transparently to pursue latent nuclear capability. These are all things China cares about most.

F5: Acceptable if China can come in as a mediator, though it is wary of North Korea tilting toward the United States
F2: Stability without unification, lower risk of war
F3: More nuclear powers on its periphery
F4: Collapse and U.S. forces moving north

intent.read: Denuclearization survives only in words. In action, Beijing embraces North Korea and props it up economically. Its military personnel moves concentrate decision-making in one man, making a wobble in its North Korea policy unlikely. This is the basis for the judgment that "North Korea's nuclear weapons are uncomfortable, but better than collapse."

watch.t: Monthly China-North Korea trade statistics (Chinese customs) (f23)
Whether Kim Jong Un visits China
Military personnel changes ahead of the Party Congress

items.means: Nuclear weapons and missiles, the choice of whether to negotiate, the timing of provocations. Only North Korea can open the door to inter-Korean relations
items.frame: The regime's perpetuation is everything, and nuclear weapons are its insurance. South Korea is not a kindred nation but the most dangerous foreign country. South Korean information is more dangerous than South Korean weapons.
goals: Perpetuation of the regime
Recognition of its status as a nuclear weapons state
Sanctions relief and the economy (Russia and China, and the United States if possible)
items.strategy: Pyongyang seeks to entrench nuclear weapons as a premise rather than a subject of negotiation and to trade arms control and sanctions with the United States as one nuclear power to another. It excludes and cuts off South Korea (the two-state doctrine). It positions itself between China and Russia and makes use of both.
tactics: At the February Party Congress, it formalized its nuclear status and the two-state doctrine

Its position is that it will not negotiate with the United States as long as Washington demands denuclearization. On September 17, Kim Yo Jong called its nuclear status "absolute" but did not name the United States directly

On September 21, 2025, Kim Jong Un said Pyongyang could talk with the United States if Washington dropped its demand for denuclearization, but would not bargain anything away in exchange for sanctions relief
It supplies Russia with troops and artillery shells and receives technology in return (suspected help with nuclear-powered submarines)
It has tightened information control to the point of executing people for watching South Korean dramas
red: Negotiations premised on denuclearization
Large-scale people-to-people exchanges with South Korea (an influx of information)
Attempts at regime change
Making human rights a condition
items.ext: The lesson of Iran (countries without nuclear weapons get attacked and their leaders killed) has reinforced the lesson of Libya. Pyongyang sees U.S. retreat and U.S.-China rivalry as opportunities, and an end to the Russia-Ukraine war as a risk of losing a source of income.
items.want: That South Korea stay out of the talks. If it asks for anything, it would be a halt to joint exercises and to leaflets and broadcasts aimed at the North
items.onrec: Pyongyang would reject a phased freeze with South Korea at the table (A1) and insist on a direct deal with Washington. It would refuse the exchanges of special-relationship coexistence (A2) and counter the special-relationship framework with "two states." It would use a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as a pretext for its own nuclear buildup. North Korea's most capable response would be to ignore Seoul's proposals while signaling to Washington that leaving South Korea out would make for a faster deal.
items.lever: The substance of sanctions relief (without South Korean money and goods its economic effect is small), the scale of joint exercises, humanitarian aid, and information tools aimed at the North. Because North Korea fears South Korean information more than South Korean weapons, switching the information tools on and off is the card North Korea would pay the most for. What North Koreans lose when the tools are switched off is set out under "What it means for people."

F5: Gains recognition of its nuclear status and sanctions relief without South Korea
F2: Brings inter-Korean contact and an influx of information
F3: Its own nuclear weapons are justified, but South Korea's would be a threat

intent.read: Of all the countries, North Korea's words and deeds match most closely. It entrenches nuclear weapons as a premise rather than a subject of negotiation and cuts off contact with South Korea. The one opening is that Kim Yo Jong's statements have not named the United States directly, and that opening faces only toward Washington.

watch.t: How the report to the Party plenary meeting describes the United States and South Korea
Signs of preparation for a seventh nuclear test
Whether statements begin naming the United States directly

items.means: A veto on the UN Security Council, the 2024 mutual defense treaty, military technology, food and energy
items.frame: North Korea is the ally that helped Moscow fight its war, and a card for tying down the United States in Northeast Asia.
goals: Prosecuting the war in Ukraine (troops and artillery shells)
Counter the United States in Northeast Asia and deter South Korean and Japanese support for Ukraine
Keep North Korea as a counterweight to China even after the war
items.strategy: Moscow de facto accepts North Korea's nuclear weapons (Lavrov said the denuclearization issue was "closed") and binds Pyongyang with technology. It has not cut ties with South Korea completely, leaving a door open to revive economic relations after the war.
tactics: It transfers technology in return for North Korean troops and artillery shells
In 2024, it vetoed the extension of the Security Council's panel of experts on North Korea sanctions
The war in Ukraine continues after the collapse of a 32-hour truce in April
red: Collapse of the North Korean regime
South Korean lethal military aid to Ukraine
A U.S. military buildup in the Far East
items.ext: An end to the Russia-Ukraine war changes everything. North Korea will be less useful after the war, but Russia may keep using it to avoid depending on China.
items.want: That Seoul send no lethal weapons to Ukraine and revive economic cooperation (shipbuilding, energy) after the war
items.onrec: Moscow would be indifferent to, or at least not obstruct, a phased freeze (A1) and special-relationship coexistence (A2). It would use a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as propaganda claiming that the nonproliferation regime has collapsed and as a pretext for expanding technology transfers to North Korea.
items.lever: The level of support for Ukraine; the door to postwar economic cooperation

F5: If North Korea tilts toward the United States, Russia becomes less useful
F3: Japanese nuclear weapons would threaten Russia too

intent.read: Moscow de facto accepts North Korea's nuclear weapons and binds Pyongyang through the mutual defense treaty, its Security Council veto, and military technology. As long as the war continues after the collapse of the 32-hour truce in April, this direction will not change.

watch.t: A Russia-Ukraine ceasefire and the return of North Korean troops
Russian technology revealed in the launch of a North Korean nuclear-powered submarine
Signals of economic cooperation with South Korea after the war

items.means: The weight of the U.S.-Japan alliance, economic cooperation funds, latent nuclear capability (plutonium), U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation
items.frame: North Korean missiles are a direct threat, and the abduction issue is an unhealed wound. If Washington limits only ICBMs, Japan remains within range of medium- and short-range missiles.
goals: Keep U.S. extended deterrence in place (prevent the U.S. defense commitment from being decoupled from Japan)
Medium- and short-range missiles and the abduction issue
A deterrence posture that does not fall behind South Korea's
items.strategy: Tokyo is strengthening the U.S.-Japan alliance and building counterstrike capabilities. It keeps its non-nuclear principles while leaving room to revisit the principle of "not permitting the introduction" of nuclear weapons, one of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles.
tactics: In Hiroshima in August, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan currently maintains the Three Non-Nuclear Principles but dropped the pledge to uphold them going forward
She said that, in revising the three security documents by the end of the year, the government would not prejudge whether to keep the Three Non-Nuclear Principles
Japan is expanding its counterstrike capabilities and U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation
red: An agreement in which Washington limits only ICBMs and leaves medium- and short-range missiles untouched
Japan-North Korea normalization that leaves out the abduction issue
South Korea alone acquiring latent nuclear capability
items.ext: A Taiwan crisis is a crisis for Japan (Okinawa). U.S. retreat opens the door to a debate on Japan's own nuclear weapons.
items.want: That Seoul maintain U.S.-Japan-South Korea cooperation and coordinate with Japan before pursuing latent nuclear capability
items.onrec: Tokyo would support a phased freeze (A1) if medium- and short-range missiles are included in what is frozen. If South Korea opens the door to a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b), Japan would use it as a pretext to "normalize" its own reprocessing.
items.lever: Prior coordination on latent nuclear capability (a joint Japanese-South Korean norm); a joint demand that medium- and short-range missiles be included in any agreement with North Korea

F1: The threat remains, but it is familiar
F5: If only ICBMs are limited, Japan is left with the threat from medium- and short-range missiles
F3: Some welcome it; most fear it

intent.read: In words, Tokyo keeps its non-nuclear principles, but the language has weakened, and it is accelerating moves to acquire counterstrike capabilities and raise defense spending. It is leaning toward "keeping the door open" rather than toward nuclear armament. This is the basis for the judgment that Japan could move first in nuclear dominoes (F3).

watch.t: Wording on the non-nuclear principles in the revised three security documents (f19)
Changes in reprocessing and plutonium policy
How much of the U.S.-Japan extended deterrence consultations is made public

reads.t: "Armed stalemate" (F1) is the only future that none of the deciding powers rejects.
reads.d: That is why it is the most likely. Everyone is somewhat dissatisfied, but no one is willing to pay the cost of breaking it.

reads.t: Of the three powers with the greatest say (the United States, China, and North Korea), two (the Trump administration and North Korea) prefer "a U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea" (F5), and China can accept it.
reads.d: For South Korea, exclusion is a risk as real as war. This future was hidden because, among the four futures first sketched, it had been folded into armed stalemate (F1).

reads.t: North Korea holds the key to managed coexistence (F2). And what North Korea rejects is not a freeze but contact.
reads.d: North Korea fears South Korean information more than South Korean weapons. That is why a freeze (A1) comes before exchanges (A2). Because North Korea rejects exchanges, only the legal framework should be prepared; exchanges that benefit people directly, such as family reunions or the repatriation of detainees, should be opened separately as deals with something given in return (A7). For the same reason, the information tools (A6) become the most expensive card South Korea holds.

reads.t: Nuclear dominoes (F3) is no one's preference. It comes from fear.
reads.d: It is a future that the countries' preferences alone do not capture. External variables such as a U.S. retreat open this path. It also marks a limit of this method, which gauges futures by preferences.

reads.t: South Korea's leverage lies in "the things that cannot be implemented without South Korea."
reads.d: The practical work and funding of sanctions relief, the scale of joint exercises, a joint Japanese-South Korean norm on latent nuclear capability, and information tools aimed at the North. South Korea should make these conditional on its participation in a U.S.-North Korean deal, showing both Washington and Pyongyang that a deal without South Korea will not work. This is the tactic for turning a deal without South Korea (F5) into managed coexistence (F2).

syn.note: Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, and Rejected are provisional judgments of how readily each country's leadership would accept that future through 2030. A country's weight as a deciding power is rated by how hard it would be for a future to come about if that country opposed it.

intent.note: Each country's intentions are checked first against costly actions rather than words. For each country, dated signals are sorted into words and deeds, and a judgment is made on whether the two match.
intent.read: North Korea and Russia are the countries whose words and deeds match most closely. In the United States and Japan, actions are running ahead of words, toward retreat and toward preparation, respectively. China's words and deeds point in opposite directions: it talks of denuclearization while embracing North Korea. A recheck against these intent indicators found no signal yet that would change the judgments in the table of preferred futures. If the signals change, both the preference judgments and the probabilities of the futures will be revised.

items.t: A substantive U.S. retreat
items.def: An actual reduction of U.S. Forces Korea, or a formal weakening of the extended deterrence commitment
items.flips: C2 (the risk of exclusion grows), C5 (an independent nuclear arsenal ranks last)
items.why: If the United States pulls back from the Korean Peninsula, a U.S.-North Korean deal can more easily bypass Seoul (F5↑), and doubts about extended deterrence open the door to nuclear debates in South Korea and Japan (F3↑). While North Korea holds off on ICBM flight tests, the threat to the U.S. homeland fades as an issue in American politics, lowering the domestic cost of a decision to reduce troops.
items.sign: The USFK provision is dropped from the final NDAA, or a troop reduction is announced

items.t: A U.S.-China grand bargain
items.def: The Korean Peninsula becomes an item in a U.S.-China deal that also covers Taiwan · an extreme form of world scenario A
items.why: The risk of war falls (F4↓), but the signal that allies' interests can be traded away heightens anxiety in South Korea and Japan (F3↑), and the Korean question is handled over South Korea's head (F5↑).
items.sign: A joint U.S.-China document includes language "opposing" Taiwan independence or wording on U.S. Forces Korea

items.t: A cross-strait crisis
items.def: A blockade or quarantine of Taiwan, or armed conflict · the same event as world scenario D
items.why: U.S. Forces Korea is drawn off to Taiwan, and North Korea gains an incentive to open a "second front" on the Korean Peninsula. Pyeongtaek and Osan become targets whether South Korea wants it or not (F4↑, F3↑).
items.sign: Exercises around Taiwan shift to maritime inspections or drills to cut off energy shipments

items.t: An end to the Russia-Ukraine war and shrinking North Korea-Russia trade
items.def: North Korea's exports of troops and artillery shells stop after the war ends or after a long ceasefire
items.flips: C3 (the favorable case in which freeze negotiations open), C2 (the risk of a deal without South Korea also grows)
items.why: With its income from Russia cut off, a cash-strapped North Korea could turn toward negotiations. It is almost the only external variable that could move things in a favorable direction. But because its negotiating partner would likely be the United States alone, the probability of a deal without South Korea (F5) rises as well.
items.sign: A Russia-Ukraine ceasefire holds for more than a month, and the return of North Korean troops is reported

items.t: Cracks in North Korea's internal control
items.def: Cracks such as mass defections, market unrest, or elite defections become visible from outside
items.flips: The shape of an upheaval (peaceful transition or bloodshed)
items.why: The influx of information is less a trigger than a slow variable that determines the shape of an upheaval when it comes. East Germans watched West German television for decades, but the system fell only after the Soviet Union withdrew its backing.
items.sign: Defector arrivals in South Korea exceed 1,000 a year, or reports of executions and purges in border areas surge

items.t: Instability in China's leadership
items.def: Xi Jinping's incapacitation or a power struggle becomes visible
items.why: The ongoing military purge (the expulsion of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli) signals consolidation rather than instability. Because China's policy of keeping North Korea as a buffer rests on interests that do not change with the leader, a change in China's leadership would have only a weak effect on the Korean Peninsula. The risk lies in the succession of the 2030s.
items.sign: No succession lineup emerges at the 2027 Party Congress, or an unusual vacuum appears at the top of the leadership

items.t: Shrinking human judgment and delegated authority
items.def: Official documents confirm that the U.S.-South Korean combined command-and-control system has cut human approval steps between AI target identification and strike authorization or has predelegated strike authority, or North Korea states explicitly that it has applied AI or automation to the Nuclear Trigger or its nuclear counterattack command system (by the end of 2030). The public unveiling of AI weapons (North Korea's February 2026 reference to AI in the KN-25 and May reports of an "AI-guided" cruise missile, and the U.S.-South Korean adoption of AI decision support) is treated as a baseline that has already occurred. The AI mentioned in connection with the KN-25 may refer to the production process rather than guidance.
items.why: What destabilizes a crisis is not the announcement of a technology but the shrinking of the human judgment that screens out false alarms and the widening of predelegation (the 1983 Petrov false alarm). Right after Iran's supreme leader was killed, North Korea wrote the delegation of nuclear-use authority into its constitution (no causal link has been established). If these changes overlap on both sides, the likelihood of sudden upheaval (F4), including accidental clashes, rises, and the trust-building that managed coexistence (F2) requires becomes harder. Nuclear dominoes (F3) does not move, because it is a matter of alliance credibility, not AI.
items.sign: North Korean media explicitly mention AI or automation in the Nuclear Trigger system; the United States and South Korea announce changes to strike-authorization procedures

reads: With the exception of an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and shrinking North Korea-Russia trade (X4), every variable moves probability away from managed coexistence (F2) toward a deal without South Korea (F5), nuclear dominoes (F3), and sudden upheaval (F4). The more the outside world is shaken, the greater the chance of extremely bad outcomes.

The value of reversible insurance (a conditional latent nuclear capability, A3b) therefore rises. And if managed coexistence is the aim, Seoul must move quickly while the window is open. That window falls around China's 2027 Party Congress, the U.S. decision on U.S. Forces Korea, and the end of the Russia-Ukraine war.

Some external events have already happened. For North Korea, the fate of Iran, attacked because it had no nuclear weapons and stripped of its leader, has become a second lesson after Libya. Denuclearization is treated as having effectively disappeared from the negotiating agenda through 2030, and a freeze is set as the ceiling.

The AI variable (X7) is defined not by announcements but by changes in the structure of authority. Both the U.S.-South Korean side and North Korea have already unveiled AI weapons, but no clear rise in the probability of crisis has been detected since. Rather than creating new probabilities on the Korean Peninsula, AI raises the likelihood of accidental clashes to the extent that it shrinks the role of human judgment.
external.note: The likelihoods and conditional probabilities are provisional judgments. Because the variables overlap, they should not be added or multiplied. The table shows which way the futures tilt on the assumption that a given variable occurs.

client.name: The government of the Republic of Korea
client.note: The goals and their order are derived from the Constitution of the Republic of Korea and the government's official statements; the order is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. The preamble of the Constitution commits the nation "to ensure security, liberty and happiness for ourselves and our posterity forever," and Article 10 guarantees the right to pursue happiness. The well-being of the country's own citizens is thus already built into the South Korean government's goals.

goals.d: Deter war and protect citizens' lives
goals.src: Constitution, Article 5(2) (mission of the armed forces) and Article 66(2) (independence and territorial integrity of the state)

goals.t: A seat at the table and diplomatic autonomy
goals.d: Avoid being shut out of decisions on the Korean Peninsula; preserve the alliance and the country's foreign policy options
goals.src: Constitution, Article 66(2); address to the UN General Assembly, September 2026 (pledging to help resume U.S.-North Korean dialogue)

goals.d: Protect markets, supply chains, energy, and the country's credit standing
goals.src: Preamble of the Constitution ("security, liberty and happiness"); the state's basic duties of governance

goals.d: Preserve the legal basis for unification and the framework of inter-Korean relations
goals.src: Constitution, Articles 3 and 4 and Article 66(3)

goals.d: Protect citizens, including separated families, detainees and abductees, and North Korean defectors
goals.src: Constitution, Article 10 (right to pursue happiness and the state's duty to guarantee fundamental rights)

ranked.t: Build up conventional deterrence (A5) and secure a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) as insurance. In freeze negotiations, concentrate less on a seat at the opening stage than on securing a seat at the table for the implementation and peace-regime stages that follow a U.S.-North Korean agreement (A1). The cards to play early are not sanctions relief but tension-reducing steps, such as adjusting joint U.S.-South Korean exercises or restoring inter-Korean liaison channels; information tools aimed at the North (A6) serve as bargaining chips within this package.

A humanitarian exchange that offers something in return (A7) contributes substantially to protecting citizens (G5) at low cost, so it should be pursued in parallel whenever an opening appears. Because North Korea rejects special-relationship coexistence (A2), only its legal framework should be prepared for now.
Staying the course (A0) is the baseline for comparison. It incurs small losses on the two highest-priority goals: national security (G1) and a seat at the table and diplomatic autonomy (G2).
Nuclear sharing or the redeployment of tactical nuclear weapons adds to deterrence, but Washington is unlikely to accept it, and it would invite Chinese retaliation.

Maximum pressure (A4) ranks low even when judged by the South Korean government's own goals. China and Russia plug the gaps in sanctions, so its effect is small; it runs against the current of U.S. negotiations, leaving South Korea bypassed; and it closes the door to freeze negotiations.
An independent nuclear arsenal ranks last, because it would cost the alliance (G2) and the economy (G3) irreversibly. It should be reconsidered if U.S. extended deterrence actually collapses.

rank2.tension: Stronger deterrence (A5) and freeze negotiations (A1) are in tension with each other. North Korea can cite A5 as evidence of hostility and reject A1. This procedure does not settle how to align the pace of building deterrence with the timing of opening negotiations.
rank2.undecided: How to weigh the possibility of unification (G4) and the protection of citizens (G5) against security (G1) and diplomacy (G2) is for the South Korean government to decide. Here the goals are ordered G1 > G2 > G3 > G4 ≈ G5, following the order of the constitutional provisions and government statements.

human.note: This section reviews the rankings from the strategy evaluation from the standpoint of individual lives. It does not filter the rankings; it states where they change and by how much. The judgment belongs to readers and the South Korean government.

items.client: Switching off the information tools could be traded for restored communication lines or resumed dialogue.
items.clisa: In return for switching them off, accept only things that benefit people directly: reunions, confirmations of whether relatives are alive, and the repatriation of detainees.
items.cost: One bargaining chip can be put to fewer uses.
items.gain: The access to information that North Koreans lose is converted into gains for separated families and detainees. It remains true that the interests of different people are being traded.

items.client: A second-ranked option, pursued in parallel when an opening appears.
items.clisa: Raise it into the top-ranked package and open it at the same time as freeze negotiations (A1). The number of surviving separated-family members will fall to about 20,000 by 2030, and that loss is irreversible.
items.cost: The domestic political cost of giving North Korea something in return, and the burden of the sanctions-exemption procedure.
items.gain: The relationships dimension for separated families could rise from 0 to 50 (confirmation of whether relatives are alive, and letters). The benefit would go directly to the six detainees and to the families of abductees.

items.clisa: Keep the ranking as it is, but add food and health aid to North Korea through UN channels to the agenda of freeze negotiations (A1).
items.cost: Small. The negotiating agenda grows by one item.
items.gain: Partly eases the burden on the livelihoods of North Koreans squeezed by the arms race.
None. Viewed in terms of what it means for people, the ranking stays the same.

rows.name: Managed competition
rows.why: If Washington and Beijing manage tensions, the United States gains room to deal directly with North Korea. A deal without South Korea (F5) rises the most.

rows.name: Armed multipolarity
rows.why: If all the major powers arm, nuclear debates open in South Korea and Japan. Nuclear dominoes (F3) rises and managed coexistence (F2) falls.

rows.name: Protracted linked wars
rows.why: If the wars in Ukraine and Iran drag on, the North Korea-Russia alignment hardens. Armed stalemate (F1) becomes most entrenched.

rows.name: Taiwan Strait crisis
rows.why: A crisis in the Taiwan Strait opens a second front on the Korean Peninsula. It is the same picture as the cross-strait crisis (X3) among the external variables.

rows.name: Internal fracture in one pole
rows.why: If either China or Russia is shaken from within, North Korea, which leans on that pole, is shaken too. Sudden upheaval (F4) rises.

world.note: These are the probabilities of each future for the Korean Peninsula on the assumption that each of world scenarios A through E on the World Order tab occurs. The values are set so that, weighted by the probabilities of the world scenarios, they match the baseline probabilities under the current trend to within one percentage point (a total-probability check). They are judgment estimates by the analyst.

The order of the goals is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. Because official documents are heavy with propaganda, they have been corrected against actual behavior.

A direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out (moratorium on nuclear and ICBM tests ↔ de facto acceptance of nuclear status and scaled-back joint exercises and strategic assets)

A multilateral format does not raise the question of what inter-Korean relations are. Because it is not a bilateral inter-Korean channel, it does not clash with the two-state doctrine

Limited armed provocations to raise bargaining power
A seventh nuclear test

ranked.t: A direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out is the best move. The core of the exchange is de facto acceptance of its nuclear status and a scaling back of joint exercises and U.S. strategic assets; sanctions relief is a side item (the formula entrenched since Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020).

There is precedent for North Korea accepting multilateral formats only when they were co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. Sitting down with the South as a separate, hostile state would be considered only if the cost of exclusion grew.
If a deal with Washington is blocked, North Korea stays the course (N0).
Limited armed provocations (N4) are a way to shake up the game when negotiations stall.
Costly, because it would mean losing China.
Inter-Korean exchanges rank last: they would let in information, the greatest threat to the regime.

counter.read: North Korea's response estimated in Step 5 (dealing with Washington alone and leaving South Korea out) is also supported by precedent. What has been revised is the content of the exchange and the conditions for multilateral participation. Since the collapse of the Hanoi summit, North Korea has put withdrawal of hostile policy and recognition of its nuclear status ahead of sanctions relief, and whether it sits down in a multilateral format depends not only on the agenda but on who convenes it and how the South's status is defined. Part of the price North Korea wants (joint exercises) falls in an area where South Korea has a say, but the decision rests mainly with Washington.

The order of the goals is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. Because official documents are heavy with propaganda, they have been corrected against actual behavior.

goals.t: Peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula
goals.d: Prevent war and collapse
goals.src: China's principles on the Korean Peninsula (peace and stability, dialogue); the China-North Korea summit of June 2026 (no mention of denuclearization)

Leading a four-country freeze framework of the United States, China, and the two Koreas
