ranked.t: The best move is to lead a four-country freeze framework while propping up North Korea, because Washington and Pyongyang bypassing China (K2) is the outcome Beijing dislikes most.
If a four-party freeze framework does not materialize, China keeps propping up North Korea as it does now.
A direct U.S.-North Korean deal lowers tensions, but China is left out.
Open pressure on South Korea backfires by fostering U.S.-Japan-South Korea solidarity.
Pressure on North Korea ranks last because it shakes the buffer.

counter.read: China's best move overlaps with South Korea's at one point: both dislike a direct U.S.-North Korean deal "without South Korea" or "without China." But because precedent shows that China has not been a guarantor that brings North Korea to the table (the dual suspension China proposed in 2017 was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang in 2018, without China), it is more realistic to use a four-party framework not as a way to open negotiations but as a way to guarantee South Korea a seat at the table in the peace-regime stage after a U.S.-North Korean agreement.

pairs: South Korea
A5 + A1 + A3b (as a party to freeze negotiations)
North Korea
N1 direct U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea → fallback N2 multilateral freeze
China
K1 four-country freeze framework + propping up North Korea
twoway.equilibrium: The current equilibrium lies between "a deal without South Korea" and "armed stalemate." North Korea's best move (N1, a direct U.S.-North Korean deal without South Korea) and the Trump administration's preferences point to the same place. That is why a deal without South Korea (F5) is put at 22 percent.
twoway.zopa: There is a narrow space where the interests of the three countries overlap. South Korea wants to avoid being shut out, and China does not want Washington and Pyongyang to bypass it. But since February 2026, North Korea has said it will not deal with the South regardless of the agenda, and the only multilateral formats in which it has sat with South Korea in the past were ones co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. The realistic area of overlap is therefore a four-party framework for the implementation and peace-regime stages after a U.S.-North Korean agreement. The price for South Korea is consent to adjusting joint exercises, the practical work and funding of sanctions relief, and the restraint China will demand on Taiwan and THAAD.
traps: Nuclear dominoes (F3) is no one's preference, but it is a security dilemma that builds up from each party's rational moves. North Korea's nuclear buildup (N0), South Korea's latent capability (A3b), and Japan's preparations justify one another. Designing the latent capability to be conditional, pursued within a joint U.S.-South Korean framework, and transparent is the mechanism for breaking this cycle.

The harder South Korea tries to insert itself alone into the U.S.-North Korean channel, the more firmly North Korea shuts it out. This is the paradox: Seoul's unilateral efforts invite its own exclusion.

ai.t: AI compresses decision time, and North Korea answers by delegating authority
ai.stake: AI-enabled surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting threaten the survivability of North Korea's leadership and its mobile launchers. Historically, the weaker side has responded not with preemptive strikes but with automatic retaliation, delegated authority, and dispersal (the Soviet Perimeter system of the 1980s). Article 3 of North Korea's 2022 law on its nuclear forces policy provides that if the command-and-control system over its nuclear forces is endangered by an attack from hostile forces, a nuclear strike will be launched automatically and immediately in accordance with a predetermined operational plan. "Automatically" here means predelegation, not technical automation. Article 89 of the revised constitution, adopted by the Supreme People's Assembly in March 2026 and made public in May, provides that the chairman of the State Affairs Commission may delegate the authority to use nuclear weapons. It was adopted shortly after Iran's supreme leader was killed (February 28), but no causal link between the two events has been established.
ai.moves: What raises the risk is less AI itself than the shrinking of the human judgment that screens out false alarms and misjudgments (the Petrov false alarm and Able Archer 83, both in 1983). AI's effect therefore concentrates on raising the likelihood of sudden upheaval (F4), including accidental clashes, and on making it harder to build the trust that managed coexistence (F2) requires. Because there are also many precedents in which better reconnaissance increased transparency and stabilized crises (Cold War reconnaissance satellites and arms control verification), the introduction of AI is not in itself treated as destabilizing. The driver of nuclear dominoes (F3) is the credibility of alliances, not AI, so the AI variable does not raise its probability (external variable X7).
ai.lever: In the second quarter of 2026, South Korea accounted for about 83 percent of the world's supply of high-bandwidth memory (HBM): SK Hynix 50 percent, Samsung 33 percent. Yet when allies have used chokepoints in supply chains as instruments of coercion, it has backfired. Japan's 2019 export controls against South Korea spurred South Korean localization and alternative sourcing. Even the Netherlands (ASML) and Taiwan (TSMC), which hold chokepoints of their own, managed only to improve their terms with Washington in exchange for investment pledges. South Korea, too, did not wield HBM as leverage in negotiations over U.S. export-control exemptions (validated end-user status) and chip tariffs; HBM's defensive value worked indirectly, through the interests of American AI companies. HBM is a passive defense that raises the cost of U.S. coercion, and an asset whose value may erode as Washington presses for local production and Micron expands capacity in the United States. Because South Korea's AI base depends on American equipment and design tools and on what is in effect a single buyer (Nvidia), its leverage and its dependence sit in the same place.
signs: Changes in North Korea's delegation of nuclear-use authority and in the scope of automatic launch
The frequency of drills and the launch threshold of the Nuclear Trigger (the state's comprehensive nuclear weapons management system)
Changes in the strike-authorization procedures of the U.S.-South Korean Kill Chain
Changes in U.S. semiconductor tariffs and in HBM export controls on China

brief.q: Amid North Korea's nuclear program and great-power deal-making, what should South Korea do?
brief.a: Seoul should strengthen conventional deterrence and, as insurance, build a latent nuclear capability — enrichment and reprocessing within the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty — while tying its pace to whether North Korea freezes its program. In any negotiation over a freeze, Seoul should secure a seat at the table for the implementation and peace-regime stages that would follow a U.S.-North Korean agreement. The cards it plays early should be steps that lower tensions, such as adjusting joint U.S.-South Korean exercises or restoring inter-Korean liaison channels.
brief.eq: North Korea's best move and the Trump administration's preferences both point toward a direct deal between Washington and Pyongyang that leaves Seoul out. What Pyongyang wants most in return is de facto acceptance of its nuclear status and a scaling back of joint U.S.-South Korean exercises — and since February 2026, it has said it will not deal with the South.
brief.human: For South Koreans, the risk is concentrated in an all-out war on the Korean Peninsula, which has a 2 percent probability. If such a war broke out, their personal safety score would fall from 94.4 to 10.0. Surviving members of separated families currently have no way at all to contact their relatives, and their situation improves only if managed coexistence is achieved.

items.name: 1991: the Basic Agreement, simultaneous UN membership, and the Joint Declaration on Denuclearization
items.format: Bilateral inter-Korean talks (high-level talks). The agenda was mutual recognition of each other's systems, nonaggression, and exchanges, with the Joint Declaration on the Denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula (December 31, 1991) running in parallel. The sequence: North Korea announced its intention to join the United Nations (May 28, 1991), the two Koreas joined simultaneously (September 17, 1991), and the Basic Agreement was signed (December 13, 1991) and took effect (February 19, 1992).
items.outcome: It took effect, but its implementing bodies, such as the Joint Military Commission, were soon neutralized, and it became a dead letter with the 1993 dispute over nuclear inspections and North Korea's announced withdrawal from the NPT.
items.why: North Korea accepted simultaneous membership because, with Chinese and Soviet veto cover gone, it wanted to avoid being treated unfavorably at the United Nations. The Basic Agreement itself had no nuclear provisions, so the inter-Korean framework could not cope with the inspection issue.
items.differs: North Korea then negotiated with Seoul on the premise of a special relationship within one nation; today its constitution defines the South as a hostile state and excludes it from the category of compatriots.

items.name: 1994: the Geneva U.S.-North Korean Agreed Framework
items.format: Bilateral U.S.-North Korean talks (Geneva): a freeze of graphite-moderated reactors in exchange for two light-water reactors and heavy fuel oil. South Korea was not a party to the negotiations, but through KEDO it paid 70 percent ($3.2 billion) of the reactor costs ($4.6 billion); Japan paid $1 billion, and the United States had no designated share.
items.outcome: After the June 1994 crisis in which Washington considered striking Yongbyon, Jimmy Carter's visit to Pyongyang (June 15) produced agreement on a freeze, and the framework was signed on October 21. The plutonium facilities stayed frozen for about eight years, but the framework collapsed with the October 2002 allegations of uranium enrichment, the lifting of the freeze and expulsion of inspectors in December 2002, and North Korea's announced withdrawal from the NPT on January 10, 2003.
items.why: The freeze was limited to the verifiable Yongbyon facilities, leaving enrichment as a detour, and construction of the light-water reactors fell far behind schedule. During the crisis, President Kim Young-sam's opposition to the use of force effectively constrained a unilateral U.S. strike.
items.differs: North Korea then had not yet acquired nuclear weapons, so the freeze targeted "future capability"; today it has written its nuclear status into its constitution and declared it irreversible.

items.name: The Four-Party Talks (the two Koreas, the United States, and China; Geneva)
items.format: Jointly proposed at the U.S.-South Korean summit on Jeju in April 1996. Six plenary sessions were held, from the first in Geneva on December 9, 1997, to the sixth on August 5–9, 1999, with two subcommittees, on tension reduction and on a peace regime. The chair rotated, determined by lot.
items.outcome: The talks lapsed without an agreed document. Substantive negotiations moved to bilateral U.S.-North Korean talks, which produced a moratorium on long-range missile tests at the Berlin talks in September 1999.
items.why: North Korea delayed acceptance for more than a year and, once at the table, insisted on putting the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea on the agenda, which Seoul and Washington refused. The Taepodong launch of August 31, 1998, shifted the focus to missiles.
items.differs: The United States was then a co-proposer; the current four-party idea is a South Korean government initiative, and even South Korea's own foreign ministry has distanced itself from it, calling it an idealistic plan that had not been agreed on.

items.name: The Six-Party Talks (the September 19 Joint Statement and the February 13 agreement)
items.format: The two Koreas, the United States, China, Japan, and Russia, hosted by China (Beijing). Launched after a U.S.-China-North Korea three-way meeting in April 2003. The Joint Statement of September 19, 2005, set out nuclear abandonment in exchange for energy aid and normalization of relations, along with a separate forum on a peace regime among "the directly related parties"; the agreement of February 13, 2007, laid down an action-for-action sequence: closure of Yongbyon within 60 days in exchange for 50,000 tons of heavy fuel oil, then disablement and declaration in exchange for the equivalent of 950,000 tons.
items.outcome: The process went as far as the disablement of Yongbyon, the submission of a declaration on June 26, 2008, and removal from the list of state sponsors of terrorism on October 11, 2008, but the verification protocol collapsed in December 2008 when North Korea refused to put sampling in writing, and in April 2009 North Korea announced it was leaving the talks. The peace-regime forum provided for in the September 19 statement was never convened.
items.why: The core issues were disagreement over the scope of verification (facilities beyond Yongbyon and sampling) and the dispute over sanctions on Banco Delta Asia (BDA). As the talks broke down, Washington warned it would halt heavy fuel oil shipments while China and Russia announced they would keep supplying aid, splitting the pressure front.
items.differs: It was a framework in which North Korea nominally accepted the goal of denuclearization; today North Korea rejects denuclearization as an agenda item altogether.

items.name: 2017: China's dual suspension proposal and THAAD retaliation
items.format: Proposed by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in March 2017: a halt to North Korean nuclear and missile activities in exchange for a halt to large-scale joint U.S.-South Korean exercises (dual suspension), with denuclearization and a peace treaty pursued in parallel. In the same period, China imposed informal economic retaliation over the THAAD deployment.
items.outcome: Washington did not accept it, and on October 30, 2017, North Korea rejected it in a statement by the Committee for the Peaceful Reunification of the Fatherland and other organizations, calling dual suspension "irresponsible behavior." Yet in 2018 essentially the same exchange was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang, without China, through North Korea's testing moratorium and Trump's suspension of exercises.
items.why: North Korea saw China's mediation proposal as a framework that would constrain its nuclear status, and Washington refused to make alliance exercises an object of exchange.
items.differs: Since 2024 China has been dropping denuclearization from its official statements (Xi Jinping in September 2025, the U.S.-China outcome document in September 2026), and its November 2025 arms control white paper left it out as well. Its position on North Korea's nuclear status is closer to Pyongyang's than it was in 2017.

items.name: 2018: the Panmunjom Declaration and the September 19 military agreement
items.format: Bilateral inter-Korean summits. Article 3, Paragraph 3 of the Panmunjom Declaration committed the two Koreas to pursue "trilateral meetings involving the two Koreas and the United States, or quadrilateral meetings involving the two Koreas, the United States and China" toward declaring an end to the war and concluding a peace treaty. The September 19 Pyongyang military agreement contained conventional tension-reduction measures such as buffer zones in and around the DMZ.
items.outcome: The three- or four-party talks were never convened, even though both Korean leaders had signed the declaration. North Korea scrapped the military agreement on November 23, 2023, South Korea suspended it in full on June 4, 2024, and the Lee Jae-myung government announced in August 2025 that it would restore it.
items.why: Implementation of the inter-Korean agreements became subordinate to the U.S.-North Korean nuclear talks, and after the collapse at Hanoi, North Korea openly dismissed the South's role as "mediator."
items.differs: In 2018, North Korea used the South as a channel for dialogue; today it excludes the South as a partner in dialogue.

items.name: 2018: the Singapore U.S.-North Korean summit
items.format: A bilateral U.S.-North Korean summit. It declared four principles — new relations, a peace regime, efforts toward complete denuclearization, and the repatriation of remains — without defining a sequence for implementation.
items.outcome: It produced only an agreement in principle. At a press conference, Trump announced a halt to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises, and the South Korean government was reported to have been caught by surprise.
items.why: The top-down, leader-to-leader approach left the definition and sequencing of denuclearization to working-level talks, and alliance exercises were used as a bargaining chip without adequate coordination with South Korea.
items.differs: Trump's second administration is repeating the pattern, ordering exercises scaled back in August 2026, but North Korea now rejects any agreement that includes language on denuclearization.

items.name: 2019: the collapse of the Hanoi summit and Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020
items.format: A bilateral U.S.-North Korean summit. North Korea offered the permanent dismantlement of the nuclear-material production facilities at Yongbyon and a written pledge to halt nuclear and long-range missile tests, and demanded the lifting of five of the 11 UN sanctions resolutions. Washington presented a one-page document proposing comprehensive dismantlement, including facilities beyond Yongbyon, warheads, and missiles, in exchange for sanctions relief.
items.outcome: The summit collapsed without agreement. On July 10, 2020, Kim Yo Jong called the idea of reviving the bargain of "the partial lifting of sanctions versus the permanent dismantlement" of Yongbyon a "pipedream" and said the formula of negotiations should change to "withdrawal of hostility versus resumption of DPRK-U.S. negotiations."
items.why: The "partial" relief North Korea sought was economically the core of the sanctions, while Yongbyon was only part of its overall capability, so the values the two sides placed on the deal were far apart. North Korea had no alternative ready for Washington's demand for a comprehensive deal.
items.differs: On September 22, 2026, South Korea's president publicly proposed a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief, but North Korea has already discarded the very formula of trading concessions for sanctions relief.

items.name: 2019: U.S.-North Korean working-level talks in Stockholm
items.format: Bilateral U.S.-North Korean working-level talks (North Korea's delegation led by Ambassador Kim Myong Gil). Washington said it had brought "creative ideas"; North Korea demanded the complete and irreversible withdrawal of hostile policy as a precondition and set a year-end deadline.
items.outcome: The talks broke down the same day. North Korea called them "sickening negotiations," and Pyongyang rejected a proposal to resume two weeks later.
items.why: North Korea preferred leader-level bargaining to working-level negotiations, and it parted ways with Washington over the sequence, insisting that the hostile policy be withdrawn first.
items.differs: The working-level channel has not been restored since, and contact today is limited to letters and remarks between leaders.

items.name: The hostile two-state line and the 2026 four-party and freeze proposals
items.format: North Korea: the declaration of "two belligerent states" at the December 2023 plenary meeting; the designation of the South as a hostile state in the constitution in 2024; at the Ninth Party Congress in February 2026, the statement that the DPRK has "nothing to discuss with the ROK," along with conditions for Washington (respect for its nuclear status and withdrawal of hostile policy); and the removal of the goal of unification from the constitution in March 2026. South Korea: Minister Chung Dong-young's proposal at the Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on June 4, 2026, for four-party talks among the two Koreas, the United States, and China (to be widened later to include Mongolia, Japan, and Russia); the June 26, 2026, plan for three stages — freeze, reduction, denuclearization — preceded by U.S.-North Korean dialogue; and the president's proposal at the United Nations on September 22, 2026, of a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief.
items.outcome: In August 2026, the foreign minister called the four-party idea an idealistic notion not agreed on within the National Security Council. In August 2026, Trump ordered exercises scaled back and claimed that Kim Jong Un had responded positively, but on September 24, 2026, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea's nuclear status is irreversible and said sanctions and military pressure are incompatible with dialogue. Denuclearization was left out of the outcome document of the U.S.-China summit of September 24, 2026.
items.why: North Korea demands recognition of its nuclear status and the withdrawal of hostile policy from the United States alone, and excludes the South regardless of the agenda.
items.differs: This is the current phase itself. In November 2025, Washington formalized its support for South Korean enrichment, reprocessing, and nuclear-powered submarines, lowering the cost to the U.S.-South Korean alliance of pursuing latent nuclear capability; North Korea denounced it as an endorsement of South Korea as a "quasi-nuclear weapons state."

items.name: 2015: the August 25 inter-Korean high-level agreement (the loudspeaker exchange)
items.format: Inter-Korean high-level contact (Panmunjom). The sequence was an expression of regret by the North over the mine provocation, followed by the South's halting loudspeaker broadcasts "unless an abnormal case occurs."
items.outcome: North Korea lifted its quasi-state of war, returned its submarines to port, and agreed to resume family reunions.
items.why: The loudspeakers exposed North Koreans to information the regime could not control, so the cost to the North was high, and leaving a condition for resumption in place preserved their exchange value.
items.differs: A high-level inter-Korean channel was working then; today North Korea has closed its channels for dealing with the South altogether.

checks.reason: Given that every negotiating track over more than 30 years has collapsed within one to eight years, the judgment that an "armed stalemate" will continue is supported by the historical frequency (base rate). But 1994–2002 was a period in which a U.S.-North Korean agreement and an armed stalemate held at the same time, so the two scenarios are not mutually exclusive. And in the precedents of "a U.S.-North Korean agreement without South Korea" (1994, 2018), South Korea was left out only at the table; it still shouldered costs (70 percent of KEDO's light-water reactor costs) and adjustments to exercises.

Exclusion is a recurring fact (Geneva in 1994, the 2018 announcement halting exercises, the August 2026 order to scale them back). But as the June 1994 consideration of striking Yongbyon shows, the risk of war concentrates in the crisis phase just before negotiations collapse, and at that point South Korea's opposition to the use of force worked as a de facto veto. The real loss from exclusion was not losing a seat at the negotiating table but bearing costs without a voice.

The four-party framework operated once, in 1997–99, but North Korea insisted on the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea, and the substantive result came bilaterally between Washington and Pyongyang (Berlin, 1999); the three- or four-party peace talks agreed in writing in 2005, 2007, and 2018 were never convened. At Hanoi, even a concession bigger than a freeze (the dismantlement of Yongbyon) failed to win partial sanctions relief, and North Korea discarded that formula in 2020. On the other hand, in the August 25, 2015, agreement, loudspeaker broadcasts worked as an actual bargaining chip, and U.S. support for enrichment and reprocessing in November 2025 lowered the cost to the U.S.-South Korean alliance of pursuing latent nuclear capability.

At Hanoi, North Korea offered the dismantlement of Yongbyon — a bigger concession than a freeze — and a written pledge to halt tests, yet failed to win the lifting of five sanctions resolutions. Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020 dismissed reviving the bargain of partial sanctions relief for the dismantlement of Yongbyon as a "pipedream" and changed the formula to "withdrawal of hostility versus resumption of DPRK-U.S. negotiations," and the February 2026 Party Congress and Choe Son Hui's statement of September 24, 2026, make recognition of nuclear status and withdrawal of hostile policy preconditions. Sanctions relief is not the best outcome North Korea itself has put forward.

North Korea sat with South Korea in the Four-Party Talks of 1997–99 and the Six-Party Talks of 2003–08, but in both cases the format was co-proposed by the United States or hosted by China. Since February 2026, North Korea has said it will not deal with the South regardless of the agenda, and it refused even right after South Korea's president proposed a freeze in exchange for sanctions relief. Simultaneous UN membership in 1991 is a precedent in which North Korea, its great-power cover gone, accepted a "two states" framework to avoid exclusion.

A shared interest in avoiding exclusion is supported by Kim Jong Un's five meetings with Xi Jinping between March 2018 and June 2019 and by the Panmunjom Declaration's reference to "trilateral ... or quadrilateral" meetings. But in the Four-Party Talks China was only one of the rotating chairs; as the Six-Party Talks broke down (December 2008), it sided with the North by continuing to supply heavy fuel oil; and the 2017 dual suspension, after North Korea rejected it, was carried out bilaterally by Washington and Pyongyang without China. As for the price, China put a real cost on South Korea's security choices through informal economic retaliation over THAAD.

checks.claim: Forecast (at least one four-party consultation by the end of 2027: 15%)
checks.reason: Over the past 30 years, the four-party framework was convened only once, in 1997, and even then it took more than a year after the U.S.-South Korean joint proposal for North Korea to accept. The peace talks agreed in writing in 2005, 2007, and 2018 were never held, not even in 2018, when both Korean leaders had agreed. Today, North Korea's exclusion of the South, the foreign ministry's dismissal of the idea as idealistic, and Washington's silence all coincide; the upside factors are the president's UN proposal, the omission of denuclearization from the U.S.-China outcome document, and the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November.

precedents.insight: Since 2020, North Korea's demand has shifted from "sanctions relief" (a matter for the Security Council, where Washington and Beijing hold the keys) to "withdrawal of hostile policy" (joint exercises and strategic assets, matters for the U.S.-South Korean alliance). This means that part of the price North Korea wants lies within the scope of South Korea's consent; but the precedents of 2018 and August 2026, in which Trump raised halting or scaling back exercises first, out of step with Seoul's announcements, show that this power of consent does not translate directly into a seat at the table. South Korea's historical leverage has been not a seat at the table but a veto over the use of force (1994) and cost-sharing (70 percent of KEDO), and North Korea, too, accepted a "two states" framework in 1991 out of fear of exclusion.
uncertain: Whether North Korea's acceptance of the Four-Party Talks in 1997 was linked to food aid

The exact scope of the five sanctions resolutions North Korea sought to have lifted at Hanoi (North Korea claimed they were the 2016–17 provisions affecting civilian livelihoods) and the exact wording of the U.S. one-page document
Whether President Lee Jae-myung's September 2026 UN speech explicitly mentioned a four-party framework (the Kyunghyang Shinmun reported that it did; UPI's report does not mention it)

Whether the Chinese government formally endorsed Minister Chung Dong-young's four-party proposal (UPI reported only that Beijing supported a pragmatic approach), and whether the U.S. government has responded officially
The venue and full text of the outcome document of the September 24, 2026, U.S.-China summit, and whether Trump and Kim Jong Un will meet during the APEC meetings in Shenzhen in November
The actual scope of implementation of the restoration of the September 19 military agreement (announced in August 2025)
Whether Trump's August 2026 order to scale back exercises was coordinated with South Korea in advance

The date of North Korea's 1993 announcement of NPT withdrawal and the June 2020 demolition of the inter-Korean joint liaison office rely on general sources; the original documents were not checked in this review

links.work: Carl von Clausewitz, On War, Book 3, Chapter 16, "The Suspension of Action in War," 1832
links.idea: Military action can stop for long periods when both sides believe that waiting serves them better, or when defense is stronger than attack. Such a suspension is not peace but a tense equilibrium that can break at any moment.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that armed stalemate is the most likely future. For both Seoul and Washington and for Pyongyang, the cost of changing the status quo exceeds the cost of waiting, and the defensive advantages on the Korean Peninsula (artillery near Seoul, the U.S. reinforcement system) prolong the suspension.
links.limit: Clausewitz also saw suspension as a temporary phenomenon arising from imperfect information and fear. Unlike the conventional suspension he analyzed, a suspension under nuclear weapons tends to permit low-intensity provocations (see the stability-instability paradox below).
sources: Carl von Clausewitz, Vom Kriege, Book 3, Chapter 16 (1832); English translation by Michael Howard and Peter Paret, On War, Princeton University Press, 1976

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Balance of Power and the Balance of Terror", in Paul Seabury (ed.), The Balance of Power, 1965
links.idea: The more stable mutual deterrence is at the nuclear level, the more room there is for conventional and local provocations beneath it (the stability-instability paradox).
links.fit: It qualifies the label "armed stalemate." Stalemate is not calm: as with the sinking of the Cheonan and the shelling of Yeonpyeong Island in 2010, local clashes can become more frequent under nuclear deterrence. The 37 percent probability means only the absence of full-scale war; it says nothing about the frequency of low-intensity clashes.
links.limit: The empirical evidence for the paradox is mixed. The 1999 Kargil conflict is often cited as the classic case, but systematic evidence that provocations become more frequent once a state acquires nuclear weapons is sensitive to case selection.
sources: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Balance of Power and the Balance of Terror," in P. Seabury ed., The Balance of Power (San Francisco: Chandler, 1965), pp. 184-201

links.work: Virginia Page Fortna, 『Peace Time: Cease-Fire Agreements and the Durability of Peace』, 2004
links.idea: Analyzing ceasefires in interstate wars that ended between 1946 and 1994, Fortna showed that demilitarized zones, explicit outside guarantees, and joint commissions for handling disputes lengthen the duration of ceasefires. Arms control provisions had no clear effect.
links.fit: The Korean armistice regime has all of these — a demilitarized zone, the Military Armistice Commission, and a de facto outside guarantee in U.S. Forces Korea — which supports the judgment that the stalemate will last.
links.limit: Those elements are eroding. North Korea withdrew from the Military Armistice Commission in the 1990s, and the 2018 September 19 military agreement became effectively void in 2023–2024. With the institutional skeleton of the armistice weakened, past durations cannot simply be extended.

links.work: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 5, 17–31 (the Peace of Nicias, 421 BC)
links.idea: Sparta's allies — Corinth, Boeotia, Megara, and Elis — rejected the peace that Athens and Sparta concluded. Alienated by an agreement that did not reflect their interests, they sought new alliances, and the peace collapsed within a few years.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C2) that exclusion is a matter not of having a seat at the table but of whether South Korea's interests are reflected, and goes a step further: an agreement that leaves out the interests of an excluded party falters at the implementation stage.
links.limit: Corinth and the others had their own military forces and an alternative alliance (Argos). South Korea has no alliance alternative to the United States, so a threat to defect carries little credibility.
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 5.17-5.31; Robert B. Strassler ed., The Landmark Thucydides, Free Press, 1996

links.work: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok (The Book of Corrections, written from the late 1590s to around 1604), passages on the Ming-Japanese peace negotiations (1593–1596)
links.idea: During the Imjin War, Shen Weijing of Ming China and Konishi Yukinaga of Japan negotiated a peace while excluding Joseon. Toyotomi Hideyoshi demanded the cession of four of Joseon's eight provinces and a prince as hostage; after the intermediaries distorted each side's terms, the investiture negotiations collapsed in 1596, and the second invasion (Jeongyu War) followed in 1597.
links.fit: It is a precedent in which even Ming China, Joseon's suzerain and protector, bypassed the injured party to strike a deal, supporting the judgment that exclusion is a risk as serious as war. The territory and people of the excluded country became items on the bargaining table.
links.limit: Joseon was then on the verge of military collapse, and its relationship with Ming was one of tributary investiture, not a treaty alliance. Moreover, the harm of exclusion in this case appeared not as an unfavorable agreement but as the failure of the agreement and a second invasion.
sources: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, translated into modern Korean by Lee Jae-ho, Yeoksaui Achim, 2007

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics", World Politics 36(4), 1984
links.idea: Allies move between two risks, abandonment and entrapment; the closer an ally clings to the alliance to reduce the risk of abandonment, the greater the risk of entrapment and the weaker its bargaining power within the alliance.
links.fit: Exclusion is a form of abandonment. The theory adds a qualification: the earlier South Korea declares its support for Washington in order to win a seat at the table, the more Washington will treat Seoul's consent as already secured, and the less incentive it will have to reflect South Korea's interests when decisions are made.
links.limit: Snyder's model assumes relative symmetry between allies. In a highly asymmetric alliance such as that between Seoul and Washington, the weaker side's threats to defect struggle to gain credibility, and the model's equilibrium tilts to one side.
sources: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics," World Politics 36(4), 1984, pp. 461-495

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Chapter 2, "The Art of Commitment," 1966; The Strategy of Conflict, Chapter 8, 1960
links.idea: The credibility of extended deterrence comes from devices that bind the protector to its commitment so it cannot back out (such as tripwire forces) and from threats that leave something to chance — the risk that events slip out of control.
links.fit: The judgment ranking stronger conventional deterrence (A5) first is supported, in that South Korea's own capabilities fill the gap when North Korea's ICBM capability against the United States shakes the credibility of the U.S. commitment. At the same time, a tension emerges: adjusting joint exercises, proposed as an early card, loosens what Schelling calls the binding device, so this card and stronger conventional deterrence (A5) may erode each other's effects.
links.limit: Schelling's theory of commitment grew out of Cold War Europe (the garrison in West Berlin). The argument that tripwires lose their force when an adversary can strike the protector's homeland was the logic behind France's independent nuclear arsenal in the 1960s.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Yale UP, 1966, ch. 2
Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, Harvard UP, 1960, ch. 8

links.work: Stephen J. Stedman, "Spoiler Problems in Peace Processes", International Security 22(2), 1997; Barbara F. Walter, 『Committing to Peace』, 2002
links.idea: The greatest dangers in peace processes arise in the implementation stage after signing, when groups left out of the agreement become spoilers. Walter argued that credible outside guarantees are decisive for the implementation of negotiated settlements to civil wars.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that gives priority to a seat at the table in the implementation and peace-regime stages over the stage that opens negotiations. Implementation is where agreements actually succeed or fail, and at that stage South Korea carries weight both as a contributor to the costs and as a potential spoiler.
links.limit: Both studies draw mainly on cases of civil-war termination. They do not transfer neatly to interstate nuclear negotiations or to a peace regime for a divided nation, and if South Korea is seen as a spoiler, the cost to its alliance with the United States rises.
sources: Stephen J. Stedman, "Spoiler Problems in Peace Processes," International Security 22(2), 1997, pp. 5-53
Barbara F. Walter, Committing to Peace: The Successful Settlement of Civil Wars, Princeton UP, 2002

links.work: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, opening of Volume 1 (Sin Suk-ju's dying advice) and the passage on the 1590 envoys' reports
links.idea: On his deathbed, Sin Suk-ju urged King Seongjong not to lose peaceful relations with Japan (gyorin, "neighborly relations"). Yet when Hwang Yun-gil and Kim Seong-il went to Japan as envoys in 1590, they gave contradictory reports on the likelihood of a Japanese invasion, and the court, swayed by factional considerations, chose the optimistic view.
links.fit: It bears on the judgment that puts tension-reducing measures and the restoration of liaison channels among the early cards. Joseon's tradition of neighborly relations treated standing channels with a powerful neighbor as an instrument of security.
links.limit: The channel existed, yet it did not prevent the invasion of 1592. It is a counterexample showing that a channel by itself offers no protection when the interpretation of what it yields is captive to domestic politics.
sources: Ryu Seong-ryong, Jingbirok, Volume 1; "Jingbirok" entry, Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr

links.work: Sunzi, The Art of War, "Maneuvering" (Chapter 7)
links.idea: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free (圍師必闕); do not press a desperate foe too hard (窮寇勿迫). An enemy with no way out fights to the death.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C4) that maximum pressure (A4) ranks low even when judged by the South Korean government's goals. Pressure with no way out maximizes resistance and provocation, not submission.
links.limit: Sunzi's context is battlefield tactics. And if the "outlet" for North Korea becomes recognition of its nuclear status, it collides head-on with South Korea's goals, so the form any outlet takes has to be designed separately.
sources: 『孫子兵法』 軍爭篇; Samuel B. Griffith tr., Sun Tzu: The Art of War, Oxford UP, 1963, ch. VII

links.work: Nicholas L. Miller, 『Stopping the Bomb: The Sources and Effectiveness of US Nonproliferation Policy』, 2018
links.idea: U.S. sanctions actually imposed on nuclear programs already under way succeeded in only three of 22 cases (about 14 percent). Sanctions threats were most effective when the target depended on the United States for trade or security, and before a program began.
links.fit: North Korea, which has virtually no dependence on the United States and already possesses nuclear weapons, belongs to the type on which sanctions work least. This supports the judgment that the expected effect of maximum pressure is low.
links.limit: UN sanctions in 2016–2017 sharply cut North Korea's exports to China, so the economic blow itself was large. But it did not lead to a change in nuclear policy, and since 2023, North Korean-Russian military cooperation has weakened the sanctions net, further reducing the efficiency of pressure.
sources: Stephan Haggard & Marcus Noland, Hard Target: Sanctions, Inducements, and the Case of North Korea, Stanford UP, 2017

links.work: Nicholas L. Miller, Stopping the Bomb, 2018 (the South Korean and Taiwanese cases)
links.idea: In the 1970s, South Korea and Taiwan tried to develop nuclear weapons, but both gave up once the U.S. Congress wrote sanctions into law in the mid-1970s and the threat became credible. No country firmly aligned with the United States has launched a new nuclear weapons program since the late 1970s.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that ranks an independent nuclear arsenal last. Heavily dependent on the United States, South Korea is the type on which sanctions threats work best, and the Park Chung-hee government's program was halted along this path.
links.limit: The effect depends on the degree of dependence. If Washington lowers the value of dependence by reducing its troops or weakening its commitment, the weight of the sanctions threat falls with it.

links.work: Alexander Lanoszka, 『Atomic Assurance: The Alliance Politics of Nuclear Proliferation』, 2018
links.idea: The main trigger for allies to seek nuclear weapons is doubt about the protector's commitment, especially changes in posture such as troop reductions, and allies tend to stop when the protector restores its posture.
links.fit: It shows that the judgment ranking an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last holds only on the condition that U.S. Forces Korea and the extended deterrence commitment remain in place. Among the 2030 futures, the threshold for crossing into "nuclear dominoes" (F3, 19%) is likely to lie in changes to the U.S. posture rather than in South Korean public opinion.
links.limit: The cases center on Cold War West Germany, South Korea, and Japan. A situation in which North Korea can strike the U.S. homeland differs from the conditions of Cold War alliances.
sources: Alexander Lanoszka, Atomic Assurance: The Alliance Politics of Nuclear Proliferation, Cornell UP, 2018

links.work: Kenneth N. Waltz, "The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better", Adelphi Paper 171, 1981
links.idea: Because nuclear weapons raise the costs of war to extremes, they breed caution among their possessors, so gradual proliferation can bring stability.
links.fit: By Waltz's logic, mutual nuclear deterrence between the two Koreas might actually create stability, which contradicts the judgment that ranks an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last.
links.limit: Sagan countered, drawing on organization theory, with the risks of accidents and miscalculation by new nuclear states. Waltz's model also leaves out the costs South Korea would pay in the process of arming — NPT withdrawal, sanctions, and a rift in the alliance — and the risk of a preemptive strike during the development period.
sources: Kenneth N. Waltz, The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better, Adelphi Papers 171, IISS, 1981
Scott D. Sagan & Kenneth N. Waltz, The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: A Debate, W. W. Norton, 1995

links.work: Maximilian Horster, "The Trade in Political Prisoners between the Two German States, 1962-89", Journal of Contemporary History, 2004
links.idea: Between 1963 and 1989, West Germany bought the release of 33,755 East German political prisoners with goods and cash, at a price per prisoner that started at about 40,000 marks and rose over time, for a total of some 3.5 billion marks (with estimates as high as 8 billion marks); it also paid for exit permits for about 250,000 people.
links.fit: It supports the judgment to raise a humanitarian exchange with something given in return (A7) into the top-ranked package. It is a precedent in which exchanges that benefited people directly, between hostile halves of a divided nation, were kept separate from political relations and lasted for decades.
links.limit: Critics charged that East Germany turned the practice into a source of hard currency, creating an incentive to make arrests. It also differs from the Korean case in that intermediaries from the churches and institutional frameworks such as the 1972 Basic Treaty between the two German states supported the exchange. North Korea has tied even family reunions to political conditions, and they have been cut off since 2018.

links.work: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Section 1, Preliminary Article 6, 1795
links.idea: Even in wartime, hostile acts that would make mutual trust impossible in a future peace — employing assassins or poisoners, breaking terms of surrender, inciting treason in the enemy state — are not permitted.
links.fit: It qualifies the judgment that uses information tools as bargaining chips. By Kant's standard, means close to inciting the overthrow of the regime are something to refrain from voluntarily, before any exchange, and must be distinguished from channels through which people obtain outside information. C6, which would accept in return only things that benefit people directly, is in line with this distinction.
links.limit: Kant's article is based on trust between states; the human rights perspective of people's right to information lies outside its framework. And because North Korea defines the very influx of outside information as a hostile act, the distinction may not be accepted by the other side.
sources: Immanuel Kant, Zum ewigen Frieden (1795), First Section, Sixth Preliminary Article; Korean translation by Lee Han-gu, Yeongu pyeonghwaron, Seokwangsa

links.work: Kim Il Sung, "On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work," December 28, 1955; Supreme People's Assembly law "On the DPRK's Policy on the Nuclear Forces," September 8, 2022
links.idea: Juche proclaims independence in ideology, self-reliance in politics, and self-defense in national defense, and since the military-first (Songun) era has placed military power at the center of the state's existence. The 2022 law defined nuclear forces as a means of the state's existence and declared that there would be no denuclearization negotiations, and at the end of 2023 North Korea defined relations with the Republic of Korea as those between "two states hostile to each other."
links.fit: It supports the judgment that North Korea's best move is a direct deal with Washington that leaves South Korea out, with recognition of its nuclear status at the center of the exchange. In the discourse of independence, South Korea is not a negotiating partner in its own right, and nuclear weapons are presented as a status, not a bargaining item.
links.limit: Ideological texts and laws serve both external propaganda and domestic cohesion, and they have at times diverged from actual negotiating behavior. In 2018, three inter-Korean summits were held, and North Korea used South Korea as a channel to the United States.
sources: Kim Il Sung, Kim Il Sung jeojakjip (Collected Works), vol. 9, Workers' Party of Korea Publishing House, 1980 (speech of December 28, 1955)
https://www.ncnk.org (English translation of the September 8, 2022 law on the nuclear forces policy)

links.work: James D. Fearon, "Rationalist Explanations for War", International Organization 49(3), 1995
links.idea: When the other side has no incentive to keep its promises in the future (the commitment problem), even rational actors refuse a bargain. When one side makes concessions that are hard to reverse and the other makes concessions that are easy to reverse, a deal is hard to reach.
links.fit: It explains the judgment that North Korea puts recognition of its status and a scaling back of joint exercises and strategic assets ahead of sanctions relief. Sanctions relief is easily reversed; giving up nuclear weapons is hard to reverse (Libya's renunciation in 2003, followed by the regime's collapse in 2011, is the case North Korea cites again and again).
links.limit: The same logic qualifies the judgment. Scaled-back joint exercises can be reversed (they resumed after the 2018 suspension), and so can North Korea's moratorium on nuclear and ICBM tests. An exchange in which both sides' concessions are reversible amounts to managing a stalemate rather than resolving it, and it collapses just as easily.
sources: James D. Fearon, "Rationalist Explanations for War," International Organization 49(3), 1995, pp. 379-414

links.work: Zuo zhuan (The Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals), Duke Xi, Year 5 (655 BC): the remonstrance of Gong Zhiqi
links.idea: Gong Zhiqi, a minister of Yu (虞), warned that if Yu let Jin (晉) pass through its territory, its neighbor Guo (虢) would fall and Yu would fall with it, remonstrating that "the sideboards and the wheels of a cart depend on each other; when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold" (輔車相依 脣亡齒寒). Since entering the Korean War in 1950, China has described its relationship with North Korea through this metaphor.
links.fit: It supports the judgment that China's priority is the survival of the North Korean regime (the buffer) and that its role as a guarantor of denuclearization comes below that. A country intent on preserving a buffer is limited in how far it can pressure the buffer state to come to the table.
links.limit: "Lips and teeth" is also rhetoric. China established diplomatic relations with South Korea in 1992 over North Korea's objections and joined sanctions on North Korea in 2017. China's strategy on the peninsula also aims not only to preserve the buffer but to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington, so in a four-party framework at the peace-regime stage, China could use the seat it gains there as a channel for putting U.S. Forces Korea and the alliance on the agenda.
sources: 『春秋左氏傳』 僖公五年; James Legge tr., The Chinese Classics vol. V, The Ch'un Ts'ew with the Tso Chuen, 1872

links.work: Joint Statement of the Fourth Round of the Six-Party Talks (September 19, 2005), Item 4; the Four-Party Talks on peace on the Korean Peninsula (1997–1999)
links.idea: The September 19 Joint Statement provided that "the directly related parties will negotiate a permanent peace regime on the Korean Peninsula at an appropriate separate forum," separating denuclearization from a peace regime. Earlier, the Four-Party Talks of 1997–1999 among the two Koreas, the United States, and China had ended without results despite several plenary sessions.
links.fit: It supports the judgment (C8) that the real value of a four-party framework lies in guaranteeing South Korea a seat at the table in the peace-regime stage after a U.S.-North Korean agreement. There is already a precedent for separating peace-regime negotiations into a separate forum.
links.limit: The main reason the Four-Party Talks failed was North Korea's insistence on the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea and on a U.S.-North Korean peace treaty. As with the "three or four parties" wording of the October 4, 2007 declaration, the very range of participants can become a subject of negotiation, leaving room for South Korea or China to be left out.

theory.insight: The earlier judgment (C2) treats exclusion from negotiations as a risk for South Korea and proposes "securing" a seat at the table in the implementation stage as the remedy. Set side by side, classical and historical cases show that agreements that bypassed the local party with the most at stake were likely to be concluded but did not last. The Peace of Nicias (421 BC) collapsed because of alienated allies; the Ming-Japanese peace talks (1593–1596), conducted without Joseon amid the deceptions of intermediaries, broke down and led to a second invasion; and the Agreed Framework (1994) collapsed in 2002 under an arrangement in which South Korea paid the costs but had no part in the decisions. The F5 future (a deal without South Korea, 22%) therefore needs to be treated in terms of both the probability that it happens and the probability that it lasts, and an exclusionary deal is likely to have a path that leads back to F1 (armed stalemate). Moreover, the way an excluded South Korea actually gained weight was not by demanding a seat but through cost-sharing and the capacity to obstruct. In 1953, Syngman Rhee unilaterally released some 27,000 anti-communist prisoners of war, shaking the armistice, and Washington granted the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty as the price of his accepting it. South Korea's leverage lies in explicitly linking what it can provide or block at the implementation stage (cost-sharing, inter-Korean projects, enforcement of sanctions within South Korean jurisdiction, the conduct of joint exercises) to a seat at the table. But as Snyder's alliance dilemma shows, this capacity to obstruct wears down the relationship with Washington; in 1953, the United States even considered a plan to remove Rhee (Operation Everready). How far to push this linkage is the hidden variable in the top-ranked package.
uncertain: The exact number of ceasefires in Fortna's (2004) sample and the failure-rate figures could not be confirmed (the summary contains no figures).

The direction of the conclusions of Mehta and Whitlark, "The Benefits and Burdens of Nuclear Latency" (International Studies Quarterly 61(3), 2017) — whether latency provides deterrence or invites coercion — could not be confirmed from the original, so it was left out of the link to A3b.
The sample size in Walter (2002) and the figures for the effect of third-party guarantees could not be confirmed.
Estimates of the total West Germany paid for the release of East German political prisoners vary, from about 3.5 billion marks to as much as 8 billion marks.
Jingbirok is thought to have been completed around 1604, but the exact year could not be confirmed.
The official source for the formulation of China's Korean Peninsula priorities as "no war, no chaos, no nukes" (不战、不乱、无核) could not be confirmed, so it was left out of the links.
The number of captives repatriated by the monk Samyeong (Yujeong) in 1604–1605 (a Joseon precedent for humanitarian exchange) could not be confirmed, so it was left out of the links.

The level at which Operation Everready (1953) was considered, and the exact timing and conditions of the promise of the U.S.-South Korean Mutual Defense Treaty, were not checked against the original FRUS documents.

items.q: Do you agree that South Korea should also possess nuclear weapons?
items.read: Support for an independent nuclear arsenal has never fallen below a majority in 13 years. Other organizations' 2026 surveys point the same way: the Asan Institute for Policy Studies found 80.0 percent, the East Asia Institute 69.1 percent (on the premise that the North Korean nuclear threat persists), and the Seoul National University Institute for Peace and Unification Studies 61.1 percent.
items.caveat: Because question wording and methods differ by organization, producing results spread between 51 and 80 percent, the different surveys have not been joined into a single time series. Some surveys also find that support drops sharply when costs such as sanctions or a weakened alliance are presented alongside the question (Asan Institute for Policy Studies).
sources: Asan Institute for Policy Studies survey, February 7–11, 2026 (1,000 respondents), as cited by Segye Ilbo, April 13, 2026
East Asia Institute and Hankook Research survey, July 20–21, 2026 (1,547 respondents), as cited by Korea JoongAng Daily, August 12, 2026
Seoul National University Institute for Peace and Unification Studies, 2026 Unification Perception Survey (July 2026, 1,200 respondents), as cited by Hankook Ilbo, September 28, 2026

publics.read: Clisa Geopolitics ranks an independent nuclear arsenal (A3a) last, but a majority of the public stands on the other side. Because the domestic political cost of publicly pledging to forgo nuclear weapons is high for any government, a conditional latent nuclear capability (A3b) serves as a buffer that absorbs public demand without damaging the alliance. If Washington concludes an agreement that limits only ICBMs while leaving South Korea out (the condition for reconsidering C5), it will become harder for the government to contain the debate over nuclear armament, since public opinion already leans toward it.
publics.watch: If a majority still supports it even on questions that present the costs, that would mean the public wants nuclear weapons knowing the price, and the assumption that A3b alone can absorb public demand will be revisited.

congress.t: Conditions on cutting U.S. troops in Korea and transferring wartime operational control
congress.stage: The fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) bars the use of funds to reduce U.S. Forces Korea below 28,500 troops or to complete the transfer of wartime operational control in a way that departs from the plan Seoul and Washington agreed. On July 22, 2026, the House passed a bill extending the same conditions through fiscal 2027, and the Senate Armed Services Committee's version would require the defense secretary's certification before the transfer could be completed at all.
congress.power: Through appropriations and the NDAA, Congress attaches conditions to any presidential decision to cut troops or transfer operational control. The conditions lift 60 days after the defense secretary certifies and submits an assessment.
congress.votes: The House passed the bill 216–212, with 209 Republicans, six Democrats, and one independent voting yes. In the Senate, a July 14 vote to take up the bill stalled at 50–46, short of the 60 votes needed.
congress.sides: Both the House bill and the Senate Armed Services Committee version keep the commitment to roughly 28,500 U.S. troops in Korea among their provisions on strengthening the alliance.
congress.next: House and Senate negotiators will settle the final text. Fiscal 2027 spending continues under a stopgap through December 11.
congress.qnote: The law has been enacted and the House has voted, but no floor speech for or against addressed this provision.

congress.t: The timetable for transferring wartime operational control
congress.stage: The government told the National Assembly on September 10 that it aims to complete verification of full operational capability at the Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) in November. On September 16, the nominee for defense minister said that once verification is complete, the two defense ministers will set a year for the transfer and recommend it to their presidents.
congress.power: The transfer of wartime operational control is settled by agreement between Seoul and Washington and does not require the National Assembly's consent. The Assembly scrutinizes it through its annual parliamentary audit and through questioning.
congress.sides: Ruling-party members pressed for a swift transfer. A People Power Party member criticized the government, pointing to differences between Seoul and Washington and to the cancellation of counteroffensive drills in the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise.
congress.next: The parliamentary audit in October; the 58th SCM in November.

congress.t: Aid to North Korea and a resolution condemning North Korean land mines
congress.stage: The unification minister told the National Assembly that the government is preparing to send medical equipment to North Korea and has obtained a UN sanctions exemption (September 17). On September 29, the National Defense Committee sought to adopt a resolution condemning the North Korean land mine incident but failed to do so after the ruling and opposition parties could not agree on a clause calling for a review of aid to North Korea already in the works.
congress.power: The National Assembly can cut the budget, and inter-Korean agreements that impose a heavy fiscal burden require its consent.
congress.votes: The budget passes by simple majority, so the Democratic Party (161 seats) can protect the government's proposal on its own.
congress.sides: The People Power Party demanded a review of aid to North Korea alongside the condemnation; the Democratic Party rejected that clause, saying the resolution should focus on condemning the North. Both parties agreed that North Korea was responsible and had violated the armistice agreement.
congress.next: The parliamentary audit in October; review of the 2027 budget (constitutional deadline: December 2).

hs7.lead: For South Koreans, life through 2030 stays about the same in most futures. The risk is concentrated in an all-out war on the Korean Peninsula, which has a 2 percent probability. The people with the most at stake in this issue are surviving members of separated families and North Koreans.
hs7.read: For South Koreans and surviving members of separated families, almost all of the risk lies in an all-out war on the Korean Peninsula (2%). In the other futures, life for South Koreans stays the same or income falls by 2–3 percent, so the probability-weighted expected value is also close to today's. That expected value does not mean the risk is small. Surviving members of separated families are better off only if managed coexistence takes hold, so following the recommendation doubles this group's expected Community score, from 5.0 to 10.2.

strategies.title: The Taiwan Strait: What should South Korea prepare for, and what should it promise, in a Taiwan contingency?
strategies.recipient: Government of the Republic of Korea
facts: In the Justice Mission-2025 exercises on December 29–31, 2025, the People's Liberation Army deployed 130 aircraft on the first day (90 of them crossing the median line), along with 27 naval vessels and 29 coast guard ships. It fired 27 rockets, 10 of which landed inside Taiwan's contiguous zone, and the declared exercise zones disrupted 941 civilian flights. The drills came days after Washington approved $11.1 billion in arms sales to Taiwan on December 18.

On May 8, 2026, Taiwan's Legislative Yuan, where the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Taiwan People's Party hold a majority, passed a special act that cut the ceiling on the special defense budget the government had requested from NT$1.25 trillion to NT$780 billion. The cuts eliminated funding for some 200,000 domestically produced drones, the T-Dome air defense network, and serial production of Strong Bow (Chiang Kung) interceptor missiles. Local elections are scheduled for November 28, and the presidential election for January 2028.

In the Han Kuang exercises in August, Taiwan for the first time rehearsed evacuating the president in the event of a decapitation strike and practiced responding to a blockade. The same month, China's Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration, citing a typhoon, demanded that ships in international waters of the Taiwan Strait comply with its navigation controls. Taiwan refused.

After Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told the Diet on November 7, 2025, that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, China advised its citizens to avoid travel to Japan (Chinese visits to Japan fell 60 percent in January), halted seafood imports, imposed export controls on dual-use items and rare earths in January 2026, and sanctioned Japanese politicians in March. The dispute is not yet over.

In January 2026, the United States concluded a trade agreement with Taiwan ($250 billion in Taiwanese semiconductor and technology investment; tariffs cut from 20 percent to 15 percent), and in July it deployed Navy and Marine Corps systems to the Luzon Strait and Japan's southern islands. At the White House summit on September 24, when Xi Jinping asked Washington to oppose Taiwanese independence, Trump said that Xi understood his position.

Since 2023, more than half of China's full generals have been purged. As of August 2026, only six active-duty full generals were appearing in public, and 21 theater command posts stood vacant. On September 21, Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were expelled from the Party and the military.

Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's state visit to China in January 2026, Beijing pressed Seoul to make its position on Taiwan clear. Seoul kept the language of the 1992 joint communiqué establishing diplomatic relations, in which it "respects the position of the Chinese side." Washington's 2026 National Defense Strategy names China as the top challenge and expects South Korea to play a larger regional role; Seoul remains cautious about U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) being sent to a Taiwan contingency (so-called strategic flexibility). About 5,000 South Koreans live in Taiwan (2021).

On September 28, David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, said that no date had been set, even after the summit, for approving a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan that has been on hold since May. Washington has made no public concessions on Taiwan, but it is holding back the arms sale.

law.title: What South Korea has already promised
points: In the 1992 joint communiqué establishing diplomatic relations with China, South Korea recognized the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government of China and stated that it "respects the position of the Chinese side that there is but one China." Seoul respected the one-China position; it did not recognize it.

Article III of the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty between the Republic of Korea and the United States treats an armed attack in the Pacific area on territory under the administrative control of either party as a common danger. Taiwan is not South Korean territory, so there is no automatic obligation to intervene. The picture changes, however, if USFK bases on South Korean soil come under attack, because Article III could then apply.

In the January 2006 agreement on strategic flexibility, South Korea stated that it "respects" the necessity for strategic flexibility of U.S. forces in Korea, and the United States that it "respects" South Korea's position that it shall not be involved in a regional conflict in Northeast Asia against the will of the Korean people.
law.result: Through these two "respects," South Korea has preserved its ambiguity as a matter of law. The trouble is that in a crisis this ambiguity can no longer hold, and Seoul will be forced to choose in an instant. Option A1 below, designing conditional rear-area support in advance, would turn the two "respects" of the 2006 agreement into concrete procedures before a crisis comes.

client.name: Government of the Republic of Korea
client.note: The goals and their order are the same as in the Korean Peninsula issue. In the Taiwan Strait, national security (G1) involves a gap in deterrence on the Korean Peninsula and the targeting of USFK bases; the economy and national creditworthiness (G3) involve shipping, supply chains, and trade with China; and protection of citizens (G5) involves the safety of South Koreans in Taiwan and of seafarers transiting the strait.

responses.lesson: A China that calculates with the greatest care would not retaliate against South Korea the way it did against Japan. In peacetime it would pull Seoul toward neutrality and save its retaliation for a single use just before a crisis. South Korea's risk is therefore concentrated not in peacetime but in the few days before a crisis. To avoid being forced into a decision during those days, Seoul needs to have the procedures for conditional rear-area support (A1) and economic and civilian preparedness (A4) in place in peacetime.

intent.note: Intent is judged first by actions that carry a cost, not by words. Signals are collected in each country's profile; this section shows only the signals bearing on this issue and how to read them.
intent.read: In the Taiwan Strait, only Japan's words and deeds match. China talks of peaceful unification while making pressure routine; the United States deters with arms and deployments while the president's remarks leave room for bargaining; and in Taiwan, the government's words and the Legislative Yuan's budget decisions diverge.

items.name: Tense status quo
items.story: Large-scale exercises recur once or twice a year and gray-zone pressure continues, but it does not escalate to inspections or a blockade. Political divisions in Taiwan and Washington's transactional bent push tensions up and down.
items.test: T1 applies if none of the conditions for T2 through T5 is met. Where conditions overlap, precedence goes to T4, then T3, T2, and T5.

U.S.-China summit diplomacy continues

items.name: Gray-zone escalation
items.story: China's coast guard and maritime authorities begin actually enforcing inspections, navigation permits, and ship detentions in and around the Taiwan Strait. There is no war, but Taiwan's maritime traffic and South Korean shipping start to follow Chinese rules.
items.test: T2 applies if, by the end of 2030, there is a confirmed case of Chinese authorities inspecting or detaining Taiwanese ships or ships bound for Taiwan, or enforcing navigation permits, without escalating to a blockade or combat.

Coast guard boarding inspections of Taiwanese ships
Spikes in insurance premiums and freight rates

items.name: Blockade or quarantine
items.story: China effectively closes Taiwan's major ports. Energy and food imports are cut off, and semiconductor supply chains grind to a halt. The United States and Japan are forced to choose between intervening and standing aside.
items.test: T3 applies if access to Taiwan's major ports is effectively blocked for seven days or more.

Taiwanese announcements on energy reserves
Shipping lines suspending service
items.why: Taiwan's freedom score is assumed to fall to 85 under emergency measures. South Korea's income drops because of the supply chain shock, and its risk exposure rises to 60.

items.name: Armed conflict
items.story: Fighting breaks out between Chinese forces and Taiwanese or U.S. forces. USFK is set in motion, and North Korea looks for an opening.
items.test: T4 applies if there is combat with fatalities between Chinese forces and Taiwanese or U.S. forces.
