items.who: Ukraine · Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS)
items.q: Could you accept a plan under which Ukraine withdraws from the parts of the Donbas it controls (Kramatorsk, Sloviansk, and others) in exchange for security guarantees from the United States and Europe?
items.read: In the same survey, 59 percent accepted and 31 percent opposed a plan to freeze the war on the current front line without recognizing the occupied territories, with Ukraine receiving large-scale military and financial aid. What Ukrainians reject is not a ceasefire as such but giving up land they still hold and legally recognizing the occupation.
items.caveat: Residents of the occupied territories and refugees abroad are not surveyed. The January 2026 figures are cited from press reports.
sources: January 2026 survey (601 respondents) · cited from NV, January 16, 2026

items.who: Ukraine · Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS)
items.q: Can Ukraine give up some territory to achieve peace quickly and preserve its independence, or should it not give up territory under any circumstances, even if the war lasts longer?
items.series: May 2022 about 10 → May 2024 32 → Dec. 2024 38 → Feb.–Mar. 2025 39 → May–June 2025 38
items.latest: May 15–June 3, 2025 (the most recent survey with this question)
items.read: Willingness to give up territory, around 10 percent in the first year of the war, rose to nearly 40 percent by late 2024 and has stalled since. In the June 2025 survey, opposition varied widely depending on what would be given up: 48 percent opposed de facto recognition of the occupation, 68 percent legal recognition, and 78 percent the surrender of unoccupied areas.
items.caveat: This is a different question from the scenario question above, so the two results are not joined into a single time series. Figures before May 2024 are cited from press reports.

items.q: Should military operations continue, or should peace negotiations begin?
items.read: Most Russians want negotiations, but in the same survey 68 percent said they supported the actions of the Russian armed forces. Support for negotiations peaked in February 2026 and has been declining since. Because the question does not ask about terms, support for negotiations cannot be read as consent to territorial concessions.
items.caveat: The Levada Center is an independent polling organization that the Russian government has designated a "foreign agent." Under wartime censorship laws, respondents may hide their true views or decline to answer, so the survey is used as an indicator of direction rather than level. The trend figures were read from charts the center published.

publics.read: Public opinion shows that the ceasefire in the top-ranked combination (B1), a freeze that does not legally cede the occupied territories, falls within what Ukrainians will accept. Withdrawal from the Donbas, by contrast, is rejected by 60 percent even with security guarantees attached, and Russia demands the rest of Donetsk Oblast (C5). That the ranges of agreement public opinion permits in the two countries do not overlap supports, from the side of public opinion, the assessment that a ceasefire is unlikely until Russia concludes that it cannot bear the cost (C1).
publics.watch: If acceptance of the Donbas withdrawal plan in the KIIS survey exceeds 50 percent, a ceasefire that gives up territory will be considered politically possible inside Ukraine, and the ceasefire outlook will be revisited. If continued fighting overtakes negotiations in the Levada survey, the room for agreement on the Russian side will be judged to have narrowed further.

congress.t: Enforcing tariffs under the Russia sanctions law
congress.stage: The Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act was signed into law on September 18, 2026. On October 16, two days before the tariff deadline, President Trump issued an executive order waiving the tariffs under Sections 112 and 113 and most of the sanctions, and submitted a national-interest certification to Congress. The law provides no procedure for Congress to disapprove the waiver.
congress.power: Congress made the tariffs mandatory but left the president a way to waive them in the national interest. Any lifting of sanctions on Russia is subject to congressional review.
congress.votes: Senate 86–11 (August 7); House 262–159 (September 16). In the House, 152 Democrats voted no, objecting not to sanctions on Russia but to giving the president more tariff authority.
congress.sides: Supporters argued, in the words of Rep. Michael McCaul, that “you can evade sanctions … but you cannot evade tariffs.” Opponents said the broad waiver provision makes the sanctions effectively optional (Rep. Gregory Meeks).
congress.next: The October 18 deadline for imposing tariffs; whether the president grants waivers, and which countries are targeted.

quotes.role: Representative; former chair, House Foreign Affairs Committee
quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5843
quotes.ex: Because, as we have heard from President Zelenskyy's team, you can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years, but you cannot evade tariffs. … That is why they are the teeth of this bill. Pursuant to the bill's rule of construction, only the top five importers of Russian oil will be tariffed. If a country falls off of the top-five list, the tariffs are removed.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5846
quotes.ex: I share concerns that the tariffs in the bill could backfire. They could harm our trading partners while sparing the main importers of Russian oil like China. The risk of the bill is that an important economy like China could be spared, but tariffs could be used aggressively on smaller U.S. allies. … Despite these design shortcomings I have outlined, I urge a ‘yes’ vote today.

quotes.role: Ranking Democrat, House Foreign Affairs Committee
quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5843
quotes.ex: These sanctions that are proposed now, the President of the United States, if this were urgent, could do them right now. … We said let's make sure that our friends in the European Union will not be subject to tariffs. In this bill, my friends from Europe can be tariffed. … Let's make stronger waivers if we really care about the Ukrainian people, so that no President can waive the sanctions that we are putting on Russia. No, can't do that.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5847
quotes.ex: The new sanctions on Russia in this bill would be strong and sweeping if they were enforced, but the bill gives Trump the power to simply ignore them. … The bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions.

quotes.body: House floor debate · Congressional Record H5846
quotes.ex: If we vote for this bill, it will be a Churchill moment because we will tell the President he needs to do something that he doesn't want to do. He may not do it, and we can't force him to do it … If we fail to pass this bill, there will be cheers in the Kremlin and tears in Kyiv.
quotes.devnote: voted yes, unlike most Democrats (152 voted no)

congress.t: Extending martial law and the territorial provisions
congress.stage: On July 14, 2026, the Verkhovna Rada approved presidential decrees extending martial law and general mobilization for 90 days, from August 2 to October 31. It was the 20th extension approved by the current convocation.
congress.power: Presidential decrees on martial law and mobilization take effect only with the Rada's approval (Article 85 of the Constitution). Changes to Ukraine's territory can be decided only by a national referendum called by the Rada (Articles 73 and 85), and the Constitution cannot be amended under martial law (Article 157).
congress.votes: The martial-law extension passed 313–2, and the mobilization extension 311–2 with one abstention (a majority of the full chamber is 226).
congress.next: A vote on extending martial law in late October (the current extension runs through October 31).

quotes.ex: We cannot fail to extend the legal regime of martial law, because the survival of our state depends on it. The aggressor state keeps stressing that the goals it set for itself in 2022 remain unchanged.

This is the 20th time parliament has backed Zelensky's decree on mobilization and martial law, because it is vital for the country. And note that Zelensky's own Servant of the People faction has long been unable to supply 226 votes for it on its own.

qnone.no: No one spoke against it on the floor. The chair invited two members to speak for the extension and two against, but every member who spoke supported it.

hs7.lead: Ukrainians are already in the middle of a war. About 47 people per 100,000 die from violence each year, and 23 percent of the population has been forced from home. In 57 of 100 futures through 2030, a ceasefire or peace makes life better than this; in 7, the collapse of the front makes it much worse.
hs7.read: For Ukrainians, this issue puts their whole lives at stake. The expected value for 2030 is higher than today (Personal safety 44.0 → 60.2), because futures that bring a ceasefire or peace carry high probability. But the score counts only deaths in that year. The risk that peace on Russia's terms (20%) leads to a renewed invasion a few years later is handled not in the score but in the scenario probabilities and the strategy assessment. Following the recommendation adds futures in which a ceasefire comes with guarantees, lifting the expected value a little further. For Russians, too, a ceasefire or peace means fewer soldiers killed, raising the Personal safety score from 40 to around 65.

changes.why: After Washington opened a sanctions exemption for Russian diesel and criticized Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, the probability of peace on Russia's terms was raised and that of a favorable end to the war lowered.

Even after the energy truce announced by President Trump, Russia kept attacking power plants and Ukraine lifted its restraint on striking refineries, so the truce collapsed; the probability of a continued war of attrition was therefore raised.

external.note: Likelihoods and conditional probabilities are provisional judgments. The variables overlap, so they should not be added or multiplied. The table shows which way the future leans if one variable occurs.

items.t: The United States halts support for Ukraine
items.def: The United States halts intelligence sharing or U.S. weapons transfers to Ukraine for more than 30 days
items.flips: C1 weakened (peace on Russia's terms overtakes the war of attrition) · C2 weakened · C5 strengthened
items.why: If the United States walks away, Ukraine is left alone to withstand pressure to cede territory, raising the odds of peace on Russia's terms (U3) and of a front-line collapse (U4). Because any territorial change requires a referendum, however, the pressure could also end in a ceasefire without guarantees (U6). How Ukraine responds can also ease the pressure, so this is not a purely external variable.
items.crit: Met if the U.S. government halts intelligence sharing with Ukraine or transfers of U.S. weapons to it (including weapons Europe buys and passes on) for more than 30 days, and this comes to light through notification to Congress or confirmation by U.S. officials. Temporary sanctions waivers do not count.
items.sign: U.S. demands that Ukraine stop striking refineries, and warnings of an intelligence cutoff; one-on-one U.S.-Russian summits; public U.S. demands for territorial concessions; delays in delivering U.S. weapons bought by Europe for Ukraine.
items.basis: After the White House meeting on February 28, 2025, ended in a public clash, the United States suspended weapons deliveries on March 3 and intelligence sharing on March 5, then resumed both about eight days later, on March 11, when Ukraine accepted a 30-day ceasefire proposal. According to the Ukrainian side, U.S. envoys at talks in Miami on October 9, 2026, warned that they would cut off intelligence unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries; the U.S. side denied this ([secondary]). Trump and Putin spoke by phone the same day, and the U.S. Treasury issued General License 135, allowing trade in Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.

items.t: U.S. tariffs enforced on buyers of Russian oil
items.def: Under the Russia sanctions law, the United States imposes tariffs of 25% or more for over six months on at least one of China, India or Turkey
items.why: Lower oil export earnings make the war harder for Russia to pay for, raising the odds of a ceasefire along current lines (U2, U6) and a favorable end to the war (U5), and lowering the odds of peace on Russia's terms (U3).
items.sign: Falling Russian crude imports by India and China; publication of the U.S. Trade Representative's list of countries subject to the tariffs; whether the president submits waiver certifications.
items.basis: The Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act became law on September 18, 2026, requiring the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas by October 18. But the law sets no minimum rate, and the president can waive the tariffs indefinitely by certifying that doing so is in the national interest. President Trump actually used this waiver on October 16, 2026. In August 2025 the United States imposed an extra 25 percent tariff on India over its purchases of Russian oil and withdrew it in February 2026 when India agreed to stop importing Russian oil. In March, however, when the Iran war pushed up oil prices, Washington itself temporarily allowed trade in Russian oil. While oil prices stay high, enforcement is unlikely.

items.t: The limits of Russia's war finances
items.def: Liquid assets in Russia's National Wealth Fund fall below 1 trillion rubles, or new emergency measures such as limits on deposit withdrawals or forced currency conversion are announced
items.why: If the money to sustain the war runs out, Russia gains an incentive to scale back its demand for all of Donetsk, raising the odds of a ceasefire (U2, U6) and a favorable end to the war (U5).
items.sign: Sales of National Wealth Fund assets at a record pace; repeated upward revisions of the deficit target; an expanded requirement for exporters to sell their foreign-currency earnings; a sharp fall in the ruble.
items.basis: The Russian government raised its 2026 budget deficit forecast to 3.2 percent of GDP (about 7.3 trillion rubles), double the planned 1.6 percent. Liquid assets in the National Wealth Fund stood at 3.8 trillion rubles (about $44.5 billion) on October 1, less than half the pre-invasion level (about $113.5 billion). Even so, defense spending for 2027 has risen to about 17.147 trillion rubles, with the shortfall to be covered by domestic borrowing (about 6.1 trillion rubles), tax increases and social spending cuts, so the fund's depletion may be delayed. In 1917 Russia's war finances collapsed and revolution followed; in 1918 it left the war through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, giving up vast territory.

items.t: Europe scales back its support
items.def: France, Britain or Germany withdraws from the multinational force or cuts its military aid by more than half, or the EU fails to agree on support from 2028 onward
items.flips: C2 weakened · C1 weakened (the gap between the war of attrition and peace on Russia's terms narrows to two percentage points)
items.why: France and Britain lead the multinational force meant to secure a ceasefire, so if Europe pulls back, a ceasefire conditioned on great-power troops (U2) recedes and the odds of peace on Russia's terms (U3) and a front-line collapse (U4) rise.
items.sign: France's presidential election in April 2027; discussion of the 2028–2034 budget framework at the EU summit on October 15–16; cuts to Ukraine aid budgets in major European countries.
items.basis: The EU agreed to lend Ukraine €90 billion over 2026–27, and member states were reported to have no major differences over Ukraine's roughly €100 billion share of the 2028–2034 budget framework ([secondary]). Viktor Orbán's departure after Hungary's April 2026 election has also lowered a barrier to EU unanimity. This variable's likelihood therefore rests mainly on France's presidential election in April 2027 and Britain's general election in 2029. In French polls the National Rally candidate leads the first round with around 35 percent (March and June 2026), and a July appeals court ruling cleared the way for Marine Le Pen to run, leaving it open whether the party's candidate will be Le Pen or Jordan Bardella. The National Rally has opposed sending troops to Ukraine and supplying long-range missiles.
items.crit: Met if a new government in France, Britain or Germany withdraws from the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U) or cuts military aid to Ukraine to less than half the previous year's level, or if the EU fails by the end of 2027 to agree on Ukraine's share of the 2028–2034 budget framework.

items.t: North Korea and China expand support for Russia
items.def: At least 10,000 more North Korean regular troops deployed to Russia or the occupied territories, or a Chinese transfer of finished weapons officially confirmed
items.why: If Russia's shortages of troops and weapons ease, the war of attrition (U1) drags on and the odds of a front-line collapse (U4) rise.
items.sign: North Korean troop quarters in regions bordering Ukraine such as Voronezh; more North Korean ballistic missile launchers shipped in; finished Chinese weapons, not just components, found on the battlefield.
items.basis: North Korea sent about 11,000–12,000 combat troops to Russia's Kursk region in October–November 2024 and about 3,000 more in early 2025, and in June 2025 Russia said it would receive 1,000 deminers and 5,000 reconstruction workers. On July 25, 2026, President Zelensky said Russia wanted 30,000 more North Korean troops, and in August he said as many as 30,000–50,000 could come. There is no confirmation that North Korean troops have fought inside Ukrainian territory.
items.crit: Met if at least 10,000 more North Korean regular troops are deployed to Russia or to Ukrainian territory, including the occupied areas, or if the U.S. government or the EU officially confirms transfers of finished weapons (shells, missiles or drones) by the Chinese government or Chinese state-owned defense firms.

items.t: A new Ukraine aid package from the U.S. Congress
items.def: Congress passes, and the president signs, new military aid for Ukraine of $10 billion or more by the end of 2030
items.why: If U.S. aid resumes, Ukraine is better able to withstand the stalemate, lowering the odds of a front-line collapse (U4) and peace on Russia's terms (U3) and bringing a guaranteed ceasefire (U2) closer.
items.sign: The November 3, 2026, midterm elections; the November 2028 presidential election; whether Ukraine provisions are included in must-pass bills such as the National Defense Authorization Act or appropriations bills.
items.basis: The last large Ukraine aid package Congress passed was the roughly $61 billion approved in April 2024, which cleared a Republican-majority House. The National Defense Authorization Act of December 2025 includes $400 million a year for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative in fiscal 2026 and 2027. In early October the U.S. prediction market Kalshi put Democrats' chances of winning the House at 90 percent and the Senate at around 60 percent. The real obstacles are less the House than the president's signature and the 60 votes needed in the Senate.

items.t: A sharp fall in oil prices
items.def: Brent averages below $60 a barrel in any one year
items.why: Russia's budget depends heavily on oil and gas revenue, so prolonged low prices make the war harder to pay for, raising the odds of a ceasefire (U2, U6) and a favorable end to the war (U5). Low prices also make it easier for Washington to enforce its tariffs on buyers of Russian oil (see the external variable 'U.S. tariffs enforced on buyers of Russian oil').
items.sign: An end to the Iran war and a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz (I2 in the Iran and Hormuz issue); increased output by OPEC+; a wider discount on Urals crude.
items.basis: The Iran war pushed Brent above $105 a barrel on October 8, 2026. Conversely, when Urals fell to about $39 a barrel in December 2025, Russia decided in January 2026 to sell National Wealth Fund assets at the fastest pace on record. Russia's 2027 budget assumes about 7 trillion rubles in oil and gas revenue. After the 1986 oil price collapse left it in fiscal trouble, the Soviet Union agreed in the 1988 Geneva Accords to withdraw from Afghanistan.

items.t: A change in Russia's leadership
items.def: Putin dies, becomes incapacitated or steps down
items.why: If the leader who started the war is gone, a successor gains political room to drop the demand for all of Donetsk, sharply raising the odds of a favorable end to the war (U5) and a ceasefire (U2, U6). If hard-liners take power, however, the opposite could happen.
items.sign: Gaps in Putin's public schedule; succession talk ahead of the March 2030 presidential election; open clashes among the elite.
items.basis: Putin turned 74 on October 7, 2026, and Russia's next presidential election is in March 2030. After Stalin died in March 1953, the new Soviet leadership pressed for a ceasefire, and the Korean War armistice was signed a little over four months later.

reads: The external variable that moves the odds in the Russia-Ukraine war most is a halt to U.S. support. If the United States cuts off intelligence and weapons for more than 30 days, peace on Russia's terms (U3) rises to 30 percent and overtakes the war of attrition (U1, 26%). Weighted by how likely each is to occur, the next is Europe scaling back its support.

Europe scaling back its support lowers the odds of a guaranteed ceasefire (U2) from 12 percent to 7 percent, because France and Britain would lead the troops on which the top-ranked combination, a ceasefire conditioned on great-power troops (C2), depends.

The variables unfavorable to Ukraine (a U.S. halt in support, Europe scaling back, more help for Russia from North Korea and China) each have roughly a 30 percent chance of occurring, while the favorable ones (tariff enforcement, the limits of Russia's war finances, new U.S. aid, a fall in oil prices, a change of leadership) range from 10 to 30 percent. Ukraine cannot by itself prevent either the United States or Europe from pulling back, which is why defense-industrial self-reliance (B5) ranks first.

strategies.title: The Iran war and Hormuz: What should the United States and South Korea each do?
strategies.recipient: Government of the Republic of Korea
facts: The war that began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, is now in its seventh month. Ali Khamenei was killed, and his son Mojtaba succeeded him. After the April cease-fire and the June 17 memorandum of understanding effectively collapsed on July 8 (the MOU formally expired on August 17), the United States reimposed its naval blockade. Iran restricts passage through Hormuz with attacks on merchant ships and with mines, and the U.S. military counters with escorted transits. On September 25, U.S. Central Command said it had turned back 122 merchant ships since the blockade began in April. Estimates of traffic through the strait diverge sharply between ship-tracking data and U.S. government statements. Ship-tracking data in early September showed five to 12 ships a day, roughly 10 percent of normal traffic (about 100 a day). Yet Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on September 28 that about 13 million barrels a day were passing through, and the ship-tracking firm Kpler counted 19 tankers transiting in the week to September 27. Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have captured a U.S. unmanned underwater vehicle.

On September 25, Iran put forward a seven-day roadmap for a cease-fire and the reopening of the strait; Trump rejected it. Natanz and other sites were destroyed again, but about 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent has been beyond IAEA verification since June 2025.

Seventy percent of South Korea's crude oil imports and 35 percent of its naphtha pass through Hormuz, and 64.7 percent of its helium comes from Qatar. Government stockpiles stood at 34 days of actual consumption (about 67 days including private stocks). They fell to 26 days after the coordinated IEA release in March, then rose by eight to nine days' worth once Seoul secured 24 million barrels of crude from the UAE.

In March, 26 South Korean ships were stranded in the Gulf. That month Iran called South Korea a "non-adversarial country" and said it would allow passage subject to prior coordination. After the June MOU, 24 ships had left with Iranian approval by July 1, leaving two ships and 35 South Korean sailors inside the strait (Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries figures as of July 1). In early April, the KOSPI suffered the worst day in its 43-year history and the won fell to a 17-year low. The government responded with a $17 billion supplementary budget, a cap on fuel prices, and an accelerated restart of nuclear reactors.
The Middle East's share of South Korea's crude oil imports fell to 53.1 percent in April 2026 from 65.2 percent a year earlier, as imports from the United States, Canada, and Australia rose.

On September 18, President Lee Jae-myung said South Korea would not send troops to take part or intervene in the war. The next day, the presidential office explained that this was not a rejection of Trump's request regarding Hormuz. Expanding the mission of the Cheonghae Unit, the navy's antipiracy flotilla, is discussed as the most likely option. Separately, South Korea has pledged $20 billion of investment in Texas energy projects.

Iran has not closed the strait; it opens it selectively. Ships from "friendly" countries—China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Malaysia, Thailand, and others—pass after coordination or payment of a toll (one reported case: $2 million per ship), while ships of the United States, Israel, and Western allies are blocked.

The war has badly shrunk Iran's economy. GDP in the first quarter of the Iranian year (March 21 to June 20) was 10.1 percent lower than a year earlier, and crude loadings fell from about two million barrels a day in March to 220,000–250,000 in August. The rial went from about one million to the dollar to more than 2.2 million, and 12-month average inflation stands at 69.9 percent.

Iran's conditions for ending the war, as set out on September 20 by its security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, are an end to the fighting on all fronts including Lebanon, the return of frozen assets, the lifting of the naval blockade, noninterference in Iran's internal affairs, an end to support for opposition forces, and a halt to attacks on Iranian territory. The United States, by contrast, demands first that Iran give up nuclear weapons and allow freedom of navigation through the strait. Iran's position is that it will not discuss the nuclear question until its conditions are met.

On May 4, 2026, the Panamanian-flagged Namu, operated by HMM, was struck in the strait. A South Korean investigation pointed to the possibility of Iranian-made weapons, but the government attributed the attack to "unidentified aerial objects," and Iran denied involvement.

On September 7, 2026, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei warned in a Korean-language post that any country stationing forces in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz or joining military operations there would be regarded as directly supporting the aggressor and would face serious consequences. Two days earlier, on September 5, a senior Iranian official told the Lebanese outlet Al Mayadeen that Iran would regard South Korean involvement of any kind in the strait as direct military participation in the aggression and war against Iran.

On October 1, the United States sent a carrier strike group and an amphibious ready group to the Middle East, and on October 2 G7 leaders agreed to release 100 million barrels of strategic oil reserves. On October 4, Iran said through parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf that it would not open the strait until seven conditions were met, and its Foreign Ministry said the latest U.S. proposal still put the nuclear question first.

law.title: The legal threshold for deployment
points: Article 60(2) of the Constitution requires the consent of the National Assembly for dispatching the armed forces to foreign states.
Article 5(1) of the Constitution renounces wars of aggression. Interpretations diverge on whether joining an operation to secure the strait counts as self-defense or as taking part in hostilities.

The Cheonghae Unit has operated with the National Assembly's consent for its antipiracy mission. Extending its area of operations to Hormuz has a precedent: in 2020, the unit's independent deployment to Hormuz was handled as an expansion of its area of operations.
law.result: A noncombat expansion (H1) is possible within the existing consent, but a combat deployment (H2) would require new consent from the National Assembly.

syn.note: The ratings in the table (Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, Rejected) are provisional judgments of how readily each country's leadership would accept each of the six futures (I1–I6) through 2030.

reads.t: The futures most deciding powers could accept are those in which a cease-fire is followed by reopening (I2, I6), but what Iran prefers is an incomplete reopening (I6) that leaves it leverage.
reads.d: The 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War held without a peace treaty, and in the Gulf between 2019 and 2023, Iran repeatedly seized selected ships in an "open" strait. Israel's October election and Washington's sense of whether it is winning are the wild cards.

reads.t: South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war.
reads.d: In that South Korea cannot determine the outcome of the war, the structure is the same as in the Taiwan Strait issue. What Seoul can do is reduce the price it pays in each future—above all, the energy shock.

reads.t: The future in which South Korea loses most is a collapse of Gulf exports (I4), in which the flow of Gulf oil breaks down again.
reads.d: Even if the strait reopens, supply will not return if the Gulf producers' facilities are destroyed. The energy transition (H3) is therefore a longer-lasting safeguard than any response aimed at the strait itself.

expect.note: The expected value is the sum of each future's 2030 indicator values weighted by that future's probability. It is calculated separately for each dimension—life and safety, livelihood, freedom, and so on—and the dimensions are not combined.
expect.read: For South Koreans, the expected value for livelihood is 93.9, close to the baseline (93.5), but in the worst future (all-out escalation in the Gulf) it falls to 93.4. An energy shock could shake South Koreans' livelihoods. The lives of some 90 million Iranians are not entered as numbers in this table. Still, the 10 percent contraction in Iran's GDP and the 70 percent average inflation rate in the first quarter of the war show that Iranians' livelihoods already lie close to the worst future.

futures.note: Probabilities and inputs are judgment estimates; ranges are in parentheses. Because South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war, no separate probabilities are given for the case in which the recommendations are followed. What South Korea's choices change is the price it pays in each future.

ranked.t: Build around the energy transition (H3), keep a separate channel to Iran (H4), and pursue the Cheonghae Unit's expansion (H1) in parallel only on three conditions: its area of operations stays outside the strait and the Gulf, it is not placed in a coalition led by the United States or by Britain and France, and Tehran is notified in advance. This combination does not try to change the probabilities of how the war ends; its aim is to reduce South Korea's exposure to energy shocks and ship detentions. Economic contributions to the United States (H5) serve alongside it as a buffer to soften Washington's demand for troops.
Economic contributions to the United States (H5) soften the demand for a deployment, but Washington can reply that troop contributions are a separate matter.
Riding out the crisis with emergency measures and no deployment (H0) leaves energy vulnerability and friction with the alliance in place.
Deploying combat forces ranks last. It would divide South Korea's forces on the peninsula, make South Korean ships and nationals targets of retaliation, and be hard to reverse.

rank2.tension: What has led Iran to detain ships has been action against Iranian assets and cargo more than participation in combat. The cooperation in enforcing the blockade and sanctions that Washington is likely to ask for therefore collides head-on with the channel to Iran (H4). How far to go in meeting U.S. demands is a line that procedure alone cannot draw.
rank2.undecided: How far to go in meeting the ally's demands is for the National Assembly and the public to decide.

human.note: Revisits the ranking from the strategy evaluation from the standpoint of individual lives.

items.cost: It could arouse U.S. suspicion and carries the burden of going through sanctions-exemption procedures.
items.gain: Helps sustain the livelihoods of Iranians living under blockade. It is almost the only means by which South Korea can directly help people in this war.

items.gain: Keeps the energy shock from falling hardest on the most vulnerable households.

conclusions.t: As a single future, the most likely is a continuation of the current state of war without an agreement (32%, range 23–41%). The futures in which an agreement reopens the strait and holds through the end of 2030 total 40 percent. Within them, the case in which Iran demands transit permits or tolls or seizes selected ships (24%) is slightly more likely than the case in which such incidents are rare for more than six months after the agreement (16%). The remaining 28 percent comprises the collapse of the Iranian regime (12%), a renewed collapse of Gulf exports (11%), and a nuclear-armed Iran (5%).
conclusions.why: The 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War never led to a peace treaty, and from 2019 to 2023 Iran repeatedly seized selected ships even while the strait remained open. The U.S.-Iranian memorandum of understanding of June 17, 2026, collapsed three weeks after it was signed, and Washington, believing it was winning, has since rejected a phased roadmap.
conclusions.flip: If, after a phased agreement is signed, the reopening of the strait and the lifting of the blockade both hold for more than 90 days, the probability of a full reopening will be raised.

conclusions.t: South Korea's choices will do little to change the outcome of this war. The future in which South Korea loses most is one in which the flow of Gulf oil breaks down again. Gulf crude exports fell to about 36 percent of prewar levels in March 2026 but had largely recovered by September, thanks to shuttle tankers operating under U.S. military escort. Petroleum products, however, remain at 60 percent of prewar levels, and disruptions to Qatar's LNG supply will last into the winter. The recovery in crude is also fragile, because it depends on an external condition: U.S. military escort.
conclusions.why: Even if the strait reopens, crude supplies will not return if the Gulf producers' production and export facilities are destroyed.
conclusions.flip: To be revisited if a South Korean contribution is explicitly made a condition for reopening the strait.

conclusions.t: Measured against the South Korean government's goals, the top-ranked combination is to build around the energy transition (H3), keep a separate channel to Iran (H4), and pursue an expanded mission for the Cheonghae Unit (H1) only if its area of operations is confined to waters outside the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf (the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea).
conclusions.why: In 2020, Japan sent a destroyer while excluding the strait and the Gulf from its area of operations and briefing Iran in advance, winning acceptance from both Washington and Tehran. That same year South Korea chose an independent deployment that extended the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations to Hormuz; this limited Iran's reaction to a diplomatic protest but did not prevent the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi a year later. In September 2026, Iran warned that it would regard any intervention inside the strait as participation in the war.
conclusions.flip: The ranking will be reconsidered if Iran declares even noncombat activity outside the strait a hostile act, or if Washington formally makes participation inside the strait a condition of the alliance.

conclusions.t: Deploying combat forces (H2) ranks last.
conclusions.why: It would divide the forces defending the peninsula, make South Korean ships and nationals targets of retaliation, require new consent from the National Assembly, and be hard to reverse once troops were sent.
conclusions.flip: To be revisited if the North Korean threat diminishes substantially and the operation in the strait becomes a multinational noncombat mission.

conclusions.t: Judged by its effect on individual lives, humanitarian aid for Iranians should be added to the agenda of the diplomatic channel with Iran.
conclusions.why: It is almost the only means by which South Korea can directly help people in this war.
conclusions.flip: If aid is confirmed to be diverted to the Iranian regime, the delivery route will be changed.

conclusions.t: Iran's best move is not to make an enemy of South Korea. But Iran has gained from detaining South Korean ships over frozen funds without ever labeling South Korea an enemy. In wartime, South Korean ships face the same risk of attack as every vessel transiting the strait; the additional risk that South Korea alone bears comes from action against Iranian assets in South Korea and from keeping South Korean warships inside the strait.
conclusions.why: In 2021, the Hankuk Chemi was released only after South Korea agreed to unfreeze $1 billion of the Iranian funds frozen there, and Iran's seizure of two Greek tankers in 2022 followed the same pattern: it aimed to recover Iranian oil that Greek authorities had seized at Washington's request. In May 2026, the HMM-operated Namu was struck before South Korea had any military involvement in the strait. On September 7, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson warned in Korean that any country stationing forces in the strait and the Persian Gulf or joining military operations there would be regarded as directly supporting the aggressor.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if a South Korean ship that has nothing to do with Iranian assets and stays outside the strait suffers an attack confirmed to be Iran's doing.

conclusions.t: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened, and the room for a deal lies in trading the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions in phases. But such a phased agreement is not stable on its own. For a deal to be reached and to hold, asset transfers through a third country must be executed simultaneously with each side's steps, adjacent fronts such as Lebanon must be explicitly included, and implementation must proceed in stages tied to verification by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
conclusions.why: A phased agreement was already signed once, in the memorandum of understanding of June 17, 2026, but it collapsed within three weeks because it did not cover the Lebanon front. The exchanges that held—the Algiers Accords of 1981 (the release of the U.S. embassy hostages) and the 2023 prisoner swap—were executed simultaneously and in one step, with funds held by a third country. The 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA), which was divided into several stages, was undone by the Trump administration's withdrawal in 2018. And the 1988 cease-fire in the Iran-Iraq War came only after Iran concluded that military victory was impossible.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if a single comprehensive deal without phases emerges or if Iran concedes first on the nuclear question.

conclusions.t: Measured against Washington's own goals, the top-ranked course is to keep the blockade in place while proposing a phased agreement with nuclear conditions attached, and, if that makes no progress, to fall back to an agreement that defers the nuclear issue to a second phase. On this measure, too, a phased agreement ranks above staying the course.
conclusions.why: A phased agreement secures the first and third U.S. goals (the safety of the homeland and Americans, and navigation through the strait), whereas staying the course leaves the strait closed. The nuclear conditions (shipping the enriched uranium to a third country or, at a minimum, halting 60 percent enrichment and declaring the stockpile) have precedents in the 2013 Joint Plan of Action and the 2015 shipment of uranium to Russia. But because Iran is likely to refuse verification of its stockpile, they belong on the negotiating table rather than standing as a course of their own.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if Iran rejects even a first-phase agreement without nuclear conditions, or if large-scale strikes reopen the strait.

conclusions.t: U.S. choices will do little to change the outcome of this war. If Washington follows its top-ranked course, the probability of an end to the war with full reopening rises only from 16 to 17 percent, and that of an incomplete reopening from 24 to 25 percent.
conclusions.why: The outcome depends far more on Iran's conditions for ending the war (an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the return of frozen assets; the lifting of the blockade, among others) and on its insistence that the nuclear issue come later than on anything Washington proposes. Even if the United States changes course, the chance of a deal that transfers assets and reopens the strait on the same day would rise only from 30 percent to 35–45 percent.
conclusions.flip: This assessment is wrong if a change in the U.S. proposal alone leads Iran to lower its conditions for ending the war or to agree to take up the nuclear issue first.

conclusions.t: Judged by the effect on people's lives, the ranking departs from Washington's at the top. On that measure, the top-ranked course is a phased agreement that defers the nuclear issue to a second phase, because the strait would reopen sooner, easing the hardship of Iranians and the burden on energy-importing countries more quickly.
conclusions.why: Washington's top-ranked course puts nuclear conditions up front, lowering the risk of a nuclear-armed Iran but delaying the reopening of the strait. The two rankings diverge over which weighs more heavily: the risk of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons or the cost people bear in the meantime. On the other options, the two rankings differ little.
conclusions.flip: This difference disappears if negotiations with nuclear conditions turn out not to delay the strait's reopening.

predictions.q: By the end of June 2027, the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations is formally extended to the vicinity of the Strait of Hormuz
predictions.note: Realization of the Cheonghae Unit's expanded mission (H1) within the top-ranked combination

predictions.q: The Middle East's share of South Korea's crude oil imports for the full year 2027 falls below 60 percent
By the end of 2027, Iran conducts a nuclear test or officially declares that it possesses nuclear weapons
predictions.note: The condition for a nuclear-armed Iran (I5)

falsify: If Washington rejects a noncombat contribution and applies pressure through tariffs or the question of U.S. Forces Korea, the top-ranked combination will be reconsidered.

If crude exports from the Gulf excluding Iran fall below 60 percent of the prewar average for two consecutive months, the probability of a collapse of Gulf exports (I4) will be reassessed, and the recommendation will be revised to bring forward the stockpile expansion within the top-ranked combination (exports were about 36 percent in March 2026 and about 89–100 percent in September). The threshold is set above the I4 criterion (half) so that a warning comes before a collapse is confirmed.

If a motion the government submits to the National Assembly for consent to the Cheonghae Unit's deployment, or to a change in it, places waters inside the Strait of Hormuz within the area of operations, the government's actual choice will have diverged from the condition of the top-ranked combination (C3) that confines the area of operations to waters outside the strait, so the ranking and the forecast that the Cheonghae Unit's area will be extended to Hormuz will be revisited.

rows.name: Managed competition
rows.why: In a world where nuclear limits are traded for an end to the blockade on Iran, an end of the war and full reopening (I2) is the most likely outcome.

rows.name: Armed multipolarity
rows.why: When everyone arms, Iran's incentive to acquire nuclear weapons grows too.

rows.name: Protracted linked wars
rows.why: This world scenario corresponds directly to this issue's prolonged, escalated war (I1).

rows.name: Taiwan Strait crisis
rows.why: If Washington's attention turns to Taiwan, the standoff drags on.

rows.name: Internal fracture in one pole
rows.why: In a world in which one pole is shaken from within, the probability of regime collapse or civil war in Iran (I3) rises sharply.

world.note: The probability of each of this issue's futures if each of the world scenarios A through E on the World Order tab materializes. The figures are set so that, weighted by the probabilities of the world scenarios, they match this issue's baseline probabilities within one percentage point (a total-probability check). All are judgment estimates.

counter.name: Iran (Hormuz)
counter.note: This is not a recommendation to Iran. It is Iran's best move, evaluated against goals derived from Iran's own documents and actions. The ranking of those goals is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. Because propaganda looms large in official documents, they have been calibrated against behavior.

goals.d: Preserve the system of the supreme leader (guardianship of the jurist) and consolidate Mojtaba Khamenei's succession
goals.src: Articles 5 and 57 of the Constitution; Article 177 (the Islamic character of the system and the institution of the supreme leader are not subject to revision)

goals.t: Rejecting foreign domination and expelling U.S. forces from the region
goals.d: Drive U.S. military bases out of the Gulf
goals.src: Article 152 of the Constitution (rejection of foreign domination; nonalignment with hegemonic powers); Mojtaba Khamenei's written message of May 2026 ("the nations and lands of the region will no longer serve as shields for American bases")

goals.d: Get the blockade and sanctions lifted and recover frozen assets
goals.src: Rezaei's conditions for ending the war (September 20, 2026); Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's seven-day roadmap of September 25 ($12 billion in frozen assets, lifting of oil sanctions, an end to the blockade)

goals.t: Preserving the right to enrich and nuclear capability
goals.d: Refuse to give up enrichment and hold on to a threshold capability—the ability to build a nuclear weapon if it chooses—as insurance for the regime
goals.src: The July 2025 law suspending cooperation with the IAEA; keeping about 440 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium beyond verification

goals.d: Protect allied forces in Lebanon and elsewhere
goals.src: Article 154 of the Constitution; the first of its conditions for ending the war (an end to the fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon); its abandonment of the June MOU over the Lebanon front

alts.name: Staying the course (selective passage and tolls, outlasting the blockade)
ev: Rallying effect and risk of economic collapse offset each other
Imposes costs on the United States

alts.name: Phased agreement with the United States (reopening the strait in exchange for lifting the blockade and sanctions and releasing frozen assets; nuclear issue deferred)
ev: De facto acceptance of U.S. forces remaining
Weakens ties with Hezbollah in Lebanon

alts.name: Expanding passage for non-adversarial countries (coordinated passage with South Korea, Japan, India, and some European states; isolating the United States)
ev: Separates the United States from its allies
alts.feas: High (already applied to China, India, and South Korea)

alts.name: Crossing the nuclear threshold (NPT withdrawal, weaponization)
ev: Loses even oil buyers such as China and India
alts.feas: Low to medium (nuclear facilities destroyed, so weaponization would take time)

alts.name: Gulf escalation (strikes on Saudi and Emirati facilities, Red Sea offensive)
ev: Makes Gulf states pay for hosting U.S. bases
alts.feas: High (about 70 percent of its prewar missile stock remains)

alts.name: Accepting a multilateral framework guaranteed by China
ev: Possible recognition of the right to enrich
alts.feas: Low (U.S. rejection; China's weak willingness to act as guarantor)

ranked.t: The best course is to widen passage for non-adversarial countries, prying the United States away from its allies, while pursuing a phased agreement that trades the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions step by step and defers the nuclear question. The strait is greater leverage when opened selectively than when closed.
If a deal with Washington stalls, hold to the status quo and wait it out. The constraint is how long the economy can hold out.
A multilateral framework guaranteed by China would favor Iran, but it cannot come about unless the United States accepts it.
Gulf escalation could upend the board, but it would also cost Iran oil buyers such as China and India.
The nuclear threshold is the ultimate insurance. The moment Iran crosses it, it hands its enemies a pretext for strikes aimed at regime change, so it ranks last.

counter.read: The earlier step that estimated adversaries' responses (Step 5) concluded that Iran might view an expanded Cheonghae Unit as siding with the United States and target South Korean ships. Judged by Iran's own goals, its best move is to keep treating South Korea as a non-adversarial country. The precedents show, however, that Iran has detained even non-adversarial countries' ships when there was an asset dispute, and has profited from doing so (the Hankuk Chemi in 2021, the Greek tankers in 2022). Iran's criterion for treating South Korea as an enemy is not whether it joins the fighting but what action it takes against Iranian assets and whether it keeps warships inside the strait.

pairs: South Korea
H3 + H1 + H4 (energy transition, noncombat escort, channel to Iran)
Iran
J2 + J1 (expanded passage for non-adversarial countries and a phased agreement; nuclear issue deferred)
United States (from the deciding powers table)
Use blockade and airstrikes to force through the demand that the nuclear question be settled first, and ask allies to contribute to securing the strait
twoway.equilibrium: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened. The sticking point is sequencing: who gives what first. Iran wants the lifting of the blockade and access to its assets first and the nuclear question later; the United States demands the nuclear question first. The memorandum of understanding of June 17 papered over this sequencing problem but collapsed over the Lebanon front. The current equilibrium is therefore a deadlock over sequencing, somewhere between a prolonged, escalated war (I1) and an end to the war (I2). Two clocks could break the deadlock: Iran's economic clock (a 90 percent drop in crude shipments and a collapsing rial) and America's political clock (the November midterm elections). Because a collapse of Gulf exports (I4) ranks low in Iran's own preferences and its economy is running out of time, the probability of regime collapse or civil war (I3) was raised from 10 percent to 12 percent.
twoway.zopa: The room for a deal lies in breaking the exchange into phases. In the first phase, the strait's reopening would be traded for the lifting of the blockade, and the removal or downblending of the roughly 440 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium would come in the second. The United States would get the outcome it wants—no Iranian bomb—and Iran the claim that it never surrendered its right to enrich. South Korea is not a party to such a deal. But as long as Iran treats it as a non-adversarial country, it has a narrow role in negotiating passage and providing humanitarian aid. Yet a deal of this structure was already signed once, in the June MOU, and then collapsed. For a deal to hold this time, it would need simultaneous execution through a third-country escrow, inclusion of the Lebanon front, and phased implementation tied to IAEA verification.
traps: A U.S.-Iranian deal is hostage to the Lebanon front. A single clash between Israel and Hezbollah could bring down the entire agreement on the strait, as it did in June. The next test of this link between the Lebanon front and the strait deal is Israel's election on October 27.

The deeper Iran's economic collapse, the stronger its incentive to deal—but the greater the risk of regime collapse (I3) as well. At the very point at which Washington concludes that a little more pressure will make Iran give in, there may be no one left to negotiate with.

The harder South Korea tries to satisfy both Washington's demands and Iran's treatment of it as a non-adversarial country, the more clearly each side will demand that it choose. That choice will show up in the wording of the Cheonghae Unit's mission.

ai.t: AI creates new targets in the Gulf and changes what South Korea stands to gain or lose in each future
ai.stake: Qatar produces about one-third of the world's helium as a by-product of LNG processing, and in 2025 South Korea relied on Qatar for 64.7 percent of its helium imports. In March 2026, two data centers in the UAE were hit directly by Iranian drones, and an AWS facility in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby explosion. The Bahrain facility was attacked again in April, and in July the IRGC claimed a further strike. The U.S. military said it struck more than 13,000 targets in 38 days of air operations before the cease-fire, and the Pentagon's chief digital and AI officer said the Maven system had been used in the campaign.
ai.moves: AI investment in the Gulf has not clearly changed the Gulf states' incentives to avoid escalation. The UAE, the largest AI investor, took the hardest line. Because that hard line emerged after its own data centers were hit, AI assets may even have become a reason for retaliation. The probabilities of this issue's six futures (I1–I6) therefore do not factor in AI. AI has, however, changed the probabilities of how the war unfolds (strikes on Gulf infrastructure, the pace of early attrition) by making data centers new targets and speeding up initial U.S. strikes. For South Korea, it changes the gains and losses in each future. In the case of helium, no disruption to South Korean chip production was reported even while Qatari production was halted for several months in 2026 (thanks to four to six months of inventory, recycling equipment, and diversified suppliers). The damage that actually materialized came in prices, not production stoppages. For a helium shortage to halt chip production, the cutoff from the Ras Laffan helium facilities would have to last well beyond the inventory period, and alternative suppliers and overland detours would also have to be blocked—a risk that arises in the extreme case of a collapse of Gulf exports (I4).
ai.lever: Adding alternative supply lines and stockpiles for helium and rare gases to the energy transition (H3) would, with the same preparations, reduce the exposure of chip production to helium disruptions. Because the scale of the helium risk depends less on whether supply is cut than on how long the cutoff lasts, stockpile targets should aim to lengthen the period that inventories can cover.
signs: Continued operation of the Ras Laffan helium facilities and shipments via Jeddah
When South Korean chipmakers' helium inventories run out
Prolonged service outages after strikes on Gulf data centers

brief.q: Amid the Iran war and the blockade of Hormuz, what should South Korea protect and what should it give up?
brief.a: Build around an energy transition—diversifying sources of crude imports and expanding stockpiles—while keeping a separate diplomatic channel to Iran, and pursue an expanded mission for the Cheonghae Unit only if its area of operations is confined to waters outside the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf. Freezing or disposing of Iranian assets in South Korea and cooperating in enforcing the U.S. blockade and sanctions are the most direct paths to Iranian retaliation.
brief.eq: Both the United States and Iran want the strait reopened, but a deal trading the strait's reopening for the lifting of the blockade and sanctions in phases was signed once, in June 2026, and collapsed within three weeks. Since then Washington, believing it is winning, has rejected a phased roadmap.
brief.human: The harm of this war falls most heavily on Iranians. In the future in which the Iranian regime collapses (12%), about 100 people per 100,000 would die each year and 10 percent of the population would be driven from their homes. For South Koreans, the risk in this issue is to income: if Gulf exports collapse again (11%), incomes would fall by about 5 percent from today's level.

items.name: The Iran-Iraq "Tanker War" and Iran's acceptance of Security Council Resolution 598
items.format: A war on each other's shipping: Iraq first attacked Iranian tankers and terminals, and Iran retaliated against ships linked to Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. On July 20, 1987, the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 598 (an immediate cease-fire, withdrawal to the borders, and repatriation of prisoners of war), and Iraq promptly accepted it.
items.outcome: Iran held out for nearly a year before accepting it on July 17, 1988, and the cease-fire took effect in August 1988. No peace treaty was ever concluded, and even at the height of the attacks, only about 2 percent of ships transiting the Gulf were damaged.
items.why: Iran's acceptance came only after its military commanders reported that victory was not possible within five years—which is why Khomeini likened accepting it to drinking from a poisoned chalice. What drove the decision was military pessimism more than diplomatic sequencing.
items.differs: Iran did not actually close the strait then; now it controls the strait through selective passage and tolls. And the adversary then was Iraq, whereas now the United States and Israel are direct belligerents.

items.name: U.S. Operation Earnest Will (reflagging and escort of Kuwaiti tankers) and Operation Praying Mantis
items.format: The United States reflagged 11 Kuwaiti tankers under the Stars and Stripes, making them American ships, and the navy escorted them. Mine clearance relied heavily on minesweeping forces from the Netherlands and other allies.
items.outcome: On the first convoy, the Bridgeton struck a mine (July 24, 1987). The Sea Isle City was hit by a Silkworm missile in Kuwaiti waters (October 16, 1987), and the U.S. frigate Samuel B. Roberts also struck a mine (April 14, 1988). The United States retaliated with Operation Nimble Archer (October 19, 1987) and Operation Praying Mantis (April 18, 1988), after which Iranian attacks on neutral shipping dropped sharply. On July 3, 1988, the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing 290 people.
items.why: The United States, as the escorting power, and Kuwait, as the protected state, immediately became direct Iranian targets. After a series of limited retaliatory strikes, the United States ended up fighting the Iranian navy head-on.
items.differs: Then, the United States claimed the role of protector rather than belligerent; now it is already a party to the war and is enforcing a blockade. The moment South Korea becomes an escorting power, it will stand where Kuwait and the United States stood in 1987.

items.name: The Algiers Accords (release of the hostages and unfreezing of assets)
items.format: Algeria mediated. About $7.955 billion in Iranian assets was moved into an escrow account at the Bank of England, and the Central Bank of Algeria confirmed the release of the hostages and the deposit of the assets simultaneously. Claims disputes were referred to the Iran-United States Claims Tribunal, and a $1 billion security account was set up.
items.outcome: The asset transfer was carried out overnight on January 19–20, 1981, and the hostages were freed just after Reagan's inauguration. The claims tribunal went on to serve as a forum for settling disputes for decades.
items.why: A credible third country certified both sides' performance simultaneously, and because the exchange was completed in a single step, neither side had to rely on the other's later compliance. Iran was also under separate pressure from Iraq's invasion (September 1980).
items.differs: The agenda then consisted only of hostages and assets; now the strait, the blockade, sanctions, the nuclear program, and the Lebanon front are all entangled. Disposing of nuclear material cannot be settled in a single simultaneous exchange.

items.name: From the JPOA interim deal through the JCPOA to the U.S. withdrawal
items.format: The P5+1 and Iran first concluded an interim agreement (the Joint Plan of Action), easing about $7 billion in sanctions in return for a halt to 20 percent enrichment and the dilution of highly enriched stocks. Frozen oil revenues were paid out in installments of $550 million. The JCPOA (July 14, 2015) then adopted an "Implementation Day" structure (January 16, 2016), under which sanctions were eased after the IAEA verified that the nuclear limits were being implemented.
items.outcome: Phased implementation premised on verification did work, but the first Trump administration withdrew from the deal on May 8, 2018. From 2019, Iran scaled back its commitments step by step.
items.why: The deal collapsed not because of how the sequence of implementation was designed but because of U.S. domestic politics and a change of administration. As an executive agreement rather than a treaty, it could not bind the next administration.
items.differs: Washington's negotiator today is the very president who tore up the JCPOA, and Iran's president has said publicly that he has no trust in the United States. Another difference from 2015 is the existence of about 400–440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent.

items.name: The 2019 tanker attacks and seizures: the U.S.-led IMSC and the European-led EMASoH compared
items.format: The IMSC (Operation Sentinel) is an escort arrangement launched in Bahrain by the United States, Britain, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the UAE, and others. EMASoH/Agenor is a low-intensity surveillance mission designed to avoid escalation; led by France, it drew participants including Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, and Norway, with political support from Germany and Portugal, and was launched on January 20, 2020, with its headquarters in Abu Dhabi.
items.outcome: After Britain detained the Iranian tanker Grace 1 off Gibraltar (July 4, 2019), Iran seized the Stena Impero (July 19, 2019). Greece, an EMASoH participant, handed Iranian oil over to the United States and then had two of its own tankers seized (May 27, 2022); it got the ships back only after promising an apology, compensation, and assurances against a recurrence. Right after the United States seized Iranian oil, the Chevron-chartered Advantage Sweet was seized (April 2023).
items.why: Iran's seizures were tit-for-tat retaliation against specific countries for actions they had taken against Iranian assets and cargo, more than a response to whether they had joined a coalition. EMASoH's defensive design did not invite attacks, but neither did it prevent retaliation arising from asset disputes.
items.differs: The 2019 episode was a peacetime gray-zone confrontation; now there is a full-scale war. Some 30 countries are reportedly considering joining the defensive navigation mission led by Britain and France in 2026, but Iran has warned that it will regard any military presence as support for aggression.

items.name: The Cheonghae Unit's independent deployment to Hormuz in 2020 (compared with Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force dispatch)
items.format: Rather than joining the IMSC, South Korea deployed independently to Hormuz by expanding the area of operations of its counterpiracy mission in the Gulf of Aden, notifying both Washington and Tehran before the decision. Japan explicitly excluded the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf from its area of operations and operated in the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea on the legal basis of "research and study."
items.outcome: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Abbas Mousavi, objected that South Korea's decision was unacceptable, but Iran did not immediately retaliate against South Korean ships over the deployment. A year later, however, a South Korean ship was seized while the Cheonghae Unit was on station (see P7, the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi).
items.why: The independent deployment succeeded in keeping Iran's reaction at the diplomatic level, but it did not demonstrate any real ability to protect ships.
items.differs: The year 2020 was a period of intermittent clashes; now there is a full-scale war. On September 5, 2026, a senior Iranian official warned that any South Korean involvement in the strait would amount to direct participation in the aggression against Iran, and on September 7 the Foreign Ministry spokesperson posted a warning to the same effect in Korean. The requirement for National Assembly consent has also been raised again for this deployment.

items.name: The seizure of the Hankuk Chemi and its release linked to frozen funds
items.format: The IRGC seized the South Korean-flagged Hankuk Chemi, citing marine pollution, but an Iranian official said the real hostage was the $7 billion tied up in South Korean banks. South Korea responded by sending diplomats and negotiating; the Cheonghae Unit was dispatched to the scene but could do nothing.
items.outcome: Iran freed most of the crew in February 2021. On February 24, 2021, South Korea agreed to unfreeze at least $1 billion (part of it used to pay Iran's arrears in UN dues), and the ship was released on April 9, 2021.
items.why: Iran seized a South Korean ship over an asset dispute without having labeled South Korea an adversary, and won substantive concessions as a result. For Iran, targeting a South Korean ship turned out to be a gain rather than a cost.
items.differs: The won-denominated funds frozen in South Korea were transferred to Qatar in 2023, removing the direct object of dispute. It has not been confirmed, however, where the $12 billion in frozen assets that Iran is now demanding is held or whether South Korea is involved.

items.name: The 2023 U.S.-Iranian prisoner swap and the transfer of $6 billion in funds frozen in South Korea to Qatar
items.format: After the United States issued a sanctions waiver, won-denominated funds held in South Korea were converted in Switzerland and moved to restricted accounts in Qatar (for humanitarian purchases only, €5.573 billion). Once this was confirmed, a five-for-five prisoner exchange took place simultaneously on September 18, 2023.
items.outcome: The exchange itself was completed. But on October 12, right after Hamas's attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, the United States and Qatar reached a "quiet understanding" that effectively blocked Iran from drawing on the funds.
items.why: A third-country escrow made simultaneous execution possible, but because the stage of actually spending the funds still lay ahead, they were frozen again when an outside shock (Hamas's attack on Israel) hit. For Iran, it became an experience of receiving money it could not spend.
items.differs: This experience, in which later stages were repeatedly reversed, underlies Iran's current demand for sanctions relief and the return of assets up front. Through this precedent, South Korea effectively extricated itself from the frozen-funds issue.

items.name: The "Twelve-Day War" of June 2025 and the verbal cease-fire
items.format: Following Israel's preemptive strikes, the United States struck Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan (June 22). After limited retaliation against Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Iran entered a cease-fire without any written agreement, following Trump's announcement and Qatari mediation.
items.outcome: Iran's parliament approved a plan to close Hormuz, but the Supreme National Security Council did not carry it out. The whereabouts of about 400–440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent became unclear, and Iran suspended cooperation with the IAEA.
items.why: Both sides, seeking to avoid the costs of escalation, chose to retaliate just enough to save face and then cease fire. But the nuclear question was left entirely unresolved, and eight months later it led to full-scale war.
items.differs: In 2025 the strait card remained a threat; in 2026 it is actually being played. The episode shows a cease-fire without a written agreement failing to prevent the next war.

items.name: The April 2026 cease-fire, the June 17 MOU and its collapse, and the rejection of the September 25 roadmap
items.format: A two-week cease-fire was reached through Pakistani mediation (with Chinese involvement), but the strait remained effectively closed, and on April 12 the United States imposed a naval blockade. The June 17 MOU was a phased agreement: free passage through the strait and mine clearance for 60 days, lifting of the blockade within 30 days, sanctions relief and access to assets, and the nuclear question deferred to follow-on negotiations. Iran's seven-day roadmap of September 25 would have eased assets, sanctions, and the blockade first, on days one through five, reopened the strait on day seven, and included cease-fires in Lebanon and Yemen.
items.outcome: A merchant ship was attacked on June 25 and the United States retaliated on June 27; on July 8 Trump said the MOU was over (it formally expired on August 17), and the blockade resumed. Trump rejected the roadmap, saying Iran wanted a deal "because they are losing so badly." During the MOU period, 23 of 26 South Korean-operated ships got out with Iranian approval (as of June 28).
items.why: The central cause of the collapse was that Article 1 of the MOU did not make clear whether it covered the Israel-Lebanon front. Since then, Washington, judging that it is winning, has turned to rejecting a phased agreement altogether.
items.differs: This precedent is the current situation itself. A phased agreement has already been signed once and collapsed within three weeks.

checks.reason: The Hankuk Chemi case (P7) shows that Iran seized a South Korean ship over an asset dispute without having labeled South Korea an adversary, and gained a concrete payoff—the unfreezing of $1 billion—in return. The subproposition that targeting South Korean ships is costly for Iran is therefore refuted. The Stena Impero, the Greek tankers, and the Advantage Sweet (P5) were all cases of retaliation for specific actions against Iranian assets and cargo, not for joining a coalition. On May 4, 2026, the Panamanian-flagged Namu, operated by South Korea's HMM, was hit by two unmanned aerial vehicles (Washington blamed Iran, Iran denied it, and the South Korean government has withheld judgment on who was responsible), and in early September 2026 Iran warned that any South Korean involvement in the strait (a senior official, September 5) and any military presence or operational participation in the Gulf and the strait (the Foreign Ministry spokesperson, in Korean, September 7) would be treated as joining the aggression.

The defensive design of EMASoH, which the United States did not lead, did help keep participants from being targeted, but Greece, a participant, still had ships seized over an asset dispute (P5). The Cheonghae Unit's independent deployment in 2020 kept Iran's reaction at the diplomatic level but did not prevent the seizure of the Hankuk Chemi a year later (P6, P7). Japan won acceptance from both sides by excluding the strait and the Gulf from its area of operations and briefing Tehran in advance. This time, with Seoul weighing patrol aircraft, a logistics support ship, and a mine-clearing unit, Iran has warned against any military presence in the Gulf and the strait, so an H1 that extends the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations into the strait could clash with the separate channel to Iran (H4).

In Earnest Will, the United States as escort and Kuwait as protected state immediately became targets of mines and missiles, which led to the head-on fighting of Operation Praying Mantis and the mistaken downing of Iran Air Flight 655. Because Iran has already warned, through a senior official on September 5 and in a Korean-language post by its Foreign Ministry spokesperson on September 7, that South Korean involvement in the strait would amount to direct participation in the aggression, sending combat units would immediately undermine the premise of key assessment C6—that Iran will not make an enemy of South Korea. Ranking the deployment of combat forces (H2) last fits the precedents.

A phased agreement was already signed in the MOU of June 17, 2026, but it collapsed within three weeks because the Lebanon front was left out (P10). The proposition that the room for a deal lies in breaking the exchange into phases does not, by itself, explain the conditions under which a deal can be reached and sustained. The exchanges that held (the 1981 Algiers Accords and the 2023 prisoner swap) were one-time simultaneous executions through a third-country escrow, whereas multistage agreements (the JCPOA and the spending stage of the 2023 funds) were overturned by a change of U.S. administration or by an outside shock. Trump's rejection of Iran's September 25 roadmap—which had the same structure as the MOU—on the grounds that Iran was losing also suggests that the current obstacle is not sequencing but differing perceptions of who is winning.

The Iran-Iraq War ended in a cease-fire a year after the cease-fire resolution was adopted, amid military pessimism, but it remained a cease-fire without a peace treaty (P1). After the collapse of the JCPOA, selective seizures recurred in an "open" strait from 2019 to 2023 (P5). Dividing the future into only two branches—cease-fire and reopening versus a protracted standoff—would leave out the intermediate state that has been most common in history (incomplete reopening).

checks.claim: Forecast: an 80 percent probability that Iran will not attack or seize South Korean-flagged or South Korean-operated ships through mid-2027
checks.reason: There are already the 2021 seizure of the Hankuk Chemi and the May 4, 2026, strike on the HMM-operated Namu (responsibility for which is disputed). Iran's Korean-language warning, the prospect of renewed U.S. bombing after the midterm elections, and the debate over expanding the Cheonghae Unit all fall within the forecast period. Given that seven months of war have already produced one event (the strike on the Namu) whose status under this forecast is ambiguous, 80 percent is too high.

checks.claim: Forecast: a 25 percent probability that the United States and Iran will sign a phased agreement by the end of March 2027
checks.reason: In 2026 two signed or declared agreements—the cease-fire and the MOU—emerged within four months, so the base rate for signing as such is not low. Twenty-five percent is a reasonable level that reflects Trump's rejection of the roadmap and the Iranian parliamentary speaker's insistence on seven conditions on October 4. But since both agreements collapsed within weeks, a signing alone carries little policy significance.

precedents.insight: Since 2019, Iran's seizures of ships have been tit-for-tat retaliation for actions specific countries took against Iranian assets and cargo, more than a response to whether they joined a coalition, and both Greece and South Korea recovered their ships through concessions. For South Korea, then, cooperation in enforcing the blockade and sanctions and asset disputes are more direct risk variables than participation in combat. Moreover, of the phased exchange agreements, the only ones that held were one-time simultaneous exchanges through a third-country escrow, and the settlements of 1981 and 1988 came when Iran was under other pressure (Iraq's invasion at the time of the 1981 Algiers Accords, military pessimism at the time of the 1988 cease-fire) or coincided with a change of U.S. administration.
uncertain: Final attribution of the May 4, 2026, strike on HMM's Namu (the South Korean government has withheld judgment, Washington blames Iran, and Iran denies it)
Where the $12 billion in frozen assets Iran is demanding is held, and whether any Iranian funds remain in South Korean financial institutions

The departure of 23 of 26 ships is confirmed as a post-MOU figure as of June 28, 2026; the number that left right after Iran's "non-adversarial" remark in March could not be confirmed. Whether South Korean ships paid tolls is also unconfirmed.
Whether any ships of countries participating in the 2026 defensive navigation mission led by Britain and France have been targeted by Iran
The precise dates for the Resolution 598 cease-fire (reportedly announced on August 8, 1988, and effective on August 20)
Whether the "military presence" Iran has warned against includes patrol aircraft and logistical support outside the strait (in the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea)
Annual statistics showing whether Iranian attacks on shipping increased after escorts began in 1987

links.work: Martin S. Navias & E. R. Hooton, 『Tanker Wars: The Assault on Merchant Shipping During the Iran-Iraq Crisis, 1980-1988』, 1996
links.idea: In the tanker war of 1981 to 1988, 451 merchant ships were attacked (283 by Iraq, 168 by Iran), yet even in the most intense period the attacks never stopped more than 2 percent of the ships transiting the Gulf. Because Iran's own oil exports depended on the same strait, it never carried out its threat to close it.
links.fit: Attaches a condition to the assessment that ranks a prolonged, escalated war (I1) first. By the base rate of the 1980s, a "blockade" persisted for long periods not as a physical cutoff but in the form of selective attacks and rising insurance premiums, which comes close to an incomplete reopening (I6). In 2026, by contrast, traffic through the strait remains at a fraction of peacetime levels according to ship-tracking data (five to 12 ships a day in early September, around 10 percent of the roughly 100 a day in peacetime), so the disappearance of the factor that restrained an Iranian blockade in the 1980s—Iran's own dependence on the strait for its crude exports—is grounds for setting the probability of a prolonged, escalated war (I1) higher.
links.limit: The main reason Iran kept the strait open in the 1980s was its dependence on its own exports. In 2026, Iran's exports are already blocked by the U.S. blockade, so closing the strait imposes almost no additional cost on Iran.
