hs7.split: Incomes for South Koreans, Europeans, Americans, Gulf residents and Russians are measured against the war continuing as it is today (no change in income). Iran's income baseline is a 2026 estimate.
hs7.method: Seven UN human security categories: Personal safety, Community, Political and Economic are scored 0–100; food, health and environment are alerts

changes.why: The scenarios for the Iran issue (Step 6) were reviewed again and their probabilities revised.

With attacks on tankers inside the Gulf continuing for three straight days and direct fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis widening, the probability of a collapse of Gulf exports was raised and that of an end to the war with full reopening lowered.

external.note: Likelihoods and conditional probabilities are provisional judgments. The variables overlap, so they should not be added or multiplied. The table shows which way the future leans if one variable occurs.

items.t: The United States resumes large-scale strikes
items.def: Three or more consecutive days of strikes on the Iranian mainland, announced as a resumption of operations
items.why: Large-scale strikes provoke retaliation and pressure on the strait rather than Iranian concessions, delaying a deal (I2, I6) and raising the odds of a prolonged war (I1) and of retaliation against Gulf facilities (I4). Repeated strikes on command facilities also raise the odds of regime collapse (I3).
items.sign: On October 8, President Trump said the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. Signs to watch after the vote: additional deployments of aircraft carriers and bombers, advisories urging U.S. citizens in the Gulf to leave, and an ultimatum with a set deadline (forecast 'U.S. resumes strikes on the Iranian mainland', 50% by the end of 2026).
items.basis: When struck in June 2025, Iran retaliated with missiles against Israel and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar; in the 2026 war it added control of the strait. Even after the June memorandum of understanding, U.S. strikes on coastal facilities on June 27 and Iranian restrictions on passage fed off each other, and the deal collapsed.
items.crit: The United States strikes military, energy or command facilities on the Iranian mainland on three or more consecutive days, and the White House or the Pentagon announces it as a resumption of operations. Strikes no larger than the June–July 2026 attacks on coastal facilities do not count.

items.t: Hormuz bypass routes cut off
items.def: Saudi exports via the East-West Pipeline and Yanbu, or traffic through Bab el-Mandeb, halted for a long period
items.why: If Saudi Arabia's Red Sea bypass is also blocked for an extended period while passage through Hormuz is restricted, the Gulf moves closer to a collapse of exports (I4).
items.sign: Three or more Houthi attacks a month on tankers carrying Saudi crude or leaving Yanbu; repeated attacks from Iraq on pipeline pumping stations; Pakistani or Turkish forces deployed under the Mecca defence pact joining combat in the Saudi-Houthi war.
items.basis: In June 2026 Saudi Arabia rerouted about two-thirds of the crude it normally shipped through Hormuz to the East-West Pipeline and Yanbu (Kpler data, [secondary]). On September 11, drones flying in from Iraq damaged two of the pipeline's pumping stations, halting flows for 11 days until September 22; Saudi Arabia made up the gap by shipping more through Hormuz. The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi ships on July 20, took most of Yemen's Red Sea coast in early September (in October government forces claimed to have retaken parts of it), and on September 24 fired six ballistic missiles at Yanbu and Taif (all intercepted). Tankers sailing from Yanbu to Asia must pass through Bab el-Mandeb.
items.crit: Met if crude loadings via the East-West Pipeline or Yanbu fall below 1 million barrels a day for more than 30 days, or if tanker traffic through Bab el-Mandeb stays below half its first-half 2026 average for more than two weeks.

items.t: Splits in Iran's leadership
items.def: A formal process to replace the Supreme Leader, defection of Revolutionary Guards commanders, or anti-government forces seizing a city
items.why: A split in the leadership could lead to regime collapse or civil war (I3) or to military rule by the Revolutionary Guards, and it unsettles the counterpart to any deal.
items.sign: Written messages in the Supreme Leader's name stop; reports of an extraordinary session of the Assembly of Experts; a string of replacements among senior Revolutionary Guards figures.
items.basis: Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded Ali Khamenei after he was killed in the February 28 strikes, has not appeared in public in person since; there are only videos of uncertain date released by the Iranian authorities and written messages ([secondary]). The 1979 revolution was decided when the military command declared neutrality. Unlike the shah's professional army, however, the Revolutionary Guards are both the regime's ideological army and an economic actor, so a split could lead not only to regime collapse or civil war (I3) but also to military rule in which the Guards replace the clerical leadership. Either way, custody of the roughly 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent that lies outside IAEA verification becomes a new risk.
items.crit: Met if any of the following occurs: (1) a formal process to replace the Supreme Leader or declare him incapacitated begins, such as a convening of the Assembly of Experts; (2) the dismissal or defection of the Revolutionary Guards commander-in-chief or a major military commander becomes public; (3) Kurdish, Baluch or other armed anti-government groups hold a county seat for a week or more.

items.t: An Israel-Lebanon ceasefire
items.def: A ceasefire takes effect and a timetable for Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon is announced
items.why: If the Lebanese front is settled, one major obstacle to a U.S.-Iran deal (I2, I6) disappears.
items.sign: Coalition talks after Israel's October 27 election (early-October polls put Netanyahu's bloc at 51–55 seats, with the opposition also short of a majority without the Arab parties; forecast 'Netanyahu returns as prime minister', 20%); wider deployment of the Lebanese army in the south; U.S. or French ceasefire proposals.
items.basis: Iran has insisted that any end to the war must cover every front, including Lebanon, and the June memorandum began to unravel when Iran again restricted passage after Israeli strikes on Lebanon on June 20. Israel was not a party to the memorandum. In June the Israeli government said it would not withdraw from southern Lebanon.

items.t: A deal that transfers assets and reopens the strait on the same day
items.def: Permission to transfer assets and a timetable for lifting the blockade and reopening the strait set out in a single agreement
items.why: A mechanism that spares each side from conceding first raises the chance that a deal is reached (I2, I6), though it does not guarantee the deal will hold.
items.sign: Mediation proposals from Pakistan, Qatar or Oman that set out a schedule for asset transfers through third-country accounts alongside a schedule for lifting the blockade; a general license issued by the U.S. Treasury.
items.basis: On September 18, 2023, a prisoner exchange took place on the same day it was confirmed that about $6 billion in Iranian funds frozen in South Korea had been transferred to accounts in Qatar. A month later, after the Hamas attack, the United States and Qatar blocked Iran from using the funds. Same-day execution helps a deal get done but does not guarantee it lasts. The June 2026 memorandum postponed asset transfers until a final agreement and collapsed within three weeks amid fighting on the Lebanese front. South Korea was a party to the 2023 transfer, so Seoul has a small part it can play in this variable.
items.crit: Met if the U.S. Treasury permits the transfer of Iranian assets through an institution in a third country and the same agreement sets out a timetable for lifting the blockade and reopening the strait.

items.t: Congress restrains the war
items.def: Congress limits military action against Iran by law or through the budget by the end of 2028
items.why: If Congress restricts the war through appropriations, Washington has fewer means of pressure, lowering the odds of a prolonged war (I1) and tilting the outlook toward reopening (I6).
items.sign: Provisions restricting funds for military action against Iran in the new Congress's defense appropriations bill or a continuing resolution in January 2027; Brent crude holding at $100 a barrel or more and gasoline and diesel prices that keep rising.
items.basis: The House passed resolutions restricting military action against Iran three times in 2026 (the third on September 15, 220–204), but the Senate rejected one 49–50 on September 24. If Democrats win both chambers in the November midterms, restricting the war through appropriations becomes possible, but appropriations bills are also subject to presidential veto, so Congress would have to be willing to risk a government shutdown. In 1973 Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment with more than two-thirds majorities in both chambers, barring funds for U.S. combat in Indochina, and the bombing of Cambodia ended on August 15 that year, though U.S. ground forces had already withdrawn.

items.t: A new U.S. administration changes course
items.def: The president inaugurated in 2029 formally lifts the blockade or resumes direct talks within the first year
items.why: If a new president does not want to inherit the war, the balance tilts toward lifting the blockade and negotiating, raising the odds of a reopening (I2, I6).
items.sign: Candidates' positions on the Iran war in the 2028 presidential race; the November 2028 election result.
items.basis: The U.S. presidency may change hands before 2030. The Biden administration, inaugurated in 2021, began talks in Vienna to restore the Iran nuclear deal within three months of taking office. If the war lasts into 2029, a new president will have a strong incentive not to inherit it. However, the variable becomes moot if the successor stays the course or the war ends before then.

items.t: Iran declares it is crossing the nuclear threshold
items.def: Iran announces withdrawal from the NPT or the start of 90% enrichment
items.why: A withdrawal announcement would sharply raise the odds of a nuclear-armed Iran (I5) and strengthen the U.S. and Israeli case for attack, also raising the odds of a prolonged war (I1).
items.sign: A bill to withdraw from the NPT introduced or voted on in Iran's parliament; signs that underground facilities at Fordow or Isfahan are back in operation; expulsion of IAEA inspectors.
items.basis: About 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent has been outside IAEA verification since June 2025. On September 9, 2026, the IAEA Board of Governors referred Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, and on October 4 an Iranian lawmaker said withdrawal from the NPT would be considered. North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003 and conducted its first nuclear test three years later, in 2006.

reads: The variable most likely to occur is one that prolongs the war (large-scale U.S. strikes, 65%), and that is already reflected in the baseline probabilities. Conversely, if strikes do not resume, the odds of a reopening (I2, I6) rise to around 53 percent.

The greatest danger for South Korea is that the bypass routes are cut off while passage through Hormuz is restricted. When the pipeline stopped in September, Saudi Arabia filled the gap by shipping more through Hormuz, but if both routes are blocked there is no way to make up the shortfall. That is why South Korea's response should rest on larger reserves and more diverse suppliers (H3).

The variables that would bring a deal forward (an Israel-Lebanon ceasefire, a deal that transfers assets and reopens the strait on the same day, a change of course in Washington) are all decided outside South Korea. A split in Iran's leadership or a declaration that Iran is crossing the nuclear threshold would not end the war but change the nature of the risk.

s2.subject: USA

client.name: U.S. government
client.note: The goals are taken from the December 2025 National Security Strategy, the January 2026 National Defense Strategy and President Trump's statements of war aims. The order among them is not written in those documents; it is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. On September 25 the United States rejected Iran's roadmap for reopening the strait, and it has kept demanding since then that the nuclear issue come first. Because Washington put the nuclear issue first even at the cost of keeping the strait closed, G2 is ranked above G3. The National Security Strategy promised to reduce the weight of the Middle East and shift burdens to allies, yet two months later the United States went to war, and on October 1 it sent an additional carrier strike group. Where documents and actions diverge, this analysis gives more weight to actions.

goals.t: Safety of the homeland and Americans
goals.d: Remove Iran's threat to the U.S. homeland, its citizens and U.S. forces abroad
goals.src: 2025 National Security Strategy ('first and foremost, the continued survival and safety of the United States as an independent, sovereign republic'); the president's statement of February 28, 2026; the first line of effort of the 2026 National Defense Strategy (defending the homeland)

goals.d: Keep Iran from getting even close to nuclear capability
goals.src: War aims stated by the president on March 20, 2026; the strikes of June 2025 and of 2026

goals.t: Gulf energy and navigation through the strait
goals.d: Keep Gulf energy out of enemy hands and keep shipping moving through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea
goals.src: The 2025 National Security Strategy's core interests in the Middle East

goals.t: Security of Israel and regional allies
goals.d: Protect Israel and Gulf partners
goals.src: 2025 National Security Strategy; war aims stated by the president on March 20, 2026

goals.d: Remove Iran's ability to threaten through ballistic missiles, its navy, its defense industry and proxy forces
goals.src: War aims of March 20, 2026; the April 1 address to the nation; 2025 National Security Strategy (the region must not be an incubator or exporter of terror)

goals.d: Keep the United States from bearing the costs alone, have allies do their part, and keep the Middle East from again becoming the top priority of U.S. foreign policy
goals.src: Third line of effort of the 2026 National Defense Strategy (burden-sharing); 2025 National Security Strategy ('shift burdens, build peace')

s2.deciders: The decision-maker is President Trump. Congress can constrain him through the War Powers Resolution and appropriations, and Israel could derail a phased agreement with a unilateral strike.

alts.name: Staying the course
alts.desc: Keep the naval blockade and intermittent strikes in place and demand that the nuclear issue come first.

alts.name: Resuming large-scale strikes
alts.desc: Widen strikes on the Iranian mainland again to hit remaining nuclear, missile and naval capabilities.

alts.name: Phased agreement (nuclear issue in phase two)
alts.desc: In the first phase, trade the reopening of the strait for the lifting of the blockade, and defer the enriched-uranium question to a second phase.

alts.name: Phased agreement + enrichment halt in phase one
alts.desc: Include in the first phase a halt to 60 percent enrichment and a declaration of the enriched-uranium stockpile (or its downblending inside Iran under monitoring), and return frozen assets in installments tied to each stage of verification.

alts.name: Phased agreement + third-country shipment in phase one
alts.desc: Ship the enriched uranium to a third country in the first phase.

alts.name: Forcing the strait open
alts.desc: Open the strait by clearing mines, suppressing coastal missile sites and carrying out amphibious landings.

alts.name: Pursuing regime change
alts.desc: Back opposition forces and target the leadership.

alts.name: Declaring victory and withdrawing
alts.desc: Declare the goals achieved, lift the blockade and draw down forces.

alts.name: Special operation to seize the enriched uranium
alts.desc: Send in ground forces to find and secure the enriched uranium.

alts.name: Escort coalition and allied burden-sharing
alts.desc: Ask South Korea, Japan and Europe to escort shipping through the strait and share the costs. Used alongside other options.

alts.name: Pressure through China
alts.desc: Ask China, the largest buyer of Iranian oil, to apply pressure. Used alongside other options.

alts.name: Restraining unilateral Israeli strikes
alts.desc: Ask Israel not to strike on its own while a deal is in force. Used alongside other options.

responses: U0
Expand selective passage to drive a wedge between 'friendly' countries and U.S. allies, and extend how long it can hold out.
U1
Hit Gulf infrastructure and the Red Sea bypass routes, and keep the enriched uranium as a bargaining chip.
U2
Accept the first phase, secure the lifting of the blockade and the assets up front, and stall on the second phase.
Offer easily reversible commitments, such as halting enrichment, but possibly refuse verification of the stockpile, claiming it is buried under rubble and its whereabouts unknown.
Refuse, because the enriched uranium is its last lever.
U3
Lay more mines and strike desalination plants in the Gulf.
U4
Rally the public against the outside threat and bring forward a declaration of crossing the nuclear threshold.
U5
Declare victory and entrench transit tolls and selective passage as a standing arrangement.
U9
Call the operation an invasion and widen the scope of retaliation.
U6
Single out ships from contributing countries for pressure to unsettle the coalition.

eval.base: Each score shows how that goal would stand at the end of 2027, compared with today, if the option were chosen: +2 achieved, +1 progress, 0 unchanged, −1 setback, −2 major setback (judgment estimates).

rows.why: The restrictions on the strait remain, as do the roughly 440 kg of unverified enriched uranium. The blockade keeps shrinking Iran's economy, while the costs of releasing strategic oil reserves and of high gasoline prices mount.

It would destroy more facilities, but as long as the location of the enriched uranium is unknown it cannot settle the nuclear issue. If large-scale strikes resume, the probability of the futures in which the strait reopens (I2, I6) falls from 40 percent to 33 percent, and that of a collapse of Gulf exports (I4) rises.
The strait reopens and risks and costs for U.S. forces fall, but lifting the blockade gives Iran resources to rebuild and pushes the nuclear issue back. Assets once returned are hard to claw back.
As in the 2013 Joint Plan of Action, assets are returned in tranches tied to verification. Iran may accept a halt to enrichment yet refuse verification of the stockpile.
The 2015 shipment of low-enriched uranium to Russia is a precedent, but the enriched uranium is Iran's last lever and its location has not been confirmed.
Landings and seizure would be needed under the threat of mines, coastal missiles and drones, and harassment could continue even after the strait opens.
Regime change by air power alone has rarely succeeded, and if the regime collapses the whereabouts of the enriched uranium become even less certain.
Costs fall sharply, but pressure is lifted with the enriched uranium still unverified, and Iran entrenches its control of the strait as leverage.
If it succeeds it settles the nuclear issue, but the location is unconfirmed and the risks of a ground operation are high.
During the 1987–88 escort operation, escorted ships were rarely hit. But Iran singles out ships of contributing countries for pressure.
Chinese ships pass through the strait as those of a 'friendly' country, so Beijing has little reason to pressure Iran, and its price would be trade concessions.
A unilateral Israeli strike could derail a phased agreement. Restraining Israel is a condition for an agreement but strains the alliance.

s2.rule: The goals were compared in order of priority: the score on the higher-ranked goal decides first, and the next goal counts only in a tie (scores are not added across goals). Options with a high escalation risk or that cannot be reversed were moved down one place (R8), and options rated 'low' on feasibility were not treated as courses in their own right, only as terms to put forward in negotiations. A phased agreement (U2) ranks above staying the course (U0) on the first goal, the safety of the homeland and Americans.

ranked.name: Phased negotiations with nuclear conditions
ranked.id: U0 → U2″·U2′ → U2, with U6 and U8
ranked.t: Keep the blockade in place while proposing a phased agreement with nuclear conditions. Open by demanding that the enriched uranium be shipped to a third country (U2″), and be prepared to settle for a halt to 60 percent enrichment and a declaration of the stockpile (U2′). If there is no progress within 60 days of the midterm elections (November 3), or if signs of a collapse in Gulf exports emerge (the Red Sea bypass is cut off or Gulf infrastructure is attacked), fall back to a phased agreement that defers the nuclear issue to a second phase (U2). Pair this with escort burden-sharing (U6) and restraint of unilateral Israeli strikes (U8).

ranked.name: Phased agreement (nuclear issue in phase two)
ranked.t: Secures the strait and lower costs at the price of deferring the nuclear issue.

ranked.name: Staying the course
ranked.t: Reversible, but the strait stays closed.

ranked.name: Declaring victory and withdrawing
ranked.t: Lifts pressure with the enriched uranium still unverified. It ranks above large-scale strikes because it does not sacrifice the first goal (the safety of the homeland and Americans).

ranked.name: Resuming large-scale strikes
ranked.t: Sharply reduces Iran's power projection but sacrifices the other goals, with a high risk of escalation.

ranked.name: Pursuing regime change
ranked.t: Irreversible and unlikely to succeed.

ranked.name: Special operation to seize the enriched uranium
ranked.t: Would settle the nuclear issue if it succeeded, but the location of the enriched uranium is unconfirmed and the risk of escalation is high.

ranked.name: Forcing the strait open
ranked.t: Carries the highest risk of U.S. ground casualties and escalation.

rec.basis: If the United States takes its top-ranked course, the likelihood of a deal that transfers assets and reopens the strait on the same day (external variable X5) would rise from 30 percent to 35–45 percent (a judgment estimate), and the futures were recalculated with the probabilities conditional on that variable. The change is small because the outcome depends far more on Iran's conditions for ending the war than on U.S. choices.

prec: Joint Plan of Action, November 24, 2013: Iran diluted or converted its 20 percent enriched uranium and stopped enriching above 5 percent (enrichment to 5 percent remained permitted); in return, it received $4.2 billion in frozen oil revenue in installments tied to IAEA verification. That stockpile had been declared and monitored; today's 60 percent stockpile must first be located.

The 2015 shipment to Russia: on December 28, 2015, five months after the nuclear deal was signed, Iran shipped a little over 11,000 kg of low-enriched uranium to Russia. It is the precedent for a third-country shipment (U2″).

The 1987–88 Tanker War: escorted ships were rarely hit during the U.S. escort operation. U.S. naval strikes on April 18, 1988, and Iraqi ground offensives were the pressure that led Iran to accept the cease-fire resolution (July 1988); the cease-fire took effect on August 20. Today no force is pressing Iran on the ground.

After the U.S. strikes and the cease-fire of June 2025, about 440 kg of 60 percent enriched uranium disappeared from IAEA verification. This underpins the assessment of declaring victory and withdrawing (U5).
people: Life scores change little in any future. If Gulf exports collapse, incomes fall by about 2 percent. The risk falls mainly on U.S. service members and rises under large-scale strikes, a forced opening of the strait or a special operation.

The group hit hardest. Staying the course keeps the blockade in place and so drags out, longer than any other option, the hardship of 69.9 percent inflation and a collapsing rial; large-scale strikes, forcing the strait open and regime change raise the risk of casualties, regime collapse and civil war.
Gulf residents, migrant workers and seafarers
Large-scale strikes and forcing the strait open carry a high risk of attacks on desalination and power plants and of ships being hit or seized. Most migrant workers in the Gulf come from South Asia.
They rely on Iranian gas and electricity, so strikes on Iranian infrastructure affect them.
South Koreans and Europeans, and people in low-income South Asian countries facing worse fuel shortages, see their burden ease under a phased agreement that reopens the strait.
The risk of a nuclear-armed Iran grows with a declaration of victory and withdrawal and with regime change, and falls under phased negotiations with nuclear conditions.

diff.note: The people-centered ranking weighs the harm to affected groups' lives through 2027 together with the risk of a nuclear-armed Iran (a value judgment).
rows: Hardship for Iranians and the energy burden last longer because the strait opens later, but the risk of a nuclear-armed Iran falls.
Phased agreement (nuclear issue in phase two)
The war stops and the strait reopens soonest. The nuclear risk then depends on the second-phase talks.
The blockade harms Iranian civilians for the longest time.
Fighting stops quickly, but the risk of a nuclear-armed Iran remains, as does a system of transit tolls.
Harm to Iranian civilians rises, as do the chances of regime collapse and Gulf export collapse.
Carries the greatest risk of civil war and of losing track of the enriched uranium.
Special operation to seize the enriched uranium
Its low chance of success means it does little to reduce the nuclear risk, while the risk of escalation is high.
High risks to Gulf infrastructure and seafarers.
diff.pay: The more Washington insists on nuclear conditions up front, the better it secures the goal of preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon (G2), but the longer Iranians and people in energy-importing countries bear the cost. The choice between the two is left to readers and to the strategic actor.

s2.fit: South Korea's top-ranked combination (the energy transition, noncombat escorts and a separate channel to Iran) does not conflict with Washington's top-ranked course. Because South Korea has ruled out sending combat forces, its share of escort burden-sharing (U6) extends only to noncombat escorts; and if Washington opts for negotiations with nuclear conditions, South Korea's channel to Iran also becomes useful to the United States as a conduit for talks.
falsify: If Iran formally offers, for the first phase, a halt to 60 percent enrichment and downblending under monitoring, the feasibility of the 60 percent enrichment halt (U2′) will be raised and that step moved earlier in the top-ranked course.

If, after the midterm elections, Washington resumes large-scale strikes (U1) or forces the strait open (U3), the judgment that U.S. choices do little to change the outcome (Conclusion 9) will be recalculated using the probabilities conditional on a resumption of large-scale strikes.
If the Senate passes a war powers resolution (f71), the place of limiting costs and sharing burdens (G6) in the order of goals will be reexamined and the ranking of options reviewed.

If approval of the president's handling of Iran rises above 40 percent in Quinnipiac polling (28 percent in the September 24–27 poll), the judgment about domestic constraints on escalation will be revisited.

If Israel formally announces a unilateral operation aimed at toppling the Iranian regime (following up on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's remarks of October 21), the feasibility of restraining unilateral Israeli strikes (U8) will be lowered from medium.
pub: American public opinion runs against escalation. In Quinnipiac's July poll, 74 percent opposed sending ground troops, and in its September 24–27 poll 28 percent approved of the president's handling of Iran (66 percent disapproved). In the September 3–6 poll, 39 percent favored keeping forces in place while negotiating, 30 percent withdrawing without negotiations and 22 percent expanding operations (the questions differ, so the results are not linked as a single time series). Forcing the strait open (U3) and the special operation (U9), which require ground forces, therefore face the tightest domestic constraints, while the top-ranked course of keeping the blockade in place while negotiating sits closest to the most common response.

No congressional resolution has ever halted military action. But the Senate defeat on September 24 came down to a single vote, and Republican defections are growing (four in the House in July, seven in the House and four in the Senate in September). If the balance of seats changes after the midterm elections, the weight of limiting costs and sharing burdens (G6) would rise, and the trigger in the top-ranked course for falling back to a phased agreement (U2) could be brought forward.

strategies.subject: POL
strategies.title: The Russia-NATO standoff: How should Poland prepare for the Russian threat?
facts: Russia's attacks below the threshold of war have intensified in 2026. On July 30 a Russian cruise missile, believed to be a Kh-101, came down in a field in Poland's Lublin province (Polish press reports). On August 4 a drone carrying explosives was found among Ukraine-bound cargo planes at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, and on September 1 the German federal government formally named Russia as responsible. On August 31 fire broke out at the Polish plant of WB Electronics, the EU's largest drone maker; Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it arson beyond any doubt and said it appeared to have been carried out on Russia's behalf (Polish press reports).

September brought a string of incidents along NATO's eastern flank. On the 14th a Russian warship fired flares at a Danish helicopter, and on the 15th NATO fighters shot down a drone over Lithuania. On the 23rd a Russian Mi-8 helicopter that had taken off from Kaliningrad entered Polish airspace, penetrating about 300 meters and remaining for 42 seconds (according to Poland's Operational Command). It was the first publicly reported case of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland's land border.

A Russian diplomatic document reported by Reuters on September 30 claimed that NATO was preparing an air and sea blockade of Kaliningrad and warned that Russia was ready to use every means, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance tried to isolate the exclave. The text of the document has not been made public. On October 1, at the Valdai Discussion Club, President Vladimir Putin confirmed that its contents were accurate.

The U.S. posture in Europe is wavering. In May 2026 Washington announced the withdrawal of about 5,000 troops from Germany and canceled the deployment of an armored brigade to Poland. Then, on May 21, President Donald Trump announced that he would send 5,000 U.S. troops to Poland. In September, Poland's deputy defense minister said the number of U.S. troops stationed in the country had fallen to about 6,500–7,000, down from roughly 10,000 before (press reports). In June, Poland formally requested a new permanent base.

Poland is paying a heavy price. By NATO's measure, its defense spending has risen from 2.21 percent of GDP in 2022 to an estimated 4.68 percent in 2026. It has signed contracts for South Korean K2 tanks, K9 self-propelled howitzers, and Chunmoo rocket launchers, as well as 128 deals for U.S. weapons (about $63 billion), and it is spending about 10 billion zlotys through 2028 on fortifications along its eastern border, known as the East Shield.

Poland's president and government are at odds over security policy. On March 12 President Karol Nawrocki vetoed the law implementing the EU's SAFE defense loans, and the government took a different route to sign the loan agreement on May 8 (press reports). On nuclear deterrence, the president's office puts U.S. nuclear sharing first, while the government gives priority to cooperation with France.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave wedged between Poland and Lithuania. It has about 1.03 million residents and hosts Russia's Baltic Fleet and Iskander missile units. The stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border between Kaliningrad and Belarus, known as the Suwałki Gap, is the only land route linking the three Baltic states with the rest of NATO.

people.how: Sabotage, airspace violations, the burden of defense spending, the risk of war
The risk of the Suwałki Gap being cut off, price shocks from war and sanctions
Hybrid attacks on undersea cables, airports, and power plants
A blockade crisis, becoming a target in a war
Shifts in Polish politics, resentment stirred by the issue of sabotage proxies
Border closures and the suspension of the right to seek asylum

alts.name: Staying the course
alts.desc: Keep defense spending at around 4.5–4.8 percent of GDP and continue buying South Korean and U.S. weapons and building the East Shield. Pursue the bilateral relationship with Washington (including a request for permanent bases) alongside EU defense loans and cooperation with Germany and France in Europe. Respond to attacks below the threshold of war with public attribution, consulate closures, and arrests and prosecutions; send no troops to Ukraine.

G1.t: Baseline

alts.name: A permanent U.S. troop presence
alts.desc: Expand the permanent presence of U.S. troops, even if Poland must shoulder more of the cost of permanent bases. Use purchases of U.S. weapons and the Polish president's personal channel to President Trump as leverage.

G1.t: With allied troops on the ground, a territorial grab becomes hard to attempt. The score assumes combat power of brigade size or larger (including air defense and fire support); if the presence stays symbolic, it drops to +1

G6.t: Diverts money and attention from the debate on European self-reliance

G7.t: Poland bears the cost of the bases

alts.name: Strengthening the European pillar
alts.desc: As insurance against dependence on the United States, take an active part in EU defense (SAFE), regional defense with Germany, the Nordic countries, and the Baltic states, and the debate on extending France's nuclear deterrent to Europe.

G1.t: Insurance in case the U.S. commitment wavers

G2.t: EU defense loans are already part of staying the course (A0), so they add nothing

G3.t: EU defense loans are already part of staying the course (A0), so they add nothing

alts.name: Joining NATO nuclear sharing
alts.desc: Ask for U.S. nuclear weapons to be deployed in Poland. This is the option the president's office puts first.

G1.t: Deterrence rises, but so does the risk of escalation, because this is precisely the danger Russia's nuclear deterrence doctrine targets

G4.t: Deepens ties with the United States

alts.name: Nuclear cooperation with France
alts.desc: Seek cooperation with France's nuclear forces and their rotational deployment to Poland. The government is taking part in the discussions.

G1.t: Deterrence rises, but so does the risk of escalation

G6.t: Builds up Europe's capacity to deter

alts.name: An independent nuclear arsenal
alts.desc: Withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and develop nuclear weapons. The option is examined rather than ruled out on moral grounds.

G1.t: High risk during the development period

G7.t: Sanctions and capital flight would badly damage the economy

alts.name: Airspace and border response
alts.desc: Loosen the rules of engagement for drones and helicopters that violate Polish airspace, close the border with Belarus, and respond with cyber operations against those behind sabotage. Press NATO to spell out the criteria under which its Strategic Concept allows Article 5 to apply to hybrid attacks as well.

G1.t: Shooting down a crewed Russian aircraft would itself be a deadly incident, so the net effect is set at zero

G3.t: Directly blunts attacks below the threshold of war

G7.t: Closing the border hurts revenue from China-Europe rail freight

alts.name: Cracking down on the shadow fleet
alts.desc: Take part in boarding and seizing tankers of Russia's shadow fleet in the Baltic Sea.

G1.t: The measure with the highest risk of a naval clash

alts.name: Exercises near Kaliningrad
alts.desc: Hold NATO exercises near Kaliningrad to pressure Russia into pulling troops from the Ukrainian front, while taking no offensive action against Kaliningrad itself. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski proposed this on September 11, 2026.

G1.t: Russia lists large-scale exercises near its borders among the dangers it would answer with nuclear deterrence

G5.t: Could draw Russian troops away from the Ukrainian front

alts.name: Backing restrictions on transport to Kaliningrad
alts.desc: Support the restrictions on transit and maritime transport to Kaliningrad led by Lithuania and the EU. Because the overland transit route to Kaliningrad runs through Lithuania, Poland holds almost no levers of its own.

G1.t: Could directly trigger a Kaliningrad blockade crisis

alts.name: Risk-reduction mechanisms (decoupled)
alts.desc: Pursue risk-reduction mechanisms, such as hotlines and agreements to prevent accidental clashes, at the NATO level and keep them separate from the question of forward deployment.

G1.t: Keeps accidental clashes from escalating into war

G7.t: Lowers the economic cost of crises

alts.name: Risk-reduction mechanisms (traded)
alts.desc: Pursue risk-reduction mechanisms in exchange for scaling back NATO's forward deployment.

G1.t: No change

G4.t: Concedes Russia's core demand and badly undermines the allied troop presence

G5.t: Increases Russia's leverage in negotiations over the war in Ukraine

G7.t: Lowers the economic cost of crises

alts.name: Expanding support for Ukraine
alts.desc: Increase military aid to Ukraine and, after a ceasefire, either send Polish troops to a multinational force or serve as its rear support hub.

G1.t: Puts Poland near the top of the list of sabotage targets

G5.t: Contributes the most to this objective

alts.name: Total defense and resilience
alts.desc: Finnish-style total defense. It combines large-scale military training (a target of 400,000 people in 2026; actual participation could not be confirmed), protection of critical infrastructure such as the power grid, railways, and telecommunications, and stronger sabotage investigations and counterintelligence. Training and parts of the East Shield are already included in staying the course, so what is new is the actual spending of the civil defense budget and stronger counterintelligence. One caveat: in an IBRiS survey in the summer of 2026 (as reported in the press), 27.0 percent said they would take part in the country's defense if war threatened.

G1.t: Reduces the damage from attacks below the threshold of war

G3.t: The most direct means of countering attacks below the threshold of war

alts.name: Scaling back involvement in Ukraine
alts.desc: Reduce, or attach conditions to, Poland's role as a logistics hub for Ukraine and its support for refugees, and lower the level of direct confrontation with Russia (the Hungarian and Slovak model).
alts.prob: Low under the current government; medium after the 2027 parliamentary election
alts.esc: Low in the short term, high in the long term

G1.t: Weakens the motive for hybrid attacks in the short term but invites Russia's next demand

ev.esc2: Low in the short term, high in the long term
ev.feas: Low under the current government; medium after the 2027 parliamentary election

alts.name: A security accord between the president and the government
alts.desc: The president and the government adopt a joint national security strategy and agree on joint procedures for responding to airspace incidents and sabotage, as well as on a division of roles between U.S. nuclear sharing and nuclear-deterrence cooperation with France.

G1.t: Closes off the domestic rifts Russia seeks to exploit

G4.t: Consolidates Poland's channels to Washington into one

G6.t: Removes obstacles to using EU funds

alts.name: Interceptions over western Ukraine
alts.desc: Intercept Russian missiles and drones headed toward Poland in the skies over western Ukraine. The Polish government reportedly considered this in July 2024.

G1.t: Would give Russia grounds to declare Poland a co-belligerent

G5.t: A major contribution to Ukraine's air defense

alts.name: Leverage over China and Belarus
alts.desc: Use Małaszewicze, a main transit point for China-Europe rail freight, to press China to rein in Belarus and Russia, or strike a conditional border deal with Belarus.

G1.t: No change

G3.t: Could ease pressure on the border, though the effect is uncertain

G7.t: Could put rail transit revenue at risk

alts.name: Deterrence by punishment through long-range strike
alts.desc: Expand long-range strike capabilities that can hit military targets on Russian soil (joining the European Long-Range Strike Approach, Chunmoo long-range guided missiles, and others) to build a deterrent that makes clear an attack will carry a price.

G1.t: Poland already has long-range strike capabilities, so the added effect is small; and because practically the only Russian territory within range is Kaliningrad, the deterrent gain and the risk of escalation cancel each other out

responses.note: Each counterpart is assumed to respond in the most calculated way available to it. The EU/NATO column reflects the responses of the German government and the EU.

rows.RUS: Frames the U.S. buildup as NATO pushing up to its borders and expands countermeasures in Belarus, including more Oreshnik deployments.
rows.USA: Accepts on condition that Poland pays its share and buys U.S. weapons, but keeps the troops largely on rotation.
rows.EUR: Welcomes it but sees it as a damper on the debate over European self-reliance.
rows.BLR: Uses it as a pretext for further deployments.

rows.RUS: Uses it in propaganda to widen the gap between the United States and Europe.
rows.USA: Welcomes it as burden sharing but is lukewarm about extending France's nuclear umbrella.

rows.RUS: Moves Poland to the top of its target list and puts Belarus's tactical nuclear weapons and Oreshnik missiles on display.
rows.USA: Likely to turn down a request for nuclear sharing, and strongly opposes an independent Polish arsenal.
rows.BLR: Asks for a larger nuclear deployment.

rows.RUS: Denies involvement and switches proxies; if a shootdown occurs, portrays it as aggression in its propaganda.
rows.USA: Could urge caution out of concern about escalation.
rows.BLR: Suffers economic losses from the border closure and pushes back.

rows.RUS: Escorts the shadow fleet with warships and fighter jets and brands seizures a "blockade."
rows.USA: Worries about escalation.

rows.RUS: Raises its nuclear threats along the lines of the diplomatic document Reuters reported on September 30, and answers in kind with exercises and troop deployments around the Suwałki Gap.
rows.USA: Likely to object (in keeping with a stance that puts strategic stability with Russia first).
rows.BLR: Joins in the pressure from the other side of the corridor.

rows.RUS: Agrees to talk but demands a reduction in NATO's forward deployment in return.
rows.USA: Welcomes it.
rows.BLR: Demands a seat at the table.

rows.RUS: Steps up its targeting of Poland and its propaganda casting Poland as a co-belligerent.
rows.USA: Welcomes it as burden sharing.

rows.RUS: Shifts its sabotage targets and turns to information warfare to stoke social unrest.
rows.USA: Welcomes it.

rows.RUS: Welcomes it and demands bigger concessions (a reduction in allied forces).
rows.USA: Could tolerate it as a way to press for a ceasefire in Ukraine.

rows.RUS: With its operations to exploit domestic rifts losing their effect, shifts the targets of its information warfare.
rows.USA: Little bearing.

responses.lesson: Russia, calculating as the most capable adversary, is unlikely to wage open war on Poland while the war in Ukraine goes on. It will instead use five moves. First, in direct talks with Washington, it will tie a ceasefire in Ukraine to limits on forces on NATO's eastern flank, sharply reducing the effect of the U.S. buildup without firing a shot. Second, it will protect its Baltic Sea export routes with escorts for the shadow fleet, claims that Kaliningrad is being "blockaded," and nuclear signaling. Estonia's decision in April 2026 to halt inspections of shadow-fleet vessels in its exclusive economic zone is a gain Russia has already secured. Third, it will use sabotage carried out by Ukrainian and Belarusian proxies to drive wedges into Polish-Ukrainian relations and Polish domestic politics. The perpetrator of the November 2025 bombing of a railway line was a Ukrainian national who had been working with Russian intelligence. Fourth, it will keep limited military action with murky attribution in reserve as an option. Fifth, it will consider openly seizing the Suwałki Gap or a Baltic state only if it concludes that the U.S. commitment to Europe has actually been withdrawn. Against a standoff below the threshold of war and deadly incidents, Poland's answers are therefore resilience (A8), the airspace and border response (A4), and the accord between the president and the government (A10); its insurance against a limited use of force and all-out war lies in arrangements that keep allied forces on the ground (A1 and A2) and in deterrence by punishment (A13). Because Russia's first move, a U.S.-Russian deal tying a ceasefire to limits on force posture, could badly weaken that insurance at the negotiating table, it is important for Poland to keep its own forces at the center and to have European insurance ready.

items.name: A sustained standoff below the threshold of war
items.story: Airspace violations by drones and helicopters, sabotage, GPS jamming, threats to undersea infrastructure, and nuclear threats continue, but there is no fighting between NATO and Russian forces that leaves anyone dead. The pattern of 2025–2026 persists through 2030.
items.test: If none of the conditions for P2–P6 is met, the outcome is P1. Each future is classified by the single highest stage reached by 2030, ranked from highest to lowest as P5 > P4 > P3 > P2 > P6 > P1.
signs: Airspace violations and announcements attributing sabotage continue, but no one is killed
U.S.-Russian talks remain confined to a ceasefire in Ukraine

items.name: A deadly incident, then a patch-up
items.story: One or more incidents, such as the downing of a Russian aircraft, a naval clash in the Baltic Sea, or a missile or drone that kills people on Polish territory, set off a crisis, but it is patched up without escalating into an Article 5 war.
items.test: The outcome is P2 if, after October 10, 2026, Russian or Belarusian state bodies, or proxies acting on their instructions, cause deaths on the territory or in the territorial waters or airspace of a NATO member through military equipment or infrastructure sabotage (targeted assassinations excluded), or if a NATO member shoots down or sinks a crewed Russian aircraft or vessel. The conditions for P3–P5 must not be met.
signs: Sabotage capable of causing deaths increases
Looser rules of engagement or boardings of shadow-fleet vessels are actually put into effect
Russian weapons (drones or missiles) kill people just outside NATO members' territorial waters or airspace

items.name: A Kaliningrad blockade crisis
items.story: Restrictions on transit to Kaliningrad or maritime inspections lead Russia to declare a "blockade" and escalate its nuclear threats, setting off a coercive crisis. It is resolved through negotiation or agreed rules, without fighting.
items.test: The outcome is P3 if Russia formally claims a "blockade" over actual restrictions on, or inspections of, land or sea transport to Kaliningrad, and a crisis accompanied by military measures, such as troop deployments or a higher alert level, lasts 30 days or more. Claims that a blockade is being prepared, like those in the diplomatic document Reuters reported on September 30, 2026, do not count on their own.
signs: Lithuania or the EU actually imposes restrictions on transit to Kaliningrad
Russia announces a higher alert level in Kaliningrad

items.name: Limited use of force
items.story: Russia (or Belarus) briefly seizes part of a Baltic state with unmarked forces, or carries out deliberate, limited strikes on the military facilities or infrastructure of a NATO member, testing the credibility of Article 5. This covers both a path with murky attribution during the war in Ukraine and a path after a ceasefire, once Russia has rebuilt its forces.
items.test: The outcome is P4 if regular Russian or Belarusian forces, or unmarked forces, occupy territory of a NATO member, or carry out deliberate, limited strikes on the military facilities or infrastructure of a NATO member. NATO's response must not meet the conditions for P5.
signs: Washington formalizes a drawdown of its forces in Europe or a weakening of its commitment
Russia rapidly rebuilds its forces in the western military district after a ceasefire

items.name: Full-scale NATO-Russia war
items.story: A limited clash escalates, and Polish territory comes under large-scale attack. Nuclear weapons could be used.
items.test: The outcome is P5 if NATO invokes Article 5 and Russian forces and the forces of NATO members engage in sustained combat, or if Polish territory comes under a large-scale attack spanning several cities and military facilities.
signs: A limited use of force (P4) occurs first
Russia publicly raises its nuclear alert level

items.name: Lower tensions
items.story: Alongside a ceasefire in Ukraine, NATO and Russia set up risk-reduction mechanisms (hotlines, notification of exercises, prevention of accidental clashes), and attacks below the threshold of war decline markedly.
items.test: The outcome is P6 if a ceasefire in Ukraine takes hold, at least one NATO-Russia risk-reduction mechanism (a hotline, notification of exercises, or an agreement to prevent accidental clashes) is established, and incidents on the eastern flank (airspace violations and publicly attributed sabotage) fall to half their 2025 level or less and stay there for at least a year.
signs: Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks reach a deal
A hotline between NATO and Russian military authorities reopens

futures.note: Probabilities are judgment estimates; ranges are in parentheses. Each future is classified by the single highest stage reached by 2030 (P5 > P4 > P3 > P2 > P6 > P1). The figures "if the recommendation is followed" assume that the top-ranked combination (a permanent U.S. troop presence, A1, and total defense and resilience, A8) is launched by 2027 and carried out by 2030. On the judgment that an allied troop presence reduces the expected gains from a limited use of force, only P4 was lowered, from 5 percent to 4 percent. Because Poland cannot determine Russia's decisions, the changes are kept small.

client.name: Government of Poland
client.note: The objectives below are drawn from Poland's 2020 National Security Strategy and from the prime minister's and foreign minister's addresses to the Sejm between 2023 and 2026. Some of the priorities among them are not stated in those documents; Clisa Geopolitics has inferred them from the order in which the documents present them and from actions that carry a cost (defense spending, arms contracts). In particular, defense of the eastern border (G3) and the presence of NATO and U.S. forces (G4) may in practice carry equal weight. A new national security strategy has not yet been adopted.

goals.t: Independence, territorial integrity, and the safety of citizens
goals.d: Preserve independence and territory and guarantee the safety of citizens. In his 2026 address to the Sejm, the foreign minister called security the condition for achieving all of the state's other goals.
goals.src: 2020 National Security Strategy, national interest 1; foreign minister's 2026 address to the Sejm

goals.t: Deterrence and defense capabilities of Poland's own armed forces
goals.d: Raise defense spending and build up the armed forces' capacity to deter and defend. This is the objective on which spending is most heavily concentrated.
goals.src: Same strategy, Pillar 1, strategic objective 3; 2022 Homeland Defense Act (defense spending floor of 3% of GDP)

goals.t: Defense of the eastern border and national resilience
goals.d: Secure the eastern border and build the national resilience to withstand hybrid attacks such as sabotage and airspace violations. Prime Minister Tusk has said that Poland's task is, above all, to defend its own eastern border.
goals.src: Same strategy, Pillar 1, strategic objective 2; prime minister's address to the Sejm

goals.t: NATO deterrence and the presence of allied and U.S. forces
goals.d: Strengthen NATO's deterrence and expand the permanent presence of allied and U.S. forces.
goals.src: Same strategy, Pillar 2, tasks 1.4 and 2.1

goals.t: Ukraine's continued independence and checking Russian expansion
goals.d: Preserve Ukraine's independence and halt Russian expansion. The means are support, logistics, and sanctions, not sending troops.
goals.src: Same strategy, Pillar 2, task 2.3; foreign minister's 2026 address to the Sejm

goals.d: Build European defense capabilities that complement NATO.
goals.src: Foreign minister's 2025 address to the Sejm; same strategy (EU defense as a complement to NATO)

goals.d: Sustain economic and social development so as to protect the resources for defense. The 2027 draft budget trims the share of defense spending slightly. That could be a sign that fiscal constraints are starting to bite, or the result of funding shifting to the EU defense loans.
goals.src: Same strategy, national interest 4

ranked.t: Measured against the order of Poland's objectives, a permanent U.S. military presence (A1) comes first and total defense and resilience (A8) second. The two are not mutually exclusive and can be pursued together. In negotiating a U.S. presence, Poland should aim not at troop numbers but at real fighting capability: air defense, long-range fires, and the speed of reinforcement. A1's score of +2 against the first objective assumes combat capability at brigade level or above; if Washington settles on a mainly rotational or token deployment, the score drops to +1 and resilience (A8) moves to first place. U.S. forces are the arms of others and could waver once Washington and Moscow start dealing, so Poland's own forces belong at the center.

These options serve the objectives but come with conditions. A security accord between the president and the government (A10) is unlikely to be achieved. Joining NATO nuclear sharing (A3a) and nuclear cooperation with France (A3b) carry a high risk of escalation, and it is uncertain whether Washington and Paris would accept them. Risk-reduction mechanisms belong here only when decoupled from forward deployment (A6a). A stronger European pillar (A2) is insurance against a wavering U.S. commitment. It sits in this group because the EU defense loans are already part of the current course and add nothing further to the capabilities of Poland's own armed forces or to its national resilience.

These have little or no net effect on the first objective (G1). An airspace and border response (A4) contributes substantially to national resilience (G3), but a shootdown under relaxed rules of engagement could itself become a deadly incident.

ranked.id: A6b, A4b, A11, A5a, A7, A5b, A9, A3c
ranked.t: These harm the first objective (G1) or do serious damage to the presence of NATO and U.S. forces (G4). Expanded support for Ukraine (A7) and interceptions over western Ukraine (A11) contribute substantially to Ukraine's continued independence (G5) but undermine Poland's own security. Scaling back involvement in Ukraine (A9) and an independent nuclear arsenal (A3c) rank at the bottom.

rank2.tension: Efforts to expand the U.S. presence rely on the personal channel between President Trump and President Nawrocki, and a single U.S.-Russian deal could nullify their effect. Yet putting the European pillar first risks being read in Washington as a sign that Poland wants less of an American commitment. Even when the scores for each objective are summed with weights that halve at each step down the order, the top two (A1 and A8) stay the same.
rank2.undecided: How to weigh support for Ukraine against Poland's own security is for Polish voters to decide in the 2027 parliamentary elections.

human.note: This section revisits the strategy rankings from the standpoint of individual lives. The most likely developments are a standoff below the threshold of war and deadly incidents (P1 and P2, 70% combined), and most of their victims are civilians.

items.clisa: Ranked first. The test is whether the civilian-protection budget set by the 2025 civil defense law (at least 0.3 percent of GDP a year, according to press reports) is actually spent on warnings, evacuation guidance, and compensation for damage.
items.cost: Shifts some of the money and personnel meant for equipment purchases to civil defense.
items.gain: Because the victims of attacks below the threshold of war (the 2025 railway bombing, the 2026 factory arson) are mostly civilians, the benefits reach the widest range of people.

items.cost: Poland takes on the political burden of talking to Russia and risks being seen within the alliance as appeasing it.
items.gain: If an accidental clash escalated into war, Poles, Baltic citizens, Germans, Nordic citizens, and Kaliningrad residents would all suffer. Mechanisms that prevent such escalation bear on the worst case for several groups. The size of that effect, however, has not been calculated.

items.clisa: If the rules of engagement are loosened, set standards to prevent civilian harm at the same time, such as where interceptions take place and which weapons are used, and keep border closures and suspensions of the right to seek asylum to a minimum.
items.cost: Responses may be slightly slower, and Poland may be criticized for lax border controls.
items.gain: There were press reports that damage to a house in Wyryki in September 2025 may have been caused by a missile fired by a Polish fighter jet (not confirmed by the government). More than 100 people are estimated to have died along the Belarus-EU border since 2021 (according to tallies by the press and nongovernmental groups).

items.clisa: Against the shadow fleet, use nonmilitary tools such as insurance and port sanctions first, rather than boardings.
items.cost: The effect on Russia's oil revenue takes longer to show.
items.gain: Naval clashes are the most likely trigger of a Kaliningrad crisis or a deadly incident, so this reduces that risk.

items.clisa: Same as the assessment against the Polish government's objectives. It also states, however, that the short-term benefit of a weaker motive for hybrid attacks is real for Poles, and that the cost falls on Ukrainians and on Ukrainian refugees in Poland.
items.cost: Not applicable (the ranking is the same).
items.gain: The effects on individuals are set out alongside the ranking rather than filtered out.

conclusions.t: The most likely future through 2030 is a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (40%, range 30–50%). Next comes an incident that costs lives but is then patched up (30%, range 20–40%). Limited use of force is put at 5 percent (range 2–10%) and a full-scale NATO-Russia war at 2 percent (range 0.5–3%).
conclusions.why: Since 2022, incidents on the eastern flank have grown both more frequent and more severe (the Kh-101 missile that came down in July 2026, the explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport in August, and the intrusion into Polish airspace by a helicopter from Kaliningrad in September). Yet there has been no deadly clash between armed forces. During the Cold War, every fatal shootdown between NATO and the Soviet Union was patched up. Schelling saw such incidents as adjacent rungs on a single ladder: each one makes the next rung more likely.
conclusions.flip: A deliberate Russian strike on a NATO member's territory before a ceasefire in Ukraine would raise the probability of limited use of force (P4). A drop in incidents on the eastern flank to half the 2025 level or less, sustained for more than a year, would raise the probability of lower tensions (P6).

conclusions.t: Measured against the Polish government's objectives, the top priority is to strengthen a permanent U.S. military presence and national resilience (total defense) together. The negotiating goal for the U.S. presence is not troop numbers but the ability to fight: air defense, long-range fires, and the speed of reinforcement. A stronger European pillar should be kept as insurance against a wavering U.S. commitment.
conclusions.why: In the precedents where deterrence failed (Poland in 1939, South Korea in 1950), no allied forces were on the ground. Yet empirical studies (Reiter and Poast 2021; Blankenship and Lin-Greenberg 2022) find that the local balance of forces and real fighting capability matter more for deterrence and reassurance than a small tripwire force as such. Because U.S. forces are, in Machiavelli's phrase, the arms of others (The Prince, chapter 13) and could waver once Washington and Moscow begin bargaining, Poland's own forces must be at the center. The EU defense loans (about €44 billion) are already part of the current course, so further strengthening the European pillar adds only insurance against a wavering U.S. commitment. Polish public opinion points the same way: in a January 2026 SW Research poll, 53.2 percent of respondents said that today's United States is not a reliable ally.
conclusions.flip: If Washington settles on a mainly rotational or token presence in Poland, the score of a permanent U.S. presence (A1) against the first objective will drop from +2 to +1, and national resilience (A8) will move into first place. If a cap on troops along NATO's eastern flank is confirmed to be on the agenda of U.S.-Russian talks, a stronger European pillar (A2) will join the top-ranked combination.

conclusions.t: Armed attacks on allied territory and attacks below the threshold of war call for different tools. Sub-threshold attacks cannot be stopped by a tripwire; they require resilience combined with selective punishment (public attribution, sanctions, and proportionate responses at the alliance level).
conclusions.why: As Schelling showed with the Berlin Wall, wherever a commitment leaves room for interpretation, the adversary expects the defender to read it in a way that avoids the need for a forceful response. Russia's choice of sub-threshold tools exploits this structure. That no full-scale ground attack has occurred is likely owed less to the tripwire than to the alliance as a whole, Poland's own forces, and the fact that Russia's forces have been tied down in Ukraine. Mazarr (2015) recommends selective punishment and clear red lines alongside resilience.
conclusions.flip: If sabotage keeps growing in frequency and damage even after resilience and punishment have been strengthened, this assessment will be revisited.

conclusions.t: The probability-weighted expected value barely changes, but if a full-scale war, put at 2 percent, does break out, Poles' personal safety would fall below the current level for Ukrainians, a nation at war (on median values). Clisa Geopolitics therefore places civilian protection and safeguards against accidental clashes ahead of the ranking based on the Polish government's objectives.
conclusions.why: On the personal-safety score used for human security (0–100, higher is safer), the expected value for Poles moves by 1.3 points, from 91.5 today to 90.2, and the result is the same if the recommendation is followed. In a full-scale war, however, Poles would drop from 91.5 to 30.5 and Baltic citizens from 82.5 to 17.3. Ukrainians currently score 44.0. The judgment estimate of deaths in a full-scale war spans a wide range, though, so the score for Poles lies somewhere between 0 and 49.9. The damage from war would also extend to Kaliningrad residents (about 1.03 million). And most of the victims in the futures that are actually likely, a standoff below the threshold and deadly incidents (70% combined), are civilians as well.
conclusions.flip: If safeguards against accidental clashes prove attainable only in exchange for a reduced forward deployment, the decision to put risk-reduction mechanisms first will be revisited.

predictions.note: Whether the permanent U.S. military presence (A1) in the top-ranked combination is actually moving forward

predictions.note: One of the conditions for lower tensions (P6)

falsify: If a cap on troops along NATO's eastern flank or limits on exercises near the border are confirmed to be on the agenda of U.S.-Russian talks, the assessment of a permanent U.S. presence (A1) will be lowered and a stronger European pillar (A2) added to the top-ranked combination.
If Washington settles on a mainly rotational or token presence in Poland, A1's score against the first objective will be lowered from +2 to +1 and national resilience (A8) moved to first place.

If Russia deliberately strikes the territory of a NATO member before a ceasefire in Ukraine, both the assessment of Russia's best move (no direct fight with NATO while the war goes on) and the probability of limited use of force (P4) will be revisited.
If Poland's president and government agree on a joint national security strategy, the feasibility of a president-government accord (A10) will be raised and the ranking revisited.
If transport restrictions around Kaliningrad are actually imposed, the probability of a Kaliningrad blockade crisis (P3) will be raised.

twoway.equilibrium: While the war in Ukraine continues, Russia is unlikely to fight NATO directly. Instead it imposes costs through sub-threshold means such as sabotage, drones, airspace violations, and nuclear threats, and drives wedges between Poland's president and government and between the United States and Europe. The point where the two sides' best moves meet is therefore a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (40%) and an incident that costs lives but is patched up (30%).
twoway.zopa: What both sides could accept are mechanisms that keep accidental clashes from escalating into war (hotlines, agreements to prevent accidental clashes). But Russia would demand a reduced NATO forward deployment in return, so the only version that serves Poland's interests is one decoupled from forward deployment (A6a).
traps: Poland's two insurance policies, U.S. forces and Europe, are both the arms of others, so a single U.S.-Russian deal could shake them both at once.

Relaxing the rules of engagement for airspace violations or boarding shadow-fleet vessels is meant to reduce sub-threshold attacks, yet either step could itself trigger a deadly incident (P2) or a Kaliningrad crisis (P3).

brief.q: How should Poland prepare for the Russian threat?
brief.a: Strengthen both a permanent U.S. military presence and national resilience. In negotiating the U.S. presence, aim not at troop numbers but at real fighting capability: air defense, long-range fires, and speed of reinforcement. U.S. forces belong to another power and could be unsettled by a U.S.-Russian deal, so put Poland's own forces at the center and build up a stronger European pillar as insurance against that moment.
brief.eq: While the war in Ukraine continues, Russia is unlikely to fight NATO directly. Instead it imposes costs through sub-threshold means such as sabotage, drones, airspace violations, and nuclear threats, and drives wedges between Poland's president and its government and between the United States and Europe. The two sides' best moves therefore converge on a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (40%) and on an incident that costs lives but is patched up (30%).
brief.human: The risk to Poles is concentrated in a full-scale NATO-Russia war, put at a 2 percent probability. In that event, their personal-safety score would fall from 91.5 to 30.5, and that of Baltic citizens from 82.5 to 17.3.

items.means: Missiles, troops, and the Baltic Fleet in Kaliningrad; nuclear weapons and nuclear threats; the Oreshnik deployed in Belarus; sabotage proxies run by the intelligence services; drones and GPS jamming; the shadow fleet
items.frame: Sees NATO as bringing its military infrastructure up to Russia's borders, and holds that the United States and its "satellites" have unleashed a new type of hybrid war against Russia.
goals: Regime survival and great-power status (2023 Foreign Policy Concept)
Achieving its war aims in Ukraine (securing Donetsk, neutralizing Ukraine)
Keep NATO away from its borders and split the United States from Europe (2014 Military Doctrine, 2023 Foreign Policy Concept)
Protect Kaliningrad's security and its access routes (2022 Maritime Doctrine, 2024 Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence)
Protect its seaborne export routes in the Baltic (as its military escort of the shadow fleet shows)
items.strategy: Avoid open war with Poland while fighting in Ukraine. Instead, impose costs below the threshold through sabotage and airspace violations with blurred attribution, protect Kaliningrad and the Baltic export routes with nuclear threats, and widen the cracks in Polish domestic politics and in Polish-Ukrainian relations. Russia's most capable move would be to link a ceasefire in Ukraine to limits on the posture of NATO's eastern flank in direct negotiations with Washington, sharply reducing the effect of the U.S. buildup without firing a shot.
tactics: On September 10, 2025, drones violated Polish airspace on a large scale, and NATO held Article 4 consultations at Poland's request. An estimated 19 to 23 drones entered ([secondary] press reports)

[secondary] On November 15, 2025, a section of the Warsaw–Lublin railway line was blown up; the Polish government announced that it was the work of two Ukrainian nationals who had been cooperating with Russian intelligence. Prime Minister Tusk also regarded the August 31, 2026, fire at a drone plant (WB Electronics) as arson carried out on Russia's behalf (Polish press reports)
[secondary] On July 30, 2026, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell and exploded in a field in Poland's Lublin province (Polish press reports)

[secondary] On September 23, 2026, an Mi-8 helicopter from Kaliningrad entered Polish airspace, about 300 meters in, for 42 seconds. It was the first publicly reported case of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland's land border (press reports of an Operational Command statement)

[secondary] In a diplomatic memorandum to NATO reported on September 30, 2026, Russia warned that if NATO tried to isolate Kaliningrad, it was ready to use all the forces and means at its disposal, including nuclear weapons (Reuters report; original text not verified). On October 1, 2026, at the Valdai Discussion Club, President Putin confirmed that the memorandum was accurate in every respect

[secondary] Provides armed cover for the shadow fleet. On May 14, 2025, an Estonian attempt to inspect a tanker failed to board it because of cover from a Russian Su-35, and on April 10, 2026, the Estonian navy stopped boarding operations in its exclusive economic zone
red: The isolation of Kaliningrad and the blockade of its transport routes (cited in the 2024 Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence as a danger to be met with nuclear deterrence; the memorandum reported on September 30, 2026, referred to nuclear use)
Attacks on Russian territory (Putin: the use of all the weapons at Russia's disposal would come onto the agenda)
The closing of its seaborne export routes through the seizure of ships ([secondary] Nikolai Patrushev, chairman of the Maritime Board: Russia cannot allow its key sea routes to be blockaded)

A buildup of foreign forces in neighboring countries and the deployment of nuclear weapons on Polish territory (the Military Doctrine lists a buildup of foreign forces in neighboring states as a main external military danger)
items.ext: Intends to avoid open conflict with NATO until the war in Ukraine ends, and sees ceasefire talks as a chance to tie a settlement to limits on the eastern-flank posture. The U.S. National Defense Strategy's downgrading of Russia to a manageable threat and the drawdown of U.S. forces in Europe offer an opportunity to split the United States from Europe, and the Iran war is a variable that drains U.S. military capacity. The standoff between Poland's president and government and the parliamentary elections in fall 2027 are targets for information warfare. On September 17, 2026, Prime Minister Tusk singled out lawmakers from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), warning them not to spread narratives that favor Russia ahead of the elections ([secondary] reports).
items.want: Halt the permanent U.S. presence and participation in nuclear sharing; stay out of transport restrictions on Kaliningrad and ship interdictions; scale back its role as the logistics hub for Ukraine
items.onrec: Casts a permanent U.S. presence (A1) as NATO's advance toward Russia's borders and uses it as a pretext for more countermeasures, such as the Oreshnik in Belarus. Russia's most capable response would not be to confront U.S. forces militarily but to link a ceasefire in Ukraine to limits on the eastern-flank posture (caps on rotational troops, limits on exercises near the border) in direct negotiations with Washington, sharply reducing the effect of the presence at the negotiating table. Responds to total defense and resilience (A8) by shifting its sabotage targets and using information warfare to stoke social unrest, and uses a stronger European pillar (A2) in propaganda meant to drive a wedge between the United States and Europe.
items.lever: What Poland holds is its role as the logistics hub for Ukraine and its vote on EU sanctions, but using either would mean abandoning Ukraine's continued independence (G5). Beyond that, it has only investigations, arrests, and diplomatic measures that raise the price of sabotage, and it has already used up consulate closures, the last being Gdańsk in November 2025. Tools that Russia does care about, such as exercises near Kaliningrad (A5a), also raise the risk of escalation.

P1: Matches Russia's best move: imposing costs without open war
P2: If an incident with blurred attribution is patched up, Russia can gauge the limits of NATO's response. Escalation, however, is hard to control
P3: Russia can counter with nuclear threats, but the isolation of Kaliningrad is a vital danger that Russia has named in its own documents
P4: Not its best move while the war in Ukraine continues. The risk is high until it can confirm that Washington has withdrawn its commitment to Europe
P5: Putin said on October 1, 2026, that he had no plans to attack Europe. Such a war would not serve regime survival
P6: Acceptable if gained in exchange for a reduced NATO forward deployment

intent.read: Russia's nuclear signals match its actions. The 2024 Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence, the memorandum reported on September 30, 2026, and Putin's remarks on October 1, 2026, all draw the same line around Kaliningrad and attacks on Russian territory. By contrast, the claim that Russia has no plans to attack Europe and its denials of sabotage are at odds with incidents that the Polish and German governments have attributed to Russia (the railway bombing, the drone at Leipzig airport). Avoiding open war while stepping up sub-threshold attacks it denies is the basis for judging that Russia prefers a standoff below the threshold (P1).

watch.t: How forcefully Russia responds to Steadfast Noon, NATO's nuclear deterrence exercise
Whether the supposedly accidental drone and missile attacks that Prime Minister Tusk has warned of materialize
Whether limits on NATO's eastern-flank posture come onto the agenda of ceasefire talks on Ukraine

items.means: The nuclear umbrella (NATO nuclear sharing), U.S. troops in Poland and decisions on a permanent base, air and naval forces assigned to the NATO Force Model, arms sales, direct negotiations with Russia
items.frame: Holds that the era in which the United States propped up the entire world order is over, that Europe must take primary responsibility for its own defense, and that the United States must restore strategic stability with Russia.
goals: Shift the defense burden to Europe (fulfillment of the Hague pledge to spend 5% of GDP; Europe's primary responsibility for conventional defense)
Restore strategic stability with Russia and reduce the risk of a Russia-Europe conflict
Use trade and arms sales to build up the "healthy nations" of Central and Eastern Europe
Dispel the perception of NATO as an endlessly expanding alliance
items.strategy: Hand Europe's conventional defense over to the Europeans and draw down U.S. forces, while rewarding Poland, which spends heavily on defense and buys American weapons, through bilateral deals. Those rewards depend heavily on the personal relationship between the two presidents. Washington itself is split: the administration is cutting forces in Europe, while Congress is trying to preserve a floor on troop levels there.
tactics: [secondary] On January 23, 2026, the National Defense Strategy called on European allies to take primary responsibility for conventional defense and ranked Europe third, after the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific (summary by the Polish Institute of International Affairs)

[secondary] On May 1, 2026, announced the withdrawal of about 5,000 of the roughly 36,000 U.S. troops in Germany, shortly after Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized the United States over the Iran war (U.S. press reports)

[secondary] In mid-May 2026, canceled the deployment of an armored brigade combat team (about 4,000 troops) bound for Poland, and on May 19 said it would cut the number of brigade combat teams in Europe from four to three. It described the Polish deployment as a temporary delay

[secondary] On May 21, 2026, President Trump said 5,000 U.S. troops would deploy to Poland, citing his relationship with President Nawrocki, and on September 17 he said there had been great progress in talks on a base in Poland. The actual deployment and the base location have not been confirmed

[secondary] On June 11, 2026, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe, confirmed for the first time that U.S. assets assigned to the NATO Force Model would be scaled back in favor of the Indo-Pacific

[secondary] Through the National Defense Authorization Act bill released by the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee on May 26, 2026, Congress moved to extend the floor of 76,000 U.S. troops in Europe and opposed halting the brigade deployment to Poland. Whether the bill was finally enacted could not be confirmed
red: Escalation that drags U.S. forces into a Russia-Europe conflict (likely to oppose pressure such as transport restrictions on Kaliningrad or exercises)
