Independent nuclear armament by an ally
An endlessly expanding NATO
A return to a structure in which the United States props up Europe's defense
items.ext: Sees the war in Ukraine as a problem to be settled in the course of restoring strategic stability with Russia. The Iran war, which began on February 28, 2026, is draining U.S. military capacity, and the withdrawal of troops from Germany came right after a dispute with Berlin over that war ([secondary] reports). In Polish politics, Washington has strengthened the president's hand by citing Trump's relationship with President Nawrocki as grounds for the deployment decision. There are also reports that the location of a base in Poland could be announced before the November 3, 2026, midterm elections ([secondary]).
items.want: Honor the Hague pledge of 5 percent of GDP and keep buying American weapons; bear the cost of a permanent base; take the lead in Europe's conventional defense; do not disrupt Washington's diplomacy aimed at strategic stability with Russia
items.onrec: Accepts a permanent U.S. presence (A1) on condition that Poland bears the cost and buys American weapons, but would keep the troops mainly rotational. Washington's most advantageous response is to claim a win by announcing a base while leaving the size and permanence of the force undecided, preserving room to use them in negotiations with Russia. Welcomes a stronger European pillar (A2) as burden sharing but is lukewarm about extending French nuclear deterrence. Welcomes total defense and resilience (A8).
items.lever: Purchases of American weapons (128 deals worth $63 billion, according to the Polish government), bearing the cost of a permanent base ([secondary] expected to exceed 15 billion zlotys), Poland's standing as a model of burden sharing with defense spending in the mid-to-high 4 percent of GDP range, and its ties to a Congress intent on preserving the floor on troops in Europe. The personal channel between President Nawrocki and Trump is strong, but it is not a channel the government controls, so it also carries the risk of domestic conflict.

P1: Europe bears the costs, and U.S. forces do not fight directly
P2: Washington is drawn into crisis management, but it is tolerable if the incident is patched up
P3: A crisis involving nuclear threats collides head-on with its priority of strategic stability with Russia
P4: The credibility of Article 5 is put to the test, and U.S. forces could be drawn into combat
P6: Delivers both strategic stability with Russia and a lighter burden on U.S. forces

intent.read: In words, Washington favors Poland, but its costly actions point toward cutting forces and assets in Europe. In May 2026 the withdrawal from Germany and the cancellation of the brigade bound for Poland came first, and the deployment of 5,000 troops remains an announcement grounded in the relationship between the two presidents. Poland's deputy defense minister said rotational U.S. forces in Poland had fallen to about 6,500–7,000, down from roughly 10,000 before ([secondary]). This is the basis for judging that the U.S. administration prefers lower tensions (P6) and that its favor toward Poland rests on a personal relationship.

watch.t: Announcement of the location of a permanent base in Poland, and the size and permanence of the force
The floor on U.S. troops in Europe and the Polish brigade provision in the final NDAA
Actual deployment of the 5,000 troops announced

items.means: The 45th Panzer Brigade in Lithuania (aiming for full operational readiness with more than 5,000 troops before the end of 2027) and its role as lead nation of NATO's multinational battlegroup in Lithuania, a voice over European defense funding, and diplomatic and investigative responses to hybrid attacks
items.frame: Holds that Germany is a daily target of Russian hybrid warfare but is not at war, and that Europe must take more responsibility for its own security as the United States pulls back.
goals: Take a direct part in deterrence on NATO's eastern flank with German troops (the Lithuania brigade)
Make hybrid attacks costly (public attribution, diplomatic measures, pressure on the shadow fleet)
Build Europe's capacity to take on what the United States is cutting back
Keep the standoff from sliding into a state of war
items.strategy: Station its own troops permanently in Lithuania to share the tripwire role on NATO's eastern flank, and answer hybrid attacks with public attribution and diplomatic measures while avoiding military escalation. Having clashed with Washington over the Iran war and then seen U.S. troops withdrawn, Berlin aims to fill the gap by expanding Europe's responsibilities.
tactics: Established the 45th Panzer Brigade in Rukla, Lithuania, on April 1, 2025, and on February 4, 2026, incorporated NATO's multinational battlegroup in Lithuania, about 1,700 strong, into the brigade

On June 22, 2026, led the Freedom Shield 2026 exercise in Lithuania, with about 2,900 participants; Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would demonstrate its deterrence and defense capabilities twice a year

[secondary] In late April 2026, Chancellor Merz criticized the United States, saying it had been humiliated in the Iran war, and when Washington announced on May 1, 2026, the withdrawal of about 5,000 troops from Germany, Pistorius said the move had been foreseeable (U.S. press reports)
[secondary] After a Kh-101 cruise missile came down in Poland on July 30, 2026, Merz pointed to Russia's ruthlessness and its willingness to escalate (Polish press reports)

[secondary] On September 1, 2026, formally attributed the explosive-laden drone found at Leipzig/Halle Airport (August 4) to Russia, and announced the summoning of the Russian ambassador, the closure of the Russian consulate general in Bonn (September 18), and stepped-up pressure on the shadow fleet (German press reports)
red: Escalation into a state of war with Russia ([secondary] Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt: Germany is not at war)
Letting hybrid attacks go unpunished ([secondary] Merz: those responsible will pay a price)
Independent nuclear armament by an ally
items.ext: Continues to support Ukraine within the framework of aid that allies pledged at the NATO summit in Ankara in July 2026 (€70 billion for 2026, and at least as much in 2027). Accepts the U.S. pullback from Europe as foreseeable and responds by expanding Europe's responsibilities. The Iran war caused friction with Washington, and the cut in U.S. troops in Germany was announced soon afterward ([secondary] reports). Berlin's public position on Poland's 2027 elections could not be confirmed. As the president's veto of the EU defense loans shows, however, Poland's domestic conflict sets the pace of the European pillar.
items.want: Take an active part in EU defense funding and regional defense cooperation (the European pillar); join in attributing hybrid attacks and taking joint action against them; maintain support for Ukraine
items.onrec: Welcomes a stronger European pillar (A2) and total defense and resilience (A8). Also welcomes a permanent U.S. presence (A1), but believes that if Poland leans toward bilateral deals with Washington, it will dampen the debate on European self-reliance. Germany's most advantageous response is not to block A1 but to press Poland to increase, at the same time, what it puts into the European pillar (EU defense loan projects, regional defense cooperation).
items.lever: Poland is the largest user of the EU's SAFE defense loans, taking about €44 billion of the €150 billion, which makes it the test of whether the European pillar actually works. Another basis for cooperation is that the two share the eastern flank: the United States leads the battlegroup in Poland, and Germany the one in Lithuania. Beyond that, Poland has little leverage over Germany.

P1: Not a state of war, but Germany keeps paying the cost of hybrid attacks
P2: Germany is a target too (Leipzig airport). Even if the incident is patched up, the credibility of deterrence is shaken
P3: Europe would be divided over transport restrictions on Kaliningrad
P4: The German brigade stationed in Lithuania would face a direct test
P6: The most desirable future, provided a ceasefire and risk-reduction mechanisms do not come at the price of a reduced forward deployment

intent.read: Germany has stationed troops permanently in Lithuania as it said it would, and after the Leipzig incident it formally named Russia and closed a consulate general. Yet it holds to the line that Germany is not at war, and its responses stay within diplomatic and investigative measures. This is the basis for judging that Germany prefers lower tensions (P6) but would attach conditions to any deal that pays for them by reducing the eastern-flank posture.

watch.t: Integration of the 45th Panzer Brigade's remaining units and the move into the new barracks at Rūdninkai
Completion of the 45th Panzer Brigade's buildup and full operational readiness
watch.when: Second half of 2027 to end of 2027

watch.t: Concrete steps behind the stepped-up pressure on the shadow fleet announced after the Leipzig incident

items.means: Borders with Poland and Lithuania, territory hosting Russia's Oreshnik (number of launchers undisclosed), a corridor for migrants, smuggling balloons, and drones, joint exercises with Russia
items.frame: Forms a Union State with Russia and entrusts its security to Russian nuclear deterrence and the deployment of Russian weapons.
goals: Survival of the Lukashenko regime
Security under Russia's nuclear deterrent (the Oreshnik deployment)
Economic gains from the border and transit trade
items.strategy: Gain security guarantees by serving as Russia's forward base, and pressure neighboring NATO states with cheap, deniable tools such as migrants, balloons, and drones while avoiding direct combat. No public document setting out the Belarusian leadership's goals could be found, so its goals and strategy have been inferred from its actions.
tactics: [secondary] Held the joint strategic exercise Zapad-2025 with Russia on September 12–16, 2025. The official figure was 13,000 troops, but German and Lithuanian officials put the number at about 30,000, and Poland closed its border with Belarus from September 11, 2025
[secondary] In late October 2025, smuggling weather balloons from Belarus repeatedly halted operations at Vilnius Airport, and the Lithuanian president's office called it a hybrid attack
[secondary] The Polish government announced that the two perpetrators of the November 2025 railway bombing had fled to Belarus

[secondary] On December 18, 2025, President Alexander Lukashenko announced that Russia's Oreshnik had been in Belarus since the previous day and had been placed on combat duty. The number of launchers was not disclosed
[secondary] Lithuanian authorities said the drone shot down in Lithuanian airspace on September 15, 2026, had likely come from Belarus
red: Attacks on Belarusian territory (Russia's Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence also list conventional aggression that poses a critical threat to the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Belarus, a member of the Union State, as grounds for nuclear use)
Becoming a direct party to combat with NATO
Losing transit trade to a prolonged border closure
items.ext: No public material showing how the Belarusian leadership views external variables could be confirmed this time. Judging by its actions, it follows Russia's decisions on the war in Ukraine and the NATO-Russia standoff, and its economic gains and losses depend on whether the border is open or closed. If Poland leans toward scaling back its involvement in Ukraine after the 2027 elections, Minsk could offer a conditional border deal.
items.want: Keep the border and transit trade open; do not target Belarus directly in the standoff with Russia
items.onrec: Uses a permanent U.S. presence (A1) as a pretext to demand further deployments of Russian weapons. Has almost no stake in a stronger European pillar (A2). Has little direct stake in total defense and resilience (A8) either, but stronger sabotage investigations and counterintelligence would blunt the tactic of using Belarus as an escape route.
items.lever: Opening and closing the border with Belarus is Poland's lever. Poland closed the border on September 11, 2025, and reopened it on September 25; given reports that about 85–90 percent of China-Europe rail freight passes through Małaszewicze in Poland ([secondary]), pressure via China has also been floated. But Russia makes Belarus's decisions, so the effect is uncertain.

P1: Can keep up low-cost pressure under Russia's protection, but border closures bring economic losses
P2: If a drone or proxy coming from Belarus causes deaths, Belarus becomes a direct target
P3: Would be drawn into the pressure on Russia's side, and its territory caught up in the crisis
P4: Would follow if Russia decided on it, but Belarusian territory would become both launch point and target
P5: Its own territory becomes a battlefield
P6: Border and transit trade revive, and it could demand a seat in risk-reduction talks

intent.read: The announcement of the Oreshnik deployment and the joint exercises with Russia point consistently toward Belarus serving as Russia's forward base. The scale of the Oreshnik deployment, however, has not been confirmed, nor has any Belarusian state involvement in the balloon and drone incidents been officially established. That Belarus's choices are bound to Russia's decisions is the basis for judging its decision-making power to be low.

watch.t: The number of Oreshnik launchers in Belarus and confirmation by Russia's Ministry of Defense
Renewed incursions of drones or balloons from Belarus
Closures and reopenings of crossing points on the Polish-Belarusian border

syn.note: The labels Preferred, Acceptable, Uncomfortable, and Rejected are provisional judgments of how readily each country's leadership would accept each future (P1–P6) that could unfold through 2030. Each country's weight as a deciding power is rated by how hard it would be for a future to come about if that country opposed it.

reads.t: Russia's preferred future is a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (P1), and every other deciding power accepts it.
reads.d: That is why it is the most likely outcome, at 40 percent. Washington accepts it as long as Europe bears the costs, Germany tolerates it as long as it is not at war, and Belarus keeps up low-cost pressure under Russia's protection. All have grievances, but none is willing to pay the price of breaking the status quo. Most of the damage Poland suffers in this future comes from sabotage and airspace violations, so total defense and resilience (A8) is the most direct preparation.

reads.t: Russia, the United States, and Germany would all accept lower tensions (P6), but they differ over the price.
reads.d: Russia demands a reduced NATO forward deployment in return for risk-reduction mechanisms, and Washington, which has made strategic stability with Russia a priority, may be open to that bargain. Germany wants lower tensions without a reduced forward deployment. What is dangerous for Poland is not lower tensions as such but a deal in which Washington and Moscow link a ceasefire in Ukraine to limits on the eastern-flank posture. Risk-reduction mechanisms must therefore be decoupled from forward deployment (A6a), and a version that trades them for a reduced forward deployment (A6b) should be avoided.

reads.t: Washington's favor toward Poland rests not on costly actions but on the relationship between the two presidents.
reads.d: On May 21, 2026, President Trump cited his relationship with President Nawrocki as the basis for deploying 5,000 troops, but the withdrawal from Germany and the cancellation of the brigade bound for Poland had come first that same month. The president holds the channel to Washington, while the government holds the European channels, such as the EU defense loans and nuclear cooperation with France, so both insurance policies are hostage to the domestic standoff. That is why Poland should rely on a permanent U.S. presence (A1) while keeping a stronger European pillar (A2) ready as insurance; the parliamentary elections in fall 2027 could change this alignment.

reads.t: The only leverage Poland holds over Russia would cost it its own objectives to use. The leverage it can actually use lies with its allies.
reads.d: Poland has already exhausted its diplomatic tools against Russia, down to closing consulates; using its role as Ukraine's logistics hub as leverage would mean abandoning Ukraine's continued independence (G5); and the Kaliningrad-related tools that Russia does care about also raise the risk of escalation. With its allies, by contrast, it has real leverage: arms purchases and base-cost sharing with Washington, its position as the largest user of the EU defense loans with Berlin, and the power to open and close the border with Belarus. Poland's preparation begins not with moving Russia but with using this leverage to keep allied forces on the ground in Poland.

intent.note: Intent is judged first by actions that carry a cost, not by words.
intent.read: Germany and Belarus show the closest match between words and deeds. Germany has stationed troops permanently in Lithuania as it said it would, and Belarus has taken on the role of Russia's forward base in practice. Russia's nuclear signals match its actions, but while saying it has no plans to attack Europe, it is stepping up deniable sub-threshold attacks. Washington speaks of favoring Poland, yet its costly actions point toward cutting forces and assets in Europe. If the signals change, the preference assessments and the probabilities of the futures will be revised together.

items.name: The Berlin blockade and airlift
items.format: When the Soviet Union cut off rail, road, and water access to West Berlin, the United States (on June 26, 1948) and Britain (on June 28) launched an airlift. Washington deployed nuclear-capable B-29 bombers to Britain, and the West answered with a counter-blockade of the Soviet zone of occupation. Moscow offered to lift the blockade if the West withdrew the Deutsche Mark from West Berlin; the West refused.
items.outcome: The blockade was lifted in May 1949 without armed conflict. The airlift continued until September 30, 1949, carrying about 2,325,510 tons (1,783,573 tons by the United States and 541,937 tons by Britain) on 277,569 flights, at a cost of 101 lives. NATO was founded shortly before the blockade ended, and West Germany was established about two weeks after it ended.
items.why: Rather than force a way through on the ground, the West chose an unarmed humanitarian airlift, creating a situation in which the Soviet Union would have had to use force first to stop it, shifting onto Moscow the onus of starting a war. By keeping the airlift going into the spring, the West proved it could sustain it indefinitely, and the shortages that the counter-blockade caused in the eastern zone became a political burden for Moscow. A rally of some 300,000 West Berliners stiffened the West's political resolve.
items.differs: Today the territory cut off by land is Russia's Kaliningrad. Conversely, if the Suwałki Gap were severed, the Baltic states would be cut off by land, a Berlin in reverse. The Baltic states have sea and air supply routes, but unlike the Berlin air corridors of 1948, those routes could themselves be threatened by Kaliningrad's air defense and missile forces. And in 1948 only the West had nuclear weapons; today both sides are nuclear powers.

items.name: The Berlin crises and the West Berlin garrison
items.format: In November 1958, Khrushchev demanded that the United States, Britain, and France withdraw their forces from West Berlin within six months, and after the 1961 Vienna summit he set another six-month deadline. The three Western powers kept in place a West Berlin garrison too small to defend the city, and President Kennedy called up 150,000 reservists and raised defense spending.
items.outcome: The Soviet Union never acted on its deadlines. On August 13, 1961, East Germany sealed the boundary between East and West Berlin with barbed wire and then built a wall, and the West did not remove it by force. In October of the same year, U.S. and Soviet tanks faced off at Checkpoint Charlie, but both sides pulled back after an agreement reached through informal channels. West Berlin remained part of the Western sphere until 1989.
items.why: The West Berlin garrison could not hold the city on its own, but attacking it would have meant fighting U.S. troops directly, with the attendant risk of nuclear escalation, and Khrushchev was unwilling to run that risk (U.S. State Department historical records). The West held its core line, its presence in West Berlin and its rights of access, while tolerating the construction of the wall on the East Berlin side, leaving Moscow a way out that did not require force.
items.differs: Cold War tripwires worked where boundaries were clear and the U.S. nuclear arsenal was highly credible. Today there are many ways to apply pressure below the threshold that would trigger intervention, such as sabotage and drones, so a tripwire may deter a full-scale attack without deterring gray-zone attacks. Nor is there an obvious halfway exit for the Suwałki Gap, comparable to the wall, that both sides could accept.

items.name: The withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea and the North Korean invasion of June 1950
items.format: The U.S. National Security Council paper NSC 8/2 (approved by the president on March 23, 1949) provided for withdrawing the occupation forces from Korea before June 30, 1949, leaving behind only a military advisory group, and for supplying equipment and aid to South Korean forces, including 65,000 troops. It did not adopt the option of unconditionally guaranteeing South Korea's independence, by force if necessary. In a speech on January 12, 1950, Secretary of State Dean Acheson listed the Aleutians, Japan, the Ryukyus, and the Philippines as the defensive perimeter without mentioning Korea.
items.outcome: U.S. combat units had withdrawn by the end of June 1949, and on June 25, 1950, North Korea invaded the South. Contrary to its earlier signals, the United States entered the war at once.
items.why: One interpretation holds that the withdrawal, the defense-perimeter speech, and the House of Representatives' rejection of an additional aid bill for South Korea nine days after the speech together signaled weak U.S. resolve to intervene (CFR; the scholarly debate is ongoing). [secondary] According to studies of Soviet archival documents, Stalin told Kim Il Sung in April 1950 that U.S. military intervention was unlikely, and he approved the invasion only after receiving assurances that South Korea could be overrun within a few weeks, before the United States could respond. Deterrence failed under a combination of conditions: no troops on the ground, an ambiguous commitment, and the belief that a quick war could create a fait accompli. What failed was not America's actual will but the communication of that will.
items.differs: Poland's situation differs from that of South Korea in 1949: it has a legal commitment under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty and a standing U.S. troop presence (including the permanent garrison in Poznań). Still, because every adjustment of U.S. force levels in Europe can be read as a sign of a weakening commitment, the structural lesson of this precedent remains valid.

items.name: NATO's Enhanced Forward Presence (eFP) and Germany's permanent brigade in Lithuania
items.format: The Warsaw summit of July 8–9, 2016, decided to rotate four multinational battalions through Poland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, and by August 2017 the four battlegroups were fully operational (the battlegroup in Poland is led by the United States). The 2022 Madrid summit agreed to scale them up to brigade level when needed, and Germany decided to station a permanent brigade of about 5,000 troops in Lithuania, holding its inauguration ceremony in Vilnius on May 22, 2025 (with full operational capability targeted for the end of 2027). In June 2026, a ninth forward land force was established in Finland.
items.outcome: Since 2017, Russia has launched no overt ground attack on the territory of a NATO member. In the same region, however, attacks below the threshold of war, such as sabotage, airspace violations, and damage to undersea infrastructure, have risen sharply since 2022 (see P9 and P10).
items.why: Battalion-size forces serve less as a defensive capability than as a political device: an attack would inflict casualties on the troops of several allies, leaving the alliance as a whole no choice but to intervene. Overt ground attacks were deterred, but the logic did not work against attacks that are hard to attribute and fall short of the threshold for invoking Article 5.
items.differs: This case is still unfolding, and the observation that deterrence has held largely overlaps with the period in which Russia has kept most of its ground forces tied down in Ukraine. If the war in Ukraine ends and Russian ground forces are redeployed westward, the deterrent effect of battalion- and brigade-size forces will face a new test.

items.name: The Kaliningrad transit regime: the 2002 EU-Russia agreement and Lithuania's 2022 restrictions on the transit of sanctioned goods
items.format: In a joint statement on November 11, 2002, the EU and Russia agreed to introduce a Facilitated Transit Document (FTD) and a Facilitated Rail Transit Document (FRTD) to guarantee overland travel between Kaliningrad and mainland Russia after Lithuania joined the EU (with legislation to be in place by July 1, 2003). The statement also made clear that this would not infringe on Lithuania's sovereign right to exercise controls and to refuse entry. In mid-June 2022, Lithuania began blocking rail transit to Kaliningrad of goods under EU sanctions, such as steel, and after July 10 it extended the restrictions to cement, alcohol, timber, and other goods. On June 21, 2022, speaking in Kaliningrad, Nikolai Patrushev, secretary of Russia's Security Council, warned that Russia would certainly respond and that the population of Lithuania would feel a serious negative impact.
items.outcome: On June 27, 2022, the pro-Russian hacker group Killnet claimed responsibility for distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on Lithuanian institutions. In guidance issued on July 13, 2022, the European Commission permitted rail transit of sanctioned goods only to meet Kaliningrad's own needs, kept in place the ban on road transport and on military and dual-use goods, and capped volumes at the average of the previous three years (2019–2021). LTG Cargo, the freight arm of Lithuanian Railways, resumed transit on July 22, 2022. There was no military clash.
items.why: Russia took no military action beyond warnings and cyberattacks, and the EU lowered tensions by using interpretive guidance to turn Lithuania's unilateral measure into a common EU rule. According to an analysis by OSW, the Warsaw-based Centre for Eastern Studies, Germany and the United States wanted the situation calmed diplomatically, and Lithuania accepted the guidance as a binding decision. The 2002 agreement, too, was a compromise, struck through documents and screening procedures, between Russia's demand for free transit and Lithuania's sovereign right of control.
items.differs: In 2022, Russia was concentrating its forces on Ukraine, and the legal basis for the measure was EU sanctions rather than a Lithuanian decision alone. Poland shares a direct border with Kaliningrad and could become a direct party to the same kind of transit or border dispute, and Russia could brand transit restrictions a "blockade" and use them as a pretext for intervention. The precedent shows that such a dispute can be calmed through legal compromise, but whether the same outcome would follow at a time when Russia has forces to spare remains untested.

items.name: The Suez crisis and the Soviet nuclear threat
items.format: On October 29, 1956, Israel advanced into the Sinai Peninsula, and a few days later British and French forces landed in the Canal Zone. On November 5, 1956, Soviet Premier Nikolai Bulganin sent letters to the leaders of Britain, France, and Israel hinting at the use of force. The United States pressed its allies, backing a UN ceasefire resolution and blocking International Monetary Fund (IMF) support for Britain.
items.outcome: Britain accepted the UN ceasefire on November 6, 1956 (UN General Assembly Resolution 1001 and the deployment of the UN Emergency Force followed on November 7), and British and French forces withdrew and were replaced by UN troops. British Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned in January 1957.
items.why: A CIA Special National Intelligence Estimate of November 6, 1956, judged that the Soviet letters were vague and did not commit Moscow to unilateral military action, and that the Soviet Union would almost certainly not attack the British or French homeland. What decisively forced Britain to back down was not the Soviet threat but U.S. opposition, together with the drain on its foreign exchange reserves and the pressure for devaluation (Imperial War Museums). The Soviet Union was able to claim credit afterward for the effect of its threat.
items.differs: The 1956 nuclear threat had a large effect because it targeted allies that had split from the alliance's largest power, the United States. Poland is not at odds with Washington. The lesson of this precedent is that for a Russian nuclear threat to work, a rift must first open between the United States and Europe, or within Europe itself.

items.name: Russia's nuclear signaling (2022–2025) and the 2024 revision of its nuclear deterrence doctrine
items.format: On February 27, 2022, President Putin ordered Russia's deterrence forces onto a special mode of combat duty, citing what he called aggressive statements by the West, as well as sanctions. On March 25, 2023, he announced that Russia would station tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus. The Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence, signed on November 19, 2024, treat aggression by a non-nuclear state with the participation or support of a nuclear state as a joint attack (paragraph 11), treat aggression by a member of a military bloc as aggression by the bloc as a whole (paragraph 10), and permit nuclear use even in response to a conventional attack that poses a critical threat to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Russia and Belarus (paragraph 19). In November 2024, Russia struck the Ukrainian city of Dnipro with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile, and in December 2025 it made public the missile's deployment in Belarus.
items.outcome: Nuclear weapons were not used. The doctrine was revised right after reports that the United States had allowed Ukraine to use long-range missiles against targets inside Russia, and Western support for Ukraine continued to expand step by step even after the threats. [secondary] Assessments differ on how far the threats slowed Western decisions on aid or narrowed their scope.
items.why: As far as public evidence shows, Russia's nuclear signals were not paired with attacks on NATO territory and served instead to limit the scope of Western involvement. The 2020 doctrine confined the conditions for nuclear use to threats to the very existence of the state; the 2024 doctrine's extension of those conditions to conventional attacks and to an ally, Belarus, is assessed as lowering the threshold (Arms Control Association).
items.differs: Because the 2024 doctrine names Belarus among the conditions for nuclear use and includes a bloc clause, nuclear signals could apply more directly than they did in Ukraine if Poland or Lithuania became embroiled in a clash on the border with Belarus or Kaliningrad. Poland, however, sits under NATO's nuclear deterrent, so its position differs from Ukraine's.

items.name: Attributing and responding to attacks below the threshold of war: the cyberattacks on Estonia (2007) and the Vrbětice ammunition depot explosions in the Czech Republic (2014; attributed in 2021)
items.format: (a) In April and May 2007, after the Estonian government decided to relocate the Bronze Soldier, a Soviet war memorial in Tallinn, DDoS attacks hit the government, parliament, ministries, media, and banks for about three weeks. The Russian government denied involvement and turned down Estonia's requests for cooperation with the investigation. (b) On October 16, 2014, about 50 tons of ammunition exploded at the Vrbětice depot in the Czech Republic, killing two people, and two months later another 13 tons exploded at the same site. On April 17, 2021, the Czech government announced that there was reasonable suspicion of the involvement of Unit 29155 of Russia's military intelligence agency (GRU), and it expelled 18 Russian embassy staff identified as GRU and SVR officers, giving them 48 hours to leave.
items.outcome: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was not invoked over Estonia, and the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) was established in Tallinn on May 14, 2008, and received NATO accreditation that October. In the Czech case, after Russia expelled a larger number of Czech diplomats, the Czech Republic demanded on April 22, 2021, that the two countries' embassies be cut to equal staffing (seven diplomats and 25 administrative and technical staff), and Russia complied by the end of May. There was no military retaliation.
items.why: In Estonia, the attackers looked like individuals or non-state actors; in the Czech case, investigation and attribution took more than six years. Both made an immediate collective response difficult. The responses imposed nonmilitary costs, through the expulsion of diplomats and the building of institutions, and their effect showed up in a shrinking of Russian intelligence footholds and the institutionalization of defensive capabilities.
items.differs: Attacks today are far more frequent (P10), and attribution comes faster: in 2025, Poland publicly blamed Russian intelligence services for the bombing of a railway line within days. But Poland has already closed all Russian consulates, so its means of imposing diplomatic costs are largely exhausted.

items.name: Damage to undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea and NATO's Baltic Sentry
items.format: On October 8, 2023, Balticconnector, the gas pipeline linking Finland and Estonia, was damaged by the anchor of the Hong Kong-flagged container ship Newnew Polar Bear (in August 2024, China acknowledged the incident as an accident caused by a storm). On December 25, 2024, the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S dragged its anchor for about 60 miles, damaging five undersea cables, including the Estlink 2 power cable; Finland detained the ship and charged three crew members, including the captain. On January 14, 2025, NATO launched Baltic Sentry, deploying frigates, maritime patrol aircraft, and naval drones.
items.outcome: Balticconnector resumed commercial operation about six months later, on April 22, 2024. The Helsinki District Court dismissed the Eagle S case on October 3, 2025, for lack of jurisdiction, but on August 27, 2026, the Helsinki Court of Appeal unanimously upheld Finland's jurisdiction and returned the case to the lower court (the deadline to seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court is October 26, 2026). Finnish power and transmission companies have claimed about €105 million in damages. No court has yet established state responsibility.
items.why: When a ship flying a third country's flag drags its anchor on the high seas or in an exclusive economic zone, it is hard to tell accident from intent, and the principle of flag-state jurisdiction under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea limits what coastal states can do under criminal law. The response has therefore taken the form of stepped-up patrols and broader interpretations of domestic law.
items.differs: Poland, too, has a Baltic gas pipeline (Baltic Pipe), undersea cables, and an LNG terminal at Świnoujście, making it a target for the same kind of attack. If the 2026 appellate ruling becomes final, a broader reading of coastal-state jurisdiction could add to the means of deterrence.

items.name: Russia's hybrid offensive against Poland: sabotage and drone incursions into its airspace
items.format: By CSIS's count, Russian attacks in Europe rose from three in 2022 to 12 in 2023 and 34 in 2024. The International Centre for Counter-Terrorism (ICCT) in the Netherlands counted 151 acts of Russia-linked sabotage between February 2022 and February 2026, with Poland the most frequent target, at 31 (21%). In Poland, these included the arson at the Marywilska shopping center in Warsaw in May 2024 (found in May 2025 to have been ordered by Russian intelligence services) and the bombing of the Warsaw-Lublin railway line on November 15–16, 2025. On the night of September 9–10, 2025, drones entered Polish airspace during a Russian air attack on Ukraine (Prime Minister Tusk reported 19 violations), and Polish and Dutch fighter jets and German Patriot systems responded, shooting some of them down. On September 19, 2025, three Russian MiG-31s violated Estonian airspace for 12 minutes.
items.outcome: Poland requested consultations under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty on September 10, 2025, and Estonia did so on September 19 (until then, Article 4 had been invoked five times at Turkey's request, once at Poland's in 2014, and once at the joint request of eight countries in 2022). On September 12, NATO launched Eastern Sentry to strengthen air defense along its eastern flank, and on September 23 the North Atlantic Council declared that it would use all necessary military and non-military tools and that its commitment to Article 5 was ironclad. Poland closed the Russian consulates in Poznań (October 2024), Kraków (May 2025), and Gdańsk (November 2025) one after another. On November 18, 2025, Prime Minister Tusk told parliament that 55 people had been detained, 23 remanded in custody, and 28 expelled in connection with sabotage cases, and he declared a third-level (CHARLIE) alert on some sections of the rail network. Drone debris damaged one house, but there were no casualties, and Article 5 was not invoked. The attacks continued afterward.
items.why: According to the ICCT, about 95 percent of the perpetrators were "disposable" proxies with no formal ties to Russian intelligence services; they were recruited on Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency, and about half did not live in the targeted country. The two suspects in the railway bombing entered and left Poland via Belarus. Attribution was possible, but there was no obvious party on which to impose direct costs, and the damage was limited, so the alliance responded proportionately, with stronger air defenses and police and diplomatic measures. The ICCT's analysis also suggests that the choice of targets is related to how much a country supports Ukraine.
items.differs: This case sets the baseline for the current situation. Unlike the 2007 attacks on Estonia, the attacks have escalated to physical bombings and arson that could cost lives, and the observation period (2022–2026) is confined to years in which Russia has been at war in Ukraine.

items.name: Finland's total defense after 1944
items.format: Under the September 1944 armistice with the Soviet Union, Finland ceded Karelia, Salla, and Petsamo, leased Porkkala, near Helsinki, to the Soviet Union for 50 years, and accepted heavy war reparations and caps on its armed forces (including 42,000 for the army). [secondary] During the Cold War, it concluded the Agreement of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance with the Soviet Union in 1948 and remained nonaligned, while maintaining a total defense system built on conscription and a large reserve. Today its wartime strength is about 280,000 (95 percent of them reservists), it has about 870,000 trained reservists, and about 75 percent of the male age cohort was conscripted in 2023.
items.outcome: Unlike the Eastern European countries along the Soviet border, Finland escaped occupation and communist rule and kept its independence. The price was the constraint of having to take Soviet interests into account in its foreign policy. The Soviet Union returned Porkkala in 1955, and Finland joined NATO on April 4, 2023.
items.why: The high cost of resistance that Finland demonstrated in the wars of 1939–1944, and the cost of occupation that a large reserve imposes, changed Moscow's calculations. Self-reliance without allies, however, still meant surrendering part of its political autonomy.
items.differs: As a NATO member, Poland combines alliance deterrence with self-reliance. The Finnish model of a large reserve and total defense is the direction Poland is taking as it expands its forces and fortifies its borders, and Finland itself has moved to the same combination since 2023.

items.name: Failed commitments to small states beside great powers: Czechoslovakia (1938), Georgia (2008), and Ukraine (1994–2014)
items.format: (a) Czechoslovakia had concluded an alliance with France in 1924 and also had a treaty with the Soviet Union, but on September 29–30, 1938, in Munich, Germany, Britain, France, and Italy agreed, without Czechoslovak representatives present, that it would cede the Sudetenland, home to about three million ethnic Germans. (b) On April 3, 2008, NATO's Bucharest summit declared that Georgia and Ukraine "will become members of NATO" but did not grant them a Membership Action Plan (MAP). (c) In the Budapest Memorandum of December 5, 1994, the United States, Britain, and Russia gave Ukraine, which was giving up its nuclear weapons, "assurances" that they would respect its territorial integrity.
items.outcome: (a) Germany annexed the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. (b) The Russo-Georgian War broke out in August 2008, and Russia recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. The EU fact-finding mission (the Tagliavini report, September 30, 2009) concluded that Georgia's shelling of Tskhinvali on the night of August 7–8, 2008, triggered the war, but that Russia's military action went far beyond the reasonable limits of defense. (c) Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 effectively nullified the memorandum.
items.why: In all three cases, the states making the commitments had no troops on the ground, and the commitment was either a political promise rather than an obligation to intervene automatically (Budapest), a declaration with no date set for membership (Bucharest), or a pledge whose makers were themselves trying to avoid war (Munich). In each case, the attacker had grounds to believe that the patron would not respond militarily.
items.differs: Poland is a full member of the North Atlantic Treaty and hosts a permanent U.S. garrison and NATO forward-deployed forces on its territory. These cases are therefore better used not to judge Poland itself but as a benchmark for the risks that arise when the alliance's resolve wavers, and for situations in the non-member buffer states along Poland's borders with Ukraine and Belarus.

items.name: Britain's 1939 guarantee and the German and Soviet invasions of Poland
items.format: On March 31, 1939, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons that if Polish independence were threatened, the British government would feel bound "at once to lend the Polish Government all support in their power," and the Anglo-Polish Agreement of Mutual Assistance was signed on August 25, 1939. But the secret protocol of the German-Soviet Nonaggression Pact of August 23, 1939, had already divided Poland into German and Soviet spheres of influence along the Narew, Vistula, and San rivers.
items.outcome: Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, and Britain and France declared war on September 3, but [secondary] they launched no offensive on the Western Front that could have saved Poland. The Soviet Union invaded from the east on September 17.
items.why: There was a written guarantee and a mutual assistance agreement, but no allied troops were in Poland, and the attacker believed a quick war could create a fait accompli. Before the invasion, Germany and the Soviet Union had already fixed in their secret protocol the line along which they would partition Poland.
items.differs: This experience became the historical basis for a conviction in Poland's strategic culture that written guarantees are not enough and that allied troops must be on the ground. Today Poland is a member of the North Atlantic Treaty and hosts a permanent U.S. garrison and NATO forward-deployed forces on its territory (see P12).

items.name: The Solidarity crisis of 1980–81 and the Soviet threat of intervention
items.format: According to the minutes of the Soviet Politburo meeting of December 10, 1981, Andropov said that Moscow had no intention of sending troops into Poland, Gromyko that sending in troops was out of the question, and Suslov that doing so would be a catastrophe. The Polish leadership under Jaruzelski, by contrast, signaled indirectly that if Polish forces could not cope on their own, it expected support that could extend to the dispatch of Soviet troops.
items.outcome: Three days later, on December 13, 1981, Poland declared martial law.
items.why: The minutes show that the Soviet leadership's actual willingness to intervene was weaker than the threat of intervention perceived from outside. The case shows that a threat of outside intervention can be inflated beyond the real intent to intervene and exploited for domestic political purposes.
items.differs: The threat of intervention in 1981 concerned a domestic crisis in Poland; today the standoff is between Russia and Poland as a NATO member. Still, the lesson that there can be a gap between the threats an adversary brandishes and its actual intentions remains relevant in assessing Russia's threats.

items.name: NATO membership and the building of deterrence on the eastern flank
items.format: Poland joined NATO on March 12, 1999. At the Warsaw summit in July 2016, NATO decided on the Enhanced Forward Presence (eFP), rotating multinational battalions through Poland and the Baltic states, and it became operational in 2017 (the battlegroup in Poland is led by the United States). On March 21, 2023, the U.S. Army established its first permanent garrison in Poland (USAG Poland) at Camp Kościuszko in Poznań.
items.outcome: Poland requested Article 4 consultations on March 3, 2014, right after the annexation of Crimea; again on February 24, 2022, together with seven other countries; and on its own on September 10, 2025, after the drone incursions.
items.why: Since joining NATO, Poland has steadily widened the arrangements that put allied troops on the ground, moving from the rotational deployment of multinational battalions to a permanent U.S. garrison. Behind this lies the experience of 1939 (P13), which taught that written guarantees alone are not enough.
items.differs: These arrangements are still in place, and the observation that there have been no overt ground attacks largely overlaps with the period in which most of Russia's ground forces were tied down in Ukraine (see P4).

items.name: Rearmament and the fortification of the eastern border since 2022
items.format: By NATO's count, Poland's defense spending rose from 1.86 percent of GDP in 2014 to 2.21 percent in 2022, an estimated 4.25 percent in 2025, and an estimated 4.68 percent in 2026 (July 2026 figures). The government's 2026 budget bill set defense spending at about 200 billion zlotys (about 4.8 percent of GDP). East Shield (Tarcza Wschód), announced in May 2024, is a program to spend about 10 billion zlotys by 2028 building barriers, anti-tank ditches, and counter-drone systems along roughly 800 kilometers of the borders with Belarus and Russia.
items.outcome: Poland's defense spending as a share of GDP is the highest in NATO. East Shield is under way, with 2028 as its target.
items.why: Alongside alliance deterrence, Poland is building up its own strength, and like Finnish total defense (P11), it is aiming to raise the cost of occupation by expanding its forces and fortifying its borders.
items.differs: Because this case is still unfolding, its deterrent effect has not yet been tested. The defense spending ratios for 2025 and 2026 are NATO estimates.

checks.reason: The precedents show that pressure below the threshold of war has often been contained without military conflict. The 2014 explosion at the Vrbětice ammunition depot killed two people, yet the response went no further than public attribution and the expulsion of diplomats in 2021; the 2022 Kaliningrad transit dispute was settled through EU guidance, and the 1961 tank standoff at Checkpoint Charlie through an informal agreement. Russian attacks in Europe rose from three in 2022 to 34 in 2024 (by CSIS's count), but Article 5 was not invoked even during the drone incursions of September 2025. This is consistent with C1, which sees a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (40%) and a deadly incident that is then patched up (30%) as the most likely futures. The observation period, however, coincides with the years in which most of Russia's ground forces were tied down in Ukraine, so precedent alone cannot show whether this pattern will hold after the war in Ukraine ends.

Where deterrence collapsed, in Poland in 1939 and South Korea in 1950, and in Czechoslovakia, Georgia, and Ukraine, there were no allied troops on the ground; where it held, in Berlin and under NATO's forward presence, allied troops were there. This supports C2, which ranks a permanent U.S. troop presence first. Finland, which preserved its independence by raising the cost of occupation with a large reserve, and Poland's own rearmament and border fortification are consistent with the judgment that national resilience should be built up alongside it. The 1956 Suez crisis shows that nuclear threats work when an alliance is divided, so stronger European defense must go hand in hand with solidarity with the United States rather than replace it. Yet deterrence held in Berlin even though the West Berlin garrison was too small to defend the city, so the criterion of making fighting capability rather than troop numbers the goal of negotiations rests more on empirical research than on precedent. And as with South Korea in 1949, any adjustment to the troop presence can itself be read as a sign of a weakening commitment, so capability-focused negotiations must not come across as a drawdown.

Since 2017 there have been no overt ground attacks on NATO territory, but in the same region cyberattacks, sabotage, drone incursions into airspace, and damage to undersea infrastructure have increased sharply since 2022. In Berlin in 1961, too, the West defended its presence and access rights but did not stop the building of the wall. In Estonia, the Czech Republic, Finland, and Poland alike, the response to attacks below the threshold of war was to impose nonmilitary costs: public attribution, the expulsion of diplomats, stepped-up patrols, and broader legal interpretation. This is consistent with C3, which holds that tripwires cannot stop below-threshold attacks. But Poland has already closed all Russian consulates, largely exhausting its means of imposing diplomatic costs, and the attacks have continued since then, so the precedents do not answer the question of what selective punishment should consist of.

The 1961 tank standoff at Checkpoint Charlie ended with both sides pulling back after an agreement reached through informal channels, and the 2022 Kaliningrad transit dispute was likewise calmed through legal compromise. That channels for defusing accidental standoffs have actually been used is consistent with C4's judgment to give priority to mechanisms for preventing accidental clashes. Moreover, Russia's 2024 nuclear deterrence doctrine names Belarus among the conditions for nuclear use and permits nuclear use even against a conventional attack that poses a critical threat to sovereignty and territorial integrity, so if Poland or Lithuania became embroiled in a clash on the border with Belarus or Kaliningrad, nuclear signals could apply more directly than they did in Ukraine. The risk that an accidental border clash could escalate into something far larger is correspondingly high. During the drone incursions of September 2025, however, only one house was damaged and there were no casualties, and the precedents do not directly show how much harm civilians would suffer in a full-scale war.

precedents.insight: In the cases where deterrence held (Berlin in 1948–1949 and 1958–1961, and NATO's forward presence since 2017), great-power allied troops were on the ground, so an attack would have meant immediate direct combat, and the alliance's largest power showed through action, with an airlift, a reserve call-up, and permanent deployments, that it would not back down. In the cases where deterrence failed (Czechoslovakia in 1938, Poland in 1939, South Korea in 1950, Georgia in 2008, and Ukraine in 2014), there were no allied troops on the ground or the commitment was ambiguous, and the attacker believed a quick war could create a fait accompli. Pressure through isolation or blockade was more often relieved not by breaking through by force but by unarmed means that left the other side to use force first (the 1948 airlift) or by multilateral rules (the EU's 2022 Kaliningrad guidance). Nuclear threats substantially changed the outcome when an alliance was divided (Suez in 1956), but in 2022–2025, with the alliance united, they did not lead to nuclear use and only affected the scope and pace of decisions. No overt ground attack took place, but tripwires did not stop attacks below the threshold of war, such as cyberattacks, sabotage, drones, and damage to undersea infrastructure, and the responses went no further than imposing nonmilitary costs: public attribution, the expulsion of diplomats, stepped-up patrols, and broader legal interpretation. Finland preserved its independence through self-reliance that raised the cost of occupation, but without allies it had to give up part of its political autonomy; Poland, by contrast, combines self-reliance with alliance deterrence. Precedent alone, however, cannot tell whether attacks on Poland stay below the threshold today because of deterrence or because Russia's forces are tied down in Ukraine. The real test will come after the war in Ukraine ends.
uncertain: Sources give different dates for when Lithuania began restricting rail transit of sanctioned goods to Kaliningrad in 2022 (after June 17, June 18, or June 20), so the date could not be established.
Even within the U.S. State Department's historical records, the end of the Berlin blockade is dated both May 11 and May 12, 1949.

The U.S. State Department's historical records date Khrushchev's 1958 Berlin ultimatum to November 10. The date of the formal notes sent to the three Western powers could not be confirmed from primary sources.

The U.S. State Department (Britain's acceptance on November 6, 1956) and Britain's Imperial War Museums (the UN resolution of November 7) use different reference points for the Suez ceasefire. The original text of Bulganin's letters could not be checked directly because the CVCE website blocked access, and the wording of the threatened rocket attacks relies on secondary accounts.

The exact date on which the withdrawal of U.S. forces from South Korea was completed in 1949 (reportedly June 29) and the size of the U.S. military advisory group in Korea could not be confirmed from primary sources. The account of the April 1950 conversation between Stalin and Kim Il Sung rests on researchers' summaries rather than the original records.

No confirmed official figures could be found for the exact number of drones that entered Polish airspace on September 9–10, 2025, or for the number shot down (Prime Minister Tusk cited 19 violations; Ukraine's air force, at least eight drones).

Even within materials from the Polish prime minister's office, accounts differ on whether the train passing at the time of the November 2025 railway bombing was a passenger train carrying 475 people or a freight train.

Whether the Eagle S case will be appealed to the Supreme Court (the deadline to seek leave is October 26, 2026) and what will follow could not be confirmed. The appellate ruling was confirmed through press reports (The Record); the text of the judgment itself was not reviewed.
Whether Russian tactical nuclear weapons have actually been deployed in Belarus, and in what numbers, could not be confirmed from primary sources beyond official announcements.
The 1948 Finnish-Soviet Agreement of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance and the exact amount of Finland's war reparations could not be confirmed from primary sources.
Researchers differ on whether Russia's nuclear threats slowed Western decisions on support for Ukraine, and no quantitative evidence could be found.

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Yale University Press, 1966, chapter 2, "The Art of Commitment," pp. 47–49 (the Berlin garrison)
links.idea: Schelling located the reason a small garrison in Berlin could hold Soviet forces in check not in the troops' fighting power but in the fact that there was no way out of the commitment: "What can 7,000 American troops do, or 12,000 Allied troops? Bluntly, they can die. They can die heroically, dramatically, and in a manner that guarantees that the action cannot stop there." (p. 47) He went on to argue that when a commitment is ambiguous, the adversary expects the defender to choose the lenient interpretation. The sectors of West Berlin were "a tightly defined piece of earth," so the commitment to them was "credible because it is inescapable," but the commitment to the city as a whole was ambiguous. As he put it, "When the Wall went up the West was able to construe its obligation as not obliging forceful opposition." (p. 48)
links.fit: The distinction drawn in C3 is already present in Schelling's own logic. A tripwire becomes an "inescapable commitment" only for a clearly bounded object, namely an armed attack on allied territory. Sabotage, drones, and attacks on undersea infrastructure fall, like the Berlin Wall, within the room for interpreting the commitment, and the alliance has an incentive to read them as not requiring a forceful response. If Russia anticipates this and chooses to stay below the threshold, the tripwire's failure to stop sub-threshold attacks is not an accident but a structural outcome.
links.limit: Schelling was explaining the U.S. commitment against the Soviet Union to American readers from the perspective of the protector, the United States. The context—a protector's forward-deployed garrison facing Russia (then the Soviet Union)—matches this issue, but the interests differ: the protected party, the Polish government, wants the commitment to be inescapable, whereas the United States wants to keep its options open. Schelling also cited the fact that the Soviets never crossed that boundary as evidence of deterrence, but in this passage he did not examine whether the Soviets had any intention of invading (see Reiter and Poast below).
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, Arms and Influence, Yale University Press, 1966 (Veritas paperback edition, 2020, retaining the original pagination), ch. 2, pp. 47–49 — checked against the text

links.work: Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, Harvard University Press, 1960, chapter 8, "The Threat That Leaves Something to Chance," pp. 187–203
links.idea: The force of a strategic threat can come not from a firm commitment to carry it out but from a risk that may slip out of control. The crux is that "the final decision is not altogether under the threatener's control" (p. 188), and Schelling used this logic to reinterpret the forces stationed in Europe: "What we have is a graduated series of trip wires, each attached to a chance mechanism, with the daily probability of detonation increasing as the enemy moves from wire to wire." (p. 192) He also held that the probability of accidental war rises with a crisis (p. 188), and he criticized the dichotomy of a tripwire that either works or does not as "mistaking two simple extremes for a more complicated range of probabilities" (p. 203).
links.fit: For C1, it is a reminder that an incident that kills people but is then patched up (30%) and limited use of force (5%) are not separate events but neighboring rungs on the same ladder, and that each incident raises the probability of the next rung. The point that the probability of accidental war rises with a crisis is consistent with C4, which gives priority to mechanisms that keep accidental clashes from escalating into war. Russia's nuclear threats, too, can be seen less as a commitment to actual use than as a device for making the other side share the risk and thereby constraining the range and speed of its decisions; the observation that they did not lead to nuclear use in 2022–2025, while the alliance held together, is what this device looks like when it works as designed.
links.limit: The assessment comes with conditions. First, the observation that nuclear threats did not lead to use was made in the absence of actual combat. According to Schelling, the risk grows as a crisis deepens and part of it is beyond anyone's control, so this regularity cannot be carried over to a phase in which fighting breaks out in the Suwałki Gap. Second, in Schelling's logic of the threat that leaves something to chance, the risk of uncontrolled escalation is itself a source of deterrence. Mechanisms to prevent accidental clashes may therefore weaken deterrence somewhat even as they guard against escalation, and C4 is a judgment that accepts this cost.
sources: Thomas C. Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict, Harvard University Press, 1960 (1980 edition, with a new preface), ch. 8, pp. 187–203 — checked against the text of the 1980 edition

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, Deterrence and Defense: Toward a Theory of National Security, Princeton University Press, 1961, chapter 1, pp. 14–15
links.idea: Snyder divided deterrence into deterrence by punishment and deterrence by denial. Deterrence by punishment is the threat to impose costs greater than what the adversary stands to gain; deterrence by denial is the capability to reduce the adversary's chances of achieving its objective in the first place. The credibility of a threat of punishment depends on the cost the punishing side would bear in carrying it out, while denial capabilities also serve for actual defense if deterrence fails, so in their case the functions of deterrence and defense overlap.
links.fit: Supports C2, which does not give top priority to deterrence by punishment through long-range strike—the message that an attack will be made to pay—and instead sets the goal of negotiations over the U.S. military presence as the capability to fight. If the targets that Polish long-range strike could reach are limited to Kaliningrad and carrying out a strike could provoke Russian escalation, the cost of execution is high and the threat loses credibility. The same resources spent on denial capabilities remain available for defense even if deterrence fails.
links.limit: Snyder's distinction assumed all-out nuclear and conventional war. Polish long-range strikes could be aimed not at the Russian heartland but at operational targets such as launch bases and command posts, doubling as denial, so the line between punishment and denial is blurrier than in the 1961 distinction. The original text could not be checked directly, and the page numbers follow citations in the secondary literature.

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, Deterrence and Defense: Toward a Theory of National Security, Princeton University Press, 1961, chapter 1, pp. 14–15 (an extended application of deterrence by denial)
links.idea: Deterrence by denial removes the motive for action by depriving the adversary of what it would gain. For deterrence to work, the adversary's objective must be a gain that can be denied.
links.fit: C3's call to answer sub-threshold attacks with resilience extends deterrence by denial to the protection of infrastructure. It is supported in that, if the damage sabotage aims to cause (paralysis of power, communications, and rail) can be repaired quickly, the payoff from an attack shrinks.
links.limit: With conditions. By denial, Snyder meant military force capable of preventing the seizure of territory. If the aim of sub-threshold attacks is not physical damage but a show of menace, a test of alliance cohesion, or the division of domestic opinion, the attacker has already achieved much of its aim even if the damage is quickly repaired. In that case resilience limits the damage but does not deter, and it must be accompanied by attribution and an alliance-level response (see Mazarr below). C3's call to combine resilience with selective punishment is its answer to this condition.

links.work: Glenn H. Snyder, "The Security Dilemma in Alliance Politics," World Politics 36(4), July 1984, pp. 461–495
links.idea: Allies maneuver between the risks of abandonment and entrapment (being dragged into an unwanted conflict). Clinging to the alliance to reduce the risk of abandonment raises the risk of entrapment and weakens one's bargaining power within the alliance; keeping one's distance does the opposite. This alliance game interacts with the choice between firmness and conciliation toward the adversary. Snyder held that the dilemma is acute in a multipolar system and weak in a bipolar one, in which the superpowers have no choice but to defend their allies for the sake of their own interests.
links.fit: Supports C2's condition of preparing European insurance against the risk of abandonment through a U.S.-Russian deal. In Snyder's logic, fears of abandonment grow as the system moves closer to multipolarity with U.S. attention shifting to China, and so does the need for insurance. Stronger European defense lowers dependence on the United States and thus reduces the cost of abandonment.
links.limit: Two conditions apply. First, in Snyder's model, a signal that one side is keeping its distance can trigger the other side's fears of abandonment and its own distancing. If stronger European defense is read in Washington as a signal that Europe wants less of the U.S. commitment, it risks hastening a U.S. exit. Second (an inference by Clisa Geopolitics), spreading insurance across several policies pays off most when each policy fails independently. A weakening of the U.S. commitment through a U.S.-Russian deal is likely to strengthen the case for accommodating Russia within Europe as well, so the U.S. troop insurance and the European insurance could falter together; the risk that diversification reduces may therefore be smaller than C2 expects. Moreover, as in the U.S.-South Korean relationship, the U.S.-Polish relationship is highly asymmetric, so threats of exit by the weaker side are hard to make credible.

links.work: Dan Reiter and Paul Poast, "The Truth about Tripwires: Why Small Force Deployments Do Not Deter Aggression," Texas National Security Review 4(3), Summer 2021
links.idea: Tripwire forces do not change the local balance of forces and are therefore insufficient for deterrence. Even when casualties occur, publics and leaders do not necessarily demand intervention (Beirut in 1983, Mogadishu in 1993), and an attacker will strike if it can create a fait accompli before reinforcements arrive. In the case of Berlin, the documentary record shows that the Soviet and East German leaderships had no plans to invade West Berlin, so it is unclear what the garrison deterred. On the Korean Peninsula in 1949–1950, Stalin approved the invasion after U.S. forces had been cut to tripwire levels. The authors conclude that "Tripwire-force deployments are insufficient to bolster deterrence because deterrence is about more than signaling," and that deterrence depends on the ability of forward-deployed forces to slow or stop an attack.
links.fit: Does not conflict with C3's assessment that a tripwire cannot stop sub-threshold attacks. Attacks aimed at a fait accompli and sub-threshold attacks both exploit the gap in which a tripwire cannot compel a response.
links.limit: It refutes the causal claim that the tripwire deterred a full-scale ground attack. The absence of a full-scale attack does not by itself show that the tripwire deterred one; whether Russia had any such plans, and how much it mattered that Russian ground forces were tied down in Ukraine after 2022, have to be examined separately. Clisa Geopolitics accepts this rebuttal and attributes the absence of a full-scale ground attack less to the tripwire itself than to the forces of the alliance as a whole and of Poland itself, and to the fact that Russian forces were tied down in Ukraine. The study has its own limits. The number of cases is small, and it does not directly test the effect of tripwires linked to the nuclear umbrella after 1945. In addition, unlike the Baltic states, which host only battalion-sized multinational battlegroups, Poland has U.S. forces that the authors recorded as "brigade-sized," which places them closer to a capability than to a pure tripwire.

links.work: Brian Blankenship·Erik Lin-Greenberg, 「Trivial Tripwires? Military Capabilities and Alliance Reassurance」, Security Studies 31(1), 2022, pp. 92–117
links.idea: The reassurance that allies draw is the product of resolve and capability, and high resolve cannot make up for low capability. A survey of European foreign policy and security experts and case studies of U.S. and NATO reassurance measures in the Baltic region found that tripwire forces on allied territory reassure no more than high-capability forces deployed outside it.
links.fit: Attaches a condition to C2, which ranks a permanent U.S. military presence first. If what the Polish government seeks is reassurance as well as deterrence, the value lies less in the fact that U.S. troops are present than in the ability of those troops and the reinforcement system to actually fight. This is why C2 sets the goal of negotiations over the U.S. presence not as troop numbers but as capabilities such as air defense, long-range fires, and speed of reinforcement, and the capabilities that European allies provide can be judged by the same yardstick.
links.limit: The survey respondents were experts; the study did not measure the judgment of the Polish government itself. In the ensuing exchange (Security Studies 31(4), 2022), Goldgeier and Wojtowicz pointed to the differing requirements of deterrence and reassurance and to the role of allies other than the United States, and Mastro to the concept of the tripwire and the reassuring effect of temporary operations, as questions for further work. The study rests on data from before the full-scale invasion of 2022.

links.work: Michael J. Mazarr, Mastering the Gray Zone: Understanding a Changing Era of Conflict, Strategic Studies Institute and U.S. Army War College Press, December 2015
links.idea: A gray-zone strategy is an integrated campaign that moves toward its goals gradually rather than seeking decisive results and tries to stay below key escalation thresholds; it is an instrument tailored to measured revisionists, who seek to alter the system bit by bit rather than overturn it. Mazarr hypothesized that such strategies erode the credibility of U.S. deterrence and reassurance commitments and heighten the risk of miscalculation and accidental war. At the same time, observing that "Avoiding thresholds of response turns out to be very difficult," he argued that gray-zone offensives tend to be self-defeating. In his recommendations, he held that outcomes are shaped chiefly not by tactical skill but by the strength of the rules-based order and the social and political resilience of the target state, and he urged: "Punish selected revisionist actions and broadcast true red lines."
links.fit: Supports C3, which centers the response to sub-threshold attacks on resilience. It is also consistent with C1, which sees a sustained standoff below the threshold of war (40%) and an incident that kills people but is then patched up (30%) as the most likely futures. The observation that thresholds are hard to avoid explains the path by which sub-threshold offensives sometimes escalate into deadly incidents.
links.limit: With the condition that resilience alone is not enough. Mazarr recommended selective punishment and the clear public declaration of red lines alongside denial (resilience). C3's call to combine resilience with selective punishment (public attribution, sanctions, and proportionate responses at the alliance level) against sub-threshold attacks reflects this recommendation, but C3 does not include declaring red lines. The study was written before 2022 with U.S. policy as its subject, and its hypotheses were not systematically tested.

links.work: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (Il Principe), chapter 13, "De militibus auxiliariis, mixtis et propriis" (titled "De' soldati ausiliari, misti, e propri" in the Wikisource edition), written in 1513 and published in 1532
links.idea: Machiavelli defined auxiliary arms (ausiliarie) as what one has "quando si chiama un potente, che con l'armi sue ti venga ad aiutare e difendere" (when one calls in a powerful man to come with his arms to help and defend you), and he held that such troops, however useful in themselves, are harmful to those who call them in. Citing the story of David refusing Saul's armor, he summed up: "l'armi d'altri o le ti cascono di dosso, o elle ti pesano, e le ti stringono" (the arms of others either fall off your back, or weigh you down, or constrict you). Mixed forces that combine one's own troops with those of others are far better than pure auxiliaries but far inferior to one's own ("molto migliori ... e molto inferiori alle proprie"), and his conclusion was "senza avere arme proprie, nessuno Principato è sicuro" (without arms of its own, no principality is secure).
links.fit: The context fits. In a book dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, Machiavelli was writing about Italian princes who called in the armies of powerful states to protect themselves (Pope Julius II calling in the army of King Ferdinand of Spain), and the Polish government's request for a permanent U.S. military presence is a call for auxiliaries in exactly his sense. Falling off, weighing down, and constricting correspond, respectively, to abandonment through a U.S.-Russian deal, the costs and price of the deployment, and the entrapment of being bound to the protector's priorities. C2 therefore comes with a condition. U.S. forces and Europe are both the arms of others, so spreading the insurance between them reduces the risk but does not eliminate it. Poland's own forces must be placed squarely at the center of the judgment, with U.S. forces and European defense layered on top of them as a mixed force.
links.limit: The greatest danger Machiavelli warned of—that if the auxiliaries win, the one who called them in becomes their prisoner ("vincendo resti loro prigione")—does not apply directly to NATO, a treaty-based alliance, or to the U.S.-Polish relationship. And because he wrote in an age without nuclear deterrence, his argument does not cover the realm of nuclear deterrence, where Poland cannot rely on its own forces and has no choice but to depend on the arms of others. Machiavelli's conclusion should therefore be read not as "one's own forces only" but as "a mixed force built on one's own forces." The quotations follow the Italian Wikisource edition and differ in spelling and word forms from critical editions (e.g., "...o le ti caggiono di dosso, o le ti pesano, o le ti stringono").

theory.insight: Set against the theory, the framework of C3—that an armed attack on allied territory and sub-threshold attacks call for different instruments—holds up. Schelling himself, citing the Berlin Wall, wrote that where a commitment leaves room for interpretation, the adversary expects the defender to choose the lenient reading. Reiter and Poast's empirical work, however, does not support the causal claim that the tripwire deterred a full-scale ground attack. Clisa Geopolitics therefore locates the source of deterrence in the forces of the alliance as a whole and of Poland itself, and in C2 it sets the goal of negotiations over a permanent U.S. military presence not as the mere presence of troops but as the capability to fight. Snyder's alliance dilemma and Machiavelli's account of auxiliaries support C2's condition of preparing European insurance in case the U.S. commitment falters, but they add a condition of their own: because U.S. and European insurance could falter together during a U.S.-Russian deal, and because both are the arms of others, Poland's own forces must be placed squarely at the center of the judgment. Schelling's threat that leaves something to chance supports C1 and C4 in that the risk of accidental war grows as a crisis deepens, while also requiring that the observed regularity—nuclear threats that did not lead to use—not be carried over to a phase of actual combat, and that the risk of escalation be counted not only as a cost but also as a source of deterrence. Mazarr's gray-zone study supports a resilience-centered response but holds that it must be accompanied by selective punishment and clear red lines; of these, C3 has adopted selective punishment.
uncertain: The volume and issue of the Reiter and Poast article (vol. 4, no. 3, Summer 2021) were confirmed through the TNSR author page and a War on the Rocks podcast page, but the page range could not be confirmed. The issue's table of contents on tnsr.org could not be accessed because of request limits, and Project MUSE returned a security-check page.

The cited page numbers from chapter 8 of The Strategy of Conflict (pp. 187, 188, 192, and 203) were confirmed in the text of the 1980 edition (with a new preface). The text was assumed to have the same pagination as the 1960 first edition, but it was not checked against a copy of the first edition.

The cited page numbers from Arms and Influence (pp. 47–48) were confirmed in the 2020 Veritas paperback edition (whose pagination and index match the 1966 Yale edition). They were not checked against a copy of the 1966 first edition.

The page numbers for the denial-punishment distinction in Snyder's Deterrence and Defense (1961) (pp. 14–15) follow the citation in Zilincik and Sweijs (Contemporary Security Policy 44(2), 2023). The original text and the title of chapter 1 could not be checked directly, and the point that the credibility of a threat of punishment depends on the cost of carrying it out was likewise summarized without checking it against the original.

The finer points of Snyder's 1984 article (such as the passage on signals of distancing triggering the other side's fears of abandonment) rely on the abstract and existing summaries and were not rechecked against the full text.
The argument that the U.S. troop insurance and the European insurance could falter together during a U.S.-Russian deal is an inference by Clisa Geopolitics, not a claim made by Snyder.

The quotations from Mazarr's report were confirmed in the SSI executive summary.
