The full-text PDF (DTIC) returned a blocked page and could not be accessed, so the total page count (154 pages, according to a retailer's listing) and the page numbers of the quotations in the main text could not be confirmed.

The bibliographic details of the Blankenship and Lin-Greenberg article (Security Studies 31(1), pp. 92–117) were confirmed through Crossref, and the gist of its findings through a summary by the MIT Security Studies Program. The full text could not be accessed.
The quotations from chapter 13 of Machiavelli follow the Italian Wikisource edition and differ in spelling and word forms from critical editions such as Inglese's.

Reiter and Poast's description of U.S. forces in Poland as "brigade-sized" reflects the situation in 2021 and may differ from their size, or from their permanent or rotational status, as of October 2026.

items.q: Is there currently a threat to Poland's independence?
items.latest: September 11–22, 2025; 969 adults; mixed mode (face-to-face, telephone, online)
items.read: In the September 2025 survey, 63 percent said a threat exists and 26 percent said it does not, the highest figure since CBOS began asking this question in February 1991. The survey was conducted just after Russian drones entered Polish airspace on September 9–10, 2025.
items.caveat: Survey values between May 2022 and September 2025 could not be confirmed, so only the two data points are connected. The sample was drawn at random from the national population register (PESEL).

items.q: Poland's security rests on its NATO membership. Can Poland today be confident that its allies will take part in defending its borders?
items.latest: September 11–22, 2025; 969 adults; mixed mode (face-to-face, telephone, online)
items.read: In the September 2025 survey, 68 percent said Poland could be confident (14 percent definitely, 54 percent somewhat), while 24 percent said it could not. That is lower than the 81 percent recorded in March 2022, just after the full-scale invasion, but 7 percentage points higher than in March 2025. In the same survey, 62 percent said the U.S. response to the drone incursion of September 2025 was inadequate, while 51 percent rated the response of European allies positively.
items.caveat: The report does not quote the exact wording of the question on the U.S. response. A separate CBOS survey asking whether U.S. forces would come to Poland's aid if Russia attacked (commissioned by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna, October 2025; 63.8 percent said they would help) asked a different question and is not joined to this series (press reports).

items.q: Which should take priority: ending the war and restoring peace, even if Ukraine has to give up part of its territory or its independence, or continuing to fight without concessions to Russia?
items.unit: End the war first / keep fighting, %
items.latest: November 27–December 8, 2025; 948 adults; mixed mode (face-to-face, telephone, online)
items.read: The share saying that ending the war should come first held steady at 54 percent, while the share saying the fight should continue without concessions rose from 28 percent to 33 percent. Poles regard Russia as a threat, yet a majority want the war in Ukraine to end even if it means giving up territory.
items.caveat: Because the option also includes giving up independence, the figures cannot be compared directly with questions that ask only about territorial concessions. The September 2025 figure is the comparison value given in the December 2025 report.

items.q: Do you have a favorable or unfavorable opinion of NATO (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization)?
items.latest: February 8–May 13, 2026 (fieldwork period for the full 37-country survey); telephone survey; Polish sample size not confirmed
items.read: In the 2026 survey, 78 percent viewed NATO favorably (29 percent very, 50 percent somewhat) and 13 percent unfavorably. In the same survey, 7 percent viewed Russia favorably, and 4 percent said they had confidence in President Putin to do the right thing regarding world affairs. Favorable views of NATO remain high but have declined for two consecutive years since 2024.
items.caveat: The timing and method of the 2025 survey could not be confirmed. The 2024 figure comes from a telephone survey.

items.q: Do you regard today's United States as a reliable ally of Poland?
items.latest: Late January 2026 (fieldwork dates, sample, and method not disclosed)
items.read: Asked whether today's United States is a reliable ally, 53.2 percent said it is not, 29.9 percent said it is, and 16.9 percent did not know. Set against the CBOS finding that 68 percent are confident their allies would take part in defending the border, this suggests that Poles' doubts are aimed at the United States rather than at the alliance as a whole.
items.caveat: A single survey. The fieldwork dates, sample, and method were not disclosed, and the original survey could not be checked, so the figures rely on reporting by Notes from Poland.

publics.read: Poles feel the Russian threat more keenly than at any time since 1991 (63 percent say a threat exists), yet they are broadly confident that their allies would take part in defending the border (68%). Only about 30 percent, however, regard today's United States as a reliable ally (press reports). This fits the assessment (C2) that Poland should lean on a permanent U.S. troop presence while keeping its own forces at the center and having European insurance ready. On the war in Ukraine, though, a majority of 54 percent say ending it should come first, even at the cost of territory. This trend signals that after the 2027 parliamentary election Poland could move toward scaling back its involvement in Ukraine and lowering the level of confrontation with Russia (A9).
publics.watch: If the share in CBOS surveys who are confident that allies would take part in Poland's defense falls below 60 percent, or the share who say ending the war in Ukraine should come first rises above 60 percent, the assessments of strengthening the European pillar (A2) and scaling back involvement in Ukraine (A9) will be revisited, taking into account the standoff between the president and the government and the shape of the 2027 election.

rows.name: Managed competition
rows.why: A world in which the Russia-Ukraine war is frozen without a legal end. Risk-reduction mechanisms could emerge alongside a ceasefire, so the probability of lower tensions (P6) is higher than in the other world scenarios. Russia may rebuild its forces after a ceasefire, but because the U.S. commitment to Europe holds in this world, the probability of limited use of force (P4) is judged low. Incidents decline, but the standoff below the threshold continues.

rows.name: Armed multipolarity
rows.why: As the U.S. retreat accelerates, Russia has a greater incentive to test whether the alliance's commitments will actually be honored. The probabilities of a deadly incident (P2) and limited use of force (P4) therefore rise, and that of lower tensions (P6) falls.

rows.name: Protracted linked wars
rows.why: A world in which the Russia-Ukraine war continues and U.S. military capacity is tied down in the Gulf. More frequent sub-threshold attacks raise the probability of a deadly incident (P2), but because Russia's ground forces are also tied down in Ukraine, the probabilities of limited use of force and full-scale war do not rise much. With a ceasefire in Ukraine further off, the probability of lower tensions (P6) is the lowest of any world scenario.

rows.name: Taiwan Strait crisis
rows.why: If U.S. attention and forces shift to Taiwan, Russia gains room to maneuver in the Baltic. The probabilities of a Kaliningrad blockade crisis (P3) and limited use of force (P4) therefore rise. In the world scenario table for the Russia-Ukraine war issue, however, the probability of a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in this world is higher than in C, so the probability of lower tensions (P6) is also set slightly higher than in C.

rows.name: Internal fracture in one pole
rows.why: Within this world scenario, the case used as the baseline is a collapse of Russia's war economy. Lower tensions (P6) then become more likely, but so does the risk that a cornered regime acts recklessly, so the probabilities of limited use of force (P4) and full-scale war (P5) also rise slightly. Internal fractures in Iran or China are judged to have little effect on this issue.

world.note: These are the probabilities of this issue's futures under each of the world scenarios A through E in the World Order tab. They are set so that, weighted by the probabilities of the world scenarios and summed, they match this issue's baseline probabilities to within one percentage point (a law-of-total-probability check). All figures are judgment estimates.

counter.name: Russia
counter.note: This is not a recommendation to Russia. It is an assessment of Russia's best move, measured against objectives derived from its own documents and its actual conduct. The ranking among those objectives is Clisa Geopolitics' interpretation. Because Russia's official documents carry a heavy load of propaganda, its objectives were adjusted on the basis of its actual conduct. For example, its documents list the isolation of Kaliningrad as a danger to be deterred with nuclear weapons, yet Russia sent Kaliningrad's ground forces to the Ukrainian front. Its war aims in Ukraine are therefore ranked above Kaliningrad. The Baltic Sea export routes do not appear separately in the documents but were included as an objective on the strength of Russia's military escort of the shadow fleet.

goals.d: Preserve the regime and be recognized as a great power. The Foreign Policy Concept treats the United States as an influential center of world development and as the main source of threats to Russia's security
goals.src: Foreign Policy Concept, March 2023, paragraphs 59 and 62

goals.d: Secure the four annexed regions (starting with the rest of Donetsk Oblast) and neutralize Ukraine
goals.src: Putin's conditions of June 14, 2024; the annexation of October 2022 (Russia's objectives in the Russia-Ukraine war issue)

goals.t: Keeping NATO away from its borders and splitting the United States from Europe
goals.d: Stop NATO military infrastructure and foreign troops from moving closer to its borders, and drive a wedge between the United States and Europe
goals.src: Military Doctrine of 2014, paragraph 12; Foreign Policy Concept of 2023, paragraph 59; Maritime Doctrine of 2022, paragraph 54

goals.t: Security of Kaliningrad and its access routes
goals.d: Protect Kaliningrad and secure the transport routes to and from the Russian mainland. The Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence list the blocking of transport routes that would isolate part of Russia's territory as a danger to be deterred with nuclear weapons
goals.src: Maritime Doctrine of July 2022, paragraph 56(2); Basic Principles of State Policy on Nuclear Deterrence of November 2024, paragraph 15(g)

goals.d: Protect the Baltic Sea export routes, including those used by the shadow fleet. [secondary] Nikolai Patrushev, chairman of the Maritime Board, responded to ship seizures by European countries by saying that Russia cannot allow its key sea routes to be blockaded (press reports)
goals.src: Confirmed by conduct (armed escort of the shadow fleet); remarks by the chairman of the Maritime Board

Draws out caution in Washington but unites Europe

Deepens divisions within Poland but also rallies NATO
Invites retaliation and tougher maritime inspections
alts.feas: High (as long as proxies can still be recruited)

ev: Gives NATO a reason to strengthen its eastern posture
alts.feas: Medium (some assess that it is possible even during the war in Ukraine; [secondary] press reports on a 2026 assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service)

ev: All-out war with NATO and nuclear risk
Draws troops away from the Ukrainian front
If the U.S. commitment holds, prompts NATO to close ranks and build up

alts.name: Accepting lower tensions and risk-reduction mechanisms (without a reduction in forward deployment)
ev: Lowers the risk of escalation but gains nothing in return
Accepts forward deployment as it stands and gives up a bargaining chip
Lowers the risk of accidental clashes
alts.feas: Low (Russia would agree to talk but demand a reduction in NATO's forward deployment in return)

ranked.t: Russia's most advantageous move at present is to keep imposing costs below the threshold of war while bundling, in direct talks with Washington, a ceasefire in Ukraine with limits on NATO's force posture on the eastern flank (caps on rotational forces, limits on exercises near the border). If that deal went through, Russia could sharply reduce the effect of the U.S. buildup without firing a shot. In the draft treaties it sent to the United States and NATO in December 2021, Russia likewise demanded that no forces be stationed in countries that joined NATO after May 1997. Because it is uncertain whether Washington would accept NATO's eastern-flank posture as a subject for negotiation, the feasibility of this move is rated medium; in the meantime, the standoff below the threshold of war (P1, 40% probability) continues. If the deal went through, the result would come close to lower tensions bought with a reduction in forward deployment (P6), which is better for Russia than P1. The deciding-powers analysis rates Russia's preference for P6 as Acceptable because that judgment also covers lower tensions that come without any such price. [secondary] The U.S. National Defense Strategy of January 2026, which characterized Russia as a "persistent but manageable" threat (according to a research institute's summary), widens the room for such a deal.

Claims of a Kaliningrad "blockade," nuclear signaling, and military escort of the shadow fleet serve together as supporting tools for protecting Kaliningrad and the Baltic Sea export routes. [secondary] With the diplomatic document addressed to NATO that Reuters reported on September 30, 2026 (the original has not been seen), and President Putin's Valdai remarks on October 1, Russia has already marked out that line. Estonia's decision on April 10, 2026, to halt inspections of shadow-fleet vessels in its exclusive economic zone after encountering escorting Russian Su-35s ([secondary] press reports) is a gain this tool has already delivered. An actual blockade crisis, however, is an unwelcome future for Russia as well, so it is better served by keeping its threats at the level of warnings.

Expanded sabotage and limited military action with murky attribution remain on the table, but at a high price. If people were killed, the situation would spiral into a crisis that is hard to control and would provoke a NATO buildup and retaliation. When drones violated Polish airspace on September 10, 2025, NATO launched Eastern Sentry on September 12. [secondary] On September 1, Germany formally named Russia as responsible for the August 4, 2026, explosive-drone incident at Leipzig airport and responded by closing the Russian consulate general in Bonn and increasing pressure on the shadow fleet (German press reports).

Russia has little reason to accept risk-reduction mechanisms alone while forward deployment remains in place. It would agree to talk but demand a reduction in NATO's forward deployment in return, and lower tensions obtained that way would in the end become one form of the direct deal with Washington (R1).

Openly seizing part of a Baltic state would stake the regime's survival in the middle of the war in Ukraine, so it ranks last. It comes under consideration only if Russia concludes that Washington has actually withdrawn its commitment to Europe.

counter.read: That Russia's best move lies in a deal with Washington rather than on the battlefield affects Poland's choices in three ways. First, the value of a permanent U.S. troop presence (A1) could shrink sharply at the negotiating table. If Russia succeeds in tying a ceasefire in Ukraine to limits on force posture on the eastern flank (caps on rotational forces, limits on exercises near the border), the U.S. presence that Poland secured by paying for bases would lose its effect without a shot being fired. Poland should therefore set its negotiating goals for a U.S. presence in terms of air defense, long-range fires, and speed of reinforcement rather than troop numbers, and keep its own forces at the center while preparing a stronger European pillar (A2) as insurance. Second, for Russia, risk-reduction mechanisms are not an end in themselves but a bargaining chip for winning a reduction in forward deployment. If Poland pursues risk-reduction mechanisms, then, they should be kept separate from forward deployment (A6a). Trading them for a reduction in forward deployment (A6b) would amount to Poland offering, unprompted, the very deal Russia most wants. Third, Russia already gets the future it wants (a sustained standoff below the threshold of war, 40% probability) simply by staying its current course of imposing costs through sabotage and airspace violations. Total defense and resilience (A8), which helps Poland withstand those costs, and a security accord between the president and the government (A10) are therefore more direct preparations for Poland than measures aimed at changing Russia's calculus.

ai.t: Cheap drones and signal jamming lower the cost of incursions and blur responsibility
ai.stake: The uses of AI that can be confirmed in this issue are fusing and interpreting multiple streams of surveillance data and producing AI-generated disinformation; no official source was found showing that AI has been used in the attack weapons themselves. The standoff on the eastern flank is both a war of attrition between expensive interceptors and cheap drones and a contest between one side trying to prove quickly where an incident came from and the other trying to hide it. Russia launches decoy drones such as the Gerbera, which has a foam airframe and carries neither warhead nor camera, to wear down air defenses; jams satellite navigation (GNSS) signals from Kaliningrad; and hands reconnaissance and sabotage to proxies recruited on Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency (Polish press and Ukrainian military trade publications). Poland, NATO, and the EU are racing to build systems that pool data from multiple sensors and intercept threats with cheap means. On January 14, 2025, NATO launched Baltic Sentry to protect undersea infrastructure in the Baltic Sea and deployed naval drones; over three weeks in June 2025, more than 70 aerial, surface, and underwater unmanned systems tracked hundreds of vessels a day, including the shadow fleet. The cost was about a third of what it would have been to patrol the same waters with crewed frigates (NATO Allied Command Transformation).
ai.moves: First, cheap drones lower the attacker's costs and raise the defender's in a standoff below the threshold (P1). At least three of the drones that entered Polish airspace on September 10, 2025, were Gerbera decoys carrying no explosives (Polish press reports). A Gerbera is reported to cost about $10,000, while an AIM-120 air-to-air missile, which appears to have been used to shoot them down, is estimated at $1.5 million–$2 million per round (Ukrainian military trade publications). The longer P1 lasts, the more the question for Poland becomes not whether it can shoot drones down but how much each shot costs. Second, the same tools make a deadly incident (P2) more likely. More frequent interceptions mean more damage from falling debris, and proxies cheaply recruited on Telegram also carry out attacks that could cost lives (the November 2025 bombing of the Warsaw–Lublin railway). Third, controlling escalation becomes a race to prove the source. Poland's National Institute of Telecommunications found that in both May and June 2026, jamming across all GNSS bands lasting several hours occurred around Gdańsk on 70 percent of days (satellite navigation trade press). Amid such jamming, the explanation that a drone strayed off course because of a navigation error sounds plausible. The effect of public attribution and selective punishment (C3) therefore depends on how quickly sensor records can establish the source. And the more interception is automated under relaxed rules of engagement for airspace violations (A4), the more important the procedures for telling crewed aircraft from drones become.
ai.lever: What Poland has is money and fast procurement. On January 30, 2026, it signed a contract for 18 batteries of the SAN counter-drone air defense system, worth about 15 billion zlotys (excluding VAT); the first three fire platoons are due by the end of 2026 and the full system within 24 months of the contract (Polish aviation trade press). Part of the funding comes from the EU defense loans. What it lacks is time. During this late fall and winter (with the outlook running into early spring), the period Prime Minister Tusk identified as the most dangerous, SAN will have only its first three fire platoons, and the EU's European Drone Defence Initiative and Eastern Flank Watch will still be in their early stages. GNSS jamming in the Baltic, moreover, originates outside Poland, which cannot stop it directly, and Poland's drone industry is itself a target. In December 2025 the Internal Security Agency (ABW) opened a Telegram chatbot for reporting recruitment attempts by foreign intelligence services (Polish press reports).
signs: Whether SAN's first three fire platoons are actually delivered by the end of 2026
Whether the next airspace violation is met with cheap means, such as cannon or rockets, instead of missiles
How long public attribution takes after an incident, and whether the explanation that it was an accident keeps recurring
The number of days of GNSS jamming along Poland's northern coast and the number of prosecutions for sabotage recruited via Telegram

congress.t: The law implementing the EU's SAFE defense loans and the presidential veto
congress.stage: On February 13, 2026, the Sejm passed the government's bill implementing SAFE, 236–199, with four abstentions, and on February 27 it accepted the Senate's amendments and sent the bill to the president. President Nawrocki vetoed it on March 12; on March 25 the Sejm referred the veto to committee and has held no override vote since. Using the existing Armed Forces Support Fund (FWSZ) instead, the government signed a €43.7 billion loan agreement with the EU on May 8 (Polish press reports).
congress.power: A law that the president has returned for reconsideration takes effect only if the Sejm passes it again by a three-fifths majority of votes cast, with at least half of its statutory members present (Article 122(5) of the Constitution). The Senate plays no part in the override.
congress.votes: The five caucuses of the governing coalition hold 239 seats, 37 short of the 276 needed if all members are present. In seven override votes on other laws between December 2025 and September 2026, support ranged only from 232 to 246 votes.
congress.sides: The president vetoed the law, citing the long-term debt burden and the risk that the EU could withhold funds arbitrarily, and put forward as an alternative a "Polish SAFE 0%" bill that would raise the same amount from central bank profits. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz criticized it as a veto directed not at the government but at Poland's security (Polish press reports).
congress.next: No date has been set for an override vote. The 2027 draft budget states that part of defense spending will be financed with SAFE funds through the Armed Forces Support Fund.

congress.t: The 2027 budget law and defense spending
congress.stage: The government submitted the 2027 draft budget to the Sejm on September 29, 2026, and the Sejm held its first reading on October 8. Defense spending totals 198.1 billion zlotys (4.51 percent of GDP), combining 131.7 billion zlotys from the state budget (3.0 percent of GDP) and 66.4 billion zlotys from the Armed Forces Support Fund.
congress.power: Only the government may introduce a budget bill, and the Sejm may not raise the deficit above the level in the government's draft. The president must sign the budget law within seven days and cannot veto it; he can only refer it to the Constitutional Tribunal for review (Articles 220, 221, and 224 of the Constitution).
congress.votes: Like an ordinary law, it passes by a majority of those present, so the governing coalition (239 seats) can pass it on its own. The 2026 budget law passed 233–197 on December 5, 2025.
congress.sides: President Nawrocki signed the 2026 budget law while denouncing it as a budget of chaos, and referred it to the Constitutional Tribunal for review. The government does not recognize the Tribunal's legitimacy (Polish press reports).
congress.next: The Sejm vote is scheduled for December 2026 (Polish broadcast reports). If the budget has not been presented to the president within four months of its submission (by January 29, 2027), the president may shorten the Sejm's term within the following 14 days (Article 225 of the Constitution).

congress.t: The legal basis for military operations in the Baltic and in the airspace
congress.stage: On November 21, 2025, the Sejm passed a bill to improve military operations when national security is threatened in Polish waters and to secure the Baltic Sea, 263–2, with 172 abstentions, and the president signed it on January 9, 2026.
congress.power: The law amends provisions on operations abroad and on forward-presence activities on allied territory (according to the Sejm's explanatory memorandum). Peacetime military operations on Polish soil are ordered by the president, at the government's request, for up to 60 days, and any extension requires the Sejm's consent. Forces engaged in such operations may destroy or disable drones that threaten people or facilities (Homeland Defense Act, Articles 11a and 25, based on the consolidated text before the amendment).
congress.next: It could not be confirmed whether a new bill further broadening the rules of engagement has been submitted to the Sejm.

hs7.lead: In most futures, life for Poles and Baltic citizens stays nearly the same as today. The risk is concentrated in a full-scale NATO-Russia war, with a probability of 2 percent. What shapes life for Kaliningrad residents most is not this standoff but the war in Ukraine.
hs7.read: Expected scores for Poles and Baltic citizens move by only one to three points, because 84 percent of the probability lies in futures where the standoff continues (P1), an incident is patched up (P2), or tensions ease (P6). In a full-scale war, however, with a probability of 2 percent, Poles' personal safety would fall below the current level for Ukrainians. That is why Clisa Geopolitics places civilian protection, and safeguards that keep accidental clashes from escalating into war, ahead of the ranking based on the Polish government's objectives.

law.title: The legal thresholds for armed response and invoking the alliance
points: Armed responses in self-defense, such as shooting down drones that violate Polish airspace, do not require a declaration of a state of war, as when Polish and Dutch jets shot down Russian drones on September 10, 2025. Under Article 116 of the Polish Constitution, the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, may declare a state of war only in the event of armed aggression against Polish territory or when an international agreement creates an obligation of common defense; the president declares it only if the Sejm cannot convene.

Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty treats an 'armed attack' on one member as an attack on all, but each member decides for itself on 'such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force.' It is not an automatic commitment to go to war. Article 4 provides for consultation when territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened; Poland requested Article 4 consultations right after the drone incursion on September 10, 2025.

Since the 2014 Wales summit, NATO's position has been that the North Atlantic Council decides case by case whether a cyberattack amounts to an armed attack under Article 5, and the 2016 Warsaw summit applied the same principle to hybrid attacks. There is no predefined threshold.

The 'Safe Baltic' law, signed on January 9, 2026, allows navy ships and military aircraft to use weapons to protect critical infrastructure such as undersea gas pipelines and offshore platforms, and lets the defense minister, rather than the president, decide on deploying ships to the high seas.
law.result: The tools Poland can actually use against sub-threshold attacks are therefore infrastructure protection and airspace responses under domestic law, Article 4 consultations, public attribution and sanctions, and the resilience to repair damage quickly. Only a clear armed attack would make invoking Article 5 all but certain, and even then each ally decides how far to respond. That is why the actual presence of U.S. and other allied troops in Poland matters more than the wording of the treaty.

methodology.purpose: Clisa Geopolitics analyzes geopolitics and proposes strategies with the happiness of individual human beings as its mission. It assesses the situation without value judgments, evaluates strategies against the strategic actor's goals, and sets out separately what the results mean for people's lives.

flow.d: Facts, decision-makers, options, the most capable adversary, futures and external variables
The strategic actor and its goals, scorecard, ranking
Seven categories of human security (four scores and three alerts), differences in ranking
Resolution dates, Brier scores, notices of changed assessments

update: When the facts change, the assessment process is rerun from step one (Situation assessment). Conclusions are never revised in isolation.
When a conclusion changes, the earlier one is not deleted; what changed and why is recorded under "Did this process change the assessment?"

Once a forecast's resolution date passes, the source listed under "Resolves on" determines whether it came true. Where several bodies are listed, an official announcement from any one of them is enough; if there is no official announcement, a report by Reuters or the AP settles it. The test for whether a forecast came true is written into the question itself. A forecast's score is the average of the Brier scores for each day's probability, from the day it is published to its resolution date, or to the day the event occurs if it comes true sooner. Probabilities can be revised right up to the resolution date as new facts warrant, but revisions made in the last seven days of the scoring period, ending on the resolution date, do not count toward the score; each of those days is scored at the probability that stood the day before the window opened (for an October 31 resolution date, October 25–31 are scored at the October 24 probability). For forecasts open only briefly, the window is shortened so that it never exceeds a quarter of the period from publication to the resolution date, rounded down to whole days. With each result, the scores based on the first and the final probability are published side by side with the 0.25 benchmark that a 50 percent forecast on everything would earn. When missed forecasts pile up, the stage of analysis that produced them is reviewed.

The likelihood terms next to each forecast probability follow the wording used in UK government intelligence assessments. The UK leaves deliberate gaps between terms (for example, 5–10%), while Clisa assigns a term to every probability.

When new source data for measuring human security are released (conflict deaths, refugees and displaced persons, V-Dem, and World Bank income data are updated every year), current values are recalculated and the reference date is changed.
When an external variable materializes or shows signs of doing so, its conditional future becomes the new baseline, and any conclusions it unsettles are reviewed again.

When the probabilities of the world scenarios are revised, a check confirms that the baseline probabilities of each issue's futures still equal the sum of their scenario-conditional probabilities weighted by the scenario probabilities (a law-of-total-probability check).
terms: Historical precedent
A past event whose structure resembles the present situation
Most capable adversary
An adversary whose response neutralizes the strategic actor's signals and leaves it with nothing but the costs
Judgment estimate
A value assigned by judgment, with its reasoning, where no measured data exist. Labeled to distinguish it from measured values
Brier score
The mean of the squared differences between forecast probabilities and actual outcomes (1 if the event occurred, 0 if not). Zero is perfect
Decision-maker / deciding power

In the strategic analysis, a deciding power is a country whose opposition would make an outcome hard to achieve, or the only country that can make the outcome possible. In Power Structures, the decision-maker is the person who holds decision-making authority in a country
External variables
Events outside an issue that shift the probabilities of its possible futures
Conditional future
The probabilities of possible futures on the assumption that an external variable occurs
Strategic actor
The party that would adopt and carry out the strategy. Its goals are drawn from its own documents
Situation assessment · Ⅰ
The part that assesses what will happen, without value judgments
Strategy evaluation · Ⅱ
The part that evaluates options against the strategic actor's goals
What it means for people · Ⅲ
The part that shows how outcomes affect individual lives. Options are not excluded on this basis; it is presented separately from the strategy evaluation
Editorial principle
The sole criterion for what is not recommended: acts that international humanitarian law clearly prohibits
Ranking gap
The cost the strategic actor would bear, and what people would gain, if Clisa's ranking were followed in place of the actor's own
Sequence of strategic reasoning
A step-by-step assessment process that runs from establishing the facts to issuing forecasts
Indicators of resolve
Dated signals that reveal a country's resolve, divided into words (declarations) and deeds (costly signals)
Costly signals
Signals that are expensive to send and hard to reverse, and therefore hard to fake: money, legislation, people, and troop movements
Military capability and posture
Each country's personnel, nuclear arsenal, key forces and proficiency (capability), and dated changes in deployments, exercises and procurement (posture). Only what bears on an assessment is included
The other side's best move
The other country's best strategy as judged by its own goals. Not a recommendation to that country
Likely outcome (equilibrium)
The point at which, with each side making its best move given the other's choice, no one has reason to change strategy unilaterally
Bargaining space
The zone in which the two sides' goals overlap, making agreement possible
Shared trap
A structure in which each side acts rationally yet all end up with an outcome none of them wanted. The security dilemma is the classic example
Prior attempts
The history of solutions previously tried on an issue: the format, agenda, and sequencing of negotiations; how agreements were reached, implemented, and broke down; and why they succeeded or failed
Precedent check
A procedure that sets an assessment against past cases of the same kind to determine whether they support it, call for adjusting it, or refute it
Independent challenge review
A procedure in which a reviewer who does not share the context of the analysis searches for contrary precedents and the strongest counterarguments
Seven categories of human security
The scope of human security as defined by the UN. There are seven: personal safety, community, political, economic, food, health, and environment
methodology.editorial: Acts that international humanitarian law clearly prohibits — deliberately targeting civilians, using starvation as a method of warfare, taking hostages, and the like — are not recommended. Analysis of such options, however, is kept in full in Situation assessment (Ⅰ). Basis: Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, Articles 51 and 54; Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, Article 8.

division.t: How people and AI divide the work
p: Like other major events, geopolitical ones are hard to predict. The July Crisis that followed the assassination in Sarajevo in June 1914 shows that this holds even for an event as large as a world war: in the month or so before it broke out, those involved responded without truly foreseeing the catastrophe ahead. That is why Clisa Geopolitics does not promise accuracy. It states each forecast as a probability, then measures how accurate it proved and publishes the result.

The analysis and forecasts at Clisa Geopolitics are written and reviewed with an AI, Anthropic's Claude. The AI does not tire or give up; it can review every forecast against the same standards as many times as needed. It may also be less likely than people to make a wrong decision while held captive by a plan or forecast already made, as Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, chief of the German General Staff, did when he insisted in 1914 that the war plan could not be changed.

This holds, however, only if people work alongside the AI and give it sound guidelines. So the editors set the standards and guidelines for judgment and oversee the results; when an error comes to light, they correct it and revise the guidelines so it does not recur. The AI must follow those guidelines every day without exception, and people keep checking that it does.

Because those who set the guidelines may have biases of their own, every forecast carries a resolution date and a source for checking the outcome, and the results are published so that readers and outside observers can verify them as well.

indicator.title: Measuring human security
indicator.unit: People's lives are measured across the seven categories of human security defined by the UN. Personal safety, community, political, and economic are scored from 0 to 100 (higher is better), while food, health, and environment are shown as alerts that switch on when a threshold is crossed. The scores belong not to countries but to the people in each group, and the categories are never combined.

dims.name: Personal safety
parts: x is violent deaths per 100,000 people a year (intentional homicides plus deaths from the organized violence the group experiences)
dims.src: UN Office on Drugs and Crime intentional homicide statistics (compiled by Our World in Data) and the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP GED). Conflict deaths use confirmed data for the previous year; only for groups in which new violence broke out during the year are the most recent 12 months used (including candidate data)

dims.name: Community
parts: s is the forced displacement rate (%) (refugees and asylum seekers abroad plus people internally displaced by conflict and violence)
For surviving members of separated families, the possibility of contact with family is used instead (0 = impossible, 100 = free movement)

dims.name: Political
parts: The degree of freedom from torture and political killings by the government (0–1)

dims.name: Economic
parts: Loss is the percentage by which real gross national income per capita (constant 2021 PPP dollars) is below its highest level of the past five years; for future scenarios, the scenario's change in income is added

A 10 percent fall in income lowers the score by 20 points. This follows research that treats a fall of more than 10 percent in per capita consumption or income as a macroeconomic disaster (Barro and Ursúa, 2008). The straight-line scale down to 0 (a 50 percent loss) is a judgment made by Clisa Geopolitics
An income gain counts only to the extent that it recovers an earlier loss, because the measure tracks whether lives are disrupted, not growth
Futures in which income changes by less than 2 percent are treated as within the margin of error of our estimates and are not counted in the classification

Per capita income level and the unemployment rate are shown for reference and are not part of the score. Until October 21, 2026, this measure used the Human Development Index method (per capita income level)
dims.src: World Bank World Development Indicators (GNI per capita, unemployment). Iran's current loss is an estimate that reflects the IMF World Economic Outlook growth rates for 2025 and 2026. Taiwan's income is the IMF World Economic Outlook figure converted using South Korea as the benchmark; no unemployment data are available for Taiwan

dims.name: Food, health, and environment alerts
dims.formula: Switched on if any one of the criteria below is met
parts: Food: any area of the territory is in IPC/CH Phase 4 (Emergency) or higher; a famine classification or famine-risk warning; food imports or supply routes are cut off in the scenario; the country is on the FAO list of countries requiring external assistance for food

Health: under-five mortality rises by more than 10 percent within a year; a WHO Grade 3 emergency or a public health emergency of international concern; more than 10 attacks on health facilities in a year
Environment: an attack on, seizure of, or loss of power at a nuclear facility; the destruction of a large dam; residents evacuated after a large-scale attack on chemical or industrial facilities
dims.src: IPC, CH, FEWS NET, FAO GIEWS, the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), WHO, IAEA, UNEP

limits: Future values are judgment estimates. For each scenario, low, middle, and high values are set for the death rate, the forced displacement rate, the V-Dem index, and the rate of change in income, and only that scenario's effect is added to the current value. Deaths in ceasefire, peace, and de-escalation scenarios are the values for one year after the ceasefire has taken hold.

The colors in the "100 futures" chart are judgment estimates. A future is classed as "Much worse" if any one of the four categories falls by more than 20 points or two or more categories fall by more than 10 points, "Worse" for a drop of more than 1 point, and "Better" for a rise of more than 1 point. Groups whose personal safety cannot be measured are classified by a judgment estimate of deaths (100 or more per 100,000 a year counts as Much worse).
Probability-weighted expected values barely move when life hardly changes in the most likely scenarios. Gauge the size of a risk by the worst case and its probability.

For North Koreans, there are no homicide statistics or purchasing-power income figures, and deaths in prison camps and by execution are not captured in conflict data, so the personal safety and economic categories are marked "not measurable." Because North Korea was dropped from the FAO list in March 2025, the food column reads "data gap."

Kaliningrad residents are calculated using Russia-wide values as a proxy, with income adjusted to 82 percent of the Russian average (University of Turku report, 2019). For Gulf residents, citizens and migrant workers cannot be distinguished, so values for each country as a whole are used.
The "personal well-being index" used before October 2026 (life and safety, livelihood, freedom, relationships and community) has been replaced by this measure.

notices.text: One key assessment and four forecasts (f54–f57) were added to the Korean Peninsula issue. They address the mismatch between the pace at which the United States is handing South Korea primary responsibility for deterring North Korea and the pace at which South Korea is acquiring the means to carry that responsibility.
notices.h: The security vacuum the Korean Peninsula can expect in the 2030s
South Koreans' well-being hangs by a thread
notices.text: A second feature based on population projections, "South Koreans' well-being hangs by a thread," has been published. The October 1 feature has been retitled "The security vacuum the Korean Peninsula can expect in the 2030s."

notices.h: What it took for a country to invent an alphabet
notices.text: A third feature, "What it took for a country to invent an alphabet," was published for Hangul Day. It traces the two conditions, one domestic and one external, that sustained King Sejong's 32-year reign: where they came from and why they lasted only a generation. It then puts the same question to the Korean Peninsula of 2026.

notices.h: Issue change: AI and Chips removed, Russia-NATO standoff added
notices.text: The AI and Chips issue has been removed from the issues under analysis, and a new issue has been published: "The Russia-NATO standoff: How should Poland prepare for the Russian threat?" Forecasts f46–f53, which are tied to the AI and Chips issue, will remain until their resolution dates.

notices.h: Russia-Ukraine war: U.S. waives Russia sanctions; top-ranked combination stands
notices.text: President Trump's October 16 executive order waived most of the tariffs and sanctions in the Graham Russia sanctions law, meeting a warning signal in the Russia-Ukraine analysis: the United States lifting tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. The order cited only the national interest, but it came a week after a deal to import Russian diesel, and Trump has pointed to diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections. Washington has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and has even suggested Ukraine needs a new president, but no U.S. demand for territorial concessions has been confirmed, and Europe has kept its line of increasing pressure on Russia. The top-ranked combination—a self-sufficient defense industry and a ceasefire that does not legally cede occupied territory—therefore stands. With Washington setting aside its means of pressing Russia, however, the burden of guaranteeing a ceasefire has shifted further toward Europe.

notices.h: The Russia-Ukraine war: why the attrition goes on
notices.text: The fourth feature, “The Russia-Ukraine war: why the attrition goes on,” uses People's Lives data to show how Russia keeps the war's impact confined to the front while Ukrainian society as a whole wears down, and identifies what could change that dynamic.

notices.h: The economic measure now tracks income loss rather than income level
notices.text: We changed the economic measure in Impact on people from income level to income loss, so that shocks that sharply reduce income, such as South Korea's 1998 financial crisis, show up properly in the scores. As a result, 29 classifications changed, including that of South Koreans in a blockade of Taiwan.

notices.h: Why North Korea is holding off on ICBM test launches
notices.text: The fifth feature, “Why North Korea is holding off on ICBM test launches,” is now up. It looks at why North Korea holds back the ICBMs aimed at the U.S. mainland while it keeps firing missiles aimed at South Korea and Japan, and at the risk that choice leaves for South Korea.

insights.t: For South Korea, a risk as real as war is being shut out of the agreements that deal with North Korea. South Korea was not a party to the negotiations over the 1994 Agreed Framework, yet it paid 70 percent of the cost of building the light-water reactors, and right after the 2018 Singapore summit the United States announced a halt to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises without consulting Seoul beforehand.

What North Korea wants most out of negotiations is not sanctions relief but de facto U.S. acceptance of its nuclear status, and what South Korea can influence lies at the edges of that: adjustments to joint U.S.-South Korean exercises and to deployments of U.S. strategic assets. Since Kim Yo Jong's statement of July 2020, North Korea has given priority, over sanctions relief, to the withdrawal of the U.S. "hostile policy," including a halt to joint exercises and to strategic-asset deployments. Even here, however, what South Korea holds is limited influence, not a veto.

South Korea's troop shortage around 2040 cannot be closed by lengthening military service, and it coincides with a period when South Korea's share of the burden within the alliance grows. Under the current system, South Korea's armed forces would shrink to about 270,000 by 2040, widening the troop ratio with North Korea from 1:2.8 to 1:4.7, and keeping 250,000 enlisted soldiers would require extending compulsory service to 31–33 months. The 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy states that South Korea is capable of taking primary responsibility for deterring North Korea.

A ceasefire on the current front line in the Russia-Ukraine war is unlikely until Russia concludes that it can no longer bear the cost of taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast. Even if a ceasefire is reached, without guarantees backed by great-power troops it is likely to be no more than a pause before the fighting resumes, as with the Minsk agreements of 2014–2015. Yet Russia rejects the very presence of Western troops.

The course of events in the Taiwan Strait depends heavily on the deal the U.S. administration strikes with China, but the administration cannot set the terms of that deal on its own. When the Carter administration broke diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 1979, Congress enacted the Taiwan Relations Act, offsetting much of the effect. Because the power to initiate arms sales rests with the executive branch, however, Congress can slow the administration's concessions to China but would find it hard to reverse them.

Iran has detained a South Korean ship without ever declaring South Korea an enemy. The Hankuk Chemi, seized in January 2021, was released only after Seoul agreed to unfreeze $1 billion of the Iranian funds frozen in South Korea. On top of the risks every ship faces in wartime, South Korea bears additional risk from two sources: measures to freeze or dispose of Iranian assets in South Korea, and the presence of South Korean warships inside the Strait of Hormuz. On September 5, 2026, Iran warned through a senior official that it would regard any South Korean involvement in the strait as joining the aggression, and on September 7 its Foreign Ministry spokesperson issued a warning to the same effect, in Korean, to any country stationing forces in the Persian Gulf and the strait.

A permanent U.S. military presence is aimed at a large-scale ground attack, but the sabotage, drones, and airspace violations Poland is actually experiencing cannot be stopped by a tripwire. As Schelling showed with the case of the Berlin Wall, where a commitment leaves room for interpretation, the adversary expects the defender to avoid a forceful response. Russia's choice of sub-threshold means exploits this structure. What Poland should seek in negotiations over the U.S. presence, therefore, is less troop numbers than the capability to actually fight—air defense, long-range fires, and speed of reinforcement—and against sub-threshold attacks it should combine resilience with selective punishment (public attribution, sanctions, and proportionate responses at the alliance level).

blocks.p: According to Japan's Ministry of Defense, North Korea has launched 16 ICBM-class missiles since 2017 (Figure 1): three in 2017, seven in 2022, five in 2023 and one in 2024, with none in 2018–2021 or since 2025. The last was a Hwasong-19 on October 31, 2024, five days before the U.S. presidential election.

blocks.p: Other ballistic missile launches continued in the meantime. The ministry counted five in 2025 and at least 15 in 2026 through September 20, and North Korea fired ballistic missiles again on October 3 and 12. What North Korea has halted is not missile launches as such, but only test launches of the ICBMs aimed at the U.S. mainland.
Nor has ICBM development stopped: in place of test launches, North Korea has kept displaying its ICBM capability through ground tests and public events (Figure 2).

sections.h: Why only the ICBMs are held back

blocks.p: Conventional analysis and reporting holds that North Korea no longer needs to negotiate with the United States now that it has expanded military cooperation with Russia. The Associated Press reported in July 2025 that North Korea, focused on its cooperation with Russia, showed no near-term interest in diplomacy, and many experts took the same view. On this reading, the absence of ICBM tests has nothing to do with negotiations and is explained instead by other factors, such as the Hwasong-20's development schedule or restraint urged by Russia and China.
Clisa Geopolitics takes a different view: North Korea is using its ICBM tests as a bargaining chip with the United States and for its geopolitical goals.
First, the points at which North Korea halted and then resumed ICBM test launches have tracked the course of U.S.-North Korea summitry:

ul: 2017: In President Trump's first year in office, North Korea fired three ICBMs.
April 2018: North Korea announced a halt to nuclear tests and ICBM test launches, and the Singapore summit followed in June.

2020–2021: North Korea declared at the end of 2019 that it was no longer bound by its moratorium, but it soon sealed its borders against the COVID-19 pandemic, and its ballistic missile launches overall fell sharply during this period.
January–February 2022: In January, North Korea said it would consider resuming the activities it had suspended, and in late February it resumed test launches, firing 13 ICBMs through October 2024.
Since 2025: While President Trump has again floated a meeting with Kim Jong Un, there has not been a single ICBM test launch.

blocks.p: Halting test launches that directly threaten the U.S. mainland is the easiest concession North Korea can offer Washington before negotiations even begin. And since test launches can be resumed at any time, North Korea gives up little by making it.

North Korea stands to gain a good deal from this bargaining chip. In a September 21, 2025, speech to the Supreme People's Assembly, Kim Jong Un said he could talk with the United States if it dropped its demand for denuclearization, but that he would not negotiate any trade-off to obtain sanctions relief. The ruling Workers' Party's Ninth Congress likewise set respect for its current status (recognition as a nuclear-armed state and withdrawal of the hostile policy) as the condition for talks. This suggests North Korea needs a negotiation in which it first secures de facto recognition as a nuclear-armed state and then builds on that to win sanctions relief as well.

Second, the ICBM pause is not only about negotiations with Washington: Clisa Geopolitics judges that a calculation aimed at separating South Korean and U.S. interests is also at work. If North Korea offers to lift the threat to the U.S. mainland while continuing to hold and display a regional nuclear strike capability through its short- and intermediate-range missiles, Washington becomes more likely to weigh the cost of defending South Korea and Japan separately from its own interests, and the room for U.S. and South Korean interests to diverge grows accordingly.

Third, the ICBM pause also suits the interests of China, North Korea's patron. Test launches aimed at the U.S. mainland give Washington a rationale for its Golden Dome missile defense plan and for a U.S. military buildup, which also burdens China. By halting them, North Korea stays within the bounds China will tolerate and preserves the conditions for China's continued protection at the UN Security Council.

sections.h: Why China does not stop it

blocks.p: North Korea's nuclear missiles are a burden for China too, because the threat they pose fuels calls for nuclear armament in South Korea and Japan and gives grounds for Golden Dome (the U.S. missile defense plan) and for military cooperation among the United States, South Korea and Japan. That is why China voted for all six UN Security Council sanctions resolutions against North Korea in 2016–2017, and in February 2017 it also halted imports of North Korean coal.
Yet the same ICBM launches drew opposite responses from China at different times (Figure 3). China backed sanctions in 2017, but since 2022 it has stepped back from holding North Korea to account:

ul: May 26, 2022: The day after North Korea fired an ICBM, China joined Russia in vetoing a draft resolution imposing additional sanctions.
March 28, 2024: China abstained in the vote on extending the mandate of the UN panel of experts on North Korea sanctions.

Since 2024: China began dropping the phrase “denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula” from official statements, and did not use it in its November 2025 arms control white paper or during President Xi Jinping's June 2026 visit to Pyongyang.

blocks.p: What changed in between was not North Korea's behavior but U.S.-China relations. In 2017 President Trump linked the two issues, saying a trade deal would be far better for China if it solved the North Korean problem, and China's cooperation on sanctions was likely driven in part by the expectation of such a reward on trade. But the United States labeled China a strategic competitor in December 2017 and launched a trade war in July 2018. In 2022, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan deepened the U.S.-China confrontation further. With nothing left to gain from cooperating on North Korea, China began to treat it not as a liability to be reined in but as a buffer against the United States.

sections.h: The threat that remains for South Korea

blocks.p: If North Korea offers to halt ICBM test launches in negotiations and the United States accepts, the threat to the U.S. mainland will shrink. But the short- and intermediate-range missiles aimed at South Korea are easily left out of a deal; in 2019, when North Korea fired a string of short-range missiles, President Trump indicated that short-range missiles were not a problem.

In March 2023, North Korea unveiled its Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead alongside a chart showing it could be mounted on a range of short- and intermediate-range missiles, including the Hwasong-11 family. Its frequent recent launches are therefore closer to operational deployment and unit training aimed at South Korea than to new development. In January 2024, the U.S. government also said Russia had struck Ukraine with North Korean ballistic missiles; through these sales, North Korea is gaining both combat performance data and revenue.

If a U.S.-North Korea summit takes place without South Korea formally involved in the preparations, Clisa Geopolitics puts the chance that the agreement contains no provisions on inter-Korean relations or on short- and intermediate-range missiles at 75 percent{{fc:f14}}.

North Korea's halt to ICBM test launches is not a sign that the threat is shrinking, but a sign that the party bearing the risk and cost of the North Korean threat is changing. North Korea holds the threat to the U.S. mainland as a bargaining chip while it keeps building its nuclear strike capability aimed at South Korea and Japan, and this widens the room for Washington to weigh the cost of defending its allies separately from its own interests.

Rather than restraining North Korea, China, for its part, has held South Korea and the United States responsible for the costs of the North Korean threat, and has thereby kept U.S. military influence on the Korean Peninsula from growing. Its economic retaliation over the 2017 THAAD deployment, and the “Three Nos” position the South Korean government subsequently stated, are the clearest examples{{n:1,2}}. In Clisa Geopolitics' judgment, North Korea's strategic aim is that, even though South Korea faces the risk from North Korea's nuclear weapons head-on, the negotiations and deals over those weapons should take place among the United States, North Korea and, behind them, China, without South Korea.

The chance that North Korean state media announce an ICBM test moratorium tied to dialogue with the United States is 12 percent{{fc:f79}}.

features.title: Why North Korea is holding off on ICBM test launches
features.lead: Conventional analysis and reporting holds that North Korea lost interest in negotiating with the United States after aligning with Russia.
summary: Conventional analysis and reporting holds that North Korea lost interest in negotiating with the United States after aligning with Russia. Clisa Geopolitics, however, sees North Korea using ICBM test launches as a bargaining chip in talks with Washington and in pursuit of its geopolitical goals. One reason is that its pauses in ICBM testing have coincided with periods when U.S.-North Korea summitry was under way or under discussion.

Halting ICBM launches serves as a bargaining chip with Washington, while also helping to pry South Korean and U.S. interests apart and suiting the interests of China, North Korea's patron. Since 2022, as U.S.-China rivalry has deepened, China has stepped back from holding North Korea to account and has instead blamed South Korea and the United States.

North Korea keeps firing the short- and intermediate-range missiles that neither China nor the United States much cares about. If Washington and Pyongyang strike a deal that limits only ICBMs, the short- and intermediate-range nuclear missiles aimed at South Korea and Japan are likely to be left out of it and to harden into a North Korean lever that could reshape the security landscape of Northeast Asia.

notes.t: Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, a missile defense system. In July 2016, South Korea and the United States decided to deploy THAAD with U.S. Forces Korea against North Korean missiles, and it was deployed in Seongju, North Gyeongsang Province, in 2017. China objected that the THAAD radar could monitor Chinese territory and retaliated economically: it restricted group tours to South Korea, forced stores run by South Korean companies to suspend operations and curbed South Korean pop culture.

Three positions stated by the South Korean government in October 2017: no additional THAAD deployment, no participation in the U.S. missile defense system, and no development of South Korea-U.S.-Japan security cooperation into a military alliance. The South Korean government explained that this was a statement of existing positions, not an agreement with or commitment to China, and on October 31 that year Seoul and Beijing agreed to improve relations.

blocks.p: The {{life:ukraine|People's Lives}} tab on Clisa Geopolitics plays out the years to 2030 a hundred times and shows, each time, whether people's lives would be better or worse than today{{n:1}}. For the Russia-Ukraine war, the result splits cleanly in two. In the 60 futures where the fighting stops, life improves for both peoples. In the 40 where the war goes on, life for Russians stays about the same while only Ukrainians are worse off. Thirty-three of those 40 are a war of attrition like today's{{case:ukraine}}.

blocks.p: On the classification alone, the gap between the two countries is not large. If attrition continues, Ukraine is rated "worse" for one reason only: the share of people displaced from their homes rises from 23 percent to 24 percent. In fact, relative to population, more Russians die than Ukrainians. Violent deaths run at 62.1 per 100,000 people a year in Russia and 47.0 in Ukraine, and most of the Russian dead are soldiers at the front.

The real difference lies less in the size of the cost than in where it falls. In Russia, soldiers die but the rest of society is barely shaken; in Ukraine, the war is felt in communities and the economy, and in food, health and the environment as well.

Russia's low political score predates the war.

blocks.p: The difference exists because the front lies entirely on Ukrainian soil. Russian missiles and drones target Ukraine's cities and power plants, and about a quarter of Ukrainians have been driven from their homes. Russia, by contrast, has loaded the cost of the war onto its soldiers and their families. As Robert Pape observed in his work on economic sanctions, those who hold power can shift pain onto the powerless{{n:2}}{{acad:ir101/09|Lecture 9}}.

sections.h: Why Putin can afford to wait

blocks.p: The bargaining model of war shows why this matters. Because war is costly, there is a bargaining range of deals that both sides should prefer to fighting{{n:3}}{{acad:ir101/05|Lecture 5}}, and the side that pays less to keep fighting can demand a correspondingly larger share of the deal. Russia, able to keep the war's impact confined to the front, is in exactly that position.

blocks.note: With 100 to divide and Russia's chance of winning set at 60 percent, cutting Russia's cost of war from 10 to 2 raises the smallest share Russia will accept from 50 to 58.

blocks.p: Russia's behavior fits the model. Since the start of 2026, Moscow has repeatedly demanded that Ukrainian forces withdraw from all of Donetsk Oblast as a condition for a cease-fire. Putin has rejected proposals to stop the war along the current front line, and on October 16 he again called the "liberation" of Donetsk one of his main goals.

Public opinion narrows the bargaining range as well. Surveys by the Levada Center, an independent Russian pollster, show that most Russians want peace talks, but only a minority would accept talks that hand occupied land back. Most Ukrainians support a cease-fire as such, but they reject giving up land they still hold or legally recognizing the occupation, according to the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS). In short, the deals the two publics would accept do not overlap.

blocks.note: In a September 2025 survey, 80 percent said they would support a decision by Putin to end the war, but only about a third favored returning occupied territory to Ukraine to end it.

blocks.p: An end to the fighting would clearly benefit Russians too, as the rise in their personal-safety score from 40 to about 65 shows. The war goes on anyway because the winning coalition{{n:4}}{{acad:ir101/06|Lecture 6}} that keeps Putin in power, groups such as the security services and big business, bears almost none of its cost, and the deaths at the front have little bearing on them.

On the battlefield, neither side is likely to win easily. On September 26, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington think tank, assessed that Russian forces had gained almost no ground since March, and in a September KIIS survey 62 percent of Ukrainians said they could endure the war for as long as necessary. With Russia able to wait despite making little headway and Ukraine determined to hold its ground, the grinding war of attrition is likely to drag on.

sections.h: When the bleeding spreads beyond the front

blocks.p: Russia's strategy rests on the premise that it can keep the war's impact confined to the front, and Ukraine's long-range drones seek to break that premise. Striking deep behind enemy lines once required bombers or long-range missiles; cheap drones have sharply lowered that bar. In September and October, Ukraine struck Russian refineries, export terminals and data centers belonging to Yandex, Russia's largest internet company, one after another. Reuters reported on October 8 that, as a result, fuel was running short in many parts of Russia, lines were forming at gas stations and consumer prices were climbing.

Russia's budget is growing tighter. The 2026 deficit forecast has doubled from the original plan to 3.2 percent of GDP, and the liquid assets of the National Wealth Fund have fallen below half their pre-invasion level. Even so, the government has decided to raise defense spending in 2027 and cover the gap with tax increases and cuts to social spending. A cost once confined to the front has begun to shift onto society as a whole.

blocks.p: Then the Iran war intervened{{case:iran}}. Russia's Urals crude, which sold for about $45 a barrel before the United States and Israel struck Iran on February 28, reached $113.89 on April 8 and still averaged more than $90 in September. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) in Finland estimates that higher oil and gas prices added $35.9 billion to Russia's seaborne export revenue over six months. Moscow is spending much of that windfall to hold down domestic fuel prices: in September alone it paid refiners 305.5 billion rubles in price compensation, about two-thirds of that month's oil and gas tax revenue of 452.4 billion rubles. In effect, Moscow is using its oil-price windfall to keep the fuel shortages caused by Ukraine's strikes from spilling over into everyday life.

In the United States, meanwhile, as fuel prices rose, the Trump administration decided on October 9 to import Russian diesel. It also pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, and on October 16 it waived the tariffs it had planned to impose on countries buying Russian oil. President Donald Trump himself pointed to the burden of diesel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. As far as the war in Ukraine is concerned, the Iran war has brought Russia extra revenue while leading Washington to give up some of its own leverage over Moscow.

Higher fuel prices from the Iran war are also shaking European societies. In France, protests that began in mid-September, when diesel topped €2.37 a liter, merged with anger over schools, living costs and public services; on October 17, about 550,000 people took to the streets nationwide, according to the authorities. The protesters have not demanded cuts to aid for Ukraine, but the more frustration grows over living costs and public debt, the harder it becomes for European governments to spend money on Ukraine. European aid fatigue is precisely what Russia is counting on most. Russia can keep the war's impact confined to the front; Europe's democracies cannot shield their citizens from the shock of rising living costs.

As a result, Putin's strategy has become even harder to shift. For that to happen, the cost of the war would have to go beyond inconveniences such as gas station lines and reach the war budget and the winning coalition. There is no evidence yet that it has reached that stage, and higher oil prices and U.S. imports of Russian diesel, among other things, have made it less likely to do so. Still, Washington's easing of sanctions has not upended the situation entirely: existing sanctions on Russia remain in place, nothing confirms that Washington has pressed Ukraine to cede territory, and Europe is keeping up its pressure on Russia.

features.title: The Russia-Ukraine war: why the attrition goes on
features.lead: The longer the war runs, the more it wears down Ukrainian society as a whole, while Russia can keep the war's impact confined to the front. That is why Russian President Vladimir Putin keeps up the war of attrition, and his strategy will change only once that impact spreads through Russian society as a whole.
summary: Even if the war of attrition continues, Russian society will look much as it does today, while Ukrainian society will be worse off.
The side for which fighting on is cheaper has no reason to scale back its demands, so Putin can afford to keep up the war of attrition and wait.

Ukraine's drone strikes and the strain on Russia's budget are unsettling that dynamic, but higher oil prices driven by the Iran war and Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia are cushioning their impact on Russia.
falsify: Whether Russia formally proposes stopping the war along the current front line, or accepts armed foreign troops stationed in Ukraine—a sign that Putin no longer has a reason to wait.
Whether Russia declares a new mobilization—a sign that a cost once confined to the front has spread to society as a whole.
How far Russia's fuel supply deteriorates and its budget deficit widens this winter—a gauge of how fast the cost is spilling beyond the front.

Whether Congress moves to reverse the sanctions waiver after the November 3 midterm elections—lawmakers from both parties have already objected to the Russian diesel imports and the waiver, and if Congress revives pressure on Russia, Moscow's costs will rise again.
Whether Washington revisits the tariff and sanctions waivers in mid-December, when the 60-day grace period cited by Secretary of State Marco Rubio runs out.

Whether Europe settles its support after France's presidential election in the spring of 2027—the EU's €90 billion loan covers 2026–2027, and if Russia concludes that support will continue indefinitely, time will no longer be on its side.
