features.title: What it took for a country to invent an alphabet
features.lead: Hangul is the only script known to have come with a book in which its inventors explained how it was designed. The achievement belongs to the 32-year reign of King Sejong, and that reign rested on two things: a domestic order his father, King Taejong, had secured in blood, and an external order that Ming China kept stable. The domestic order lasted barely a generation before the bloodletting resumed. Hangul Day, October 9, is a fitting moment to ask where that stability came from and why it did not last.
summary: Slow work with no immediate payoff, such as inventing an alphabet, was possible only when no one at home threatened the throne and no one abroad threatened the state. Sejong's 32 years had both conditions: a royal authority his father had secured in blood, and an international order Ming China held steady.

That stability rested less on institutions than on the will and action of a single monarch, and it did not outlast a generation. A coup came three years after Sejong's death, and within six the Hall of Worthies, the academy that had produced the book explaining the alphabet, was abolished. Hangul survived not by the will of the state but because ordinary people used it.

The Korean Peninsula in 2026 faces an unsettled external order, but its domestic stability rests on democratic institutions rather than, as in Sejong's day, on a single ruler. Democracy entrusts the succession of power to a constitution and elections rather than to one person's temperament or lifespan; what it does not supply by itself is the consensus needed to carry a task across changes of government. What is the task this peninsula must take on for the next generation, and is there a national consensus to carry it forward whoever holds power? Those are questions worth asking on Hangul Day.

sections.h: An alphabet that came with its own manual

blocks.p: In December 1443, King Sejong of Korea's Joseon dynasty (r. 1418–1450) devised a set of 28 letters. In September 1446 he completed the Hunminjeongeum, "the correct sounds for instructing the people," a book that set out the principles behind the letters and how to use them. The royal annals record both events without a date, noting only that each happened "this month," because the alphabet was not a project debated at court; the king drove it himself, and quietly. Scholars still differ over how much the Hall of Worthies, the royal academy, contributed, but the annals and the Hunminjeongeum both credit Sejong with the invention, and that remains the mainstream view. The preface the king wrote himself, at the head of the book, opens with a plain statement: "The speech of this country differs from that of China and does not match its characters, so that among the ignorant people there are many who wish to say something but cannot express their meaning." A different language needs a different script. The logic has held for 580 years, and Hangul is now the one script that South and North Korea share.

Hangul was not the first script a state had invented. The Khitan rulers of Liao created their scripts around 920 and 925; Li Yuanhao, founder of the Tangut state of Western Xia, issued a Tangut script in 1036, on the eve of declaring his empire; the Jurchen rulers of Jin promulgated their scripts in 1119 and 1138; and in 1269 Kublai Khan proclaimed the 'Phags-pa script the official writing of the Mongol Yuan empire. Choe Mal-li, deputy director of the Hall of Worthies, pointed to exactly these precedents when he petitioned against the new alphabet in 1444. Only the Mongols, the Tanguts, the Jurchens, the Japanese and the Tibetans had scripts of their own, he wrote, and those were the affairs of barbarians; to invent one was to abandon China and make Korea barbarian too. Sejong knew the precedents his critics named and went ahead anyway. Every one of those state-made scripts, from Khitan to 'Phags-pa, has since vanished. The Khitan scripts were banned by the Jin in 1191; 'Phags-pa fell out of use after the Yuan collapsed; the Tangut and Jurchen scripts lingered for roughly two centuries beyond their dynasties and then died. A script made by a state declined when the state lost its power.

Hangul differs from them in two respects. The first is survival. Among scripts invented outright rather than borrowed or adapted, those that serve today as the de facto sole official script of a nation come down to Hangul and the Armenian alphabet. The second is the manual. Other scripts have a known inventor and date; what no other script has, as far as is known, is a book in which its makers systematically explained the design. The Hunminjeongeum explains that the five basic consonants depict the shape of the speech organs as each sound is made, and that the three basic vowels stand for heaven, earth and humanity. The book was rediscovered in 1940. Hangul Day falls on October 9 because a postscript by the scholar Jeong In-ji at the end of the volume is dated to the first 10 days of the ninth lunar month of 1446, and the last of those days, converted to the solar calendar, is October 9. UNESCO inscribed the book on its Memory of the World register in 1997.

Survival, though, did not mean that Hangul was the script of the state all along. It became the default script of official documents only in 1894, under the Gabo Reforms, 448 years after its invention. In the interval, Joseon's official documents were written in classical Chinese, and Hangul was the script of women and children, of Buddhist texts and popular fiction. The Joseon state did not keep Sejong's alphabet alive. Through the centuries in which the state declined to make it official, it was kept alive and handed down by the people who wrote in it.

sections.h: The two conditions behind a 32-year reign

blocks.p: Once the letters existed, the book explaining them (the Hunminjeongeum) took another three years. Before and after that work Sejong re-established and enlarged the Hall of Worthies (1420), published a manual of Korean farming (1429), built six garrisons along the Tumen River frontier (1434–1449), devised a rain gauge (1441), calculated a calendar fitted to Korea's own sky (1442), and, after 14 years of debate, settled a land tax graded by soil quality (1444). Each took about a decade from start to finish, and each required that the king not change his mind along the way. That is why the usual account of these 32 years dwells on Sejong's character and intelligence. The account is not wrong, but the conditions that allowed Sejong to use those gifts lay elsewhere.

The first condition was stability at home. Sejong's father, Taejong (Yi Bang-won), took up arms in August 1398 and killed the chief minister Jeong Do-jeon and his own half-brother, the crown prince Yi Bang-seok. In 1400 he fought and defeated his elder brother Yi Bang-gan in the streets of the capital, Kaesong, and that same year abolished the private armies kept by princes and by the merit subjects, the officials rewarded for their part in founding the dynasty. As king he had his wife's four brothers put to death in turn (1410 and 1416). After passing the throne to his third son in August 1418 he kept military affairs in his own hands, and at the end of that year he had the new king's father-in-law, Sim On, executed; the pretext was that Sim's brother had criticized the retired king's grip on the army. When Taejong died in 1422, Joseon had no royal kinsman, no merit subject and no in-law left who could stand against the king. Many ministers opposed Sejong's policies, but in 32 years no one challenged his throne, and that security was not something Sejong built. He inherited it from his father.

The second condition was stability abroad. Sejong's reign coincided with a settled stretch of Ming rule under the Yongle, Xuande and Zhengtong emperors, and Joseon kept to the tributary relationship the Ming had defined, sending envoys every year and receiving investiture for each new king. The Ming left Korea's position undisturbed, and Korea had no reason to fight the Ming. One purpose of the Hall of Worthies was to train officials who could manage relations with the Ming smoothly; the Ming order was the premise of Sejong's government. There was fighting with the Jurchens on the northern frontier and a punitive expedition against Japanese pirates in the south, but no war that put the state's existence at stake. Sejong died in 1450, the year after the Tumu crisis, in which Mongol forces from the northern steppe captured a Ming emperor.

With no rival to the throne at home and no threat to the state's existence abroad, a king could spend 10 years at a stretch on work that showed no immediate result. The alphabet was one such piece of work, and the one that lasted longest. Without those conditions, even the most gifted king would have struggled to do the same.

From 1445 Sejong delegated the business of government to his heir, and in 1450 he died. The heir was Munjong, who had been crown prince for 29 years, since 1421. Munjong reigned a little over two years before dying of illness in 1452, and his son Danjong became king at 12. Sejong had spent 29 years preparing the succession. But the heir died young, and in the meantime the princes to whom Sejong had entrusted various tasks in his final years had built up followings of their own.

Taejong had abolished the princes' private armies and kept royal kinsmen out of politics. Sejong, late in life, charged his second son, Prince Suyang, with translating and publishing Buddhist scriptures and with compiling musical scores, while his third son, Prince Anpyeong, moved among the scholars of the Hall of Worthies and became a central figure in learning and the arts. Publishing and pious works were not politics, but through them the princes acquired followers and standing. In October 1453 Prince Suyang led troops to kill Kim Jong-seo and Hwangbo In, the ministers guarding the boy king, and exiled his brother Anpyeong to Ganghwa Island, then had him put to death. In 1455 he took the throne from his nephew as King Sejo. In 1456 he executed the officials who had tried to restore Danjong, abolished the Hall of Worthies and suspended the royal lectures. In 1457 he had Danjong killed. All of it came within seven years of Sejong's death.

Sejo did not stop everything. He began compiling a code of law and reformed the land system; the code was completed in 1485 as the Gyeongguk daejeon, Joseon's Great Code. What he cut off were the Hall of Worthies and the royal lectures: the institutions at the king's side that produced books and could tell him no, among them the very body that had explained the Hunminjeongeum. Sejong's tax law, his frontier and his calendar survived; the institution that had helped produce them could not withstand a single coup.

Hangul, for its part, did not owe its survival to the protection of the Joseon state. Within six years of Sejong's death, Joseon abolished the body that had explained the alphabet, and in 1504 King Yeonsangun, seizing on an anonymous denunciation written in Hangul, went so far as to ban the teaching and learning of the script. For nearly 400 years afterward the documents of the state were written in classical Chinese. Hangul survived not through official recognition or protection but through use. It lived in mothers' letters to their daughters, in the Buddhist translations the court printed, and in the novels that passed from hand to hand.

sections.h: The question for the Korean Peninsula in 2026

blocks.p: Hold the two conditions behind Sejong's 32 years up against the Korean Peninsula of 2026, and the external one is being shaken. The international order is strained by rivalry between the United States and China; Washington is moving to reduce the role of U.S. forces in Korea; and in February 2026 North Korea's party congress formalized its status as a nuclear-armed state and its "two states" doctrine toward the South{{case:korea}}. The domestic condition differs in kind from Sejong's. Where Joseon's progress depended heavily on the temperament and lifespan of one monarch, South Korea's stability rests on democratic institutions: a constitution, elections, a National Assembly and courts. That the country holds steady when its president changes every five years is the work of those institutions, a system that South Koreans rebuilt in blood after the tragedy of dictatorship. In that respect South Korea has what Sejong never had.

Under absolute monarchy, the direction and pace of progress depend heavily on the disposition of one ruler, and a change of ruler often halts or reverses them. That is why Sejong's 32 years ended with his generation. Democracy entrusts the succession of power not to a monarch's lifespan or an heir's quality but to a constitution and elections. What democracy does not supply by itself is continuity of policy: a change of government normally brings a change of policy, and for any undertaking to outlast a government there must be a separate consensus that it should. South Korea's large infrastructure projects and long-term reforms have carried across governments because such a consensus existed. Its approach to North Korea, by contrast, has not. The alliance with the United States has remained the foundation of South Korea's foreign policy under every government; policy toward the North has reversed course each time power has passed between conservatives and progressives. Dealing with the North is strategic and in part philosophical work, and its results are slow to appear; no consensus, it seems, has formed around it, and policy has hinged instead on the judgment of each president in turn.

Of everything Sejong left behind, what lasted longest and survives to this day is an alphabet, and what preserved it for 450 years was not the state or those who held power but the people who wrote in it. It may be that what ultimately sustains work that is strategic and philosophical, invisible yet important, is the steady attention and will of the people themselves. The 450 years of Hangul after Sejong suggest as much.

features.title: South Koreans' well-being hangs by a thread
features.lead: Even under the most favorable assumptions, South Koreans' well-being index will be hard to keep at its current level, and a set of shifts converging around 2030 could drag it down sharply: the handover of primary responsibility for deterring North Korea, the transfer of wartime operational control, China's rise, a crisis in the Taiwan Strait, and the de facto formalization of North Korea's nuclear status.
summary: Even in the best-case scenario, South Koreans' well-being index will be hard to keep at its current level, and geopolitical shifts could send it sharply lower.

The geopolitical shifts of this period (the transfer of primary responsibility for deterring North Korea from U.S. to South Korean forces, the transfer of wartime operational control, China's rise and growing influence in East Asia, a Taiwan Strait crisis, and the de facto formalization of North Korea's nuclear status) are converging, and South Korea urgently needs to examine them carefully and prepare its response.

blocks.p: The Clisa Geopolitics well-being index is a modified version of the UN Development Programme's (UNDP) Human Development Index{{n:1}}. It scores South Koreans' lives on two dimensions, safety and living conditions, each from 0 to 100, and combines the two into a single score the same way the Human Development Index does, by taking their geometric mean. Safety is calculated from life expectancy and exposure to war and state violence; living conditions from per capita income, the dependency burden, the old-age poverty rate, and the youth employment rate, with the worst-performing OECD member set at 0 and the best at 100. Unlike the World Happiness Report{{n:2}} (published by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network and others), which asks respondents how satisfied they are with their lives, the index is built from measurable living conditions, so projected changes in population and the security environment can be built into it.

South Koreans' well-being index currently stands at 58.1 (safety 71.1, living conditions 47.5). Weighted by the probabilities of the scenarios the peninsula could follow through 2030, the index falls to 54.5 in 2030, 41.0 in 2040, and 20.9 in 2050. In no scenario does the 2030 index exceed today's level, and even if the best scenario, in which inter-Korean tensions ease, holds, the index reaches only 24.2 in 2050. Safety varies widely from one scenario to another, but living conditions deteriorate in every scenario as the working-age{{n:3}} population shrinks and the number of older people grows.

blocks.p: These calculations assume that old-age poverty and youth employment stay at current levels. Even in the best case, with old-age poverty falling to the OECD median, youth employment rising to the OECD median, and people aged 65 to 69 continuing to work, living conditions score 49.5 in 2050, below today's score on the same basis (about 61, with 65- to 69-year-olds counted as working age). Even if 65- to 69-year-olds work, the number of people supported by every 100 working-age people more than doubles, from about 29 today to 68.5 in 2050. On the well-being index, the best case yields 59.5 in 2050, short of today's 65.9 on the same basis. With the current level hard to hold even in the best case, the geopolitical shifts described below come on top.

blocks.p: The United States is handing its role on the Korean Peninsula over to South Korea. The 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy states that South Korea is capable of taking primary responsibility for deterring North Korea{{n:4}} with "critical but more limited" U.S. support. With the South Korean government citing 2027–2028 and the commander of U.S. Forces Korea the first quarter of 2029, expectations for the transfer of wartime operational control{{n:5}} are converging on 2028–2030{{fc:f55}}. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 sets a floor of 28,500 U.S. troops in Korea but allows a reduction if the secretary of defense certifies it{{fc:f56}}.

North Korea's nuclear status has, in effect, been formalized. In September 2023, Pyongyang wrote its policy of strengthening its nuclear forces into its constitution, and it has been adding warheads and has effectively fielded the means to deliver tactical nuclear weapons against South Korea and Japan. After Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Pyongyang in June 2026, denuclearization was absent from both sides' statements, a sign that Beijing has tilted toward tacitly accepting North Korea's nuclear weapons. China has made "the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" its national goal and is extending its influence in East Asia.

The Taiwan Strait is a risk that bears directly on South Korea's economy and security. Clisa Geopolitics puts the likelihood of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan and U.S. intervention by 2030 at 2.5 percent{{case:taiwan}}. The likelihood is low, but if it happened, South Korea's trade with China, its shipping, and its semiconductor supply chains would be cut off even if South Korea itself were not a battlefield. Applying Bloomberg Economics' estimates, South Korea's per capita income would fall by about a quarter in the first year. If North Korea raised tensions on the peninsula during a crisis over Taiwan, both U.S. Forces Korea and the South Korean military might have to devote themselves entirely to defending the peninsula.

These shifts threaten a well-being index that is precarious to begin with. In 2030, the index ranges from 52.3 to 57.7 in the scenarios without war, but it falls to 50.3 if a limited clash breaks out and to 42.6 in a full-scale war on the peninsula. Clisa Geopolitics puts the likelihood of a full-scale war on the peninsula by 2030 at 2 percent. The likelihood is low, but if it happened, applying Bloomberg Economics' estimates, income would fall to two-thirds of its no-war level and, even after recovering to its prewar level, would remain about 12 percent below the no-war path as late as 2050.

Bloomberg Economics' first-year loss estimates are applied, with 10 percent of the first-year loss assumed to be recovered each year from the second year on.

blocks.p: These shifts also enlarge the share of the burden South Korea must carry on its own. Yet over the same period, the troops and workers available to carry it will dwindle.

The number of 20-year-old men will fall from about 240,000 in 2024 to about 140,000 in 2040 and about 130,000 in 2045. Those who turn 20 in 2040 were born in 2020 and are about six years old today. According to material the Ministry of National Defense submitted to the National Assembly in September 2025, if the current system is maintained, the armed forces will shrink from about 450,000 in July 2025 (250,000 enlisted soldiers and 200,000 officers and NCOs{{n:6}}) to about 270,000 in 2040 (150,000 enlisted soldiers and 120,000 officers and NCOs). North Korea's military is estimated at about 1.28 million (2022 Defense White Paper).

Keeping enlisted strength at 250,000 by lengthening service would require, assuming about 69 percent of 20-year-old men enlist as they do now, about 31 months of army service in 2040 and about 33 months in 2045, nearly double the current 18 months. Even then, the decline in officers and NCOs would leave total strength below a third of North Korea's, and young men on the verge of starting careers and families would serve more than a year longer. Longer service cannot make up for the shrinking force{{fc:f57}}.

In its June 2026 force-restructuring plan, the Ministry of National Defense said it would keep defense manpower, meaning active-duty troops plus military civilian employees and standing reservists, at 500,000 in 2040, raise the share of officers and NCOs (career soldiers) among active-duty personnel to 63 percent, and expand drone forces to about 30 times their current size. Unlike the figure of 270,000 above (active duty only), the 500,000 includes military civilian employees and standing reservists. The plan works only if the number of career soldiers rises sharply, yet the army's NCO fill rate fell from 95 percent in 2020 to 42 percent in 2024 (data submitted to the National Assembly's National Defense Committee). Career soldiers, too, must be drawn from the same population of young people. How much of the shortfall around 2040 can be made up depends on how far unmanned systems can substitute for troops.

North Korea's total fertility rate is 1.78 (2024, UN estimate), and about 340,000 to 350,000 babies are born there each year. Projected from births, North Korea will match or overtake South Korea in the number of people in their 20s around 2043, at 3.46 million against 3.3 million (the North Korean figures are UN estimates with wide margins of error). South Korea's military is already only a little over a third the size of North Korea's, so this crossover does not open a new gap, but under the current system the troop ratio widens from about 1 to 2.8 today to about 1 to 4.7 in 2040. That said, the North Korean figure has been the same estimate for years and the North's equipment is aging, so the real gap in military strength is smaller than the troop ratio suggests.

Because of the U.S.-South Korean alliance and U.S. Forces Korea, a shrinking military does not translate directly into a gap in the country's defenses. But as noted above, troop numbers are falling just as South Korea's share of deterring North Korea grows, and without fundamental measures a defense gap will be hard to avoid.

sections.h: Fewer workers and more older people through 2050

blocks.p: Statistics Korea (now the Ministry of Data and Statistics) publishes several population projections under differing assumptions about fertility, life expectancy, and migration; its baseline is the medium variant{{n:7}}. Actual births (254,000) and the total fertility rate (0.80) in 2025 came closer to the high variant, which assumes the highest fertility, so the table below, which shows the number of children and older people supported by every 100 working-age people (ages 15 to 64), uses the medium variant as its baseline and also gives the high-variant totals. Raising fertility alone to the high-variant level puts the 2050 burden at 94.4, almost the same as the high variant.

blocks.h: People supported by every 100 working-age people (ages 15–64)
blocks.note: Statistics Korea population projections, medium variant. High-variant totals are included in the figures below.

blocks.p: The working-age share of the population falls from 69 percent in 2025 to 52 percent in 2050. Nearly all of the added burden comes from supporting older people. The working-age population shrinks 32 percent, from 35.91 million in 2025 to 24.45 million in 2050; the population aged 65 and over grows 80 percent, from 10.51 million to 18.91 million; and the population aged 0 to 14 falls from 5.26 million to 3.75 million (medium variant). Those who will be 65 or older in 2050 were born in or before 1985 (people now in their early 40s or older), and those of working age (15 to 64) at that point were or will be born between 1986 and 2035.

Compared with other countries over the same period, South Korea's dependency burden in 2050 is similar to that of Japan, Italy, and Spain, and its old-age burden alone is the heaviest in the OECD. (The cross-country comparison uses World Bank projections, which apply a common standard and differ slightly from Statistics Korea's projections.)

What sets South Korea apart is the speed of the change and old-age income. The increase in the burden from 2025 to 2050 (46.6) is the largest in the OECD, eight more than the next-largest, Spain's (38.6). The poverty rate among people aged 66 and over (39.8%) is the highest in the OECD, double Japan's and triple those of Italy and Spain. If that rate holds, about 7.5 million of the 18.91 million people aged 65 and over in 2050 will be poor. The rate may come down somewhat as generations with longer National Pension contribution records reach old age. Per capita income at purchasing power parity{{n:8}} rises from $64,210 in 2025 to $82,195 in 2050 (applying the Korea Development Institute's potential growth projections), but the number of people each working-age person supports doubles.

sections.h: The limits of a fertility rebound

blocks.p: The total fertility rate fell below the replacement level (2.1) in 1983, to 2.06, and kept falling to 0.72 in 2023 before rebounding to 0.75 in 2024 and 0.80 in 2025.

But the older people of 2050 have all been born already. The rebound cannot change the old-age burden through 2050, and by adding children it actually enlarges the dependent population slightly. Even if the rebound continues, the burden falls below the medium variant only in the late 2050s, and even then it merely grows more slowly rather than shrinking (109 in 2065). Where the rebound pays off before 2050 is the young adult population: children born from 2026 on begin turning 20 in 2046, adding to the pool of workers and conscripts.

Around 2030, the transfer of primary responsibility for deterring North Korea, the transfer of wartime operational control, China's rise and growing influence, the risks in the Taiwan Strait, and the de facto formalization of North Korea's nuclear status are expected to arrive at once. Over the same period, falling births will shrink the military, and by 2050 the working-age population will make up only a little over half of the total. Even in the best case, South Koreans' well-being index will be hard to keep at its current level, and a single geopolitical shock could send it sharply lower.

As South Korea's share within the alliance grows, Seoul needs to secure the U.S. commitment to extended deterrence{{n:9}} in more clearly institutionalized form. The Ministry of National Defense's plan to offset a shrinking force with career soldiers and unmanned systems faces problems that must be solved, as the difficulty of recruiting officers and NCOs shows. South Korea also needs to prepare in advance for how it would handle both the defense of the peninsula and the alliance's demands during a Taiwan Strait crisis. South Korea is far ahead of North Korea economically and technologically, so if this review and response come in time, technology and the alliance can make up for the decline in troop numbers.

method.t: Based on Statistics Korea's population projections (December 2023, medium and high variants). Working age follows the 15–64 definition of the working-age population used by Statistics Korea and the OECD. For cross-country comparisons, World Bank population projections are used to apply a common standard.

Per capita income starts from the World Bank's per capita gross national income at purchasing power parity and applies the Korea Development Institute's (KDI) potential growth projections (1.5 percent a year through 2030, 0.7 percent in the 2030s, and 0.1 percent in the 2040s), adjusted for population change.

Poverty rates for people aged 66 and over from the OECD Income Distribution Database (2023; 2021 for Japan). With no official projections available, current levels are assumed to persist and are applied to the population aged 65 and over.
The dependent and working-age populations are recalculated with ages 65 to 69 counted as working age.

method.k: Population in their 20s and troop strength
method.t: The population in their 20s is estimated from annual births; for North Korea, UN estimates and World Bank projections are used. Length of service is calculated for the army, assuming about 69 percent of 20-year-old men enlist, as they do now.

A modified index that adds other indicators to the life expectancy and income components of the UNDP's Human Development Index. Safety averages life expectancy with a 0–100 rating of exposure to war and state violence in each scenario (a judgment estimate by Clisa Geopolitics). Living conditions averages per capita income, the dependency burden, the poverty rate for people aged 66 and over, and the employment rate for people aged 15 to 29, each rescaled so that the worst-performing OECD member scores 0 and the best 100. The well-being index is the geometric mean of the two scores, the same method as the Human Development Index. Values for 2040 and 2050 assume the 2030 scenario persists. Because the best case counts ages 65 to 69 as working age, it is compared with the current score on the same basis.

The 2030 scenario probabilities are taken from the Korean Peninsula issue in Strategic Analysis. In this essay, inter-Korean détente (13%) corresponds to managed coexistence and North Korean regime transition in Strategic Analysis; continued standoff (63%) to armed stalemate, a deal without South Korea, and a North Korean leadership succession that leaves the regime intact; and nuclear arms race (19%) to nuclear dominoes. Sudden upheaval (10%) is split into full-scale war on the peninsula (2%), limited clash (3%), leadership succession (2%), and North Korean regime transition (1%), with the remaining 2 percent added to armed stalemate. Where a case falls under more than one scenario, its score is the probability-weighted average of those scenarios' scores.

Likelihoods through 2030 are Clisa Geopolitics estimates. The 2 percent probability of full-scale war on the peninsula takes into account that, since the armistice, the only inter-Korean clash with 100 or more deaths was the DMZ conflict of the late 1960s; the share of such clashes since 1945 that escalated into war (37%); and forecasts on prediction platforms. Income losses from full-scale war apply Bloomberg Economics' first-year estimates (37.5 percent for the Korean Peninsula, 23 percent for Taiwan) and assume that 10 percent of the first-year loss is recovered each year from the second year on.

features.events_h: Events that could unfold in this configuration

events.t: The first test is whether the joint communiqué of the Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) explicitly commits to maintaining 28,500 U.S. troops in Korea{{fc:f54}}.

The transfer of wartime operational control could be completed, launching the Future Combined Forces Command under a South Korean four-star general{{fc:f55}}. Around the time of the transfer, U.S. Forces Korea could fall below 28,500 troops{{fc:f56}}.

In response to the shrinking force, one of three options (longer active-duty service, mandatory service for women, or a shift to an all-volunteer force) could be formally pursued as a government proposal or a bill{{fc:f57}}. South Korea's own nuclear armament could become a major issue in a South Korean presidential election{{fc:f19}}.

The target year of the Ministry of National Defense's force-restructuring plan. Whether it achieves 500,000 defense personnel, a 63 percent share of officers and NCOs, and a roughly thirtyfold expansion of drone forces will determine whether the shrinking force can be offset.
North Korea matches or overtakes South Korea in the number of people in their 20s, at about 3.46 million against about 3.3 million.

A full-scale war on the peninsula by 2030 (2%) and a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with U.S. intervention (2.5%). An armed clash on the peninsula with 100 or more deaths and a change of North Korea's supreme leader are also considered unlikely{{fc:f20}}.

features.paths_h: Paths to add to the scenarios
features.paths_lead: Adding demographic change to the Korean Peninsula scenarios means the following paths also need to be watched{{case:korea}}.

paths.t: NCO recruitment shortfalls persist and unmanned systems arrive late, pushing back the Ministry of National Defense's 2040 targets. If the manpower gap extends into the 2040s, public support for South Korea's own nuclear weapons could grow{{fc:f19}}.

U.S. Forces Korea is reorganized around air power, missile defense, and reconnaissance, and the South Korean military takes on nearly all of ground defense{{fc:f56}}. South Korea's share would be largest just when its ground forces shrink the most.

A full-scale war breaks out on the Korean Peninsula or in the Taiwan Strait. The likelihood is low, but if it happened, applying Bloomberg Economics' estimates, per capita income would fall by roughly a quarter to a third in the first year and would not regain its no-war level even by 2050, pushing an already declining well-being index down once more{{case:taiwan}}.

features.falsify_h: Signals that this assessment is wrong
features.falsify_lead: If any of the following is confirmed, this essay's assessment is wrong or has been weakened.
falsify: The army's NCO fill rate climbs back to 80 percent or higher.
A new Statistics Korea population projection raises the working-age share of the population in 2050 to 60 percent or more in the medium variant.

A Security Consultative Meeting joint communiqué or an agreement on the transfer of wartime operational control includes both a commitment to maintain the size of U.S. Forces Korea and the institutionalization of extended deterrence.
North Korea returns to denuclearization talks and removes its nuclear force policy from its constitution.

notes.t: An index the UNDP has published every year since 1990 that combines life expectancy, education, and per capita income to measure each country's level of development. The Clisa Geopolitics well-being index borrows its methods for calculating life expectancy and income.

An annual report that ranks countries by the life satisfaction respondents assign themselves (0 to 10) in the Gallup World Poll. It is published jointly by the Wellbeing Research Centre at the University of Oxford, Gallup, and the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. In the 2026 report, South Korea scored 6.040, ranking 67th of 147 countries.

Ages 15 to 64, which Statistics Korea and the OECD define as the working-age population. It is a statistical category that applies whether or not people actually work; this essay's "best case" assumes that people aged 65 to 69 also work.

notes.k: Primary responsibility for deterring North Korea
notes.t: A division of roles, set out in the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy, under which the South Korean military bears primary responsibility for deterring and repelling a North Korean attack and U.S. forces provide support.
The authority to command South Korean military units in operations if war breaks out. Since 1978 it has been exercised by the ROK-U.S. Combined Forces Command, headed by a U.S. four-star general.
Career soldiers, namely commissioned officers and noncommissioned officers, as distinct from enlisted soldiers doing compulsory service.

Statistics Korea publishes several population projections assuming low, medium, and high levels of fertility, life expectancy, and international migration. The medium variant is the baseline projection calculated from the medium assumptions; the high variant uses the assumptions under which the population stays largest.
A conversion that adjusts for differences in price levels across countries so that what the same amount of money actually buys can be compared.
The U.S. commitment to treat an attack on an ally as an attack on itself and to deter it with all its military capabilities, including nuclear weapons. It is often called the "nuclear umbrella."

The well-being index in this feature was built specifically for it, on two dimensions: safety and living conditions. Since October 2026, the "What it means for people" sections of the issue analyses have been measured across the UN's seven categories of human security, so the figures in this feature cannot be compared with those in the issue analyses.

features.title: The security vacuum the Korean Peninsula can expect in the 2030s
features.lead: This essay assumes that the trends that will shape the Korean Peninsula's future continue on their present course, and it sets out the configuration they form as they overlap and the events likely to occur within it. Where the scenarios for the Korean Peninsula issue address which futures could arrive, this essay addresses when the risks grow.

flows.t: The Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) in November 2026 will take up verification of the Future Combined Forces Command's full operational capability (FOC){{n:2}} and a target year for the transfer. The South Korean government has floated 2027–2028 and the commander of U.S. Forces Korea the first quarter of 2029, so the timing of the transfer is converging on 2028–2030{{fc:f55}}.

China has set as its national goals "the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" and becoming a "great modern socialist country" by the middle of the century. After Xi Jinping's visit to Pyongyang in June 2026, denuclearization was missing from both sides' statements, and Beijing has in effect tilted toward tacit acceptance of North Korea's nuclear weapons.

In South Korea, majorities in several polls favor an independent nuclear arsenal, and young people's interest in unification is waning. In the United States, support for defending allies splits sharply along partisan lines, and the administration makes cost sharing a condition of alliance. In China, a 2025 Tsinghua University survey found that 79.2 percent of respondents expected China's international standing to rise over the next decade.

The number of warheads is growing, and the delivery systems for tactical nuclear weapons aimed at South Korea and Japan are effectively in place. Reentry technology for intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) that could reach the U.S. mainland, however, has not yet been demonstrated. North Korea's nuclear weapons are pointed at South Korea, while its ICBMs serve as a shield against U.S. intervention.

The 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy says South Korea is capable of taking primary responsibility for deterring North Korea with "critical but more limited" U.S. support. The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA){{n:3}} for fiscal year 2026 restored the 28,500-troop floor for U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) but allows reductions if the secretary of defense certifies them, and the 2026 Ulchi Freedom Shield combined exercise was cut to five days{{fc:f56}}.

flows.k: A shrinking pool of young people
flows.t: The number of 20-year-old men will fall from about 240,000 in 2024 to about 130,000 in 2045. The number of conscripted soldiers could drop to around 150,000 by 2040, and even with officers and NCOs included, total troop strength is projected to fall short of a quarter of North Korea's estimated forces. Defense spending will rise to about 3.5 percent of GDP, but the population that must sustain it is shrinking as well{{fc:f57}}.

features.window_h: The gap between handing over and filling in
window: Taken together, these trends point to one core problem: a difference in speed. The U.S. handover of roles—the transfer of wartime operational control, the realignment of U.S. Forces Korea, and the shift of primary responsibility—is concentrated around 2028–2030. South Korea's effort to fill those roles—offsetting a shrinking force with career soldiers and unmanned systems, and acquiring the means to counter North Korea's nuclear weapons—is aimed at 2040 even in the Ministry of National Defense's own plans. In between, from around 2028 and throughout the 2030s, South Korea will have taken on the roles without yet having the means to carry them out. Clisa Geopolitics calls this stretch a "security vacuum." It may be the longest period during which the U.S. defense commitment looks shaky. Because the Mutual Defense Treaty and U.S. Forces Korea remain in place, the situation differs from 1950, when the United States publicly left South Korea outside its defense perimeter. But a transition in which roles are being handed over is when North Korea has the most room to discount Washington's willingness to intervene.

In this period, three things are likely. The U.S.-South Korean alliance will endure but become a division of labor in which the United States backstops from behind; North Korea, China, and Russia, though not formal allies, will band together and shield one another; and South Korea will be pushed toward becoming an armed middle power{{n:4,5}}, with fewer troops, a growing defense budget, and mounting latent nuclear capability.
features.events_h: Events that could unfold in this configuration

events.t: The SCM will set out a target year for the OPCON transfer and the direction of "alliance modernization." The first test is whether the joint communiqué explicitly commits to keeping 28,500 U.S. troops in Korea{{fc:f54}}.

Another meeting between President Trump and Kim Jong Un{{fc:f22}} is possible, as is a partial deal trading a halt to ICBM tests for sanctions relief{{fc:f21}}. If South Korea is left out of preparations for the talks, inter-Korean relations and short-range missiles are likely to be missing from any agreement{{fc:f14}}.

Taiwan's presidential election in January{{fc:f25}} and the U.S. presidential election in November will shake up the configuration. Around the OPCON transfer, a realignment shifting U.S. Forces Korea from a ground-force posture toward air power, missile defense, and surveillance could be announced{{fc:f56}}.

Debates over lengthening military service, expanding women's service, and moving to an all-volunteer force will become part of the official agenda{{fc:f57}}. While keeping up low-intensity provocations in the Yellow Sea and along the DMZ, North Korea may begin to use nuclear threats not as a bargaining chip but as an instrument of coercion.

An independent nuclear arsenal could become a major issue in the South Korean presidential election for the first time. A formal move by South Korea or Japan to develop nuclear weapons or abandon its non-nuclear principles remains a minority path{{fc:f19}}.
An actual blockade of Taiwan's ports (see the forecast of no blockade{{fc:f36}}); an armed clash on the Korean Peninsula that kills 100 or more people{{fc:f20}}.

features.paths_h: Paths to add to the scenarios
features.paths_lead: Among the scenarios for the Korean Peninsula issue, a deal without South Korea (F5) and nuclear dominoes (F3) are paths along which this vacuum widens, and sudden upheaval (F4) is a path that would upend every calculation. To these, this essay adds the following paths.

paths.t: A crisis in the Taiwan Strait or a major North Korean provocation draws U.S. attention back to the Korean Peninsula, extended deterrence{{n:6}} becomes institutionalized, and the vacuum is filled.

paths.k: Two fronts in a Taiwan contingency
paths.t: As a crisis unfolds in the Taiwan Strait, North Korea simultaneously raises tensions on the Korean Peninsula, pinning down South Korean forces and U.S. Forces Korea on the peninsula. South Korea is caught between its ally's demands and North Korea's nuclear threat{{case:taiwan}}.

The agreement on the OPCON transfer also institutionalizes extended deterrence.
Unmanned systems to offset the shrinking force are deployed faster than planned.
U.S.-North Korean negotiations cover short-range missiles, and South Korea takes part as a party.

notes.t: The authority to command South Korean military units and conduct operations in the event of war. Since 1978 it has been exercised by the ROK-U.S. Combined Forces Command (CFC), whose commander is a U.S. four-star general (peacetime operational control passed to the South Korean military in 1994). Seoul and Washington agreed on the transfer in 2007, but it was postponed once in 2010, and in 2014 the approach shifted from a fixed date to a transfer once set conditions are met.

notes.k: Full operational capability of the Future Combined Forces Command
notes.t: The Future Combined Forces Command is the new combined command that, after the OPCON transfer, will be led by a South Korean four-star general, with a U.S. four-star general as deputy commander. Before the transfer, whether it works properly is verified in three stages—initial operational capability (IOC), full operational capability (FOC), and full mission capability (FMC). Full operational capability is the second of these.

The basic law on defense policy and budgets that the U.S. Congress passes every year. For several years it has included a provision barring the use of funds to reduce U.S. Forces Korea below a set level, with an exception if the secretary of defense certifies to Congress that certain conditions are met, such as that the reduction is in the U.S. national security interest.

A country that is not a great power but has enough economic, military, and diplomatic weight to play a meaningful role in its region and on the international stage. Australia, Canada, and South Korea are commonly cited; in 2013, South Korea joined Mexico, Indonesia, Turkey, and Australia in founding MIKTA, a consultative group of middle powers. Middle powers are often characterized by mediation between great powers, multilateral diplomacy, and security that relies on alliances.

A term used in this essay. Unlike middle powers that entrusted their security to alliances and expanded their role through diplomacy and economics, it describes a country that, as the United States hands over primary responsibility for deterring North Korea, raises its defense spending, builds up latent nuclear capability (the technology and materials to build nuclear weapons quickly), and arms itself to hold its ground. It is an in-between state: neither becoming a great power nor relying on an alliance as before.

A U.S. commitment to treat an attack on an ally as an attack on itself and to deter it with all its military power, including nuclear weapons. It is often called the "nuclear umbrella." Seoul and Washington consult on carrying out this commitment through the Extended Deterrence Strategy and Consultation Group (EDSCG) and the Nuclear Consultative Group (NCG), created by the 2023 Washington Declaration.

summary: Around 2028–2030, the United States will hand roles over to South Korea through the transfer of wartime operational control, a realignment of U.S. Forces Korea, and a shift of primary responsibility for deterring North Korea.

Offsetting a shrinking force with career soldiers and unmanned systems, and acquiring the means to counter North Korea's nuclear weapons, will not come to fruition until around 2040. In between, South Korea will be in a security vacuum, having taken on the roles without yet having the means.
In this period, South Korea is likely to be pushed toward becoming an "armed middle power," with fewer troops, a growing defense budget, and mounting latent nuclear capability.

The paths that would widen the vacuum are a U.S.-North Korean deal that leaves out South Korea and moves by South Korea and Japan toward nuclear armament. The joint communiqué of the November 2026 SCM is the first test.

fc_reviews.note: After the October 21 resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal went through without being blocked, the probability on the related forecast was lowered. Two new forecasts ask whether North Korea will resume ICBM flight tests and whether it will tie an ICBM test moratorium to talks or an agreement with the United States.

items.why: The Philippine military completed a rotation and resupply mission to the BRP Sierra Madre on October 21, and the China Coast Guard announced that the resupply had taken place "with China's permission." The first resupply since China blocked a mission on September 24 went unobstructed, and Beijing chose to cast the mission as permitted rather than stop it, lowering the chance that it will block a mission again by November 30.

fc_reviews.note: Last week the three-way talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine slipped to November, and Washington repeatedly signaled renewed strikes on Iran while cutting embassy staff in several Middle Eastern countries. With the Hormuz blockade continuing, Brent crude rose to its highest level since April. Of the two forecasts on the U.S.-South Korea Security Consultative Meeting, one was lowered to correct an error in its basis and the other to reflect a precedent that was not fully weighed when it was published. Probabilities were adjusted for eight forecasts and left unchanged for one.

items.why: After meeting special envoy Witkoff on October 21, Russian presidential aide Ushakov said Moscow was in principle ready to resume three-way talks around November 10, and President Zelensky said on October 23 that the negotiating teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November. With both sides pointing to November, three-way technical talks among the United States, Russia, and Ukraine are now very unlikely to take place by October 31. Because the change falls within the final seven days before the resolution date, it does not count toward the score.

President Trump repeatedly hinted at further strikes on Iran on October 22 and 23. Beyond words, the State Department ordered nonemergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia on October 21 and cut embassy staff in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates on October 23, and there were reports that U.S. military personnel at Middle Eastern posts were also being reduced. Because costly actions point toward renewed strikes, the probability was raised slightly. It was not raised further because the president said on October 25 that he was deciding between a deal and military action.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned on October 22 that the conflict would spread to U.S. bases in the region if Washington kept supporting tanker transits, and U.N. Ambassador Waltz said the U.S. Navy could maintain the blockade for the time being. Iran's Foreign Ministry said on October 25 that messages were still being exchanged through mediators, but neither side has changed its terms, so the probability that a ceasefire takes effect and the strait's reopening is officially announced by the end of the year was lowered.

Brent crude settled at $116.72 a barrel on October 23, its highest close since April 29. With Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and the Hormuz blockade continuing, a year-end close below $90 would first require the strait to reopen; because the probability of a U.S.-Iran ceasefire and Hormuz reopening was also lowered, this forecast was lowered with it.

A cargo ship sank after a drone attack off Constanța, Romania, on October 23, killing one crew member and leaving three missing, and Romania's president blamed Russia. Because the ship went down just outside Romania's territorial waters, the event does not meet this forecast's conditions, but attacks on merchant ships in the western Black Sea are becoming more frequent, so the probability of a similar event inside a NATO member's territorial waters was raised slightly.

Reuters reported that South Korean and U.S. officials see little chance of a Trump-Kim summit this year and that Washington has received no answer from North Korea. With no sign of preparations for a meeting around the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, the probability was lowered.

The probability of a U.S.-Iran ceasefire and Hormuz reopening was lowered, but this forecast runs to the end of March 2027. Iran says messages are still being exchanged through mediators, and the U.S. president has not ruled out a deal, so the probability is left unchanged.

When this forecast was published, its basis said the figure of 28,500 troops had been dropped from the 57th joint communiqué, but a check of the original communiqués showed that the number has not appeared in any communiqué from 2019 on. They said only "current level," without a number, and in 2020 and 2025 not even that. The forecast therefore overstated, from the start, the chance that the number would be spelled out; the basis has been corrected and the probability lowered. There are also reports that this year's meeting will be pushed back to around December by disagreement over the conditions for transferring wartime operational control (OPCON), making it likely that no communiqué will be issued in November at all. Whether the communiqué uses the words "current level" is asked separately in a new forecast on whether the 58th Security Consultative Meeting's communiqué will explicitly commit to keeping U.S. forces in Korea at the current level.

The "current level" language on U.S. forces in Korea has been dropped from a communiqué and later restored only once (omitted in 2020 and reinstated in 2021), and a new U.S. administration took office in between. There is no precedent for the same administration restoring language it had itself removed. The 58th communiqué will be written by the administration that dropped the phrase in 2025, so the probability, which did not fully reflect this precedent when the forecast was published, has been lowered.

fc_reviews.note: The probability of the Japan-China summit forecast has been revised down.

items.why: China rejected a proposal for Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to meet President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC summit in November and offered a meeting with Premier Li Qiang instead, according to reports citing unnamed sources. Beijing is also demanding that Takaichi clearly correct her remarks on Taiwan. The G20 summit in December offers one more chance, so the forecast now stands at 18 percent.

fc_reviews.note: Last week the United States allowed supplies of Russian diesel, but Russia stayed away from a U.S.-led meeting, and Iran kept the strait closed, calling the U.S. reply insufficient. The probabilities of four forecasts were lowered, and two forecasts with conflicting factors were left unchanged.

items.why: The October 9 meeting in Miami brought together only the United States, Ukraine, and European representatives; Russia did not attend. The same day, describing the Trump-Putin phone call, the Kremlin relayed President Putin's position that negotiations with Ukraine cannot resume for now. With less than three weeks left before the October 31 deadline and no date or venue announced for three-way talks, the probability that U.S.-Russia-Ukraine technical talks will be held was cut sharply.

Russian strikes killed at least 28 people across Ukraine on October 7, 33 in Kramatorsk on October 8, and at least 20 in Zaporizhzhia on October 10. With Russia staying away from U.S.-led negotiations, the probability that a full ceasefire signed by both sides takes effect by year-end was lowered further.

The probability of a full Russia-Ukraine ceasefire taking effect by year-end was lowered, but this forecast runs to the end of June 2027. Because the United States is pressing Ukraine to accept a ceasefire on Russia's terms, there is still room for a ceasefire, once reached, to hold for more than 30 days, so the probability is left unchanged.

Member countries of the International Energy Agency agreed on October 7 to speed up stockpile releases, and the United States allowed supplies of Russian diesel on October 9, yet Brent crude closed at $104.72 a barrel on October 9. With tanker attacks spreading north of Qatar (October 7), off the United Arab Emirates (October 9), and to Oman's Sohar anchorage (October 11), the probability of Brent falling below $90 by year-end was lowered.

On October 11, Iran called the U.S. reply insufficient and said it would not open the strait until its conditions are met, and the United States did not accept Iran's proposal for joint management of the strait. The probability that a ceasefire takes effect and the strait's reopening is officially announced within the remaining 11 weeks was lowered.

President Trump said on October 8 that he would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. But there have been reports of preparations to resume strikes after the election, and costly actions such as enforcing the naval blockade and additional aircraft carrier movements continue. With words and actions pointing in different directions, the probability is left unchanged.

fc_reviews.note: Last week the United States sent more forces to the Middle East, raising the military pressure on Iran, and North Korea fired a hypersonic intermediate-range missile while rejecting inter-Korean contact. The probabilities of four forecasts were adjusted, and two forecasts with conflicting factors were left unchanged.

items.why: On October 1 the United States sent a carrier strike group and an amphibious ready group to the Middle East, and President Trump said expanded airstrikes were possible after the midterms. Moving forces is a costly step, and it points the same way as the rhetoric, so the probability that the United States resumes airstrikes on mainland Iran has been raised.

On October 4, Iran's Foreign Ministry said the latest U.S. proposal still put the nuclear issue first, and the same day Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran would not open the strait until its seven conditions were met. The room for signing a phased U.S.-Iran agreement that separates reopening the strait from the nuclear issue has narrowed, but draft texts are still being exchanged through mediators.
With the probability that a phased agreement is signed now lower, the probability that it holds for 90 days after signing has been lowered in step.

In statements on October 2 and 3, North Korea denied responsibility for the land mine and rejected contact with South Korea, and on October 3 it launched a hypersonic intermediate-range missile. With no North Korean action in response to Seoul's calls for dialogue, the balance has tilted further toward the inter-Korean military communication lines remaining unrestored.

The G7 agreed on October 2 to release 100 million barrels of reserve oil over four months, but with the strait still blockaded and the Houthis claiming an attack on Saudi Aramco facilities, Brent remains above $100 a barrel. With factors pushing both down and up, the probability is left unchanged.

President Zelensky said on October 4 that the United States had proposed holding trilateral technical-level talks by the end of October and that Ukraine supports this timetable. Russia has not yet announced agreement on the timing or venue, so the probability is left unchanged.

retired_cases.title: AI and Chips: What should South Korea do in the U.S.-China chip rivalry?
retired_cases.h: The AI and Chips issue has been removed from the issues under analysis
d: Since October 2026, Clisa Geopolitics has measured what an issue means for people across the UN's seven categories of human security (personal safety, community, political, and economic, plus alerts for food, health, and environment), and it treats as issues for analysis those in which people's lives are heavily at stake in these categories. By this standard, AI and Chips does not stand as an issue in its own right, so it has been removed from the issues under analysis.
The U.S.-China chip rivalry remains on the map as the flashpoint "U.S.-China chip rivalry and Korean fabs in China" and is treated as an external variable in other issues, such as the Taiwan Strait.
Forecasts already published, f46–f53, will not be deleted; they will remain in the Forecasts and Track Record tab until their resolution dates, when their outcomes will be settled.
